21528-the-international-monthly-magazine:
The International Monthly Magazine began at New York in August 1850, priced at twenty-five cents a number. Stringer and Townsend issued it from Broadway, with a year's run costing three dollars. Its first volume runs from August to November of that year.

An opening essay treats the great change in how letters reach readers through periodicals. Since the Edinburgh Review, it argues, the finest minds have written for magazines. Contents range over art, portraits, tales borrowed from Household Words, and notes on statues and painters. Sir David Brewster's portrait and an essay on learning show the mix of science and letters inside.
a-suggestive-inquiry-into-the-hermetic-m: A Suggestive Inquiry into the Hermetic Mystery, 1850. The hermetic inquiry. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
alchemy-and-the-alchemists-1850: Alchemy and the Alchemists, 1850. The Victorian survey. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
anima-magica-abscondita-or-a-discourse-o: Anima magica abscondita, 1650. The hidden magical soul. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
ars-et-theoria-transmvtationis-metallica: Ars et theoria transmutationis metallicae, 1550. The art and theory. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
arxiv-2510-00250:
Elke Neuhaus, Niharika Chakrabarty Paul, and Irem Portakal wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on two families of varieties built from permutations. Matrix Schubert varieties and Kazhdan-Lusztig varieties both arise from rank conditions on matrices. Each splits off a flat factor, leaving a core piece whose symmetry the authors study. Their focus is when that core is toric under the usual torus action.

For toric cores, the authors fully characterize which simple reflections keep the core toric. They also track how the weight cone changes under those moves. For Kazhdan-Lusztig varieties, they follow complexity along chains in the Bruhat order of permutations. Special permutation patterns get their own complexity analysis in the paper. Finally, the authors connect both families to conditional independence and quasi-independence models in statistics, an unexpected bridge.
arxiv-2510-00350:
Akshaya Kumar, Anna Raymaker, and Michael Specter published this 2025 paper auditing Tile, the crowd-sourced tracker network. Tile is the second most popular service of its kind, behind Apple's AirTags. The authors give the first full security analysis of Tile's protocol. They reverse engineered how tags, phones, and servers interact, since Tile publishes no formal protocol description.

Their findings break several of Tile's stated privacy promises. Tile's servers can persistently learn where every user and tag has been. Unprivileged outsiders can also track users through the Bluetooth signals tags emit. The anti-theft mode, which weakens anti-stalking protections on purpose, turns out easy to circumvent. Its novel accountability mechanism can be subverted to frame honest users. The authors close by calling for formal definitions of accountability in such tracking systems.
arxiv-2510-00450:
Sheikh Rahman and Nasir Eisty published this 2025 systematic review of learning-based testing, a software testing approach with a long history. The method learns a model of the system under test by probing it with generated cases. That learned model then guides deeper testing than fixed scripts allow. The review traces the idea from its theoretical roots to industrial case studies.

Three core modules organize the field: model inference, model checking, and test data generation. Early work inferred state machines for procedural programs, the authors recount. Recent work folds machine learning into inference, especially for data-driven and reactive systems. Embedded reactive systems have become the emphasis as commercial interest grows. Industrial deployments show the method can work outside the lab, though adoption remains thin. The authors aim to surface this underused potential for practitioners and researchers alike.
arxiv-2510-00550:
Tai Le and nine colleagues published this 2025 paper on monitoring a baby's heartbeat before birth without sticky electrodes. A fetal electrocardiogram can flag distress and developmental problems early. Skilled staff and clinic visits limit access, especially in remote or poor regions. The team built a maternity belt with novel non-contact electrodes that read signals through clothing.

Bench tests compared the new electrodes against the standard silver-based wet type. Signal quality came out comparable, with far better comfort for the wearer. A pilot study then fitted the belt on ten pregnant volunteers at a medical center. Participants were between twenty-five and thirty-two weeks along in the study. The system performed well and proved usable and safe in practice. Future versions will add sensors to locate the fetus for better placement.
arxiv-2510-00650:
Arjmandi-Lari, Mantzarlis, and Stafford examine the health of X's Community Notes system in this 2025 arXiv paper. Community Notes lets users attach context to misleading posts, and a bridging algorithm publishes notes that raters from opposing political camps both find helpful. Other giant platforms have copied the model, so its long-term survival matters beyond X. The authors ask whether the contributor community behind it is stable or quietly eroding.

Using a regression discontinuity design, they show that having a note published raises a first-time author's retention by about five percent. That incentive is weakening, since only about ten percent of notes reach publication and the share is falling. Most notes come from a shrinking minority of contributors, and fewer authors stay active year over year. The authors warn the system is successful but increasingly fragile.
arxiv-2510-00850:
Khalid and Sturt, at the University of Illinois Chicago, make the sample average approximation practical for assortment optimization in this 2025 arXiv paper on operations research. A retailer choosing which products to stock faces a random utility model of customer choice with no tidy formula. One workable route samples many customer rankings, builds a ranking-based proxy model, and optimizes the assortment against that proxy. The bottleneck was solving the proxy problem itself at realistic scale.

The authors develop mixed-integer programming algorithms with stronger formulations and new Benders cut results for ranking-based choice. Without heuristics or parameter tuning, their solvers ran more than twenty times faster on real-world instances with thousands of products and samples. That speed turns the sampling approach from a curiosity into a tool. They showcase it on assortment problems where no practically efficient algorithm was previously known.
arxiv-2510-00950:
Pitilakis, Katsios, and Boulogeorgos design a reconfigurable metasurface for optical wireless links in this 2025 arXiv paper. Metasurfaces are thin patterned sheets that steer and shape light or radio waves. Making them tunable in the infrared is hard, since liquid crystals and bulk crystals offer weak or bulky control. The authors build theirs from GST, a phase-change alloy whose optical properties shift sharply when heated between its amorphous and crystalline states.

Their unit cell uses simple conductive patterns, and its response can be predicted with transmission line theory and equivalent circuits. Material behaviour in both states, plus partly crystallized mixes, comes from models fitted to measured data. Full-wave simulations confirmed the analytic predictions across angles of incidence. The team estimates heating crosstalk stays below ten percent in unheated neighbouring cells, though fuller thermal simulations remain future work.
arxiv-2510-01250:
Dang and D'Elia describe a challenge system that rewrites toxic sentences into neutral ones across fifteen languages. Platforms evolve faster than moderation rules, so automated detoxification offers moderators a scalable assist. Their entry competed in the PAN 2025 multilingual detoxification challenge.

A large multilingual model was fine-tuned cheaply with adapter training on thousands of human and synthetic pairs. At run time, retrieved similar examples and marked toxic spans guide the rewrite. The system ranked first on both rich-resource and low-resource languages. Few-shot examples and step-by-step prompting each added clear gains. Style transfer accuracy, meaning preservation, and fluency formed the three-part score. Language resource status predicted performance more strongly than any design choice. Synthetic pairs, machine-translated and model-generated, bulked out the training corpus. Three retrieved neighbors accompany every input at inference. Detoxification preserves meaning while removing venom from text.
arxiv-2510-01450:
Zuo and co-authors design a new attention mechanism for transformers by treating attention as a regression problem solved fresh at every step. Efficient linear attention sacrifices expressiveness, while the field rarely asks what a costlier, principled mechanism could gain. Their local linear attention interpolates optimally between the linear and softmax extremes.

A bias-variance analysis shows advantages for associative memory over both parents. Two memory-efficient primitives tame the naive quadratic costs. A blockwise hardware algorithm and a custom inference kernel make the design practical. Regression and in-context tests map where the mechanism wins and where it strains. Nonparametric statistics supplies the theoretical lens for the design. Conjugate gradient solvers run inside the blockwise forward pass. Associative memory capacity is the arena for the theory comparison. Accelerator hardware shapes what scalable means in practice. Expressiveness, not speed, is the paper's ambition.
arxiv-2510-01650:
Lee and co-authors prune ninety percent of a language model's weights while keeping it coherent, by abandoning the surrogate objectives every rival method relies on. Conventional pruning stalls near sixty percent sparsity before accuracy collapses. Their method, Elsa, attacks the constrained problem directly with a classical splitting algorithm from optimization.

Removing the surrogate removes the ceiling it imposed. Perplexity at extreme sparsity dropped several-fold below the best prior method on a seven-billion-parameter model. A quantized variant scales the recipe to a twenty-seven-billion-parameter model. Convergence guarantees accompany the empirical frontier push. Magnitude pruning and one-shot rivals populate the beaten baseline table. Alternating direction method of multipliers supplies the classical machinery. Ninety percent sparsity was the unseen frontier of the title. Memory and compute savings scale with every zeroed weight. Fidelity retention at extremes is the result that matters.
arxiv-2510-01950:
Cui and Gong rebuild the renormalization of the one-dimensional Ising model with stochastic tools in this 2025 paper. The renormalization group links a spin system across scales and explains critical behavior. Their route starts from a partial differential equation in random form, made by smoothing a discrete stochastic equation. They first prove regularity bounds for its solution.

A Clark-Ocone-Haussmann formula then yields a log-Sobolev bound that holds up to the terminal time. From it, they extract an a priori form of the renormalization relation. A partition function check verifies the procedure. Finally, two-point correlation functions of the lattice equation converge to those of the Ising model at the stable fixed point as time grows. The work ties probability inequalities to a classic physics construction. It gives the coarse-graining story a fully stochastic-analytic foundation.
arxiv-2510-02050:
Ganesh S and seven co-authors pick hurricane forecast predictors by causality rather than correlation in this 2025 paper. Intensity forecasts struggle with tangled links among weather variables. Picking by correlation can chase confounders and fail on unseen storms. The team built a dataset from the SHIPS scheme, using ERA5 reanalysis fields.

A causal discovery framework found predictors with a true causal link to intensity change. Forecast models trained on those features were compared against no selection, correlation ranking, and random forest rankings. The causal selection won on held-out storms across lead times from one to five days. Its edge was largest under three days. The chosen predictors were physical: vertical wind shear, mid-level potential vorticity, and surface moisture. Causal screening travels better, the authors argue, because it keeps drivers, not passengers.
arxiv-2510-02150:
Harder and Lee wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on mirror symmetry for singular Calabi-Yau spaces. Mirror symmetry pairs two different spaces whose hidden counts match. The pair studied here comes from branched covers, where one space wraps over another. Four earlier researchers, Hosono, Lee, Lian, and Yau, had stated a conjecture about such pairs. Harder and Lee test that conjecture and extend the construction to a wider family of covers.

Inside, the authors prove that paired mirror spaces share matching Hodge numbers. Hodge numbers count the shapes of holes inside a space. Their main tool adapts the Cayley trick from older geometry. The trick links the cover to a Landau-Ginzburg model, which is a simpler paired system. Because the method stands apart from mirror symmetry itself, other geometers can reuse it elsewhere.
arxiv-2510-02250:
Gonzalez-Pumariega and co-authors show that running many computer-use agents in parallel can beat one careful run. Their 2025 machine learning paper tackles agents that click and type on real desktops. Such agents fail often, and results vary wildly between runs. The team proposes Behavior Best-of-N, shortened to bBoN. The method runs several attempts at the same task. It then turns each attempt into a short behavior narrative. A selector reads those stories and picks the best attempt.

On the OSWorld benchmark, the method reached a success rate near seventy percent. Human performance on the same tasks sits near seventy two percent. Earlier methods trailed that score by more than ten points. Tests on Windows and Android arenas also went well. The lesson is blunt. Wide sampling works when selection uses structured summaries, not raw logs.
arxiv-2510-02350:
Pihulski and co-authors rebuild a classic database question dataset for the language model era. Their 2025 paper presents LLMSQL. The older WikiSQL set taught machines to turn questions into SQL queries. Years of use exposed deep flaws in that set. Case errors, type mismatches, and broken syntax were common. Some questions had no valid answer at all. The team classified each error type they found. Automated cleaning fixed much of the damage. Targeted manual work corrected the rest. Questions and full SQL now sit as clean plain text.

Nine major language models were tested on the rebuilt set. Large reasoning models passed eighty five percent execution accuracy. Small fine-tuned models did even better on the set. They surpassed ninety percent accuracy after adaptation. Simple queries dominate real workloads, the authors note. A clean simple benchmark still teaches a great deal.
arxiv-2510-02550:
Rocca and co-authors run quantum simulations of carbon capture inside a metal-organic framework. Their 2025 chemistry paper studies the material Fe-MOF-74. Such frameworks offer huge surface area for trapping carbon dioxide. Steel and chemical plants need that capture to cut emissions. Exposed iron sites in this framework grip the gas strongly. Standard density methods disagree widely on the grip strength. Strong electron correlation makes the physics hard classically. Quantum algorithms promise better answers for such systems. Periodic materials with plane waves strain those algorithms badly.

The team shrinks the problem with localized Wannier orbitals. Natural orbital selection trims the active space further. A number preserving quantum ansatz matched exact results within chemical accuracy. Hardware runs reached active spaces of twenty eight qubits. Noisy devices still returned meaningful correlation energies. The workflow scales toward realistic adsorption problems. Quantum chemistry for materials gains a template.
arxiv-2510-02650:
Hsiang and Burke put a number on how much human climate change raised Syria's civil war risk. Their 2025 attribution study revisits the drought before the war. Syria suffered severe drought from two thousand seven to twenty ten. The war began in twenty eleven. Earlier work linked the drought partly to human emissions. Qualitative links cannot feed cost-benefit accounting, though. The authors combine several published estimates into one calculation. A meta-analysis ties persistent drought to excess conflict risk. Attribution work sizes the human share of that drought.

Their best estimate raised Syria's baseline conflict risk by about three point six percent. The ninety percent interval ran from roughly one to seven percent. The effect was discernible but modest beside the high baseline. Future populations deserve this risk inside climate accounting. Even small percentages matter at national scale. The study shows how attribution chains get quantified.
arxiv-2510-02850:
Wu and Lu improve how language models learn from feedback. Training with human or AI feedback relies on a reward model. That model scores answers, and the main model chases high scores. A single scorer has blind spots, and models can overfit them. Routing offers a fix by picking among several scorers per query. Early routing methods explored too little and started cold.

Their system, BayesianRouter, works in two stages. An offline stage learns each scorer's strengths from past preference data. An online stage then picks a scorer for each new query. It uses Thompson sampling, guided by the offline knowledge as a prior. Beliefs update as fresh rewards arrive. Tests covered chat quality and reasoning benchmarks. The router beat single scorers, scorer ensembles, and prior routers. It did so while calling just one scorer per query. The design keeps alignment quality high at low cost.
arxiv-2510-03150:
Lin and co-authors map an ancient cold front in the Virgo galaxy cluster. Cold fronts are sharp edges in hot cluster gas. Virgo hosts two famous fronts near its core. A third, far southwest one was spotted by an earlier mission. This team imaged it properly with XMM-Newton mosaics. The front sits about two hundred fifty kiloparsecs out.

All three fronts likely share one birth event. A companion galaxy, M49, probably fell in from the northwest. Simulations of a binary merger match the swirling pattern. The outer front has endured for billions of years since. Its southern edge stays razor sharp in the images. Magnetic fields likely shield that leading edge from erosion. The western side, by contrast, is splitting in two. Kelvin-Helmholtz ripples are the suspected cause there. Brightness ripples follow the spectrum expected from turbulence.
arxiv-2510-03250:
Rüttgers and co-authors fix the scaling troubles of logic gate networks by reparametrizing the gates themselves. Differentiable logic gate networks infer fast and stay accurate. Depth, though, brings vanishing gradients and discretization pain. Prior work patched symptoms with careful initialization schemes. The authors trace the root cause to the gate parametrization. Their input-wise parametrization rethinks how each gate is described. Parameter count per gate now shrinks logarithmically with input count.

Binary inputs already show the practical payoff clearly. Models shrink to a quarter of their former size. The backward pass speeds up by nearly twofold. Convergence takes a small fraction of the earlier training steps. Accuracy on CIFAR-100 holds steady or improves. Deeper networks no longer degrade the way they did. Richer gates with more inputs become affordable to train. Edge and real-time hardware remain the natural home for these circuits.
arxiv-2510-03450:
Silenko presents a 2025 arXiv paper solving, in generality, how the orbital angular momentum of twisted particles behaves inside arbitrary gravitational fields. Twisted photons and other vortex particles carry intrinsic orbital angular momentum, a kind of twist. Gravity from massive objects can twist light, and twisted photons are candidates for free space communication and for measuring black hole spin. Yet no equation governed the twist's motion in spacetime. Silenko derives one that holds in any Riemannian spacetime.

The derivation never needs Maxwell's equations in curved spacetime to describe twisted photons. The paper also gives an account of the orbital Hall effect, in which twisted particles of opposite twist veer apart, for twisted particle types. The analysis detects a violation of the weak equivalence principle. Foundations matter because applications from black hole spin measurement to optical links assume the twist survives transport. This work supplies the equation those fields lacked.
arxiv-2510-03750:
Zhang and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper building scorecards for algorithms that estimate how far a piano's sustain pedal is pressed from audio. Pedal depth is continuous, and half pedaling shapes performances, yet work mostly detected on or off. Frame by frame error scores miss what musicians care about: whether press and release moments land, and whether gesture contours match. The proposed framework adds an action level check on direction and timing, plus a gesture level check on the shape of each cycle.

Three model variants were compared: audio only, MIDI informed, and a binary trained version. The MIDI informed model won at the action and gesture levels, despite modest gains in frame scores. Continuous depth estimation proved for capturing actions and preserving gesture shape. Music transcription systems feed analysis, education, and restoration tools. Judging them by criteria should steer builders toward models that pianists would recognize as right.
arxiv-2510-03850:
García and co-authors present this 2025 arXiv paper on signal strength statistics in fading wireless channels. Engineers model fading with the alpha-mu distribution, and receivers add several faded signal copies together. Predicting performance requires the probability distribution of that sum. Older formulas were heavy, unstable, or broke down as more copies were added.

The authors derive new exact formulas for the sum's density and cumulative distribution. Their expressions stay simple, and their computing cost does not grow with the number of added signals. They then apply the formulas to two receiver designs that combine signals from several branches. The analysis yields exact and approximate results for error rates and outage chances, plus clean measures of coding and diversity gain. Simulations showed the new formulas compute far faster than the old ones. The work gives wireless engineers a practical receiver design tool.
arxiv-2510-04150:
Hanany and Lubotzky present this 2025 arXiv paper counting characteristic subgroups of the free group. Subgroup growth studies how many subgroups of each index a group possesses. Characteristic subgroups, those preserved by every automorphism, are rarer and more rigid than normal subgroups. Rivin had asked about their growth rate for free groups. Thurston expected the answer to differ between two generators and more.

The authors show the growth type is the same for every rank at least two, settling the question against that expectation. The count of characteristic subgroups of index up to n grows like n raised to the power log n. Along the way, they answer a question about normal subgroup growth in large groups. Their discussion raises a broader question about when characteristic and normal growth types coincide. Rigidity theorems like Mostow's would then transfer the equality to many lattices in Lie groups.
arxiv-2510-04250:
Hossain, Khan, and Chao present this 2025 arXiv paper on the stability of two viscoelastic fluid layers flowing down an inclined plane. Such layered flows matter in coating processes and thin-film evaporators, where waves can ruin a film or improve transport. The study adds insoluble surfactant at both the exposed surface and the interface between layers. Each fluid follows the viscoelastic Walters B-double-prime model, allowing the authors to separate elastic effects from viscosity and density contrasts.

A normal-mode analysis produces an Orr-Sommerfeld boundary-value problem, which the authors solve with Chebyshev spectral collocation. Elasticity in either layer strengthens long surface waves, while its effect on interfacial waves reverses with viscosity ratio and wavelength. Surfactant can suppress the strong surface mode and, under some conditions, control interface instability through Marangoni forces. The mode-by-mode map helps engineers predict which layer properties stabilize an film.
arxiv-2510-04450:
Qiyuan He and seven coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on making images with autoregressive models. Such models build an image token by token, much as text models build a sentence. They trail diffusion models in image quality, and many blamed the tokenizer that turns images into tokens. The team found a different flaw: tokens the generator produces often decode badly. The generator and the tokenizer, in short, fall out of sync.

Their fix, named reAR, adds a training rule that keeps the two parts in sync. While predicting the next token, the model also learns to recover the current visual embedding. It also learns to predict the target embedding under noisy context. The rule needs no change to the tokenizer, the scan order, or the sampling code. On ImageNet tests, quality scores improved sharply with the rule in place. With a strong tokenizer, a small model matched larger diffusion models.
arxiv-2510-04550:
Pengfei He and twelve coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on testing how AI agents use tools. Agents now call search engines, file tools, and service APIs to finish tasks. Most tests grade only the final answer, so a lucky or sloppy path can pass unseen. The team built TRAJECT Bench, a benchmark that grades the path of tool calls. Tasks mimic production style APIs across domains.

The benchmark pairs tasks with tools that run, so a step can be checked as it happens. Test paths vary in breadth, with calls made in parallel, and in depth, with chains where each call feeds the next. Scores cover tool choice, argument correctness, and whether order respects the dependencies. The analysis exposed failure modes, such as picking a similar but wrong tool. It showed agents choosing parameters with little regard for the task. Performance dropped hardest when paths grew from short to medium length.
arxiv-2510-04650:
Evgeny Ryabkov and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on light trapped inside empty spheres. A Mie void is a spherical hole inside a material, and it traps light by reflection at its boundary. Fill such a void with a resonant medium and light and matter can merge into polaritons. The team studies the spectra of these coupled states in theory. They also treat the flipped case, a void carved inside a resonant material.

They derive formulas for the quality factor of void cavities, which measures how long light survives inside. Maps of the parameter space show where weak coupling ends and strong coupling begins. In the strong regime, they track side effects such as boosted quality factors and tighter field concentration. Voids are simple to carve and robust compared with layered mirrors. A clear theory of their spectra helps designers pick sizes and materials with intent.
arxiv-2510-05050:
Priyanka Boora and three co-authors study a rare particle decay as a probe for new physics in this 2025 arXiv paper. The decay turns a Lambda-c baryon into a Lambda, a muon, and an antineutrino. Small deviations from Standard Model predictions could reveal unknown interactions. The authors analyze the decay inside an effective field theory.

They fit the allowed sizes of new-physics operators using many related measurements. Adding constraints implied by the Standard Model effective theory tightened every bound. One scalar coefficient's allowed range shrank substantially. They also map what right-handed neutrinos would change in the same decay. The resulting predictions for rates and asymmetries can be tested at BESIII, Belle II, and LHCb.
arxiv-2510-05750:
Yang and colleagues ask whether heterogeneous graph networks truly earn their complexity. These models exploit multiple node and edge types for classification. Everyone assumes the fancy architectures drive their success. Their 2025 causal study tests that assumption across many benchmarks.

The team reproduced results across twenty-one datasets and twenty baselines with careful retuning. A causal framework then separated architecture effects from information effects. Architecture and complexity show no causal effect on performance at all. Heterogeneous information, by contrast, helps causally and measurably. It raises homophily and widens local-global label distribution gaps. Factual and counterfactual analyses, plus sensitivity checks, back the conclusions. Minimal sufficient adjustment sets validated the causal identification strategy. Those changes make node classes easier to distinguish. Practitioners should invest in better relational data, not bigger architectures.
arxiv-2510-05950:
Sui and colleagues classify time series with language model agents and no training. Time series classification usually demands task-specific training on scarce labeled data. Reasoning language models can read temporal patterns but underperform used purely zero-shot. Their 2025 FETA framework adds exemplar-based in-context reasoning instead.

Each multivariate series is decomposed into channel-wise subproblems. Structurally similar labeled examples are retrieved for every channel. A reasoning model compares the query against those exemplars directly. It returns channel-level labels with self-assessed confidences. A confidence-weighted aggregator fuses the channel decisions into one verdict. Pruning irrelevant channels and controlling input length keep it efficient. Exemplar grounding makes the decisions interpretable to users. On nine UEA datasets, the training-free system surpasses multiple trained baselines. Plug-and-play deployment without parameter updates is the practical promise. Heterogeneous data mixing text and signals remains future work.
arxiv-2510-06250:
Meena and seven co-authors build a framework for annotating personal data across languages in a 2025 language technology paper. Language models must handle personally identifiable information under varied regulations. Training that behavior needs quality labeled data, which barely exists for underrepresented locales.

The framework covers thirteen locales and roughly three hundred thirty-six locale-specific personal information types. Its phased, human-in-the-loop method pairs linguistic expertise with strict quality assurance. Inter-annotator agreement metrics and root-cause analysis exposed and resolved labeling inconsistencies. Recall and false positive rates improved from pilot through training to production phases. The authors catalog common annotator challenges in multilingual personal-data labeling. The resulting high-fidelity datasets suit supervised fine-tuning of language models. For responsible AI teams, the pipeline shows how analytics-driven iteration lifts both annotation quality and model reliability, where labeled data starts scarce.
arxiv-2510-06550:
Yuwei Xiao, Shuai Ma, Antti Oulasvirta, and Eunice Jun address a pain point in Bayesian statistics. Their 2025 paper concerns prior elicitation, where analysts state their beliefs before fitting a model. Beliefs about real variables must usually be translated into abstract parameter distributions. That translation is hard, especially for people new to the method.

The team built PriorWeaver, an interactive visual system for the task. Analysts draw their assumptions about variables and links between them. The system turns those drawings into a dataset and derives priors from it. Built-in checks then show analysts whether the priors match their intent. In a lab study with 17 newcomers, users reported more control, clarity, and confidence than with a baseline tool. Their final priors also matched their stated expectations more closely. The study suggests that building example data by hand beats guessing abstract parameters.
arxiv-2510-06750:
Jaeseong Lee, Dayoung Kwon, and Seung-won Hwang tackle waste in large reasoning models. Their 2025 paper notes that these models often overthink simple problems. They spend long chains of thought where a short answer would do. Running both a fast model and a slow model, then routing each query, is one fix, but it doubles deployment cost.

Their method, Gold-Switch, superposes the two styles inside a single model instead. It unlearns parts of the reasoning model at inference time, with no training. An analysis of singular values finds the right low-rank adjustments for each layer. Choosing those ranks layer by layer beat using one fixed ratio everywhere. Inference ran faster and task performance improved in their tests. One caution emerged from the results. Turning the scaling up too far sometimes increased overthinking. The work targets local deployments where a single adjustable model is cheaper than two.
arxiv-2510-06850:
Longteng Chen, an author, proves that a family of geometric shapes is stable under a smoothing flow. The 2025 paper works in Kähler geometry, which mixes complex and Riemannian structures. The shapes are expanding soliton metrics shaped like cones. Such solitons generalize Einstein metrics and anchor much of complex geometry.

Chen perturbs one of these metrics within the same Kähler class. He then runs the normalized Kähler-Ricci flow starting from the perturbed shape. Under suitable assumptions, the flow exists for all time. It converges uniformly to an expanding soliton metric of the kind. If the perturbation fades at far distances, the limit is the original soliton. Dents in the shape wash out rather than grow. The proof leans on a maximum principle argument and control of the driving vector field. Stability results like this one certify that these solitons are landmarks, not accidents.
arxiv-2510-07050:
Nicola Rossberg leads a team measuring whether people actually understand the features an AI explanation relies on. Their 2025 paper introduces the Feature Understandability Scale for explainable AI. Explanations of tabular models cite input features as reasons. A cited feature helps nobody if the audience finds that feature itself opaque.

No validated measure of feature understanding existed before this work. The team drafted a scale from the literature, then refined it through expert interviews and focus groups. A pilot study and factor analysis shaped the final instrument. Two versions emerged, one for numerical features and one for categorical ones. Each version rests on two underlying factors. An independent dataset confirmed that structure in a second analysis. Designers can now screen features before generating global explanations. Picking understandable features should make explanations land better with real users. The scale brings psychometric rigor to a corner of AI design that ran on intuition.
arxiv-2510-07150:
Smirnov and Zeng announce FIRE 7, a major update to a program used in particle physics. The 2025 paper appears in a computer physics journal. FIRE simplifies Feynman integrals, the math objects behind particle collision forecasts. A step called reduction rewrites huge numbers of integrals in terms of a small core set. That step is often the slowest part of a precision calculation. FIRE 7 aims to make it much faster.

The update leans on modular arithmetic, solving the problem with numbers first and rebuilding exact answers later. A smarter presolve step simplifies the core equations before numbers are inserted. The classic exact method also runs far faster than before. New command-line tools help users apply saved reduction tables to fresh problems with less hand work. Faster reduction supports sharper tests of particle theory at colliders.
arxiv-2510-07250:
Lou, Bresler, and Pananjady build a general machine for turning one kind of random sample into another. Their 2025 paper starts from a single observation drawn from a bell curve with unknown center. From that one sample, their procedures fake a sample from a different target distribution, uniformly for every possible center. Clever randomized constructions make the trick work approximately. The authors then weaponize the trick for hardness proofs.

If an easy problem could be converted into a hard-looking one, the hard one inherits lower bounds. Their reductions show that hardness results proved under Gaussian noise extend to many non-Gaussian noises, light- and heavy-tailed alike. One application settles a long-standing conjecture about a gap between statistical and computational difficulty in phase retrieval. Another links two planted-pattern models so their hardness maps match point by point. Such reduction machines unify scattered hardness results in high-dimensional statistics.
arxiv-2510-07350:
Chakravarty tests whether crop yield models trained in one region survive travel to new climates and years. The 2025 paper calls this the first large-scale check of its kind. Deep models using satellite and weather data have raised forecast accuracy in familiar territory. The study benchmarks leading architectures, including a graph-based recurrent model and a large vision transformer, on Earth observation data under realistic distribution shifts.

The graph recurrent model generalized across regions far better than the transformer. It also used over a hundred times less computing, aiding sustainable deployment. The transformer excelled at home but failed beyond its original four states. Both models struggled in a structurally distinct farming zone, where forecast gaps exceeded half the achievable accuracy. Alignment in space and time, not raw complexity, drives transfer.
arxiv-2510-07450:
Saavedra-Araya studies the times at which a dynamical orbit hits a sequence of shrinking targets. The 2025 paper works in ergodic theory and number theory. Fractional parts of a growing sequence times a starting point must land inside intervals whose sizes shrink. The set of hitting times depends delicately on the starting point chosen. The main theorem shows that, for almost every starting point, these hitting-time sets are good for pointwise convergence of ergodic averages. That is a strong regularity property for such thin, irregular sets of integers.

A second result proves a transversality phenomenon. Fix any set of integers whatsoever. For almost every starting point, its intersection with the hitting-time set is geometrically independent, certified by a fractal dimension computed over the integers. The two sets thus behave as if in general position, neither shadowing the other.
arxiv-2510-07550:
Motamed, Chen, Van Gool, and Laina teach video-language models to spot physics violations in generated video. Their 2025 paper starts from an embarrassment: AI videos look gorgeous while objects float, teleport, and morph against causality. Humans catch these instantly, but no robust automated judge existed. Off-the-shelf video-language models proved poor at the task, exposing weak temporal and causal reasoning. Their recipe, TRAVL, fine-tunes such models with a balanced training set plus a trajectory-aware attention module that forces the model to encode motion paths explicitly when judging plausibility of what it sees.

A new benchmark, ImplausiBench, holds three hundred videos split evenly between real and generated. Its design strips linguistic shortcuts so only visual-temporal understanding can score. Human gold judgments and a stricter automated metric both grade performance. TRAVL improved plausibility judgment on two different base models with minimal surgery to either.
arxiv-2510-08050:
Goswami and Maity wrote this 2025 mathematics paper computing an invariant cohomology group for two finite-dimensional Hopf algebras. Such groups classify ways a symmetry structure can be twisted without changing its representations. Direct computation had stalled on the first example, a certain group ring, where earlier work got only partial information. The authors instead use a categorical description of the invariant second cohomology.

For the group ring, the categorical approach settled the question cleanly. The group equals the two-element cyclic group, found without computer-aided calculation. For the eight-dimensional Kac-Paljutkin algebra, both invariant cohomology variants turned out trivial. The authors also prove useful general facts along the way. These groups govern fiber functors and ergodic actions of quantum groups. A clean categorical method should help wherever direct algebra becomes unwieldy.
arxiv-2510-08350:
Daniel Jason Tan and co-authors use deep learning to personalize tube feeding for intensive care patients, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Critically ill patients often cannot eat, so clinicians set enteral nutrition through a feeding tube. Fixed guidelines cannot match each patient's changing body state. Their system, DeepEN, learns feeding policies from records of past patients.

DeepEN trained offline on more than eleven thousand intensive care patients from the MIMIC-IV database. Every four hours it recommends calorie, protein, and fluid amounts tuned to the patient's state. A custom reward balances short-term body measures with long-term survival. Its network design discourages unsafe departures from good clinician practice. DeepEN beat clinician-derived and guideline-based policies on their metrics. Estimated mortality fell by 3.7 percentage points, from 22.5 percent to 18.8 percent, and nutrition markers improved.
arxiv-2510-08650:
Vinayak Sharma and co-authors replace the spline functions inside Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with tiny quantum circuits in a 2025 arXiv paper. KANs build functions from sums of one-variable B-spline curves, beating classic networks on scientific regression with fewer parameters. Their structure also yields closed-form equations, a prized interpretability benefit. The new variant, QuIRK, swaps each spline for a single-qubit data re-uploading model.

Data re-uploading feeds the input into a qubit circuit repeatedly to shape expressive one-variable functions. QuIRK matches or outperforms traditional KANs while using even fewer trainable parameters, the authors report. The advantage is especially clear on periodic functions, where the quantum form fits naturally. Single-qubit circuits stay easy to simulate classically, with plain GPU acceleration helping. QuIRK also retains the closed-form solution extraction that makes KANs attractive.
arxiv-2510-08750:
Udsa and colleagues examine how much training text a language model memorizes when many owners train it together, in this 2025 arXiv study. The setup is federated learning, where each client keeps its own data and only model updates are shared. Earlier checks looked at one sample at a time, which can miss subtler leaks that span many samples. The authors build a finer test that tracks memorization within one client's data and across different clients.

Their tests show that the shared models do retain client text, and retention is stronger for text from the same client than from others. How much leaks also depends on practical choices. Longer prompts given to the model, the way answers are decoded, and the training method all shift the amount. The work gives builders of shared models a way to measure a privacy risk that older tools understated.
arxiv-2510-08950:
Zhang and colleagues present the most complete spectroscopic census yet of the Rosette Nebula, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Rosette is a glowing cloud of ionized gas around young massive stars. Using a multi-fiber spectrograph on China's LAMOST telescope, the team gathered spectra across the nebula's full face. Their harvest holds three thousand eight hundred fifty-four high-quality spectra over about four and a half square degrees.

From the glowing lines of hydrogen, nitrogen, and sulfur, they measured brightness, motion, and line widths at each point. The motion map revealed a bow-shaped feature never seen before in this nebula. Combined with gas temperature and turbulence estimates, the patterns suggest the Rosette is colliding with the nearby Monoceros Loop, the remnant of an exploded star. They publish a full parameter table for testing theories of the nebula's chemistry and motion.
arxiv-2510-09050:
Ali, Islam, and Banerjee study how a company should split billboard slots among several products at once, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Roadside billboards are sold in time slots, and picking the slots whose passing traffic will most influence buyers is a known hard problem for one product. A commercial house promoting many products faces a harder version: each product has its own influence demand that must be met.

The authors formalize two variants. In one, a shared pool of slots must satisfy every product's demand. In the other, each product gets its own budget and its own disjoint set of slots. They model the problems with a cover formulation over functions that show diminishing returns, a structure that admits algorithms with guarantees. A bi-criteria approximation handles the first variant and a sampling-based method the second. Experiments on real trajectories and billboard records showed the methods effective.
arxiv-2510-09250:
Jiang and co-authors teach a sinking glider to steer by sliding its center of mass, finding the best trick depends on the water's thickness, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Tiny unpowered gliders could scatter through air or water as cheap sensor networks, if they land near their targets. The team studied a compact glider settling through a viscous fluid, shifting its internal mass as it falls. Simulations supplied the physics, and reinforcement learning searched for steering strategies.

Two winning strategies emerged. In thin fluid, where inertia is strong, the glider learns to tumble rapidly, shifting its center of mass as it rotates. Tumbling generates a large sideways inertial lift, carrying it far. In thick, syrupy fluid, tumbling fails, so the glider holds a steady inclined tilt instead. The tilt produces a gentle viscous sideways force and a much shorter range. The optimal strategy flips with the particle Reynolds number.
arxiv-2510-09450:
Ruirui Lin, Guoxi Huang, and Nantheera Anantrasirichai present DWTA-Net in a 2025 arXiv paper on low-light video enhancement. Videos shot in the dark suffer noise, weak contrast, and washed-out colour. Learning-based methods run fast but often fail under heavy real noise, because they do not draw enough on information from neighbouring frames over time.

DWTA-Net works in two stages with a recurrent design that carries information forward through the video. The first stage aligns several frames and restores local structure and colour with a Mamba-based module, an efficient sequence model. The second stage refines the result using dynamic, weight-based temporal aggregation steered by optical flow, adapting its denoising to motion. A texture-adaptive loss protects fine detail in busy regions while calming noise in flat ones. On real low-light footage, the method suppressed noise more strongly and produced fewer artefacts than leading rivals.
arxiv-2510-09750:
Michael Wyatt, Steven Furlanetto, and Mary Minasyan model how a short photon mean free path reshapes reionisation in a 2025 arXiv paper. Measurements at the tail of reionisation find that ionising photons travel a much shorter distance before absorption than guesses from earlier epochs suggested. That distance controls the size of the ionised bubbles around early galaxies.

The authors build the first analytic model that treats the mean free path as a free parameter inside the excursion set formalism. The model targets one-point summary values of the ionisation field, the quantities most relevant to twenty-one centimetre tomography with upcoming radio telescopes. A shorter mean free path matters most late in reionisation, shrinking ionised regions by about an order of magnitude near the end compared with models that ignore it. The predicted twenty-one centimetre contrast falls to one millikelvin or less at wide spacings, so finer readings are needed.
arxiv-2510-09950:
Bulatov and Amirhossein Kazeminia classify modular counting problems in this 2025 arXiv paper in computational complexity. The constraint satisfaction problem asks whether one relational structure maps into another while preserving its relations. Counting versions ask how many such maps exist, and modular counting counts them modulo a number.

The authors study this counting over 3-element domains and over conservative domains, where every unary relation is available. These restricted settings are test beds for finding the exact border between easy and hard counting. A full classification tells algorithm designers which cases admit fast counting and which are provably hard. The paper adds the modular variant to that map for the domains it covers.
arxiv-2510-10050:
Takahashi and Hiroki Saito analyze a spin-2 Bose-Einstein condensate in this 2025 arXiv paper in atomic physics. The condensate is made of rubidium-87 atoms with hyperfine spin two. It is an open quantum system: atoms leave through two-body inelastic collisions, where pairs crash and are lost.

One collision channel, with total spin four, is forbidden by angular momentum conservation. That ban leaves a fingerprint: the atoms that remain become magnetized in a characteristic way. The authors carry out a quantum many-body analysis of this decay process. Understanding the loss matters because dissipation is usually a nuisance in condensates; here it sculpts the state that survives, which experiments can measure.
arxiv-2510-10150:
Hao and co-authors rethink entropy interventions in reinforcement learning in this 2025 arXiv paper on language model training. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves reasoning, but training risks entropy collapse, a fast loss of diversity in the model's outputs. A collapsed policy explores too little and generalizes badly.

Recent fixes intervene on entropy directly, yet why they work is unclear. The authors analyze the problem from an entropy change perspective, tracking how entropy evolves during training and what drives the change. That view clarifies which interventions help and which merely mask the imbalance between exploration and exploitation. Better control of diversity could make reward-based training more reliable for reasoning models.
arxiv-2510-10250:
Krolik, Jake Lynn, John Henry Rudden, and Dmytro Vremenko detect brain tumors in MRI scans in this 2025 arXiv study of computer vision in medicine. Automated detection and segmentation of tumors could speed up radiology workflows. The authors compare several machine learning models on the task.

Their lineup runs from basic logistic regression up to convolutional neural networks and residual networks, which classify and outline tumors in the scans. Comparing simple and deep models on the same data shows how much the added complexity buys. The study is framed as an exploration of what current techniques achieve on MRI tumor detection. Such benchmarks guide hospitals toward tools that are accurate enough to assist, not just impress.
arxiv-2510-10450:
P Sangeerth and three co-authors design a controller for systems whose dynamics are only partly known, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They target incremental stability, a property where trajectories of a system converge toward each other rather than toward one fixed point. Their version, incremental input-to-state practical stability, adds guarantees that the system stays safe. The design builds on feedback linearization, a technique that reshapes a system's behavior through control input.

To handle the unknown parts of the dynamics, they approximate the model with Gaussian process regression, a statistical learning method that also reports its own uncertainty. The resulting controller comes with formal guarantees of both stability and invariance, meaning the system remains inside a safe region. They demonstrate the controller on a manipulator example. The work speaks to engineers who need provable safety when part of the model cannot be written down in advance.
arxiv-2510-10750:
Laura Weihl and three co-authors test whether AI can flag the interesting moments in underwater video, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Cameras monitor marine biodiversity, but most footage is uneventful and manual review is impractical. Visual anomaly detection promises to surface unusual events automatically. The team introduces AURA, the first benchmark dataset for underwater anomaly detection labeled by multiple annotators, and they evaluate four detection models across two marine scenes.

Their results are sobering. Model performance varies dramatically and depends heavily on how much training data is available and on how variable the normal scene looks. Choosing which frames to show the model matters a great deal. Comparing against several human annotators shows that soft labels and consensus labels carry real value, since even people disagree on what counts as anomalous. The authors offer their approach as practical support for scientific exploration and for scaling up biodiversity monitoring.
arxiv-2510-11950:
N. Sawai and six colleagues report new digital controls for a great X-ray laser. The LCLS at SLAC switched on in 2009, but its linac still runs on control electronics dating to the nineteen sixties and eighties. The Linac Electronics Modernization Plan replaces that legacy gear. Their 2025 arXiv paper describes the low-level radio-frequency system at the plan's heart, the electronics that keep the accelerating fields precisely shaped.

The design reuses boards from the newer LCLS-II machine: the open-source Marble carrier and the Zest+ digitizer. Adapting a system built for continuous-wave superconducting cavities to the old pulsed, normal-conducting linac took care. The team leaned on experience from partner laboratories including Berkeley, Fermilab, and Jefferson Lab. A prototype now runs at station 26-3. It demonstrates radio-frequency generation and control, safety interlocks, triggers, and waveform capture, the full checklist the modernization requires before wider rollout.
arxiv-2510-12050:
Mohit Daga makes thinness in graphs something you can actually check. A spanning tree is thin if it uses only a small fraction of every cut's capacity, a property behind both a famous conjecture and the best traveling-salesman approximations. Verifying thinness seemed to require examining exponentially many cuts. His 2025 arXiv paper introduces k-respecting cut identities to collapse that work.

The identity expresses the weight of any cut crossing a tree in at most k edges through pairwise cuts that cross it in at most two. That yields a local oracle: after quadratic preprocessing, each such cut evaluates in constant time. Daga then gives the first procedure computing a tree's exact k-thinness certificate, value and witnessing cut included. Sampling a few random trees extends coverage to all near-minimum cuts, each certified by some sampled tree. Planar graphs earn even sharper guarantees through duality.
arxiv-2510-12150:
Jiahuan Zhou and five colleagues keep a deployed model learning without letting old knowledge poison the new. Continual test-time adaptation fine-tunes models on streaming data from shifting domains, no advance access allowed. Prior fixes restore old weights or replay old models, underlearning the new domain or importing harmful history. Their 2025 arXiv paper, KFF, instead splits and merges knowledge by class.

A fission module adaptively separates fresh domain knowledge into a class-aware prompt pool, quarantining new patterns from clashing old ones. Left alone, endless fission would bloat computation and storage. A fusion module therefore merges new knowledge into the existing pool with a greedy strategy that maximizes compatibility at minimal cost. Discriminative history accumulates dynamically while genuinely distinct domains stay segregated. Extensive experiments on the ImageNet-C corruption benchmark verify the method against rivals.
arxiv-2510-12250:
Huang and a large team report superconductivity in a different form of a nickel based compound, in a 2025 arXiv condensed matter paper. The bilayer form of the compound La3Ni2O7, a Ruddlesden Popper nickelate, superconducts near eighty kelvin under pressure and launched a new family of superconductors. The authors synthesized the monolayer trilayer hybrid phase of the same compound, where single and triple layer blocks alternate.

Under high pressure, synchrotron X ray diffraction plus Raman spectroscopy tracked a structural change at thirteen gigapascals, from an orthorhombic to a tetragonal arrangement. Above nineteen gigapascals it showed a clear superconducting transition, confirmed by zero resistance. However, its transition point was only a few kelvin, far below the bilayer value. The sharp contrast shows that the transition temperature is governed by how layers couple, and that the bilayer block is the key building unit for high temperature superconductivity in these nickelates.
arxiv-2510-12350:
Khaitan and Ganesh couple a large language model with a computer algebra system to prove hard asymptotic inequalities, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Language models can suggest proof ideas but cannot be trusted without strict checking, which has limited their role in research. Asymptotic inequalities ask how expressions behave for large values, and their proofs often hinge on splitting the domain into the right pieces.

Their tool, O-Forge, runs an in context symbolic feedback loop. The language model proposes a decomposition of the domain, and the algebra system checks each piece axiomatically, feeding corrections back. With this loop the authors answer a question posed by Terence Tao about whether language models with a verifier can help prove intricate asymptotic inequalities. They argue the combination works remarkably well at finding useful decompositions. The work is offered as evidence that artificial intelligence can move from contest problems toward research tools.
arxiv-2510-12650:
Mauel and co-authors pretrain a neural model that can infer the equations of a dynamical system on sight, from sparse and noisy data, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Ordinary differential equations describe systems evolving deterministically in continuous time, and fitting them to data is a central, difficult problem, especially when observations are few or corrupted.

Their model, FIM-ODE, is a foundation inference model trained entirely on synthetic data. It uses a flexible neural operator to estimate the governing equations in context, meaning at use time it reads the observations and outputs an equation without further training, a zero shot capability. The authors verify empirically that its estimates are accurate, on par with a state of the art neural method built for the task. They also compare the structure of the estimated vector fields qualitatively. The work extends the foundation model idea, proven in their companion papers, to deterministic dynamics.
arxiv-2511-00050:
Dhananjaya Gowda, Seoha Song, and Junhyun Lee propose FLoRA, a family of fused forward-backward adapters for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models. Low-rank adapters already cut training cost, but much of the design space remains unexplored. Their adapters fuse operations in the forward and backward passes, aiming also to reduce inference-time latency, not just training parameters.

Language model practitioners get a new adapter family positioned against established low-rank methods. Efficiency at both training and deployment matters because fine-tuned models are served many times. Fusing passes attacks overhead that parameter counts alone do not capture, widening the practical gains of adapter tuning.
arxiv-2511-00150:
Christopher Baldwin asks whether a quantum method for hard search problems really beats a well-matched classical rival. The quantum method, adiabatic reverse annealing, starts from a good first guess to dodge harmful phase changes. Baldwin reads its gains through the shape of the free energy landscape, the map that guides the search.

From that view he builds a classical twin, simulated reverse annealing, that copies the same trick without quantum hardware. In a solvable mean-field model, the classical method wins wherever the quantum one does. It even succeeds in a narrow range where the quantum method fails, which weakens claims of a quantum edge here.
arxiv-2511-00250:
Courtney Watson, Elizabeth Blanton, Scott Randall, Tracy Clarke, and John ZuHone report very deep X-ray observations of Abell 2029, a galaxy cluster with a cool, dense core. Data from the Chandra telescope, gathered over a long exposure, reveal one of the longest sloshing spirals ever seen, reaching far from the cluster core. Sloshing is gas swaying after a past disturbance.

Fainter features tell the merger story: a broad splash of cooler gas and a possible merger shock. Radio lobes at the center bend along the sloshing flow, not the host galaxy's motion. Comparison with simulations points to a smaller cluster that passed through long ago. Even calm-looking clusters, the team shows, hide busy pasts.
arxiv-2511-00350:
Yu-Peng Wang, Chuo-Kai Chang, Ryo Okugawa, and Chen-Hsuan Hsu study localization in a non-Hermitian system, a quantum setup where energy can leak, patterned by a quasiperiodic potential. They track when states stay extended and when they collapse into small regions, using several measures at once: participation ratios, fractal dimensions, and spectral statistics.

Even without the usual self-dual symmetry, a critical potential strength exists, and it grows in a straight line with the antisymmetric hopping strength. Adding longer-range hopping enriches the picture: mobility edges appear, separating localized from extended states by energy, and fractal patterns show in the complex energy spectrum. Self-similar structures recur as the potential varies, linking localization physics with fractal geometry in a leaky system.
arxiv-2511-01150:
D. Schuricht and J. Sirker study paraparticles, hypothetical particle types with statistics beyond the usual boson and fermion kinds, arranged in interacting chains. Their Hamiltonians sum over the particles' internal flavors and use a constant interaction matrix, making the Hamiltonians blind to flavor.

For such flavor blind chains they prove the Hilbert space factors into occupation and flavor parts, with the energy acting only on occupation. With open ends, the spectrum matches the occupation Hamiltonian, flavors merely adding degeneracy. With periodic boundaries, flavor reordering splits the problem into flux sectors, making the parastatistics directly visible in the spectrum. In key cases the occupation part reduces to the solvable XXZ chain, whose gapless regime shows shifted conformal towers and a temperature dependent chemical potential.
arxiv-2511-20150:
Ehrhardt, Günther, and Ševčovič show how to merge and split energy-based system models safely. Their 2025 paper works with port-Hamiltonian systems. Such models track energy storage, loss, and exchange. Ports connect the parts to each other and the world. Coupling port-Hamiltonian parts normally preserves the structure.

The team gives a systematic two-way transformation method. Coupled parts become one single joint system. In reverse, a single system splits into weakly coupled parts. The single-system form favors stability and soundness. The split form favors distributed, parallel simulation. Operator splitting or dynamic iteration can then run it. Linear input-output relations underpin the constructions here. Energy conservation and dissipation survive both directions. Nonlinear ordinary equation systems are covered too. Future work targets adaptive coupling strategies. Structure-preserving time stepping is another open direction. Algebraic and stochastic extensions are planned as well.
arxiv-2511-20350:
McGrath measures the size of symmetry groups defined by shift rules. His 2025 paper builds size formulas for difference algebraic groups. Ordinary algebraic groups are cut out by polynomial equations. Difference versions use equations involving shift maps too. With several shifts that commute, the theory is called partial. Two main results anchor the paper.

First, the defining ideal of such a group is finitely generated. Only finitely many difference equations are ever needed. That finite generation unlocks the second result. A dimension polynomial exists for every such group in this setting. The polynomial counts the sizes of finite approximations as they grow. A special case is restated in symbolic dynamics language. There, the group is fixed by one finite window plus shift invariance. The work was supported by an EPSRC doctoral studentship. It puts this branch of algebra on the same footing as the classical theory.
arxiv-2511-20450:
Wirth settles a conjecture about distances between quantum states. His 2025 mathematics paper proves the triangle inequality for a quantum Wasserstein divergence. Wasserstein distances measure optimal transport cost classically. Quantum versions try to do the same for quantum states. De Palma and Trevisan defined one such modified distance. Whether it obeyed the triangle inequality stayed open.

A distance needs that inequality to behave like a true metric. Wirth's proof resolves their conjecture affirmatively. Complex analysis methods power the argument. The key step is a new integral representation of transport cost. Static definitions like this one generalize the Monge-Kantorovich formula. Dynamical rivals instead follow the Benamou-Brenier viewpoint. The distance has zero self-distance and symmetry by construction. Non-degeneracy depends on the chosen cost operators. Quantum optimal transport has grown rapidly in recent decades. This result firms up one of its central definitions.
arxiv-2511-20550:
Bryant, Huerta y Munive, and Foster machine-check the numeric recipes machine learning stands on. Their 2025 paper builds a checking framework inside Isabelle/HOL. Numeric methods approach solutions step by step, from root-finding to gradient descent. Bugs or shaky proofs in them undermine trust in systems built on top. Formal checking of such methods is still young.

Their language lets users state numeric programs directly. Programs carry loop invariants for correctness reasoning. A generator produces proof goals that automated methods discharge. Lemmas from the HOL-Analysis library close those goals. The bisection method shows the workflow end to end. Fixed-point iteration serves as the second worked example. Checked code exports to runnable source through Isabelle's generator. The library gained higher-order derivatives as a by-product. Taylor's theorem in Peano form was formalized too. Users need not grasp the generator's internals to use it.
arxiv-2511-20650:
Tooba Tehreem Sheikh and co-authors at MBZUAI present in 2025 MedROV, a detector that finds objects in medical scans even when it was never trained on their names. Ordinary detectors only recognise a fixed list of categories. A scan showing pneumonia is missed if pneumonia was never on that list. MedROV instead takes a text description at run time and searches the image for whatever the words describe, across scan types from X-rays to microscope slides.

To teach it, the team built Omnis, a training set of 600,000 labelled examples drawn from 35 datasets covering nine kinds of medical imaging, with machine-generated labels filling gaps. MedROV beat the previous best medical foundation model by an average of 40 points on the mAP50 accuracy score. It also topped closed-set detectors by more than 3 points on the same measure, and runs at 70 frames per second, fast enough for live clinical use.
arxiv-2511-21050:
Dongkyu Derek Cho and colleagues challenge in 2025 the belief that making a language model more capable must make it less safe. Fine-tuning normally erodes safety alignment even on benign data, across supervised tuning and human-feedback reinforcement learning alike. The team studies reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where the reward is an objective check, such as whether an answer is exactly right. Its safety behaviour had never been analysed.

Theory comes first: under KL-constrained optimisation they bound how far safety can drift, and prove conditions under which degradation vanishes entirely. Experiments across five adversarial safety benchmarks then show the method improving reasoning while holding, or even strengthening, safety guardrails. Ablations vary the optimisation algorithm, comparing GRPO with REINFORCE++, plus model scale and task domain. The authors argue the safety-capability trade-off is an artefact of training method, not a law, with direct lessons for deploying reasoning models.
arxiv-2511-21150:
Multimodal language models read images through a vision encoder, then compress the flood of visual tokens before the language model sees them. Encoding whole images at native resolution works better than slicing, but the cost balloons with resolution. Shichu Sun and colleagues present LLaVA-UHD v3 in 2025, built on progressive visual compression, a method that plugs into a Vision Transformer. Refined patch embedding allows finer patch sizes, while windowed compression inside the transformer layers merges local tokens step by step.

The rebuilt encoder, ViT-UHD, matched the strong MoonViT encoder's benchmark scores while cutting time-to-first-token by a factor of 2.4 in identical model setups. The full LLaVA-UHD v3 system matched Qwen2-VL's performance with a 1.9-fold cut in that latency. Tests span 15 benchmarks for the model and six for the encoder alone. Code and checkpoints are promised for release, aimed at cheaper high-resolution multimodal models.
arxiv-2511-21450:
Per Austrin, Johan Håstad, and Björn Martinsson ask when a promise makes a hard problem easy, in a 2025 theoretical computer science paper. Promise constraint problems hand the solver a guarantee, like a graph being 3-colorable, and ask only for a weaker prize, like a 5-coloring. A predicate is called promise-useful if some nontrivial promise version built on it is efficiently solvable, and promise-useless otherwise.

Austrin and his coauthors derive conditions settling both sides, assuming P differs from NP. Their criteria classify every Boolean predicate of arity at most four, and almost all of arity five. For large arities, they prove the vast majority of predicates are promise-useless, so helpful promises are rare gems. The engine of the work is a close study of Promise-SAT, combining the LP plus affine integer programming algorithm of Brakensiek and coauthors with new NP-hardness tests.
arxiv-2511-21550:
Thai-Khanh Nguyen and five coauthors give a sequence model a sense of momentum for recognizing human activity, in 2025. Watches and phones identify walking, sitting, or falling from inertial sensors, but the signals are noisy and activities unfold over long spans. Mamba, a state-space sequence model, handles long sequences cheaply, yet its first-order memory fades. The team borrowed momentum, the physics trick of carrying velocity, to enrich its memory.

Their Momentum Mamba adds a second-order dynamics pathway to the hidden state, damping vanishing gradients and improving robustness and long-range modeling. Two extensions push further: Complex Momentum Mamba scales memory by frequency, and Adam Momentum Mamba adapts by variance. Across multiple benchmarks, the models consistently beat both plain Mamba and transformer baselines in accuracy, noise robustness, and convergence speed. The gains cost only moderate extra training, making momentum-augmented models a scalable default for sensor data.
arxiv-2511-21650:
Francesco Capozzi, Eligio Lisi, Francesco Marcone, Antonio Marrone, and Antonio Palazzo sharpen two fundamental neutrino numbers with brand-new data, in 2025. The parameters govern how the two lightest neutrino states mix and split in mass, and they are probed by solar and reactor neutrino oscillations. A 2024 global analysis knew them only to within a few percent.

Adding the latest SNO+ constraints shifted the best fits slightly. Then the first results from China's JUNO reactor experiment cut the uncertainties dramatically. The updated global bounds put the squared mass difference at 7.48 units of a hundred-thousandth of an electronvolt squared, and the mixing measure at 0.3085, give or take 0.0073 in the same units. Those are errors of just over one percent for the splitting and about two and a half percent for the mixing. The authors also flag subtle effects that may one day break the remaining degeneracy over neutrino mass ordering.
arxiv-2511-21750:
Di Feng and eleven coauthors introduce SO-Bench, the first systematic benchmark of whether multimodal models can emit correctly structured output from images, in 2025. In real deployments, answers feed downstream software, so they must match predefined JSON schemas exactly. Text-only structured generation had been studied; the visual side had not.

SO-Bench spans four visual domains: interface screens, natural images, documents, and charts. It draws on over 6,500 diverse JSON schemas and 1,800 curated image-schema pairs with human-verified quality. Testing exposed persistent gaps. The strongest systems, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5-Pro, followed schemas with over 95 percent accuracy yet produced fully correct outputs only up to nearly 19 percent of the time on a fuzzy match. Small 3 and 7 billion parameter models lagged far behind. Follow-up training substantially improved structured output, showing the weakness is trainable rather than fixed.
arxiv-2511-21850:
Alpern and Rachev blend environmental, social, and governance scores, known as ESG ratings, into a classic portfolio-building method called Black-Litterman allocation. In their strategy, ESG scores bias the estimated equilibrium returns fed into the allocation, via shrinkage toward a stable centre. Asset returns are modelled with a heavy-tailed normal-inverse Gaussian distribution rather than a normal one, and risk is measured by CVaR, which focuses on the worst tail outcomes instead of average swings.

Portfolios were reallocated daily over a 4.7 year test period, 2017 to 2021, across many risk aversion and ESG weighting combinations. A soft limit on how much the portfolio could change each day proved important. The most successful strategies returned approximately 40 to 45 percent annually over that test period in the authors' backtest, a striking backtest result for a simple, carefully constrained ESG tilt.
arxiv-2511-21950:
Liu and colleagues study a large system of coupled random wave equations, the hyperbolic O(N) linear sigma model, with N interacting fields. Each field obeys a damped, noisy nonlinear wave equation on a two-dimensional torus, the surface of a donut, coupled to all the others through their shared average energy term. The question is what the whole system looks like when N becomes enormous, in physics language, its mean-field limit.

After proving global well-posedness, the authors prove the finite-N dynamics converge to a single mean-field equation. For local time intervals they obtain an explicit convergence rate, of order N to the power of minus one-half plus epsilon for any positive epsilon. They extend the same rate to the invariant Gibbs dynamics on large time intervals.
arxiv-2511-22050:
Bian, Wang, Tang, and Lee, neuroscientists at Carnegie Mellon, map how brain area V4. A mid-level stage of the primate visual system, organizes its coding of shape, texture, color, and three-dimensional form. Classic experiments probed each feature separately, leaving open how one neuron's preferences across features relate and how the preferences tile the cortical surface. The team attacks the question with V4 'digital twins,' neural network models fitted to wide-field calcium imaging from tens of thousands of natural images.

Probing the twins systematically, they find neurons preferring two-dimensional contour shape also prefer 3D solid surfaces and object form, while texture-preferring neurons prefer flat surfaces. The pattern suggests V4 splits its work into a shape module encoding 3D geometry and an appearance module encoding surface properties, arranged as interleaved clusters across the topographic map. A division of labor future physiology experiments can test directly.
arxiv-2511-22150:
Rottach and colleagues study how text embedding models arrange meaning in geometric space. Embeddings turn text into lists of numbers, and models differ in the shapes those numbers form. Researchers use topological and geometric measures to describe those shapes. The team compares many such measures across a wide set of models and datasets. A full view, the authors argue, is essential for understanding these spaces.

They find the measures overlap heavily, so most add little new information. Single measures also fail to tell embedding spaces apart reliably. Their answer is Unified Topological Signatures, a combined profile of a space from many angles. The signatures predict model-specific traits and reveal similarities driven by model architecture. They also link structure to ranking quality and predict how easily documents can be retrieved. That gives practitioners a fuller way to judge and compare embedding models.
arxiv-2511-22250:
Jiang, Wang, Cheng, and Ge, medical imaging researchers, reconstruct the colon's 3D shape from a single camera's video. Colonoscopy images defeat geometry models: surfaces are glossy rather than matte, the light moves with the scope, and long stretches are textureless. Their ColonAdapter fine-tunes a pretrained 3D geometric foundation model for this domain with self-supervision, keeping its priors while adapting them to clinical imagery, crucially without needing the camera's ground-truth internal parameters.

Two additions target the failure modes: a Detail Restoration Module recovers structure in low-texture regions, helped by a geometry consistency loss enforcing scale coherence. A confidence-weighted photometric loss stabilizes training where reflections corrupt the signal. On synthetic and real data it reaches state-of-the-art pose, depth, and point-map results, fixing DUSt3R's textureless-scene errors. The framework needs no ground-truth geometry labels for the colonoscopy data.
arxiv-2511-22550:
Idir and colleagues compare ten statistical models for mapping city air pollution from cheap sensors.
