Low-cost sensors on vehicles promise far denser coverage than fixed monitoring stations, but their data quality is questionable. Working in Nantes, France, the team fed fixed and mobile low-cost sensor data, plus auxiliary variables, into ten literature models. They validated outputs against reference stations. They tested both gap-filling in time and forecasting ahead.

Two lessons stand out. First, models fed low-cost data showed a pronounced bias against reference station data, in both interpolation and prediction. Second, machine learning models, random forest, XGBoost, and a hybrid, performed best at forecasting, with correlations above 0.4 on every indicator. The authors conclude that data quality matters more than model sophistication: low-cost sensors should never be used alone, but integrated with, and calibrated against, fixed station data.
arxiv-2511-22650:
Budzinskiy, Kazeev, and Olshanskii generalise tensor compression to arrays whose entries are functions. Reduced-order modelling of parametric partial differential equations needs stand-ins for the parameter-to-solution map. Low-rank tensor approximation is a compressor, except that a PDE solution at each parameter value is a whole function, not a number. The authors show Hilbert space inner-product geometry is enough: they define Tucker rank, a higher-order singular value decomposition, and a Tucker-cross decomposition for function-valued tensors, despite the field arithmetic.

On that foundation they build a cross-approximation algorithm sampling only tensor fibres, making the method non-intrusive. The PDE solver is a black box. The reduced model reads as an encoder-decoder pair: nonlinear encoder, multilinear decoder. Numerical experiments on two nonlinear parametric PDE systems demonstrate the approach, positioned for parametric workloads, inverse problems, optimal control, uncertainty quantification, and digital twins.
arxiv-2511-22750:
Mouli settles a classification question linking number fields and group theory. Drungilas and coauthors asked which triples of positive integers can occur as the degrees of two number fields and their compositum. Via the Galois correspondence, degrees become subgroup indices. A triple is index-realizable if some group has finite-index subgroups realising the first two numbers as indices and the third as the index of their intersection.

The main theorem characterises index-realizable triples completely. A triple is realizable if and only if a bipartite graph exists, with no isolated vertices and degree conditions on its parts, encoding the intersection pattern. Non-realizable triples are pinned down just as sharply, by graph-theoretic obstructions. Since every compositum-feasible triple must be index-realizable, the classification gives necessary conditions for the original problem while standing as a clean combinatorial result, proved largely by explicit constructions.
arxiv-2511-23450:
Agarwal and colleagues tackle the annotation bottleneck in object detection. Teaching a model a new object category normally demands large amounts of hand-labeled images that rare, long-tailed classes do not have. They define the object-centric data setting, in which the only material available for a new category is object-centric data such as multi-view images or 3D models. They ask how far synthetic training images can carry a detector.

Four synthesis routes are compared, from cut-and-paste compositing through 3D rendering to image diffusion models, generating cluttered scenes with realism and context for fine-tuning. Enhanced paste methods that add geometric, lighting, and perspective cues plus contextual backgrounds beat the plain cut-paste baseline. A combined 3D copy-paste method does not. The authors warn that realistic constraints like surface placement can shrink viewpoint diversity enough to cancel their own benefit.
arxiv-2512-00250:
Angular applications often suffer subtle bugs in how they handle reactive data streams. Shrinivass Arunachalam Balasubramanian presents ng-reactive-lint in 2025, a smarter linting tool for Angular apps. Misuse of Observables, Signals, and change detection can cause slowdowns that are hard to diagnose.

Later Angular versions introduced a signal-first model, yet many enterprise codebases still rely on older RxJS patterns. Those patterns can create unpredictable update flows, memory leaks, and excessive change cycles. A linter that catches such misuse early helps large teams keep web applications fast and maintainable as they grow. Linting shifts bug catching to the moment code is written, when fixes are cheapest. The tool targets reactive patterns specifically, rather than style rules in general.
arxiv-2512-00450:
Judging personality and interview performance from video and audio could speed up hiring, but datasets are scarce. Amit Kumar Gupta and co-authors at Manipal University Jaipur present RecruitView in 2025, a multimodal dataset for human resources applications. Automated assessment remains challenging because traits have geometric structure that simple methods miss.

The dataset supports predicting personality and interview performance from multimodal behavioral data. Shared data lets researchers compare methods fairly instead of training on private recordings. The work also raises the stakes for care: tools trained on such data influence real people's job prospects. Multimodal data combine face, voice, and movement, each carrying part of the signal. Personality prediction from behavior is contested, which makes shared benchmarks even more important. For firms that hire at scale, the gain is a shared test bed. New tools can be tried on the same clips, and the scores can be checked side by side.
arxiv-2512-00550:
Cells inside tissue live under constant mechanical stress, and measuring that stress explains much of development and disease. Lucas Anger and co-authors present tissue stress measurements with Bayesian Inversion Stress Microscopy in 2025. Mechanical forces shape morphogenesis, collective migration, cell division, and cell death.

Stress inside tissue cannot be probed directly, so it must be inferred from observed deformations. A Bayesian inversion states its uncertainty along with the estimate, which keeps biologists from overreading noisy maps. Better stress maps help researchers understand how tissues grow, heal, and sometimes turn cancerous. Bayesian inversion also regularizes the inference, keeping wild stress maps in check. Stress microscopy serves developmental biology, where forces sculpt growing tissues. For folks who grow tissues in the lab, the gain is a map they can trust. The pull and push in each part, with a fair sense of how sure the map is.
arxiv-2512-00850:
Haishan Wang, Mohammad Hassan Vali, and Arno Solin present Smol-GS in a 2025 computer graphics paper. A popular way to store 3D scenes is Gaussian splatting, which fills space with soft colored blobs called splats. Full scenes can take huge storage, especially when fine detail matters.

Smol-GS learns compact codes for such scenes. Splat positions are stored through a recursive voxel hierarchy, a tree of nested cubes. Features on each splat keep abstract cues like color, opacity, shape change, and material. Spatial and semantic information are packed together. Smaller scene files would help stream detailed 3D content to phones and headsets.
arxiv-2512-00950:
Arnaldo Spalvieri works out a probability law for bosonic systems in a 2025 physics paper. Bosons are particles that can share the same state, so a system is described by occupancy numbers, counts of how many sit in each state. The canonical setting fixes the temperature and lets energy be exchanged with an environment.

Spalvieri derives the canonical distribution of those occupancy numbers. He shows that canonical typicality applies here. Almost any pure state of the whole universe gives the same mixed state for the system, once the environment is traced out. In the limit, the distribution tends toward a multinomial one.
arxiv-2512-01250:
Geng Zhao, Yun Chen, Jiayuan Zhang, Jing Tang, and Yuangang Deng propose a scheme for unusual light in a 2025 physics paper. Nonclassical light, whose photon patterns no classical wave can mimic, is a resource for quantum technology. The authors work with atomic arrays that can be reconfigured, coupled to an optical cavity.

By controlling the collective interference phase of the atoms, the system switches behavior. On one side sits single-photon blockade, where photons enter one at a time. On the other, it emits high-purity bundles of several photons together. The pattern of correlations follows atom-number parity and cavity detuning, giving experimenters clear knobs to turn.
arxiv-2512-01350:
Songting Li and a large team map the halo of stars around our galaxy. The halo is a vast, sparse cloud of old stars. Its shape tells how our galaxy grew by eating smaller ones. The team used giant stars from the DESI survey's second data set.

They track stars from near the core to far out in the halo. They find the halo is both twisted and split in two zones. They also map how star counts thin with range. A twisted, split halo points to a past merger that still marks our galaxy's form today.
arxiv-2512-02050:
Gravity might be carried by a particle with a small mass, a massive graviton, and that idea has a famous catch. Th. A. Rijken and J. W. Wagenaar present in 2025 a quantization of massive and massless spin-2 particles using an auxiliary-field method, and revisit the catch directly.

The catch is the vDVZ discontinuity: a massive graviton's predictions may fail to approach Einstein's as its mass shrinks, spoiling agreement with data such as the precession of Mercury's orbit. The authors study perihelion precession in their spin-2 theory at tree level. The paper continues a long effort to learn whether massive gravity can survive contact with the solar system.
arxiv-2512-02150:
On a triangular lattice, neighboring spins cannot all oppose each other at once, and this frustration breeds exotic magnetic phases. Anna Keselman and four co-authors map in 2025 how one such antiferromagnet behaves when a magnetic field is applied, across all its coupling strengths.

They combine large-scale density matrix renormalization group simulations with self-consistent spin-wave theory, two methods that check each other. The resulting phase diagram shows quantum fluctuations stabilizing coplanar spin order everywhere in the range studied. Triangular magnets are test beds for quantum materials, and a full field-and-coupling map guides experiments hunting new phases.
arxiv-2512-02250:
Random tensors arise when analysts average noisy high-dimensional data, and one key estimate about them was proved in 2022 by Deng, Nahmod, and Yue using the moment method. Claire Kaneshiro gives a new proof of that abstract random tensor estimate in 2025, with a different central tool.

Her proof leans directly on the non-commutative Khintchine inequality, together with a probabilistic decoupling of products of Gaussians. A cleaner proof is not just elegance: it shows which parts of the original argument were essential and may extend to cases the moment method cannot reach. Tensor estimates of this kind underlie work on nonlinear waves and random data problems.
arxiv-2512-02350:
Robots and agents in different places can learn together without sharing data, but offline federated reinforcement learning inherits two problems at once. Nan Qiao and three co-authors show in 2025 that most existing methods collapse when the logged data differ in quality from client to client, and propose FOVA to fix it.

In the offline setting, agents learn from fixed logs of past behavior rather than fresh interaction, and those logs come from policies of varying quality. A method that stays robust under mixed-quality data is essential for real deployments, where no one can re-collect every client's history. The work targets federated learning's promise of collaboration without centralizing sensitive experience.
arxiv-2512-02450:
Estimating a room's 3D layout from one image works in tidy synthetic rooms and fails in real buildings with several floors. Valentin Bieri and four co-authors introduce HouseLayout3D in 2025, a benchmark for layout estimation in the wild, plus a training-free baseline that needs no task-specific learning.

Models trained on simple single-room data cannot natively handle multi-floor buildings, and splitting scenes by floor destroys global context like staircases. A benchmark drawn from real complexity exposes that gap honestly. Progress here serves augmented reality, renovation tools, and robots that must understand whole homes, not single rooms.
arxiv-2512-02750:
Kiev Gama and five co-authors study how beginners engage with vibe coding, building software by prompting AI. Instead of writing code directly, the programmer describes intent in natural language and steers the result. The style promises to open software building to far more people.

Its effects on learning, though, remain largely unexplored. Novices may gain confidence quickly, or may skip the struggle that builds real skill. The team's exploration of engagement offers early evidence for teachers. Schools need such evidence to decide how AI coding should enter the classroom. Prompt craft is a new skill, and how schools teach it will shape who gets to build with code at all.
arxiv-2512-02950:
Sungjun Lee and four co-authors create ultracold molecules from sodium and potassium atoms as a step toward dipolar gases. Feshbach molecules form when atoms bind loosely near a magnetic resonance. Coherent transfer can then move them to the ground state of rotation and vibration.

Those ground state dimers would form stable gases with strong, tunable long range interactions. The team reports creating bosonic sodium potassium Feshbach molecules by radio frequency association. Each step toward controlled dipolar gases opens studies of matter governed by long range forces. Each bound pair is a step on a stair. The stair climbs from loose pairs of atoms to a gas of true dipoles that labs can probe at will.
arxiv-2512-03150:
The Bullet Cluster is a famous crash of galaxy clusters. Boseong Young Cho, M. James Jee, and co-authors weigh its parts in this 2025 work. Past estimates of its mass ratio ranged widely, from about two to one to more than ten to one.

The team joins data from the Webb telescope and DECam in a lensing study. They report the first robust masses for the cluster's three parts from weak and strong lensing. Their title calls the crash a minor merger. Firm masses help test dark matter ideas built on this system. Mass ratios shape how the crash is read as evidence about dark matter behavior.
arxiv-2512-03450:
Finding key points on 3D objects without labels is a core challenge. Rhys Newbury and co-authors present KeyPointDiffuser in this 2025 work. Key points summarize an object's structure for grasping, matching, and generation.

Most unsupervised key point methods are not built for unconditional generation settings. That limits their use in modern 3D generative pipelines. The authors use latent diffusion models to learn key points, bridging that gap. Learned key points could help robots and design tools reason about shapes automatically. Generative key points could seed new shapes, not just describe shapes already given, extending their use in design and animation tools.
arxiv-2512-03950:
Ants leaving scent trails and cells laying chemical tracks share a trick: past paths steer future motion. Paul Pineau, Samuel Bell, Raphaël Voituriez, and Ram M. Adar build a minimal model of many such trail-following particles in a 2025 statistical mechanics preprint. Earlier work treated single particles or averaged theories, leaving collective behaviour largely unexplored.

In their model, particles wander randomly while depositing long-lasting trails that attract or repel those who come later, forming a shared memory field. Using stochastic density functional theory, the authors derive equations for the collective density and study them on paper and in simulation. With repelling trails, densities spread unusually and form temporary clusters. With attracting trails, the system condenses in finite time into frozen, localised clumps. Memory plus noise, they conclude, generates instabilities and self-organisation of its own.
arxiv-2512-04150:
A Fermi surface, the boundary in momentum space between filled and empty electron states, is usually something a material happens to have. Minho Luke Kim, Salvatore D. Pace, and Shu-Heng Shao prove some systems cannot avoid having one, in a 2025 preprint. They construct a symmetry forcing every model that respects it to be gapless in exactly this way.

The symmetry mixes ordinary fermion number conservation with a non-local Majorana translation, generating a noncompact Lie group related to the Onsager algebra. For any Fermi surface this symmetry enforces, the authors show the symmetry group always contains the even part of the ersatz Fermi liquid symmetry that such surfaces carry. They also prove these enforced surfaces generically have at least two noncontractible components, like open orbits wrapping momentum space.
arxiv-2512-04650:
Halina Wiśniewska studies a family of functions named for Weierstrass that stretch a classic inequality between sums and products. The classical rule bounds the product of two numbers by their sum in a tidy double inequality. A Weierstrass function keeps that double rule alive on a chosen interval: the sum minus one sits below the function of the product, which sits below the product of the function values. Her 2025 arXiv paper maps what such functions can do.

With these functions, the old inequality extends to trigonometric functions, the Euler gamma function, and logarithms. One case stands out: the function built from the log of one plus x, scaled to fit. It yields a new multiplicative inequality that in turn generalizes the classical rule. Such extensions give analysts fresh bounds for special functions, useful wherever products must be fenced in by sums.
arxiv-2512-05050:
Natalie Hogg, Daniel Johnson, Anowar Shajib, and Julien Larena measure a subtle distortion in strong gravitational lenses, the systems where a massive galaxy bends a distant source's light into arcs. Matter scattered along the line of sight adds its own stretch, called shear, and if that stretch can be measured reliably it becomes a new way to probe the cosmos. An earlier group study modeled a first batch of lenses from the SLACS survey.

Here the team successfully models most of a second batch, bringing the total sample to forty-five lenses. The average stretch comes out larger than expected, and a good fraction of the lenses show surprisingly strong values even under the most flexible models of the lensing galaxy. Checks against redshift, filters, image quality, and brightness explain none of the big values, leaving the strength of the effect an open puzzle.
arxiv-2512-05150:
Zhenglin Cheng, Peng Sun, Jianguo Li, and Tao Lin present TwinFlow, a training recipe that teaches large generative models to produce images in a single step. Diffusion and flow models need dozens of steps per image, which makes them slow. Existing shortcuts either distill a teacher model through procedures that degrade at very few steps, or add adversarial training with networks, unstable and hungry for memory.

TwinFlow drops both the fixed teacher and the separate adversary, using a self-adversarial flow design instead. On text-to-image tasks it reaches a strong quality score in one evaluation step, beating few-step baselines. The team also retrained a twenty-billion-parameter image model at full scale and turned it into a few-step generator. At a single step it matches the original hundred-step model on two standard benchmarks. That cuts computing cost roughly a hundredfold, with minor quality loss.
arxiv-2512-05450:
Pawel Weichbroth sorts out the messy catalogue of things that go wrong when people use mobile apps. Usability research on apps is plentiful but fragmented: studies vary in method, inputs, and depth, leaving practitioners without a shared map of the problems users actually hit. Weichbroth triangulates — a systematic literature review plus expert interviews, scholarly and practitioner knowledge side by side — to extract the traits that underlie usability issues.

The result is a catalogue of sixteen issue categories with keywords, extended into a taxonomy, plus a three-tier classification linking app, user, and resources. At the app level, issues arise from interface design, efficiency, errors, and operability. At the user level they tax cognition, learning, and memory. At the resource level they stem from network quality and hardware limits. Interface design emerges as the root cause. The paper closes with takeaways for researchers and vendors alike.
arxiv-2512-05550:
Marvin Klinger and six co-authors test rare-earth borates as working materials for magnetic refrigeration below one kelvin. Cooling by adiabatic demagnetization — magnetize a paramagnetic material, let it absorb heat, demagnetize to grow colder — is gaining importance as helium-3 supplies tighten. The classic hydrated salts degrade under heating and vacuum; frustrated rare-earth oxides promise higher entropy density and toughness, and borates are the new candidates under test here.

The team reports the structure, magnetism, and thermodynamics of two barium rare-earth borate families carrying ytterbium or gadolinium. Three of the four materials stay paramagnetic down to the lowest temperatures measured; one gadolinium compound orders just above a tenth of a kelvin. Cooling performance from two kelvin in a strong field is checked against the literature. The results add practical options to a refrigeration technology that low-temperature physics depends on more and more.
arxiv-2512-05650:
Dhorasso Temfack and Jason Wyse work on tracking an epidemic while it unfolds, from noisy and partial case reports. Health officials need estimates of hidden states, like how many people are truly infected, plus the parameters that drive spread. Fully Bayesian methods give both, but the leading algorithm is very slow. It nests one particle filter inside another, which blocks use during a fast moving outbreak.

Their 2025 paper swaps the inner filter for an ensemble Kalman filter, a cheaper approximation. A corrected density estimate keeps the swap from biasing results, and the filter is adapted to the clumpy counts typical of disease reporting. In simulations with known truth, and on United States monkeypox data from 2022, the new method matched the slow one's answers at a fraction of the cost. It rebuilt the epidemic's path and recovered key parameters well. That speed makes careful Bayesian tracking realistic during an actual response.
arxiv-2512-05850:
Haipeng An and five co-authors re-examine a puzzling excess in the world's great dark matter detectors. Three liquid xenon experiments, LZ, PandaX-4T, and XENONnT, have recorded nuclear recoil like events at energies too high for ordinary WIMP scattering to explain. Using a shared framework on public data, the team performs the first combined fit.

Two families of interaction can reproduce the spectrum: speed dependent collisions, and inelastic hits that gain or lose a fixed bite of energy. Local significance reaches about three and a half sigma. A background from double electron capture in xenon has poorly known charge yields. Varying them can move the signal from nothing to the full three and a half sigma. The decisive test will be extending the analysis to still higher recoil energies, where that background should vanish. A discovery claim is only as strong as its murkiest background.
arxiv-2512-05950:
Zalish Mahmud, Anantaa Kotal, and Aritran Piplai fill holes in datasets with a generative adversary that learns what real data looks like. Missing values are everywhere: sensors die and records conflict. Classic fixes assume tidy linear relations and fail on messy reality. Impugan instead trains a conditional generative adversarial network on complete records, learning how missing variables depend on observed ones.

At work, the generator proposes values for the gaps while a discriminator grades them against real data, pushing the fills toward realism. That contest captures bent, multi humped relationships regression cannot express. On benchmarks and on a multi-source integration task, the distance between filled and true data fell by up to about four fifths compared with leading baselines. A second measure of information mismatch fell by about seven tenths. Principled imputation decides whether the final analysis deserves trust.
arxiv-2512-06050:
L. Horoto and F. G. Scholtz propose rebuilding gravity as a genuine force, carried by a physical field, rather than as the geometry of spacetime itself. In Einstein's theory, gravity can be transformed away at a point. Their field strength tensor is the difference between the curved connection and a flat one. That object cannot be removed by any coordinate choice, so in this picture gravity has true physical degrees of freedom. The dynamics follow a Yang-Mills type Lagrangian with an extra scalar tied to the Newtonian potential.

Coupling off, the theory is general relativity; on, it is a gauge theory of gravity. Dark energy and dark matter like effects are also claimed as consequences. Gravity speaking gauge theory could ease the bridge to a quantum description.
arxiv-2512-06250:
Chris Tava asks a plain question about self guided agents: with two ways to move through a maze, when should the agent swap between them? One mode sweeps the maze in a tidy pattern, while the other heads straight for the goal. Fixed swap rules waste time in mazes that do not fit the rule.

Tava lets the agent learn the swap point on its own during each run. It needs only the maze size and the goal spot, not a map of the walls. The agent groups its state by ground covered and distance left, then tests swap points across a mid range of coverage. Across many test mazes, the learned swap beat both single mode agents and a fixed rule, cutting finish times by a clear margin. The work shows that timing a swap can be learned from progress signals alone.
arxiv-2512-06350:
Ozgecan Kocak, Phanish Puranam, and Nghi Truong ask why smart people clash so hard over the risks of artificial intelligence. Rather than count opinions, they pull apart the chains of reasoning behind them: the premises each side leans on, sorted into facts, forecasts, definitions, causal beliefs, and values. Knowing exactly where a chain splits can help policy makers answer the real points of dispute.

They test the method on guest interviews from the Lex Fridman podcast that deal with AI risk. For risks to human survival and to jobs, the guests split mainly over causal beliefs and forecasts of what comes next. For risks to human social bonds, values and definitions carried more weight, such as what counts as a genuine human connection. The team used a panel of language models to parse the talks at scale. The approach can be reused wherever public debates need their bones laid bare.
arxiv-2512-06450:
Mauli Pant, Linda Fernandez, and Indranil Sahoo model where Arctic whales gather, and in what group sizes, from a decade of aerial survey sightings. Their data cover beluga and bowhead whales in United States Arctic waters across ten years of flights. The two species share some waters but answer to different conditions. The authors model them jointly. Each species keeps its own response to the setting, while both share one hidden spatial field for their broad patterns.

Group size enters through a marked point process, so where whales appear and how many gather are read in one frame. The hidden field is built over a mesh that respects the coastline, and a fast approximation method fits the model to the full decade of effort. Results show lasting hotspots shared by both species, alongside clear differences in what draws each.
arxiv-2512-06750:
Weiqi Li and ten co authors unify three jobs that image software usually splits apart: judging an image's quality, restoring it, and enhancing it. The jobs are natural partners. A restorer that knows what damage looks like should repair better, yet most systems treat assessment and repair in isolation. Their model, UARE, is a vision language model that does all three, built to test how far quality judgment can guide repair.

Training comes in two stages. A progressive schedule moves from single distortions to stacked, mixed damage, so the model learns to handle real world mess. Then quality reading and restoration are fine tuned together on interleaved text and image data, tying the judgment signals to the repair goals. Across assessment, restoration, and enhancement tests, the unified model performed strongly, with the quality side measurably lifting the repair side. One model that both critiques and fixes is the authors' point.
arxiv-2512-06950:
Enrico Camporeale tackles a forecasting trap: when rare events matter most, standard training teaches models to please the common cases and neglect the tail. Reweighting losses or inventing extra rare examples can add noise or warp the data. His method, PARIS, instead improves the training set itself by pruning it. A theorem about how models represent data lets him compute, in closed form, exactly how removing one training point would change the validation score.

With a fast updating scheme, PARIS removes unhelpful points one by one without retraining from scratch. The test case comes from space weather, where rare storms carry outsized impact. There, pruning cut the training set by up to three quarters while matching or beating the accuracy of the full set. It also outperformed reweighting, synthetic oversampling, and boosting. Camporeale presents pruning guided by exact deletion math as a clear, cheap route to better rare-event forecasts.
arxiv-2512-07150:
Jonghyun Park and Jong Chul Ye speed up a class of solvers that reconstruct images from partial measurements using generative flow models as priors. Such solvers face a trade-off at practical step counts. Heavy optimization nails the measurements quickly but can slide into unrealistic images, especially in the warped latent spaces of flow models. Pure sampling stays faithful to the prior yet crawls toward measurement agreement.

FlowLPS mixes the two at every step of the reverse process. A few Langevin updates, random kicks guided by the posterior, jitter the current clean estimate toward plausible regions. A local refinement then rapidly enforces the measurements starting from that jittered point. Controlled re-noising steadies the whole path without breaking its coherence. Across five linear imaging problems on two standard photo sets, the balance between fidelity to the measurements and perceptual quality was strong.
arxiv-2512-07450:
Imran Ahsan, Hyunwook Yu, Jinsung Kim, and Mucheol Kim wrote this 2025 paper on privacy in graph neural networks. Such networks learn from linked data, but laws like the GDPR can require them to forget. Proving that data is truly gone is hard, since these models act like black boxes.

The authors propose a checker driven by explanations rather than raw scores. It snapshots the model before and after a deletion request. Shifts in which parts of the graph the model credits then serve as visible evidence. Five measures track those shifts, from leftover attribution to changes in graph structure. The team tests two network types and four forgetting methods on five benchmarks. Full retraining and one deletion method erase nearly all traces. Another method erases only part, and a fourth leaves clear signals behind. The readable evidence, they argue, makes forgetting claims open to audit.
arxiv-2512-07750:
Roozbeh Bostandoost and ten co-authors wrote this 2025 cloud computing paper. Public clouds place virtual machines using pipelines rich in learned models. Separate models predict processor load, memory need, and machine lifetime.

Each prediction can look harmless while quietly shifting the others. Together, those shifts compound and can badly degrade placement quality. No existing tool stress-tests how the models interact as a system. Deterministic attackers cannot capture how the models behave by chance either. The authors build SANJESH, an analyzer built as a two-level search. The outer level hunts for adversarial conditions the models could produce. It searches across what predictions are plausible under distributional uncertainty. The inner level runs the allocator against those predictions. Applied to production traces from the cloud operator, the tool bites. It uncovers scenarios far worse than the operator's own evaluator found. Correlated model drift, the paper shows, is a real risk.
arxiv-2512-08350: Zeev Nutov, a computer scientist who works on network design, posted a short paper on arXiv in December 2025. He studies the Small Cuts Cover problem. The task is to find the cheapest set of edges covering every small cut in a graph. A classic primal dual algorithm was recently shown by Simmons to guarantee an approximation ratio of five. Simmons asked whether that bound is tight. Nutov answers yes. His example makes the ratio between the algorithm solution and the optimum come arbitrarily close to five.
arxiv-2512-08450:
Besm Osman, Ruben Vink, Andrei Jalba, and Maxime Chamberland, researchers in medical computing, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their task is filling the brain cortex volume with a tetrahedral mesh, the grid that biomechanical simulations run on. For cortical simulations, the mesh must preserve exactly how the input surface is connected, or the anatomy is quietly changed.

The trouble is that automatically extracted brain surfaces arrive flawed, full of self intersections, small holes, and broken geometry. Existing meshers, constrained or not, then fail to keep the surface connectivity. The authors develop a new tetrahedralization method that maintains the input connectivity even in the presence of such defects. They also propose a metric that measures how well connectivity is preserved, so methods can be compared honestly. On that metric, their method kept connectivity correctly where existing solutions did not.
arxiv-2512-08750:
A J D Farias Junior and coauthors study vacuum energy in a system where a mass dimension one fermion field, called Elko, interacts with a real scalar field. Both fields are placed between two large parallel plates and must vanish at the plates, a setup used to study the Casimir effect. Distance between the plates sets the scale for the vacuum response.

Using the effective potential method from quantum field theory, the authors compute the vacuum energy density and its first correction from the interaction couplings. They also compute, for each field on its own, the topological mass that arises from the plate conditions and depends on the couplings. The work extends Casimir studies to this less standard fermion type. It shows how boundaries and interactions together reshape vacuum energy and effective mass in a controlled four dimensional setting.
arxiv-2512-08850:
Mohamed Benelmekki and Brahim Boulayat introduce a weaker notion of atomicity for integral domains in factorization theory. A domain is called atomic when every nonzero nonunit element factors into a finite product of irreducible elements. The new notion relaxes that demand in a specific way.

A domain is called sub atomic when every nonunit divisor of an atomic element is itself atomic. The authors study this property and several related factorization properties. They develop the basic theory, give examples, and test how the property behaves under standard constructions. Those constructions include localization, polynomial rings, and a classic composite construction for domains. Results show the sub atomic property is independent of other classical factorization properties. The work identifies a class of domains that sits strictly between atomic and non atomic domains, widening the map of factorization behavior.
arxiv-2512-09250:
Mao Nishino, Martin Bauer, Tom Needham, and Nicolas Charon work on optimal transport, the mathematics of moving mass from one distribution to another at least cost. The dynamic Benamou-Brenier form of the theory follows the moving density over time. An unbalanced version allows mass to be created or destroyed along the way, at a price.

The authors generalize an earlier constrained model. Constraints can now act on the density, the momentum, and the source term together, and they can be equalities or inequalities. Under stated assumptions they prove the resulting problems are well-posed. The paper then builds a numerical pipeline using finite differences and parallel proximal splitting methods that can actually solve them. The framework covers standard balanced and unbalanced transport plus many natural constraints, and the authors show its range on synthetic and real data examples.
arxiv-2512-09750:
Shun Inoue leads a team clarifying where the iron fluorescence line in stellar flares comes from, using a superflare on the RS Canum Venaticorum star UX Arietis. The iron K-alpha line can reveal a flare loop's latitude and size, but only if its origin is known. It could be produced by photoionization from hard X-ray photons, or by collisions from non-thermal electrons. Far-ultraviolet and X-ray observations break the tie.

Japan's Hisaki satellite watched the ultraviolet while NICER on the space station recorded X-rays. The flare released energy in both bands. The ultraviolet emission, a proxy for such activity, peaked an hour and a half before the X-rays. The iron line peaked together with the X-ray maximum instead of the non-thermal peak, supporting the photoionization origin. Calculations using the line's intensity back the conclusion and show the line can recover flare geometry.
arxiv-2512-09850:
Simone Cuonzo and Nina Deliu present Conformal Bandits, a framework that merges conformal prediction with bandit decision making. Bandits are a classic setup for choosing repeatedly among options with unknown rewards. Standard strategies chase low regret but rest on assumptions about distributions or hold only in the long run, and they ignore statistical properties. Conformal prediction instead gives coverage guarantees that hold at finite sample sizes.

The test setting is portfolio allocation, where the rewards of different arms differ by tiny amounts. In that weak separability regime, classic policies are not optimal in finite samples. Tests and the study show the new approach's regret edge, plus coverage at the promised level where a classic method can fail. Adding hidden Markov models to capture regime switching in markets improved the balance between exploring and exploiting, raised risk adjusted returns, and preserved the coverage guarantee.
arxiv-2512-10050:
Christian Millichap and Rolland Trapp classify the symmetries of a family of knots and links built from flat pieces, called flat fully augmented links. The question is which symmetry groups can occur, for the links whose crossing structure is prime in a suitable sense. Their answer is complete: exactly the finite subgroups of the rotation and reflection group of space occur, no more and no fewer. The proof builds a dictionary between symmetries of the link and automorphisms of an associated planar cubic graph.

The same machinery gives a construction kit. For any finite subgroup of that spatial symmetry group, the authors explicitly build infinitely many distinct links in the family whose full symmetry group is exactly the chosen one.
arxiv-2512-10250:
Sicheng Liu, Alexander Fengler, Michael J. Frank, and Matthew T. Harrison prove that a popular shortcut for fitting decision models is unsound in math terms. Drift diffusion models describe choices as evidence accumulating toward a threshold; they anchor computational neuroscience and the math of psychology. When drift varies within and across trials, exact likelihoods are expensive, so teams replace the varying drift with its time average, the time averaged drift approximation. Inference then runs on fast formulas for constant drift models. The authors show this estimator is inconsistent: with infinite data it still does not converge to the true drift.

The proof is by design elementary, set in perhaps the simplest possible case: Brownian motion with piecewise constant drift hitting one boundary. Numerical work shows the approximation misestimates attentional effects and can flip hypothesis test conclusions.
arxiv-2512-10850:
J Socorro and co-authors work out classical solutions for a modified gravity cosmology. Their theory generalises Einstein's by letting the action depend on the Ricci scalar and more, an F(R, ...) family. And they approach it through the Hamiltonian formalism. The test bed is the anisotropic Bianchi type I universe. It expands at different rates along different axes. It is filled with ordinary matter, modelled as a barotropic fluid. In that fluid, pressure is a fixed fraction of density.

Solutions are presented in two gauge choices for the lapse function. And the authors note that several results recover expressions inserted by hand as ansätze when solving Einstein's equations. Vacuum solutions are included for completeness. The paper is classical groundwork: before such theories can be quantised or tested against data, their exact anisotropic solutions and the gauges that make them tractable need to be on the table.
arxiv-2512-10950:
Qitao Zhao and colleagues present E-RayZer, a vision model that learns three dimensional understanding directly from unlabelled images taken from several viewpoints. Earlier self-supervised methods inferred depth and shape only indirectly, which let them take shortcuts. E-RayZer instead rebuilds scenes in explicit three dimensional space during training.

A staged curriculum moves training from easy to hard examples and blends varied data sources without any labels. The model beat its predecessor on pose estimation and matched or passed fully supervised reconstruction systems on some tests. Its learned features also outperformed leading visual pre-training models on downstream three dimensional tasks. The authors offer the approach as a promising path for spatial visual pre-training.
arxiv-2512-11050:
Zu Yan, Kohei Inayoshi, Keijian Chen, and Jingsong Guo study little red dots, a puzzling class of active galactic nuclei found by the James Webb telescope. Their spectra show strong hydrogen features that many read as signs of heavy dust. Yet the expected infrared glow from such dust is barely seen, creating a contradiction.

The authors run radiation transfer calculations through dense, dust free gas around the central black hole. They show that repeated scattering of hydrogen light naturally produces the same line ratios that dust reddening would, once the gas is dense enough. The break and broad lines in the spectrum also become linked, letting them estimate a surprisingly small gas mass nearby. Such a small reservoir suggests these nuclei saw little star formation.
arxiv-2512-11150:
Eddie Landesberg and Manjari Narayan propose a way to trust cheap AI judges when measuring how well language model systems perform. Careful human or expert scoring is expensive, so teams rely on model based judges whose raw scores can rank systems wrongly. Their method, Causal Judge Evaluation, calibrates those cheap scores against a small slice of gold standard judgments.

The calibration can then be applied at scale with valid uncertainty estimates. Crucially, a small audit in each new setting tests whether the calibration still holds, turning an uncheckable assumption into a checkable one. On thousands of chatbot comparison prompts, the method ranked system pairs almost perfectly at a fraction of the full oracle cost. A deliberately adversarial policy failed the audit and was correctly flagged, with the method refusing to report biased numbers.
arxiv-2512-11350:
Tanu Singh, Pranamesh Chakraborty, and Long Truong train a transformer system to spot traffic accidents in surveillance video automatically. Road crashes are a leading cause of death worldwide, and crowded cities generate more footage than human monitors can watch. Older vision methods read space and time poorly and failed to generalise across locations, while good training data were scarce and narrow.

The team first curated a balanced dataset spanning many traffic environments, accident types, and conditions. Their model extracts spatial features from each frame with convolutional layers, then lets a transformer track how those features evolve over time. They also tested several ways of adding motion information, a cue many earlier studies neglected. Combining ordinary video features with optical flow, which tracks pixel movement, worked best and beat the accuracy of general vision language models they compared against.
arxiv-2512-11450:
Chellasamy Jebarathinam writes a short comment correcting a claim about two kinds of quantum strangeness in pairs of qubits. Contextuality means measurement results cannot be explained by pre assigned values that ignore context. Quantum discord is a varied correlation, present even in some unentangled states. An earlier paper proposed a criterion, extending a classic proof, and argued it showed discordant states can be contextual without entanglement.

Jebarathinam shows that this test does not in general imply contextuality at all. It instead detects a distinct nonclassicality of the discordant feature, seen in practice, a notion Jebarathinam and Srikanth recently spelled out. Recast that way, the earlier paper's main conclusion, that quantum correlation cannot simply be equated with the discordant feature, becomes precise rather than wrong. The comment is a useful caution about keeping neighbouring quantum concepts separate.
arxiv-2512-11750:
Ernesto Casablanca and co-authors built LUCID, a tool that certifies the safety of black box systems that learn and wobble. Self driving and health systems pair opaque AI parts with random dynamics, and classic checkers cannot handle that mix. LUCID works from a finite set of sampled transitions alone.

It learns control barrier certificates, safety fences in state space, straight from data. Math tricks place the data in a kernel space with an ambiguity set that guards against unseen behavior, and a Fourier expansion turns a hard problem into a linear one. The team calls it the first tool with measured safety guarantees for such systems. Hard benchmark cases show the approach working in practice.
arxiv-2512-12050:
Michael Neilan, Maxim Olshanskii, and Henry von Wahl design a finite element method for Stokes flow that keeps velocity exactly divergence free. Stokes flow governs slow, syrupy motion. When a mesh does not fit the domain edge, unfitted methods cut through cells, but weak boundary rules often spoil the no compression property.

Their method pairs a Scott-Vogelius element pair on a curved cut mesh with a Nitsche and multiplier scheme for boundary data. A higher order multiplier space restores stability and pressure robustness. The paper proves stability and best order convergence in two dimensions, counting the geometric error from curved fits. Numerical tests confirm the theory.
arxiv-2512-12150:
Chenyun Luo and Hang Yu prove a local existence result for liquid crystal flow in a 2025 math paper. They study the Lin-Liu equations, which describe nematic liquid crystals that flow like a fluid with no viscosity. The fluid has a free surface, held by surface tension, and the work uses moving coordinates.

Energy bounds alone cannot prove such results, since the linearized equations lose symmetry. The authors build a stand-in system that stays close to the true model. It must track both the fluid motion and heat type flows inside, plus the smoothness of the moving edge. Their proof shows solutions exist for a short time near the start.
arxiv-2512-12450:
Sayantani Bhattacharyya, Sukanya Mitra, Shuvayu Roy, and Rajeev Singh study excitation spectra in relativistic fluids in a 2025 paper. When a fluid moves near light speed, its wave modes are computed in its rest frame. Boosting to a moving frame can bring pathologies, and pulling the modes across frames is nontrivial work.

Their framework derives boosted spectra from rest frame mode coefficients alone, skipping the usual boosted polynomial solve. Under a boost, extra solutions can appear that clash with causality; they call these spurious modes. They prove a direct link between mode conservation and causality, tying the count of modes to whether the theory stays physically sound.
arxiv-2512-12750:
Antonio Catao, Lucas Resende, and Paulo Orenstein study robust mean estimators built by shrinkage in a 2025 paper. Estimating a mean that resists outliers matters across statistics. Their class of estimators starts from a base estimate. It then shrinks the weights of sample points far from it. A data driven scaling factor sets the shrink, and a weighting function fades from 1 to 0 with distance.

Under mild assumptions on the weighting function, they prove stronger concentration bounds than the base estimator enjoys, including sub-Gaussian guarantees. Concentration means the estimate piles up tightly near the true mean. The framework unifies several known robust methods in one dimension and extends to multivariate data. Numerical tests show faster concentration even for small samples.
arxiv-2512-12850:
Duc Hoang, Aarush Gupta, and Philip Harris introduce KANELE, a way to run a special kind of neural network on FPGA chips. These chips must answer fast while using little power. The networks they use have learnable spline curves on their edges, which fit well into lookup tables.

KANELE is the first full design flow for putting such networks on FPGAs. It trains the model with pruning and low precision in mind from the start. The team reports speed gains up to 2,700 times over past work on the same task. It also matched or beat other lookup table designs on standard tests.
arxiv-2512-12950:
Lingyi Meng and co-authors tackle mapping legal terms across languages, a task made hard for Chinese and Japanese by shared written forms that carry different meanings. Few standard tools exist for this pair. Mistakes in legal terms can change what a law requires.

Their approach pairs AI agents with human legal experts in one workflow. Agents handle scanning, splitting, alignment, and first-pass term extraction. Experts review the output and apply legal judgment at each stage. The team tested the method on 35 key Chinese statutes with English and Japanese versions. It improved the precision and consistency of term mapping over manual methods alone.
arxiv-2512-13350:
Christian Nicolaisen Hansen, Line Jelver, and Christos Tserkezis study how patterning two-dimensional materials changes their response to light. They shape the materials into ribbon arrays on a surface and into spherical particles. Excitons, bound electron-hole pairs, dominate the optical behavior of these materials.

Using Fourier-Floquet methods for ribbons and Mie theory for spheres, they compute reflection, transmission, and uptake. Two materials anchor the study: hexagonal boron nitride in the UV and tungsten disulfide in visible light. Ribbon arrays showed weak tuning range, since their excitons stay local. Spheres coated with the material mixed better with other modes, offering a stronger platform for tailored light-matter work.
arxiv-2512-13450:
Julien Marche and Gregor Masbaum study signatures of vector spaces that arise in SU2 topological quantum field theory, as a function of a root of unity parameter. Such signatures are numeric invariants tied to surfaces of a given genus. Their asymptotic behavior connects topology with number theory.

For genus two, they prove a scaled signature converges to an explicit limit function along irrational directions. That limit function turns out to be the boundary value of an Eichler integral of a modular form of weight four and level two. Building on this, they propose a transformation law for the signature function, analogous to the classical reciprocity formula for Dedekind sums.
arxiv-2512-13650: Leonard Susskind argues that observers have a special role in de Sitter space, the kind of expanding space tied to cosmic acceleration. His short paper links that need for observers to a spontaneous breakdown of time-reversal symmetry. That symmetry is the idea that the laws should run the same forward and backward in time. When that symmetry breaks on its own, past and future stop being fully alike, and an observer's place in the space gains a clear physical meaning.
arxiv-2512-13950:
Alban Gauthier and co-authors judge how well material traits can be forecast for 3D scenes made with generative image models. Generative tools can now make true-to-life views of a scene that match its geometry. Other SVBRDF networks recover material traits, such as reflectance, from those images, and merging views can build a full texture atlas.

That pipeline faces a coherence problem: single-view predictions may disagree across views and yield mismatched atlases. Generated images and their conditioning signals may also carry extra information photos lack. The authors compare neural architectures and conditioning choices to find designs with high accuracy and coherence. A standard UNet proved competitive with more complex designs, a useful simplification for appearance modeling.
arxiv-2512-14650:
Sharon Mary Tomson and a large team search for gravitational wave memory in pulsar timing array data in a 2025 paper. Memory is a lasting shift left in spacetime after a gravitational wave passes. The main sources for these arrays are supermassive black hole binaries.

The team made the first search for late inspirals and mergers of such binaries using full numerical relativity waveforms that include nonlinear memory. They also searched for generic memory bursts, using kernel density and normalizing flow methods to cut computing cost. They rule out mergers of binaries with chirp mass of ten billion solar masses out to 700 Mpc over 18 years of data, at 95 percent credibility. Generic bursts above a strain of ten to the minus fourteen are also ruled out in the stated windows.
arxiv-2512-14750:
Ying Cui, Dongzhe Zheng, and a large team study a dangerous subtype of clear cell renal cell carcinoma, a common kidney cancer. The subtype, called DCCD, lacks the usual stored lipids and is linked to poor outcomes even when found early. Their 2025 work aims to spot this subtype before surgery, without a tissue sample.

The team linked three levels of evidence: molecular signatures, microscope images of tissue, and CT scans. One model, PathoDCCD, reads cell shapes and tissue patterns, while RadioDCCD reads scan features from the whole tumor and its subregions. Across five groups totaling 1,659 patients, the models matched the molecular subtype and flagged the patients with the worst outcomes. The approach could help doctors judge risk earlier and plan care sooner.
arxiv-2512-15250:
Youssef Ghallab and seven coauthors combine brain and heart signals using foundation models and a deliberately simple fusion. Electrocardiograms and electroencephalograms give complementary views of health and thought, but labeled data that pairs them is scarce, and the signals differ greatly. Their answer is to pretrain a strong encoder for each signal type alone.

They adapt the CBraMod encoder, first built for brain signals, to large scale self supervised pretraining on heart signals, with a dual masking strategy that captures links within and between leads. A matching pretrained encoder serves the brain side. The two representations are simply concatenated, and the classifier learns the cross modal interplay from there. On emotion recognition the system came near state of the art performance. The result argues that good encoders plus plain fusion can beat fancy integration when labels are few.
arxiv-2512-15450:
Gaston Nieuviarts discusses how time and Lorentzian geometry might emerge from a twisted spectral triple in a 2025 proceeding paper. Spectral triples describe geometry through algebra, and almost commutative versions underlie a noncommutative model of particle physics. A long standing problem is that this setup naturally gives a Riemannian, not a Lorentzian, signature.

The paper gathers recent results into one account of a unified algebraic mechanism. A morphism links twisted spectral triples to pseudo Riemannian ones, offering an alternative to Wick rotation. The claim is that the almost commutative structure behind the particle model may itself give rise to Lorentzian geometry from a purely Riemannian start.
arxiv-2512-15750:
Sujoy Majumder, Nabadwip Sarkar, and Debabrata Pramanik study meromorphic solutions of a nonlinear equation in a 2025 paper, dated December 11. The equation links a power of an unknown function, a power of a rational multiple of its derivative, and an exponential term. Such Fermat type equations often admit only very restricted solutions.

The authors examine the equation for all positive whole values of the three exponents. They give full rules for when such solutions can exist and find their possible forms. The results improve earlier work by Tang and Liao and by Han and Lu, both in the existence criteria and in the explicit forms obtained.
arxiv-2512-15850:
Cole Meyer and co authors reveal Callisto's near subsurface heat traits from ALMA data in a 2025 paper. Heat images at varied wavelengths probe varied depths below a surface, exposing makeup and impact history. Six archived ALMA records of Jupiter's moon Callisto, from 2012, sit at unusually short wavelengths for this moon.

Those wavelengths, 0.43 to 0.47 millimeters, sense the upper centimeter or so. The disk averaged heat reading is 133 plus or minus 15 kelvin. A two part inertia mix fits the glow best, matching longer wavelength results. The team also presents unseen Galileo radiometer maps, improving knowledge of Callisto's shallow soil.
arxiv-2512-15950:
Gregory Camilli compares procedures for modeling binary eye tracking data in a 2025 paper. Eye tracking series are correlated over time within a person, and standard logistic mixed models with random effects for persons and items ignore that serial structure. Several fixes exist, and their differences matter for reading research conclusions.

Camilli illustrates three newer approaches. Each avoids using the observed lagged outcome as a predictor. One is an autoregressive model. One is a moving average model from generalized estimating equations. One is a recurrent two state survival model for run length encoded data. Five analyses in total point to unresolved issues in eye tracking analysis. A traditional lag 1 model is included for comparison.
arxiv-2512-16250:
Sanjoy Chowdhury and eight co-authors build a test for talking-head AI in a paper uploaded to arXiv in 2025. Multimodal models that hear and see struggle in multi-speaker scenes, where they must track who speaks, keep roles straight, and ground events over time. Such skills matter for meeting analytics and conversational video assistants.

Their benchmark, AMUSE, grades models in zero-shot, guided, and agentic modes across six task families, including locating speakers in space and time and summarizing dialogues. Current models showed weak multi-speaker reasoning in every mode. The companion framework, RAFT, aligns models with reward optimization and self-evaluation while updating few parameters. It raised benchmark accuracy by up to 39.52 percent in relative terms. Together, the tools give labs a practical way to measure and improve agentic audio-visual understanding.
arxiv-2512-16450:
Mathew Thomas Arun and Ritik Pal teach a neural network the strong force in a paper shared on arXiv in 2025. Holographic QCD models the strong interaction through a five-dimensional gravity dual, where meson masses encode the hidden geometry and fields. Recovering those ingredients from measured masses is an inverse problem.

The network trains on the masses of the rho, a1, a2, and f0 mesons and their excitations, solving a discretized wave equation in the fifth dimension. It reconstructs confining potentials, a metric, and a dilaton profile that obeys the null energy condition, with an infrared dilaton far steeper than the usual quadratic guess. The symmetry-breaking potential comes out with cubic and quartic coefficients near minus 4 and 9. Using the learned ingredients, the model predicts the pion mass and spectrum accurately. Code and trained models are public.
arxiv-2512-16850:
Can Urgun and Mark Whitmeyer study real-time persuasion, where a sender shapes what a receiver learns and picks when to stop sharing. The receiver delays a decision while waiting, at a rising time cost, and the sender controls both signal clarity and the stop time.

One might expect the sender to blur the signal at times. The authors show that, under natural regularity terms, full openness is always best. The sender keeps the signal fully clear throughout and persuades only by choosing when to stop. That clean result simplifies a rich control problem: timing alone does all the work, and garbling the signal never pays.
arxiv-2512-17350:
Chenming Zhou and five co-authors find a simple trick that helps detectors spot AI-made images from generators they have never seen. Detectors often cheat: they latch onto meaning cues tied to one generator's style, then fail on the next model. The real tells sit in fine, high-frequency traces left by the making process itself.

Before detection, the team remaps pixel values across the image. That shuffle breaks the easy meaning cues, so the detector must learn the deeper traces instead. Across both GAN and diffusion generators, the shuffle lifted the cross-generator scores of leading detectors by a wide margin. Follow-up checks confirmed the gain came from blocking the shortcut, not from extra data or a bigger model.
arxiv-2512-17550:
Qian Hu and coauthors reanalyze GW231123, a gravitational wave signal read as a merger of two black holes. Their total mass comes to 190 to 265 solar masses, the heaviest merger yet detected. Waveform models of the signal disagree about the source, and the paper asks whether the data hide something more complex.

The team finds that a model with two overlapping signals fits far better, with Bayes factors around 100 to 10,000 in its favor. That reading also largely removes the clashes between waveform models. They also check the earlier event GW190521 and find no sign of the same effect there. The work warns that the loudest, heaviest signals may blend two events into one, which would change how their masses and spins are read.
arxiv-2512-17950:
Zhao Song, Song Yue, and Jiahao Zhang take on a new chore for authors at the ICLR 2026 meeting. Each paper must name one of its own authors as a reviewer, and a paper whose named reviewer shirks the job is rejected on sight. With 99 papers, one group asked which coauthor each paper should name to cut the total risk.

The basic version of the problem, lowering the expected count of rejected papers, falls to a simple greedy rule. Tougher versions cap how many papers may name the same person, guarding against one bad pick sinking many papers. Those versions link to classic flow and linear methods. The paper is the first formal study of such naming rules.
arxiv-2512-18350:
Souptik Chakraborty and Utsab Sarkar study a hard problem in the math of partial differential equations. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, concerns the fractional Hardy-Sobolev inequality. This bound helps judge the energy of waves and fields that spread in a non-local way. They ask how stable its best solutions, called bubbles, remain when several bubbles sit together.

The authors prove sharp stability in low dimensions. When a function's energy is close to that of several bubbles combined, the gap in the equation controls the distance to the true multi-bubble shape. The exact bubble layout can then be recovered. Their proof mixes localization, weighted estimates, and a spectral gap argument. A matching counterexample shows the rate they found cannot be improved.
arxiv-2512-18850:
Feeza Khan Khanzada and Jaerock Kwon teach a self-driving agent to explore before it is ever given a goal. Model-based reinforcement learning promises cheaper training through a learned world model, but it still leans on hand-designed rewards that break under change. Their system, InDRiVE, posted to arXiv in December 2025, pretrains in the CARLA simulator with no task reward at all.

Curiosity comes from disagreement: an ensemble of latent models votes, and where they disagree, the agent goes to learn. An imagination-based actor-critic turns that drive into an exploration policy inside the world model. Frozen and dropped into unseen towns, the policy transfers zero-shot with strong robustness. Brief fine-tuning then yields lane following and collision avoidance that survive town changes. The study makes intrinsic disagreement a practical pretraining signal for reusable driving models.
arxiv-2512-19050:
Amir Babak Aazami defines a higher version of self-duality for curved spaces whose dimension is a multiple of four. He builds the definition from a trace-free part of Thorpe's middle curvature operator. Self-duality in four dimensions is a classic tool in geometry, and his aim is a sound analogue in higher dimensions.

Aazami shows that metrics with the new property minimize a natural conformal energy. Their Bach tensor comes out symmetric, trace-free, and divergence-free, which answers a question posed by Kastor. He also gives a signed-square formula for the top Pontryagin density, and notes compact examples such as the Fubini-Study metric.
arxiv-2512-19250:
Prathamesh Devadiga tests whether small language models can act as compiler experts that parallelize code on their own. Classic auto-parallelizers lean on rigid rules and miss chances on mixed modern hardware. Small models, near one billion parameters, are cheap enough to sit inside a build pipeline.

Three models, Gemma 3, Llama 3.2, and Qwen 2.5, were tried with six reasoning strategies on eleven real kernels from science, graphs, and machine learning. Nearly four hundred runs averaged close to a sevenfold speedup, with convolution peaking far higher. Output was checked with sanitizers and across compilers and hardware. The results argue that small models reason well about parallel code.
arxiv-2512-19450:
Leo D'Amato, Davide Nuzzi, Alberto Testolin, and Ivilin Peev Stoianov watch number sense grow inside unsupervised generative models. A feel for how many items a scene holds underpins later math learning. Rate-distortion theory, which prices information under tight capacity, gives the authors their frame for when such a sense should appear.

Beta-variational autoencoders trained on synthetic scenes with varying item counts were tested on estimation, discrimination, and fresh stimuli. As encoding capacity rose, numerosity skill and clean separation from other visual traits grew by a power law. At high capacity the model formed a sturdy number code on its own, matching the theory's forecast.
arxiv-2512-20050:
Sourav Duari and three co-authors compute how a chiral quark-gluon plasma conducts color charge as things change in time. They use linear response theory at finite heat and density. The conductivity comes from the one-loop gluon self-energy. A chiral plasma breaks parity and charge-parity in ways a plain plasma does not. That adds a new part to the conductivity tensor. It sits beside the usual parts that run along and across the flow.

They name that new part the chiral chromomagnetic conductivity. The usual parts shift only a bit between chiral and plain plasmas, in their spectral forms. The static limit of the new part is apart. It does not depend on the medium's traits at all. The authors read that as a sign of a topological nature.
arxiv-2512-20350:
Maximilian Witte, Johannes Meuer, Étienne Plésiat, and Christopher Kadow redesign the Transformer for Earth system science. Standard attention works in a learned latent space, which scrambles the real fields climate models care about. Their Field-Space design computes attention directly in the real domain, on the sphere itself.

Every in-between state stays a continuous field, so internal states remain readable and science rules can be enforced. A fixed multi-scale split feeds structure-preserving warps of the input, avoiding the wobble of single-scale vision Transformers. On global temperature super-resolution over a HEALPix grid, the model converges faster and more stably than vision Transformer and U-Net benchmarks. It does so with far fewer parameters.
arxiv-2512-20550:
Vinayak Regmi and Christos Mousas let users author stories by arranging a scene. In their system, you drag agents and objects onto a stage; each entity arrives with semantic metadata about its identity, role, and possible interactions. The scene is serialized into plain language and handed to a large language model.

The model returns a structured string encoding who does what, when, and how. A custom parser turns that string into coordinated behaviours, animations, and interaction modules in the virtual scene. The system supports dynamic object manipulation and varied interaction types, aimed at rapid prototyping of agent narratives. Four lightweight language models were benchmarked across complexity scenarios. Response times and consistency measurements show models reliably translate scene descriptions into executable behaviour.
arxiv-2512-20650:
Esmail Gumaan lets each token choose its own attention bargain. Full multi-head attention gives the best quality but inflates the key-value cache at inference. Multi-query and grouped-query attention shrink the cache by sharing keys and values, usually at some quality cost. A static choice forces one compromise on every token.

Mixture of Attention Schemes routes dynamically instead: a learned router picks among the three schemes per token. On WikiText-2, dynamic routing edges out a static mixture of the same schemes and stays competitive with the full multi-head benchmark. The architecture promises conditional compute savings, spending memory only where the router judges it worthwhile. For deployment-minded model designers, per-token attention choice is a new dial to turn.
arxiv-2512-21150:
Yuk-Kwan Wong, Sai-Kit Yeung, and seven co-authors give marine biology the benchmark it needs for automated surveys. ORCA gathers 14,647 images covering 478 marine species, annotated with more than forty-two thousand bounding boxes and over twenty-two thousand expert-verified captions that describe each animal's morphology in words. The dataset is built to align the field's real difficulties, look-alike species, cluttered scenes, scarce examples, with standard computer-vision tasks.

Eighteen state-of-the-art models are evaluated on closed-set and open-vocabulary detection, instance captioning, and visual grounding. Performance gaps expose exactly where general models fail underwater: species diversity, morphological overlap between relatives, and domain demands no land-based dataset teaches. Conservation programs that want scalable, automatic monitoring of ecosystems gain both training material and an honest measure of readiness.
arxiv-2512-21350:
Shreehari Anand Bodas, Harsha Honnappa, Michel Mandjes, and Liron Ravner study how a service provider should set prices when customers can walk away. Their model is a single-server queue in which the provider adjusts the price over time to maximize expected revenue per unit of time. Customers who see heavy congestion may balk, meaning they choose not to join the queue at all.

The proposed pricing method is a stochastic gradient descent algorithm, which nudges the price up or down based on observed results. A key difficulty is that the provider can only observe the customers who actually arrive, not those who balked. The authors develop an infinitesimal perturbation analysis procedure that estimates the true arrival rate from that partial information. Feeding the estimate into the algorithm, they prove it settles at the revenue-maximizing price under mild conditions. The work links queueing theory with online learning for pricing.
arxiv-2512-21450:
Lei Zhao, Lei Huang, and their co-authors present RLLaVA, a software framework for training vision-language assistants with reinforcement learning. Vision-language models answer questions about images, and reinforcement learning can sharpen them. Existing training code often tangles algorithm, model, and computing setup, which makes new ideas hard to test.

RLLaVA separates the reinforcement learning logic from the model architecture and from distributed execution, and states the training task as a Markov decision process. Researchers can plug in many learning methods and many vision-language models while swapping the underlying training and inference engines. The framework is efficient enough to train models of one to seven billion parameters on common graphics cards. A four-billion-parameter model trains end to end on a single twenty-four-gigabyte card. Experiments on multimodal and agentic tasks show steady gains over the base models.
arxiv-2512-21650:
Xiao Liu, Junchen Jin, Yanjie Zhao, and Zhixuan Xing propose Physic-HM, a system for detecting anomalies in multimodal data, with robotic welding as the application. Process data such as video, audio, and sensor readings cause the final result, captured in post-weld images. Existing methods treat these streams as symmetric feature sources, ignoring that one-way physical logic.

The authors call that flaw process-logic blindness, and they add the missing structure as an inductive bias. Sensor signals guide the extraction of audio-visual features through a modulation mechanism, so process context is not drowned out by video. An architecture enforces the process-to-result direction and flags anomalies that break it. On the Weld-4M benchmark the system reached a leading detection score of about ninety-one percent. The work argues that respecting how a process generates its outputs is a powerful prior for smart factories.
arxiv-2512-21850:
Jin-Yu Ni, Liang-Jian Zou, and their co-authors find a new kind of topological phase transition for magnons, the wave-like excitations of a magnet, in a honeycomb ferromagnet. Real magnetic materials host several anisotropic exchange interactions at once, thanks to their crystal and orbital symmetries. Two of them matter here: the Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interaction and the pseudo-dipolar interaction.

Playing these interactions against each other closes and reopens the magnon bulk gap, and the reopening comes with inverted chirality, making the transition chirality-selective. The band inversion happens at the two valley points of the honeycomb Brillouin zone, which the authors read as a reversal of a magnon valley degree of freedom. A measurable consequence is a sign change in the magnon thermal Hall conductivity. The effect should be realizable in materials with strong spin-orbit coupling, such as iridates and ruthenates.
arxiv-2512-22350:
Jinyu Dai, Benjamin Riley, Qi Sun, Debayan Mitra, and Tanya Zelevinsky report the first 3D magneto-optical trap of a metal hydride molecule, calcium hydride. Trapping molecules this way opens precision readings, but molecules leak into untrapped vibrational states as they scatter light. The team scattered about ten thousand photons per molecule while covering vibrational losses up to the second excited level.

A white-light slowing technique brought the molecular beam nearly to rest, and a radio-frequency trap then captured about 230 molecules at below one millikelvin. Beam source limits and predissociation capped the number. The authors note that same predissociative loss could be turned into a tool, splitting the molecule in a controlled way to optically trap hydrogen atoms for precision spectroscopy.
arxiv-2512-22450:
Misao Sasaki and Jianing Wang show how gravitational waves could reveal the leftovers of tiny primordial black holes. Their scenario starts with black holes lighter than ten million grams, born just after inflation, which evaporate and reheat the universe before nucleosynthesis but leave Planck-mass remnants behind. Those relics could make up part or all of today's dark matter, if they exist.

The key observation is that the number density of the relics can be read directly from the peak positions of gravitational waves induced by the holes' uneven distribution. The peak frequency scales with the relic fraction of dark matter, and the peak amplitude encodes the initial abundance. For plausible densities and abundances, the signal may be large enough for planned gravitational wave tests to detect.
arxiv-2512-22750:
Jiachen Jin, Kangkang Deng, and Hongxia Wang design an optimization algorithm for problems posed on curved spaces, known as Riemannian manifolds. The objective there mixes a smooth random part with a nonsmooth regularizer. Splitting methods handle such sums well in flat settings, but existing curved-space versions were mostly deterministic, and random versions needed restrictive assumptions.

Their method, called MARS-ADMM, pairs a variance-reduced estimator for the random part with a prediction-correction update for the nonsmooth part, all in a single loop. Each step needs only two proximal updates, one curved-space gradient, and a constant number of random samples. The authors prove it reaches an approximate KKT point with fewer oracle calls than earlier stochastic methods, matching the best deterministic rates. Tests on two problem families show the method performs well in practice.
arxiv-2512-23350:
Hemant Prasad and co-authors fine-tune how the NuWro event generator simulates neutrino scattering inside atomic nuclei. When a neutrino knocks a nucleon out of a nucleus, the escaping particles re-interact on their way out, and these final state interactions distort what detectors see. Getting their strength right is essential for oscillation experiments that use NuWro to interpret data.

The team used recent MINERvA measurements of transverse kinematic variables on four targets, carbon, oxygen, iron, and lead, to recalibrate the model. They also built an event reweighting tool so future analyses can adjust the interaction strength without regenerating events. The data demand stronger nucleon reinteractions than previously assumed, though the new strength still sits inside the uncertainty band from proton transparency studies. The authors flag the shift as significant for both experimental analyses and theory work that relies on NuWro.
arxiv-2512-23450:
Yuanchao Lou, Takaaki Nomura, Xinran Xu, and Kei Yagyu test whether two-Higgs-doublet models survive once an extra gauge symmetry is added. The added symmetry blocks flavor-changing neutral currents, a long-standing problem for such models. It also forces the new particles, an extra gauge boson and heavier Higgs bosons, to stay below roughly a teraelectronvolt.

In the simplest version, Higgs bosons would decay into pairs of the new boson and then into four leptons, a signal the LHC has already searched for. The authors find that minimal setup excluded by current data. Adding a pair of vector-like fermions gives the new boson a dark decay route instead, and it can double as dark matter.
