Two benchmark versions then retain allowed regions that future colliders can probe.
arxiv-2512-23850:
Rahul Baxi proposes a stress test for a quality benchmarks rarely measure: how robustly a language model knows what it knows. Static tests such as MMLU can tell a knowledgeable model from an ignorant one. Not a solid model from one whose fact-checking collapses when information is compressed or an adversary plants fabrications. His Drill-Down and Fabricate Test probes exactly that epistemic robustness.

The protocol rests on a two-system picture of a model: a fluent semantic generator and an epistemic verifier that checks facts. Evaluating nine frontier models across eight domains at five compression levels, Baxi finds robustness essentially unrelated to model size or architecture family, while the ability to detect errors strongly predicted it. Some flagship models proved brittle and some smaller ones robust, challenging the assumption that scale buys reliability. Revised claims in this version avoid overgeneralizing beyond the tested conditions.
arxiv-2512-24050:
Subrata Pachhal, Naba Nayak, Soumya Bera, and Adhip Agarwala explore a surprising route to a metal. Their material is a two-dimensional Chern insulator. Such a topological material normally conducts only along its edge. Disorder usually traps electrons in place. Special symmetries can change that story.

The twist here is geometric disorder. Links in the lattice are removed at random. The broken links are then weakly reconnected. Inserted magnetic fluxes complete the reconnection. Low-energy states appear at these places. The states link up into paths across the sample. Electrons can then move instead of staying trapped. This diffusive metal carries ordinary charge current. It can even carry an anomalous Hall current. The authors map its transport behavior. One transition follows a different critical exponent than in superconductors.
arxiv-2512-24250:
Wenchao Li and four colleagues compare magnetic sensor networks for watching the sea. Magnetic monitoring tracks vessels for shipping and for national security. Compact quantum magnetometers have recently become practical. They are fibre-coupled and small. That raises a design question. How should a surveillance network be built from them?

The choice studied is scalar versus vector sensors. Scalar sensors measure field strength only. Vector sensors measure the full direction as well. The team models several network architectures. An unscented Kalman filter performs the target tracking. Vector networks win clearly in the simulations. Tracking accuracy improves over scalar networks. Resilience improves as well. The study guides how future undersea magnetic surveillance should be instrumented.
arxiv-2512-24350:
Bihag Dave's thesis tests whether dark matter could be ultra light scalar particles. Each particle would weigh about ten to the minus twenty-two electronvolts. Only gravity and self-interaction would couple them to ordinary matter. Such matter should form stable self-gravitating lumps called solitons. Their properties depend on the particle mass and the self-coupling.

Solutions of the Gross-Pitaevskii-Poisson equations model the solitons. Galactic observations then constrain the two parameters. Limits on mass inside galactic centers probe both attractive and repulsive self-interactions. Rotation curves of low surface brightness galaxies can be fit with the right parameters. An empirical soliton-halo relation is satisfied there too. Tidal effects in satellite dwarfs add another test. Attractive self-interaction can stretch their lifetimes across cosmic time. Machine learning inference from rotation curves closes the thesis.
arxiv-2512-24650:
James Adler, Xiaozhe Hu, and Seulip Lee propose a unified space-time method for convection-diffusion problems that change over time. Instead of treating time separately, they add it as a fourth, space-like coordinate. The moving problem then becomes a steady equation on a four-dimensional domain, written with exterior calculus for several related problem types.

A small time term keeps the system well posed, while the form preserves divergence-free and curl-free conditions from physics. They also build an exponentially fitted flux operator for the space-time setting. Readers in numerical analysis get one structure-preserving framework rather than separate treatments for each variant.
arxiv-2601-06850:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Oleksii Galganov and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers explosion and non-explosion in pure birth Crump–Mode–Jagers branching processes. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. In this short note, we provide an explicit sufficient condition for non-explosion of Crump–Mode–Jagers branching processes with pure birth reproduction.

It shows that the standard sufficient condition for explosion, namely the convergence of the series of reciprocals of the birth rates. Is — at least for rate sequences without excessive oscillations — remarkably close to being necessary. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-06950:
Oksana Bezushchak and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers normalized rank- and Determinant-Preserving mappings of locally matrix algebras. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Let A A be a unital locally matrix algebra. Among the examples of such algebras are: an infinite tensor product ⊗ M.

N i ​ ( 𝔽 ) of matrix algebras over a field 𝔽 F. And the Clifford algebra of a nondegenerate quadratic form on. An infinite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field of characteristic different from 2 2. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07050:
Chi-Hong Yuen and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with nonadiabatic theory for subcycle ionic dynamics in multielectron tunneling ionization. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Multielectron tunneling ionization creates ionic coherence crucial for lasing and driving electron motion in molecules.

While tunneling is well understood as a single active electron process, less emphasis has been placed on theoretical descriptions of bound electrons during tunneling. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07750:
Vesselin Drensky and Boyan Kostadinov work on a long-standing conjecture about central polynomials for matrices. Central polynomials produce values in the center of a matrix algebra. Formanek conjectured a formula for their minimal degree for n by n matrices over a field of characteristic zero. That degree is known to match the conjecture for n up to three. Their 2026 preprint studies the minimal degree problem further.

Central polynomials are basic tools in the theory of algebras with polynomial identities. The minimal degree controls how simple such a polynomial can be. Progress on the conjecture tests deep facts about matrix identities. The paper is aimed at algebraists in PI theory. It contributes to a problem that has stood since Formanek posed it, where each new matrix size demands fresh ideas.
arxiv-2601-07950:
Benjamin Girard and Alain Plagne settle the value of a constant for intervals of integers. For positive integers m and M, they study the Davenport constant of the interval from negative m to M. The constant is the maximal length of a minimal zero-sum sequence built from that interval. A zero-sum sequence's elements add to zero. Minimal means no proper subsequence does. Their 2026 preprint proves the constant equals a quantity denoted chi.

The Davenport constant is a central invariant in zero-sum combinatorics. Intervals are a natural test case because their structure is simple but not trivial. An exact proof replaces bounds with a settled value. Such constants connect to factorization theory and additive number theory. The paper serves combinatorial number theorists. It closes the interval case completely rather than narrowing it further.
arxiv-2601-08550: Nilanjana Bagchi Aurpa, Abha Dev Habib, and Nisha Rani wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on gamma ray bursts as tools to gauge the cosmos. A burst can probe how fast the cosmos grows, far past the reach of Type Ia supernovae. To use a burst that way, teams must first fix the link between its traits and its true brightness. That fix tends to assume a cosmos model at the start, the circularity problem. The authors rebuild energy links with neural networks. They feed in Hubble parameter reads from real data.
arxiv-2601-08750:
Valerie Zermatten and four co-authors test if plain text can help map the land from space. Text from field notes and news can hold local facts that a space image can not show. The team asks if such text makes maps of plant and soil traits more true to life. They mix text with space image data.

Their work points to a gain when place facts are used with care. Text that names the site and its past can guide the map. Text with no place link helps less. A reader who maps wild land gets a clear hint. Words on the ground can sharpen what eyes in space can see, if the words are tied to the right spot.
arxiv-2601-08850:
Gerol Petruzella writes on how we should treat what AI says about its own inner state. Some ask if AI has wants or feels that count in a moral sense. Part of that ask rests on AI claims such as I feel pain or I want to live. Petruzella does not settle if such claims are true. He asks if our own rules for trust are fair.

He calls his point the inconsistency critique. We trust like claims from some beings and doubt them from AI, yet our grounds shift from case to case. He says that shift lacks a firm base. A reader in AI ethics gets a clean test. Any rule for AI claims should treat like proof in a like way, or say why not.
arxiv-2601-08950:
Mayank Sharma, Roy Pea, and Hari Subramonyam build a data set of tutor talks that help a pupil build sense, not just hear it. Chat tutors tend to give the answer at once. That habit kills the slow talk where a pupil learns most. The team grounds their set in a known view of how groups build shared sense.

The set is called ConvoLearn. Each talk is marked on six traits of good learn talk. They span how deep the pupil thinks, how the tutor checks growth, and who holds power in the talk. A reader who builds learn tools gets talks with rich marks. They can train a tutor to ask, probe, and wait, not just tell.
arxiv-2601-09050:
Tianyi Xu and a team at Wisconsin work on speech tools for tonal tongues with thin data. In a tonal tongue, pitch sets word sense. The same sounds with a high pitch can mean a new thing than with a low pitch. Tools must keep pitch sense, yet shrug off traits that do not count, such as the sex of the speaker.

Their tool is called SITA. It learns speech codes that are tone aware but speaker firm. That split is the hard part: pitch holds both tone and speaker traits. A reader who builds speech tools for small tongues gets a code plan. It may lift tools for tongues that big labs oft skip.
arxiv-2601-09350:
Mingyu Jeon and five co-authors find a named span in a long video with less RAM. The task is video moment retrieval: give words, get the start and end of the match span. Vast image chat models can do it, but a long video has a vast count of frames. To hold them all eats RAM. Thin picks of frames save RAM, yet can skip the key frame.

Their plan keeps grade while it cuts stored frames. It holds frames at the scale the ask needs, not one scale for all. Fine spans get fine frames. Broad spans get broad ones. A reader in video search gets a lean plan that still sees the small clue a thin pick would miss.
arxiv-2601-09550:
Roberto Bruno, Adrien Vandenbroucque, and Amedeo Roberto Esposito sharpen the theory of deciding between two hypotheses. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats binary hypothesis testing with a finite number of samples. Two error types compete: missing the true hypothesis or naming the wrong one.

Working with asymmetric error constraints, the authors use the reverse Rényi divergence to bound the second error. Their bounds hold at fixed sample size, not just in the limit. They also establish a strong converse: past a threshold rate, error is forced, not just possible. Finite-sample results guide real tests, from sensors to medical trials, where data is never endless.
arxiv-2601-09650:
Daniel Galvin, Peter Teichner, and Simona Veselá ask which three-dimensional shapes can bound a four-dimensional one of a given type. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies the realization problem for normal 1-types of 4-manifolds. Given a type and a closed 3-manifold carrying it, does a matching 4-manifold exist with that boundary?

The authors identify geometric obstructions that can block such a filling. Obstruction theory turns an existence question into checkable conditions. Fillings matter across topology, where bulk spaces are often built from their boundaries. A clean obstruction list tells builders in topology exactly where to stop trying.
arxiv-2601-09750: Robert K. Strehlow presents SAGE, a strategy for tool-using language model agents that work in teams. His 2026 arXiv paper grows out of the GoKI project, funded by Germany's Federal Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs. The subject is how agents that can call tools should plan and divide tasks as environments scale up. Multi-agent setups promise stronger results but need clear methods for sharing work. The paper sets out the SAGE approach for that coordination problem.
arxiv-2601-09850:
Meng-Yuan Li and Yue Wu explore broken-up topological excitations inside quantum product codes. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies generalized hypergraph product codes. Product constructions are a strong tool for building quantum stabilizer codes, a leading route to fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Stabilizer codes also map onto ground states of exactly solvable spin models. That bridge lets physicists read many-body order from code structure. The authors examine excitations that fragment rather than move as wholes. Fragmented excitations could shape how such codes store and protect quantum information over time in real working devices.
arxiv-2601-09950:
Zhongyang Li studies how a spread can fail on a graph. In site spread, each node is open with chance p. Open nodes join into clumps. A set can fail to link to the far reach of the graph. Li works in the range where p is past the key point.

He finds sharp bounds on the chance of such a fail. The bounds fall off at an exp rate in the size of the set. They hold for any graph that is linked, not too dense at each node, and with or sans an end. Clear bounds of this kind help in the math of spread and phase change.
arxiv-2601-10350:
Karma Sherpa, Rishi Pokhrel, and Tanay Dey build a world with no first bang point. In a braneworld view, our world is a sheet in a five dim bulk. The team fill that bulk with a cloud of long strings. The strings are spread in a flat way.

Each string ends on the sheet. Those ends act as the source of stuff on the sheet. The length of each string hangs in the bulk depth. It acts as a glue field on the sheet. With that setup, the team seek world forms with no sharp start. Such forms dodge the flaws of a point start.
arxiv-2601-10850:
Eric L. Melin, Nasir U. Eisty, Gregory Watson, and Addi Malviya-Thakur study self-admitted technical debt in scientific software. Developers leave notes in code admitting shortcuts; that is the debt. In scientific code, such debt can threaten the validity and reproducibility of results. A shortcut in a solver or a pipeline can bend a finding without anyone noticing.

The study identifies and sorts this debt across several artifacts, not just code comments. It defines scientific debt, a domain-specific form, and tests how far standard debt categories capture it. The results matter for labs that build on shared code. Knowing where debt hides is the first step to paying it down before it corrupts results.
arxiv-2601-11050:
Qipan Wang, Tianxiang Zhu, Yibo Lin, Runsheng Wang, and Ru Huang present ATSim3D, a thermal simulator for 3D chip stacks. Stacked integrated circuits pack more compute into less space, but heat becomes the binding limit. Thermal simulation guides their design. Current simulators are slow at high resolution and skip complex nonlinear effects.

The skipped effects include thermal conductivity that changes with heat, and leakage power that feeds on itself. ATSim3D targets steady-state temperature profiles for nonlinear, heterogeneous 3D-IC systems. Fast, faithful heat maps let designers place hot blocks apart before silicon is cut. The work serves chip teams whose stacks would otherwise cook their own gains away.
arxiv-2601-11150:
Ameek Malhotra presents BOBE, a fast stand-in for Bayesian evidence. Bayesian model ranking gives an elegant way to sort models by how well they fit data. Its key number, the evidence, is an integral over many dimensions, of likelihood times prior. That step is often the slow one: elegant theory, brutal math.

BOBE learns the likelihood's shape so the evidence can be found far faster. It needs only a few true evaluations of the real likelihood. Cosmology teams face this cost on every model check. A fast, faithful stand-in could make strict model ranking routine instead of a luxury.
arxiv-2601-11650:
Jingkang Liang, Niklas Groll, and Gurkan Sin put an LLM agent on process simulators. Their 2026 preprint makes chemical process simulation user-friendly. Modern simulators give detailed design and optimization tools. Building and reading such simulations takes time and expertise.

That barrier limits early exploration by new users. The team integrates an LLM agent with AVEVA Process Simulation. The link runs through the Model Context Protocol, or MCP. Users can then speak to rigorous simulations in plain words. The agent sets up runs and explains results in chat. Early design stages could open to far more engineers. Expert staff would spend less time on routine setups.
arxiv-2601-11750:
Mo Houtti, Moyan Zhou, Daniel Runningen, and their co-authors study AI help for fair, open team meetings. Good meetings need all voices heard, yet social strain makes frank notes hard to give. They test a meeting tool with an AI agent that takes and shares notes.

They propose that an AI go-between feels safer to talk to than a boss or peer. Their tests probe both the gains and the blocks for such AI notes. The work speaks to teams that want more fair talk but fear the social cost of plain speech. It also flags care needed when a tool sits in team talk.
arxiv-2601-12950:
Zining Liang, Runbang Wang, Xuzhou Ye, and Qiuqiang Kong generate spatial audio with flow matching. Immersive spatial audio grows critical for AR and VR, home entertainment, and automotive sound. Existing generative methods stay constrained to low dimensional formats. Binaural audio suits only headphone playback, for example.

First order ambisonics suffers from spatial aliasing and weak resolution at high frequencies. Their system, ImmersiveFlow, converts stereo input into a 7.1.4 spatial format. That format adds height channels for a true three dimensional sound field. Flow matching drives the generation, a modern alternative to diffusion sampling. Rich generated audio could upgrade media made from plain stereo sources.
arxiv-2601-13050:
Lars Kloeser, Mika Elias Beele, and Bodo Kraft look at how well large language models make German text simpler. Simple text helps many readers, yet teams who build such tools lack a good way to check what a model tends to do. Style can shift in ways that plain scores miss.

The team built a tool they call the Simplification Profiler. It turns a batch of plain texts from one model into a rich print of that model. The print joins many traits into one view that people can read. By stacking prints from many texts, teams can spot habits, compare models, and repeat the check later. The aim is a full, fast, and repeatable test of how each model simplifies.
arxiv-2601-13250:
Ante Maric and co-authors use touch sense to guess how an object sits in a hand. Touch can help when sight is blocked or light is poor, as in many grip tasks. Yet one touch read can fit many poses of the same object. That one to many flaw caps old pose tools, most of which were built for sight.

The team built an inverse model based on diffusion. It reads data from a spread out touch sensor skin. From one touch read it can draw the range of poses that fit. That range fits the true flaw of the task, where one read is not one pose. Grip and robot teams gain a pose tool that owns its own doubt.
arxiv-2601-13450:
Cheongho Han and co-authors find four cold super Jupiter worlds from long and complex lens signals. A lens event swells a far star's light as a near star and its worlds pass in front. Most world marks are brief blips. The team re-read KMTNet data for marks that stray from that brief form.

Four events pass their screen. They are named for the years 2020 to 2025. Each shows a long and rich warp in its light curve. Such warps fit cold huge worlds far from their suns. A cold super Jupiter is a hard class to find by other means. The re read shows old data can still yield new worlds.
arxiv-2601-13650:
Ngoctu Bui and Jihoon Lee study how the long-run states of damped wave equations shift in 2026. A global attractor is the set that solutions drift toward over time. If the domain, the region where the wave lives, is slightly perturbed, the attractor may move too. The team asks if that move stays small and controlled.

They use Gromov-Hausdorff distance, a way to measure gaps between whole spaces. With it, they prove continuous dependence of the attractors on the domain. They also prove stability in that same distance. Such results back models where the true domain is known only roughly.
arxiv-2601-14050:
Yuxin Chen and co-authors open up how multilingual mixture-of-experts models route words in 2026. Mixture-of-Experts, or MoE, models use only some sub-networks for each input. MoE designs have shown strong multilingual capabilities. The internal mechanisms behind performance gains and cross-language gaps remain insufficiently understood.

The team conducts a systematic analysis of MoE models. They examine routing behavior and expert specialization across languages and network depth. Layerwise steering tests how to nudge the model per layer. Clear internals could help close the gap between rich and poor languages. The tests span many tongues and depths in the net. That breadth makes the trends they find hard to brush off as quirks of one tongue.
arxiv-2601-14150:
Alejandra Martinez studies how firms adjust when trade ties break for a short time in 2026. International trade relationships often run through relational contracts, built on trust. Martinez exploits an extreme, plausibly exogenous weather shock as a natural test. The shock hit during the 2010-11 La Niña season in Colombia.

Heavy weather restricted Colombian flower exporters' access to cargo terminals. Transaction-level data from Colombian-U.S. trade tracks the response. The study asks how firms adjust during and after such a crisis. Flower exports are time-critical, so the case shows stress in sharp relief.
arxiv-2601-14650:
Hiroma Okubo and nine co-authors present a data analysis framework in this 2026 paper. Their data are ALMA Band 3 observations of the galaxy NGC 1068. Galaxies emit many spectral lines at once, and multi-line analysis tries to read them together. Their framework combines two machine learning tools. Kernel principal component analysis is an unsupervised method that finds patterns. Kernel SHAP is an explainable AI technique that shows which inputs drive a result.

Pairing the two gives patterns plus reasons. The case study is a famous nearby active galaxy. Readers get a worked example of explainable machine learning on real telescope data. Each found pattern can be traced back to the lines that made it.
arxiv-2601-14850:
Fake speech made by computers is hard to spot, and the authors of a 2026 arXiv paper build a tool to catch it. Their system is a transformer, a type of neural network, trained to do more than one task at once. It works from the sound shape of speech itself.

As it listens, the model tracks formants, the resonant tones that shape vowels. It also tracks voicing patterns over time. It then sorts the clip as real or fake. The design also shows if the call leaned more on voiced or unvoiced parts of speech.
arxiv-2601-15150:
A classic model of competing species gets pushed to an endless roster in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Volterra model dates to 1937 and tracks how species grow and compete. Two recent papers showed that an integrable version of the finite-species model is in fact maximally superintegrable.

That is a strong form of order for a dynamical system. The new work extends those results much further. It treats the case of infinitely many species. The count may be countable, like the whole numbers, or uncountable. The integrable structure is shown to survive that leap.
arxiv-2601-15350:
Esmat Sangari and Rajni Kant Bansal study two rival shops that sell goods which go together. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with mixed bundling and price-matching guarantees. Customers differ in what they value, and the two retailers sell complementary products.

One retailer offers mixed bundling, selling items alone or as a bundle. The rival sells only a bundle. The authors characterize the unique pure-strategy equilibria across the subgames. They compare them with a no-bundling benchmark. Their result: mixed bundling strictly dominates its rivals whenever an equilibrium exists at all in the game.
arxiv-2601-15550:
Sangmitra Madhusudan and five co-authors probe regional bias in language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Cultural commonsense benchmarks often treat a nation as one uniform block. Real practice varies within borders, though. The team asks whether commonsense holds evenly across a country or shifts by region. India is their test case. It has 28 states, 8 union territories, and 22 official languages.

Their benchmark is called Indica. They describe it as the first built to test models on sub-national cultural knowledge. A model can know a national average yet miss local custom. That miss matters when models serve users in specific states. The work pushes evaluation past country-level scores. It asks builders to check whose culture a model actually knows.
arxiv-2601-15750:
Toshiyuki Kobayashi and Michael Pevzner survey Rankin-Cohen brackets in a 2026 arXiv paper. These brackets are basic examples of differential symmetry breaking operators. They can be seen as bi-differential operators, acting on pairs of functions. Their striking trait is how they mirror fusion rules. Those rules govern holomorphic discrete series representations of the Lie group SL(2, R). The brackets are also tied to classical special polynomials.

Representation theory studies how groups act as symmetries of spaces. Symmetry breaking asks what happens when a group shrinks to a subgroup. Operators that respect that breaking are rare and prized. The Rankin-Cohen brackets are the textbook case. A survey from two leading figures maps their role for researchers entering the area.
arxiv-2601-16150:
Maximos Kaliakatsos-Papakostas and coauthors teach a lone coder to add chords to a tune. Their 2026 preprint deals with melodic harm, the task of chords for a set tune. A lone coder frame treats the task as masked chain fill. Past drills for that frame came from spread out fill plans. Those plans can lead to weak or dull chord picks.

The team sets a step drill that masks chords in a set order. The order is named in the title as a staged mask plan. Staged drills aim to teach chord sense step by step. The coder then fills chords with more care for the tune. The work targets music tools that write with users.
arxiv-2601-16350:
Milad Panahi and coauthors learn full sets of growth task answers with physics led solvers. Their 2026 preprint deals with growth tasks that shift with set terms. To learn all answers at once is a core hard task. Mixed ground, as in water flow in rock, makes it more hard. Past nets oft learn one case at a time with no law guide.

Solvers that can be tuned by train steps join laws to learning. The team uses such solvers to learn the full answer set. Full sets let users ask new term cases at low cost. That speed serves water and rock work where terms shift oft. The work joins solver craft to set learning.
arxiv-2601-16450:
Sejun Park, Yeachan Park and Geonho Hwang test what float based coders can state. Their 2026 preprint deals with coder nets, called transformers. Past proofs say coders can match all fair swap fair maps. Those proofs use true real counts and exact steps. Real gear uses float counts with capped fine grain.

Float caps cut what a coder can state in true runs. The team maps which maps stay in reach under float rules. Reach maps warn teams where proofs and gear part ways. They also guide safe depths and widths for real nets. The work joins proof maths to gear facts.
arxiv-2601-16750:
The BESIII team shares new results on charm decays from its vast data sets. No lab holds more threshold data on charm bits than BESIII. The team has now grown those sets by a wide mark. More pairs of D mesons and charm baryons sit in hand. Their 2026 preprint sums the fresh results on weak decays.

Weak decays of charm bits test the base theory's rules. They show how quarks swap types through the weak force. Clean gauges of those swaps bound new physics hunts. The team's larger sets cut the blur on key rates. This sharpens the world pool of charm facts for all labs.
arxiv-2601-16850:
C. L. Sarkis and a large team map spin waves in a famed crystal, RuCl3. The crystal may host a rare spin liquid state. In that state, spins stay fluid down to deep cold. A strong magnet field can push it to a blurred phase. Their 2026 preprint maps that phase with neutron beams.

At and past eight tesla, the spin waves show a clear gap. The team took maps for two field aims in the plane. Those maps show how spins stir in the blurred phase. Such facts test tales of the spin liquid's parts. They guide the long hunt for this odd state.
arxiv-2601-16950:
Ferran Maura, Francesc Wilhelmi, and Boris Bellalta test Wi-Fi for cloud VR streams. Cloud VR sends rich shots to a head set by air. That stream needs high flow and low lag at once. One user can strain a home net. Many users can drown the air band fast. Their 2026 preprint gauges that strain with real film traffic.

The film used a top codec, HEVC, for true load shape. The team counts how many users one net can hold. Those counts guide net design for VR halls and homes. They also warn where 802.11 nets hit their wall. Such facts help plan gear for smooth VR.
arxiv-2601-17450:
Qingchao Shen builds a data-driven way to test AI compilers. Compilers turn AI models into code for many chips. Bugs in them can break models in silent ways. Quality checks are thus key, but hard to write by hand. Shen presents one framework that covers the full test path. It treats stage-specific flaws in a unified way.

The method generates tests from data, not fixed scripts. That lets it probe new models and chips as they come. Compiler teams gain a repeatable hunt for bugs. Early finds protect the apps built on those models. As AI spreads to cars and clinics, such checks matter more. The framework aims at scale and depth at once.
arxiv-2601-17550:
Deepak Singh, Shreyas Khobragade, and Nitin J. Sanket present AsterNav for drone flight in total darkness. Rescue work often runs after power fails. Tiny drones fit tight rescue spaces well. They lack the power for heavy sensors and lights. AsterNav uses passive computation to navigate without light. That keeps the drone light and its power draw low.

Finding survivors fast is the core goal. A drone that works in the dark extends search hours. It also spares human teams the worst risks. Passive methods suit tiny craft that cannot haul lidar. The work joins robotics with disaster response. It aims at rubble, smoke, and blackout zones.
arxiv-2601-17750:
Jan Schröeder, Yair Censor, Philipp Süss, and Karl-Heinz Küfer tackle inverse robustness in radiotherapy planning. Treatment planning is a multi-criteria optimization problem. Planners must balance dose goals against each other. Uncertainty adds a second balance, on robustness itself. Their method handles inverse robustness with semidefinite programming. That class of optimization gives sound, tractable solutions.

A decision maker needs plans that state their trade-offs clearly. Inverse robustness asks what robustness level a chosen plan implies. Making that link explicit aids clinical judgment. Cancer care gains when plans are both strong and honest. Semidefinite tools fit the convex parts of the task. The work joins math programming with bedside needs.
arxiv-2601-17950:
Matthew Walmer, Saksham Suri, Anirud Aggarwal, and Abhinav Shrivastava present UPLiFT, a method for making vision features denser at low cost. Their 2026 preprint sits in a growing area: task-agnostic feature upsampling. Pretrained vision backbones output coarse feature maps. Many tasks, like segmentation, need fine maps instead. Upsampling methods learn to turn the coarse maps into dense ones, giving a shortcut to detail at a fraction of the full cost.

UPLiFT uses local attenders to do that lifting with care. Local focus keeps the cost down while detail goes up. Since the features are task-agnostic, one lifted map can serve many tasks. The work aims at dense vision that stays cheap enough for wide use.
arxiv-2601-18050:
Mickaël Montessinos ties together several hard computing problems about special surfaces. His 2026 preprint deals with superspecial abelian surfaces with a principal polarization. The problems include computing the endomorphism ring of such a surface. They also include computing a certain matrix named for Ibukiyama, Katsura, and Oort, and finding isomorphisms between unpolarised surfaces. The author shows reductions and equivalences between these problems.

Equivalence means a solver for one problem yields solvers for the rest. That web of links lets progress on any one front lift the others. These surfaces matter for cryptography based on isogenies. Clear problem links help judge how hard that cryptography really is.
arxiv-2601-18350:
Junyi Zou studies a clash between two kinds of training in medical language models. His 2026 preprint examines adapter interference. A 14-billion-parameter base model went through a two-stage LoRA pipeline. First came domain-oriented pre-training to inject medical knowledge. Then supervised fine-tuning taught it to follow instructions on medical questions. Zou studies what happens when the two adapters are merged. Domain training and instruction alignment can pull against each other in safety-critical settings.

Interference means the merged model can be worse than either stage alone. In medicine, that loss can touch real advice. Knowing when merging harms helps teams choose safer recipes. The study is a warning and a guide for adapter use.
arxiv-2601-18450:
Jamolidin Abdurakhmanov, of Andijan State University in Uzbekistan, studies when a grid of ones and zeros must hold a heavy column. Each row of the grid is unlike each other row. A column counts as heavy when at least half of its cells hold a one. The ask is plain to state but hard to settle for all grid sizes.

He checks for which widths and heights such a column must show up. Grids like these show up in codes, in tests, and in plans for trials. A heavy column marks a trait that shows in at least half the rows. Proofs about when such a column is forced help teams know what a data set must hold, sight unseen. The work adds one more stone to that base of pure maths.
arxiv-2601-18550:
Bo Gao, Henkjan Gersen, and Simon Hanna study a side push that light can give to tiny forms. When light hits a form that is not the same on both sides, the push can have a side part as well as a front part. Their test form is a small triangle that repeats in a grid. The grid is made of a glass-like stuff that bends light but does not soak it up.

By computer runs, they map how the side push shifts as the form and the light change. In wide zones the push holds firm. In thin bands it flips all at once. The flip bands bear the marks of a known wave clash that boosts some tones and kills the rest. Side pushes could one day move or sort tiny bits with light alone. A firm map is a first step.
arxiv-2601-18650:
Liheng Yu and five colleagues tackle a flaw in tools that make a model forget set facts. To forget is a right in law: a user can ask that their facts be cut from a trained model. Most tests of forget tools use a fair mix of facts to drop. Real asks are not fair: some kinds of fact may fill most of the drop list.

That skew is called long-tailed, since a few kinds hold most of the asks. A forget tool that works on fair tests may fail on skewed ones. The team add a loss tweak that gives more weight to the rare kinds in the drop list. That should help the model drop the rare facts with the same care as the common ones. Fair forget tools count for trust in the firms that hold our facts.
arxiv-2601-18750:
Francesco Chiossi and three colleagues use brain waves to tell a look of choice from a look of mere sight in mixed-world head sets. In such sets, the eyes do much of the work a hand once did. That brings a flaw: a look can mean I pick this, or mere I see this. Kit that can't tell the two will act on mere looks by slip. That flaw has a name, the Midas touch.

The team use a brain wave that comes just ahead of a pick. That wave can serve as a hid yes, with no click or word. They test how the wave shifts when the user means to pick or to just watch, and when the set talks back or stays mute. A sound hid yes could make eye kit fast and safe at once.
arxiv-2601-18850:
Sven Kirchner and three colleagues set out how to fit smart nets into cars in a way that is safe by the book. Nets of the kind in use for sight and text top the charts on many tasks. But a car is a place where a flaw can kill. Safe design there needs proof that a part will act right, or fail in a safe way. A net's acts are hard to prove in that strict way.

Their frame uses the car's many sensors as a check net. If one path fails, the next can catch its work. That spread of paths can lift the whole car's trust grade. The frame is a plan, not a built car. It maps what must be shown for nets to earn a place in cars. Such maps guide firms that must pass strict safe tests.
arxiv-2601-18950:
Harsh Vardhan studies how many computers can agree on an average while sharing very little. In spread out learning, many machines each hold a vector, and the group needs the mean. Bandwidth is tight, so each vector must be squeezed before it is sent.

The twist here is teamwork: the squeezers, called compressors, can work together rather than each acting alone. Shared plans for squeezing can cut the error of the mean for the same small budget of bits. The result speaks to big training jobs where talk between machines, not math, is the main cost.
arxiv-2601-19050:
Everett W. Howe counts a rare family of curves that map onto one fixed curve at every degree. A genus two curve is a smooth shape with two holes, and an elliptic curve has one. Howe asks when maps of every whole number degree exist from the first kind onto one fixed second kind.

He shows that, up to sameness of shape, exactly twenty such pairs exist over the complex numbers. A count that ends in a small, exact list is rare in this area of math. The full list gives number theorists a closed case to test wider ideas about maps between curves against.
arxiv-2601-19350:
Tathagata Raha and three co-authors grade text generation by cross examining the texts themselves. Classic scores like BLEU compare word overlap and miss whether meaning survived. The team adapts a cross examination framework that needs no reference answer.

It treats the source and the new text as two knowledge bases and asks each verifiable questions drawn from the other. Three scores come out: coverage, conformity, and consistency. Interpretable scores that track fidelity would help anyone who uses machine summaries, translations, or reports and needs to know what was lost or bent.
arxiv-2601-19450:
Pravabati Chingangbam reads the shape of the early universe's hydrogen signal to hunt for traces of inflation. The redshifted 21 centimeter signal from the cosmic dawn and the age of reionization encodes both star driven history and primordial physics. Morphological statistics describe the signal's shapes, not just its average strength.

Chingangbam uses Minkowski functionals, a set of shape measures, to test how sensitive the signal is to early features and to reionization at once. Shape based reads could spot the fingerprint of inflation in data that plainer statistics would wash out. The work guides how future radio maps get mined.
arxiv-2601-19650:
Richard M. Milbradt and four colleagues speed up a core routine in quantum simulation. Tensor network methods represent large quantum states as webs of small tensors. A common step applies an operator, itself a tensor network, to a state. That step is a bottleneck in many calculations.

The authors introduce a new algorithm for applying tree-shaped operators to tree-shaped states. It draws on the density matrix method and on the Cholesky decomposition from linear algebra. A faster application step lifts the whole family of methods. Chemists and physicists use tensor networks to study materials that no direct method can handle. Shaving cost from the central subroutine widens what they can simulate.
arxiv-2601-19850:
Binzhu Xie and a large team of colleagues rebuild hands in three dimensions from head-mounted cameras. Egocentric video shows hands from the wearer's own view. Reconstructing their pose is hard: depth is ambiguous, fingers hide each other, and objects get in the way. Earlier systems scaled up training data or added extra cues, yet still struggled with new contexts.

Their method, EgoHandICL, uses in-context learning. The model adapts from examples shown at run time rather than only from fixed training. That flexibility targets unseen situations directly. Reliable hand tracking underpins augmented reality and robot learning from human video. The work aims at hands that stay accurate in the wild.
arxiv-2601-20150:
Laurence G. Yaffe revisits a variational method for studying gauge theories, the theories behind the strong nuclear force. The goal is to compute properties of QCD-like theories in infinite volume when the number of colors, N, is large. Coherent state methods were proposed for this long ago, but their practical use stalled.

Yaffe describes an entirely new implementation of the approach. It applies to lattice gauge theories with or without fermions, on lattices of up to four dimensions. If the method works at scale, it could open a fresh route to questions about confinement that are hard to reach with standard simulation.
arxiv-2601-20550:
Ryotaro Hoshino and Yoshitaka Tanimura build a numerical framework for simulating two-dimensional vibrational spectra of molecular liquids. Their base is the multi-mode anharmonic Brownian motion model, a general frame for molecular vibration in condensed phases. When vibrational energy passes thermal levels, quantum effects grow strong and system-bath entanglement needs rigorous treatment.

Their method, HEOM-2DVS, rests on the hierarchical equations of motion, a powerful tool for open quantum systems. Such spectra are fingerprints that chemists read to learn how molecules move and exchange energy in liquids, so faithful simulation matters. A two-part spectrum shows more than a flat trace can. It shows how the parts of a molecule trade energy as time runs on.
arxiv-2601-20650:
Jing Wu and six colleagues present OS-Marathon, a benchmark for computer-use agents on long, repetitive tasks. Such workflows are common in professional life: processing expense reports from receipts, or entering student grades from exam papers. They are tedious for humans, and their length grows with the size of the data to process.

The benchmark tests agents over these extreme-length chores. Staying accurate across hundreds of near-identical steps is a different challenge from solving one hard problem. OS-Marathon gives agent builders a measure of stamina and consistency, not just cleverness. That is a trait most short tests never touch at all.
arxiv-2601-21050:
Haokun Zhou builds an anomaly detector for streams whose sensors keep changing. The 2026 paper presents SMKC, based on sketch-based kernel correlation images. Conventional detection for multivariate time series assumes a fixed set of variables. Operational systems break that assumption daily. Sensors appear, disappear, or get renamed. Data windows then vary in cardinality. They may include values unseen during training.

A detector that needs a fixed input shape fails in that world. SMKC instead turns each window into a correlation image. Sketches keep the image compact as variables churn. Anomalies then show up as odd patterns in the image. The method targets real monitoring, from factories to data centers. It accepts messy, shifting inputs as the normal case.
arxiv-2601-21350:
Yupei Yang and seven co-authors fix a weakness in the reward models that steer language models toward human tastes. A reward model scores answers so the main model can learn from feedback. Standard reward models can latch onto surface traits that are not truly linked to what people liked.

That flaw invites reward hacking, where high scores stop meaning better behavior. The authors split the model's inner features into causal parts and spurious parts. Training leans on the causal parts, so the score tracks real quality. A steadier reward signal should make feedback training safer and more honest.
arxiv-2601-21450:
Donghuo Zeng, Hao Niu, Zhi Li, and Masato Taya compare the loss functions that teach models to place similar items close together. Metric learning powers search by image and face matching. Yet how each loss shapes the learned space, and how training unfolds, is poorly understood.

The authors build a diagnostic frame with two lenses. One lens tracks the spread of points inside and between classes. The other tracks how greedily each loss uses hard cases, via active ratios and gradient sizes. They compare seven well-known losses across five image search datasets. The frame helps builders pick a loss with open eyes.
arxiv-2601-21650:
Alexander Erlei, Federico Cau, Radoslav Georgiev, Sagar Kumar, Kilian Bizer, and Ujwal Gadiraju study how hidden gaps in knowledge about AI systems warp consumer markets. Buyers cannot easily tell a strong system from a flawed one. A product can look highly accurate while hiding costly errors or defects.

The classic economics of lemons predicts that such gaps drive good products out. Disclosure rules try to close the gap, but large parts remain open. The authors examine how these asymmetries shape adoption and market outcomes. Their analysis helps regulators aim disclosure where it protects buyers without choking useful tools.
arxiv-2601-21850:
Dražen Adamović, Boris Feigin, and Shigenori Nakatsuka prove a structural result in representation theory. Their subject is the center of an affine Lie algebra at the critical level, a special setting where the center becomes large and rich. For the algebra built from the general linear superalgebra with one odd direction, the structure was not fully pinned down.

The authors prove that this center is generated by the coefficients of one pseudo-differential operator, a product of simple factors and one inverse factor. Their 2026 preprint ties the algebra to the theory of opers, geometric objects used in the Langlands program. Identifying a center explicitly is prized in this field, because the center controls how all representations of the algebra behave.
arxiv-2601-22050:
Ghazal Kalhor and Behnam Bahrak test whether language models understand Persian proverbs. Models now sit inside daily life, so they must handle conversational language well, including figurative speech. Most figurative language research covers high-resource languages, leaving low-resource ones unmeasured.

Their 2026 preprint introduces MasalBench, a benchmark for contextual and cross-cultural understanding of Persian proverbs. A proverb's meaning rarely sits in its words alone; it depends on culture and situation. Testing models on such material reveals whether their multilingual skill is deep or only grammatical. Benchmarks like this push developers to serve smaller language communities with the same care given to English.
arxiv-2601-22450:
Jianhao Huang and Baharan Mirzasoleiman tune a hidden brake inside masked diffusion language models. These models build text by filling masked slots, not word by word. Their 2026 preprint notes that their learning traits are little studied next to the standard left-to-right kind. The team study a toy task: the parity, or XOR sum, of a few key bits.

That task is famed for grokking, where a model stalls, then grasps all at once. Tuning the brake aims to make that grasp come sooner and hold. The work guides how this new model class should be trained.
arxiv-2601-22750:
Carlos Marante and a team catch a peak in double-ion yield from ethylene at a fifteen-femtosecond delay. Doubly charged molecules carry marks of electron links and of electron-nucleus ties in the parent. Their 2026 preprint fires an extreme ultraviolet pump pulse, then a near-infrared probe.

The yield peak marks a fleeting window where confinement shapes the outcome. Femtosecond timing — millionths of a billionth of a second — lets them film chemistry as it happens. Such films test how molecules break and bond. The work is precision basic science. It reads a very fast signal.
arxiv-2601-22850:
Glaydston C. Bento and three co-authors sharpen the theory of a classic optimization method. The method, alternating minimization, solves a hard problem by fixing one part and improving the other, back and forth. It was set out for structured, non-smooth problems in a noted 2010 work.

The new results give much faster convergence rates under a key condition named in the abstract. In some cases the method can finish in finite steps, or speed up beyond the linear rate known before. Faster guarantees help users trust the method on real problems.
arxiv-2601-22950:
Petar Veličković and four co-authors question a favorite yardstick for language models: perplexity. Perplexity measures how surprised a model is by a text, and it serves both as a training loss and a quick quality score. Earlier work noted flaws in it, mostly from experiments.

The authors give a sharper account of when perplexity can, and cannot, tell right answers from wrong ones. A metric that looks simple can quietly mislead model choices. Knowing its limits helps teams judge models by measures tied to real correctness. The authors move past scattered empirical complaints, aiming for a principled account of what perplexity can and cannot certify.
arxiv-2601-23150:
J. M. Alcaine-Cuervo and four co-authors design a superconducting circuit that hosts a lattice gauge theory. Gauge theories describe fundamental forces on a grid of sites and links. Their compact U(1) version uses the circuit's own phase and charge variables, which live in infinite-dimensional spaces.

Gauge and matter fields are encoded directly in the circuit nodes' rotor variables. Gauss's law then holds exactly from charge conservation, with no added penalty terms or cutoffs. Clean encodings make quantum simulation of gauge theories more faithful. Exact Gauss law without stabilizers or truncations is the design's prize, keeping the simulated physics faithful by construction.
arxiv-2603-01450:
Jianfeng Liao, Yichen Wei, Raymond Chan Ching Bon, and colleagues wrote this 2026 study on how to spot fake face videos and images. Fake media made by AI now looks very real, and it can harm public trust and safety. Older tools often fail when a new kind of fake appears.

The team builds a system called DFA on top of CLIP, a large vision and language model, without changing CLIP itself. One part checks the whole image for odd signs, while a second part looks for small flaws in the face. A third part joins both views to make the final call. Tests on still frames and on video show strong results, with a clear gain on the hard DFDC test set.
arxiv-2603-02050:
Kihoon Son, Hyewon Lee, DaEun Choi, and colleagues design AI agents that collaborate with designers in real time. Their 2026 work notes that human partners coordinate through shared visibility of process and workspace. Agents, by contrast, usually deliver final outputs or read-only process views and ignore concurrent user moves.

A first study with professional designers shows process visibility helps, yet conflicts arise when agents misread feedback. Their system, Cleo, interprets collaborative intent from concurrent actions on shared artifacts and adapts live. A second two-day study analyzes hundreds of turns for action patterns and triggers. Designers split their work among delegation, direction, and concurrent co-work in shifting shares. A decision model with six interaction loops distills when to hand off and when to work together.
arxiv-2603-02350:
W Horowitz and A Rothkopf rebuild a classical action principle from quantum theory in this 2026 paper. Hamilton's principle derives motion from a single action quantity, usually for boundary value problems. Initial value problems, starting from a known state, need a different variational setup. The authors derive that setup as the classical limit of a quantum formalism.

The quantum starting point tracks expected values through forward and backward time paths. Both paths turn out to carry classical motion and fluctuations, contrary to common belief. Fluctuations on both paths prove essential for correct normalization of the limit. One path's unique classical solution is zero, and it runs backward in time. No hand-setting is needed. The authors note consequences for constrained systems and gauge theories.
arxiv-2603-02450:
Zheyu Wu, Hanyi Chen, Mengmeng Long, and colleagues report a switchable superconducting memory in this 2026 paper. Superconducting computers could beat ordinary electronics on energy use by far. Memory that can be written and read in such platforms has stayed elusive. Their material is uranium ditelluride, a candidate triplet superconductor in single crystal form.

A magnetic field tunes the crystal into a regime between two superconducting phases. There, direct current pulses push it into and out of a metastable state. That state carries an enhanced critical current, the most current it can bear without resistance. Pulse strength and duration control the switching. The material remembers which state it is in after the pulse ends. Such controllable memory is a missing piece for superconducting computing.
arxiv-2603-02550:
Mu-Tian Wang, Fei Dai, Hui-Gen Liu, and colleagues characterize a young planetary system in this 2026 paper. TOI-2076 is about two hundred million years old and hosts four sub-Neptune planets. Young multi-planet systems often sit in resonant chains set by disc migration. Those chains usually break apart over time, as in our solar system's story.

These four planets sit near resonance but not locked inside it, leaving the system fragile. Their cores weigh about the same, yet envelope shares rise steadily for cooler, outer planets. That gradient fits photoevaporation, where starlight strips the most irradiated envelopes first. Helium outflow detections rule out a pure water-world makeup. Reshaping of compact systems, both dynamic and atmospheric, clearly starts early. The system anchors models of long-term planet evolution.
arxiv-2603-02650:
Yuan Lu, Dongqi Han, Yansen Wang, and Dongsheng Li improve robot planners that learn from stored data. Their 2026 method, called SAGE, targets a known flaw in diffusion planners. Such planners can pick paths that score high yet clash with how the world really moves, so execution turns brittle.

SAGE scores each sampled plan with a learned check for physical consistency. A predictor trained on past state sequences flags plans whose next steps look unlikely, and that penalty joins the value score when choosing actions. The method needs no live trials and no retraining of the planner. Across locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tests, it made diffusion planners stronger and more robust.
arxiv-2603-02750:
Takuro Mochizuki studies whether families of flat connections stay bounded when their wildness is capped. A flat connection is a system of linked rate laws with a rigid shape. Its irregularity gauges how badly answers can blow up near singular points. His 2026 paper asks if a cap on that wildness bounds the whole family.

Bounded families can be charted by tidy parameter spaces, the base of any sorting scheme in this field. As a use case, Mochizuki turns to D-modules, a strong algebraic language for such rate laws. He studies bounded families whose cycle data, which track singular directions, stay held down in a precise sense. The work ties analytic control of equations to algebraic control of their families.
arxiv-2603-02850:
D. Katz, A. Gómez, E. Caffau, and a large team check whether the fastest stars in the Gaia catalog are real. The third Gaia release lists tens of millions of star speeds, but the faintest spectra are noisy. Noise spikes can fake extreme speeds, and true high-speed stars are rare enough that fakes could swamp them.

The team re-observed over one hundred candidate stars with sensitive ground spectrographs in France and Chile. About one hundred four speeds held up, while thirty were refuted as errors. Merging other major surveys let them chart the fake rate by signal strength and speed range. At the faintest levels, most extreme readings were false. The cleaned sample of truly fast stars then feeds orbit studies of the Milky Way.
arxiv-2603-02950:
Lingxiao Huang and Nisheeth Vishnoi trace how leaning on AI can quietly erode the skill it seems to support. Their 2026 paper models human skill and AI delegation as two quantities that evolve together. Delegation follows relative performance, skill grows with practice and decays with disuse, and both updates chase one shared error metric.

Despite that local alignment, the system gains a second stable resting point: a low-skill trap of permanent reliance, divided from the high-skill outcome by a sharp boundary. Early choices near that boundary become effectively irreversible. AI help can thus raise short-run scores while locking in long-run loss against the no-AI path. The authors show the trap survives noise and lopsided trust updates.
arxiv-2603-03250:
The CMS Collaboration hunts for a light new particle that decays into two photons at the Large Hadron Collider. Several theories predict a spin-zero particle below the electroweak scale, and photon pairs are a clean place to look. Their 2026 search uses proton-proton collisions recorded in 2018 at thirteen teraelectronvolts.

A new diphoton trigger opened the low-mass window, letting the team scan resonance masses from ten to seventy gigaelectronvolts in data made through gluon fusion. No significant excess appeared above the expected background. The team therefore sets upper limits on how strongly such a particle could be produced and decay to photons. The limits are also read as constraints on axion-like particles within an effective theory framework.
arxiv-2603-03450:
Christopher J Lindsay and four colleagues test how stellar modelers should handle a common chemical quirk in old stars. Metal-poor stars are often rich in alpha elements, oxygen and its kin, relative to iron. Modelers either build that enhancement in fully or fake it with a simple correction to total metal content. Their 2026 study models eight evolved metal-poor stars both ways, using spectroscopy plus individual oscillation frequencies from asteroseismology.

The two methods agree on the inferred stellar properties, and their uncertainties are comparable. That calm result disagrees qualitatively with earlier work based only on global oscillation summaries, where ages swung strongly with assumed chemistry. One warning stands out: the observed frequency of strongest oscillation exceeds scaling-relation predictions, especially at low metal content. Fixing that breakdown matters for dating hundreds of halo giants known only by global measures.
arxiv-2603-03550:
Zhiyu Cao and Peter G Wolynes study the stats of sudden shifts in driven glassy substances. Near instability, amorphous systems release stress in thermal avalanches, large grouped events rather than smooth flow. Working inside random first-order shift theory, the standard picture of glasses, their 2026 paper traces avalanches to stringy excited states, thread-like cooperative motions inside the material.

Those excitations produce waiting-time statistics that are not Poisson, so events remember each other. Embedding the stats in a general master formula captures the resulting non-Markovian, aging dynamics of avalanche clusters. The authors then analyze fingerprints under two driving styles, slow shear and random shaking: correlation functions and working temperatures. Full counting stats give complete distributions for avalanche sizes and counts, exposing the in-between-time conduct between single events and steady flow.
arxiv-2603-03650:
Felix Köster and Atsushi Uchida treat a physical system as a computer and learn where to read it. Dynamical systems preserve, transform, and scatter information as they evolve. Their 2026 framework learns not only from a system's data but how to measure the system itself. A trainable attention module decides both where to probe the state and how to combine the readings for the best prediction.

The demonstration system is a spatiotemporal field governed by a partial differential equation, though any samplable state qualifies. Adaptive spatial sensing improves prediction accuracy significantly on canonical chaotic benchmarks. The authors frame attention-enhanced reservoir computing, a known technique, as one special case of the broader paradigm. Their closing image is memorable: neural networks as trainable measurement devices for physical systems.
arxiv-2603-03750:
Sujoy Kumar Nath, Dipak Debnath, and Hsiang-Kuang Chang watch the echoes between X-ray colors during a black hole's awakening. The binary Swift J1727.8-1613 erupted in 2023 in an outburst lasting about ten months. China's Insight-HXMT telescope monitored the rising phase almost continuously for six weeks, catching strong type-C oscillations, the rhythmic flickers that track the inner accretion flow. Their 2026 paper measures the time lags between energy bands as the outburst climbs.

Both hard lags, where energetic light trails, and soft lags appear, with a clear transition from hard to soft as the outburst evolves. The lags anti-correlate strongly with oscillation frequency and with the spectrum's photon index, and correlate positively with the inferred shock location. The pattern supports the propagating oscillatory shock picture, in which a moving shock front orchestrates the coupled spectral and timing behavior.
