bastiat-the-law-1850:
Frédéric Bastiat published The Law in 1850, a short French pamphlet written months before his death. Bastiat, an economist and member of France's assembly, defended natural law against what he called legal plunder. The pamphlet became the classic statement of classical-liberal legal philosophy in miniature.

Law, Bastiat argued, exists only to defend life, liberty, and property, the gifts that come before law itself. When law takes from some to give to others, it perverts its purpose and teaches theft. He wrote with wit and plain examples drawn from French politics of his day. The Law fits in an hour's reading, yet its phrases are still quoted wherever state power is debated.
baxter-saints-everlasting-rest-1650:
Richard Baxter was a Puritan pastor who wrote The Saints' Everlasting Rest in 1650 while ill and expecting death. The book urges believers to meditate on heaven until the hope of it changes daily life. It became the Puritan classic of heavenly meditation.

Baxter paints heaven as rest after labor, reunion with the saints, and unbroken sight of God. He scolds cold hearts and gives practical rules for pondering eternal things amid business and pain. Generations of English and American readers kept the book by their bedsides for comfort in sickness and grief. Baxter wrote as a dying man speaking to fellow travelers.
bonatti-de-astronomia-tractatus-1550:
Guido Bonatti summed up medieval astrology in his Liber Astronomicus, printed at Basel in 1550 as De astronomia tractatus X. Ten treatises in Latin cover nativities, revolutions of years, elections, horary questions, and the astrology of nations and weather. Bonatti served Italian courts in the thirteenth century, and princes planned campaigns by his word.

The 1550 edition presents the complete work in its original language, as scholars of the art have always read it. Few medieval books ruled a science so fully for so long. Students of judicial astrology still treat Bonatti as the great Latin authority, the summa against which later writers measured themselves.
braid-observations-on-trance-1850:
Braid ranged across cultures and centuries in Observations on Trance, printed in 1850. Fakirs buried alive, religious ecstatics, and cases of catalepsy fill his survey. He reads them all as natural states of the nervous system. Human hybernation, his other title phrase, borrows the image of animals in winter sleep.

Reports from India, the classical world, and modern medicine stand side by side. Braid asks what one bodily scheme could cover them all. The book is the first comparative natural history of trance. It widens his science from the clinic to the whole human record. His calm tone treats marvels as data. Later students of trance still start here.
cahagnet-celestial-telegraph-1850:
Louis Alphonse Cahagnet published his somnambulist visions in French in 1848, Englished in 1850 as The Celestial Telegraph. Eight ecstatics, his entranced subjects, describe the soul's state after death. Under magnetism, they report meeting the dead and seeing the spheres above. Cahagnet records their words as evidence of the life to come.

The book became a bridge from mesmerism to spiritualism. Its trance journeys prepared readers for the seance talk that followed. Cahagnet, a French cabinetmaker turned magnetizer, built a circle around his subjects. Believers treasured the visions; critics saw dreams in costume. Either way, the text marks a turning point. It shows magnetism growing a heaven.
calmet-phantom-world-1850:
Dom Augustin Calmet, a French Benedictine scholar, wrote the treatise that appeared in English as The Phantom World in 1850, translated by Henry Christmas. Calmet studied reports of apparitions, vampires, and corpses that seemed to return from the grave. His work first appeared in the 1740s and drew wide debate.

Calmet weighed church teaching, witness reports, and tales from eastern Europe, where vampire panics were recent news. He asked whether such returns were real, fraud, disease, or error, and he did not settle every case. His careful, doubting tone made the book a key early study of ghosts and vampires, quoted by later writers for two centuries.
cia-0000008650:
November 1964 brought a second Cordoba warning: a communist terrorist group planned to seize the American consul there. A companion report a month earlier concerned an American official in the same city. Two warnings in weeks suggest a threat stream officials took seriously.

Consuls made tempting targets because they stood for the United States in public view. Security officers had to judge whether the plot was real, exaggerated, or a bluff. The file preserves that judgment process at its start, with the warning itself. Together with its companion piece, it documents a tense season for American staff in Cordoba.
cia-0000009450:
American soldiers were captured in Kontum province, South Vietnam, a May 1967 CIA report records. Kontum sits in the Central Highlands, where hard fighting raged around Dak To that year. Ground troops, unlike aircrews, were usually captured in close combat.

The report brings the infantry's captivity into a file series dominated by pilots. Soldiers taken in the highlands entered jungle camps whose conditions few survived unchanged. Their names joined the prisoner lists through reports like this one. The file widens the POW picture beyond the air war, to the men who fought the war on foot.
cia-0000009650:
A Pathet Lao prison camp in the Nam Nga Na Song area of Phong Saly province is described in a January 1970 item. Phong Saly is Laos's northernmost province, mountainous and remote, bordering China and Vietnam. Camps there sat at the far edge of the secret war.

Distance made northern camps nearly invisible to outsiders and rescuers alike. Reports like this one might rest on a single escaped prisoner or local witness. Even so, officials recorded the site, since a map point was better than none. The file adds one remote camp to the Laotian prison map.
cia-0000010850:
Turkey guarded the straits between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, and in 1951 the CIA assessed its place in the struggle between East and West. Turkey had sent troops to fight in Korea and was seeking a firm place in the Western camp. Within a year it would join NATO as the alliance's southeastern anchor.

The paper weighs Turkey's military worth and the steadiness of its politics. It also looks at the pressure the Soviet Union could bring to bear on the straits. The assessment helps explain why Washington valued Ankara so highly as the Cold War hardened across Europe and the Middle East.
cia-0000011050:
During the Arab-Israeli crisis of 1967, the CIA issued a situation report timed to noon on a day of fast-moving events. Such reports were the agency's running account of a war zone, written for senior officials who needed the latest facts. The fighting that June redrew the map of the Middle East in less than a week.

The report tracks the state of the armies and the front lines at that hour. It records what Washington knew, and when it knew it, as the crisis unfolded. For historians, these timed bulletins are a minute-by-minute record of how the war looked from inside the American government.
cia-0000013050:
A North Vietnamese Army captain said American prisoners were held in certain places in Hanoi, and a CIA item from January 1967 records his statements. Turned or captured officers were precious sources on the prison system. Their claims were tested against everything else known, since a prison's location could shape rescue plans, bombing limits, and a family's hope all at once.

The item preserves the captain's words as reported. The files weigh such testimony claim by claim, neither swallowing nor discarding it whole. For readers, the page shows the accounting of the missing being built from voices like his.
cia-0000013850: A pilot and a soldier were captured, and a CIA note dated May 2, 1967, records them together. One man came from the air war and the other from the ground war. Their joint listing shows how capture reports pooled men from very different fights. Both now faced the same prison system in enemy hands.
cia-0000014050:
Forecasting Iran's path through 1953 fills this CIA estimate from October 4, 1952. The paper judged where Iranian politics and power were likely to move in the year ahead. Iran then sat in a fierce fight over its oil, which its government had seized from British hands.

Estimates like this one weighed leaders, parties, oil, and foreign pressure, then set out the most likely course. They were written to guide U.S. officials before events forced their hand. Reading one now shows what the agency thought it knew about Iran at a tense Cold War moment, and where its judgment rested. It also marks the starting point for judging the choices Washington made on Iran soon after.
cia-0000015250: Davidson sent a copy of his article to the Pentagon, in a CIA file dated January 3, 1958. The file notes the mailing in its clipped title. Leon Davidson's saucer writings reached the top of the defense world. Tracking who got a copy was part of how offices judged a story's spread.
cia-0000015350: A telephone conversation with Dr. John A. Wheeler fills a CIA file dated January 2, 1953. Wheeler was a giant of physics, at work on the hydrogen bomb. Why his call sits in the saucer files, the title does not say. His name marks the weight of minds drawn into the question that winter.
cia-0000022750: Photo comparison case number 10,509 has its results kept in a CIA record dated in 1969. Early in the matching effort, cases in the ten thousands were already piling up. Analysts compared faces across poor prints, odd angles, and years of aging. A kept result, whatever it found, was one more firm point in a sea of rumor.
cia-0000027650: El Salvador's performance on certification issues is graded in a CIA paper dated in 1983. This entry shares its title with two sister papers of the same year, one special and one interagency. Certification linked American military aid to progress on human rights and land reform. Three papers on one test in one year show how hot the question burned in Washington.
cia-0000028650: Noel Field's story, through reports by Karel Kaplan and mentions of the Rosenbergs, fills a CIA item dated in 1977. Field was an American official who vanished behind the Iron Curtain in 1949 and fed its show trials. Kaplan, a Czech historian, later wrote on the case from secret files. A 1977 item shows old spy cases still yielding paper decades on.
cia-0000036850:
An FBIS dispatch dated September 5, 1967 reports the capture of McCain and Rice. It names John Sydney McCain and Charles Rice among the men taken in the north. FBIS gathered such reports from foreign broadcasts and passed them to officials.

The dispatch records two captures together, which was common in the Hanoi reports. Paired names helped analysts sort new prisoners from those already known to be held. For the men's families, even a short broadcast report was a thread of real news. Two men taken in the same period could end up in the same prison camp for years.
cia-0000038450:
Hanoi cited a report by its foreign ministry on the MIA question, in a CIA record dated January 2, 1986. The Vietnamese foreign ministry spoke for Hanoi in dealings with the United States. By 1986 the missing men were a standing issue between the two countries.

Inside, the ministry's position is presented as Hanoi wished it to be heard. Official statements of this kind set the terms for talks on remains and records. The file shows the diplomatic side of the accounting, where each government spoke for the record while quieter work went on between their experts in the background.
cia-0000042350:
A CIA country survey titled simply Spain is dated February 3, 1989. Spain had been a democracy for over a decade by then. General Franco's long rule had ended with his death in 1975.

Inside, the survey presents Spain as analysts saw it in the late 1980s. Country surveys covered politics, the economy, and armed forces in one brief. They were written for officials who needed the whole picture of a country on a few pages. The file gives a dated portrait of a settled democracy. Spain in 1989 stood inside NATO and the European Community, far from the isolated Spain that older files in this archive describe.
cia-0000044750:
President Duarte issued a communique on a kidnapped colonel, in a CIA record dated June 3, 1986. Jose Napoleon Duarte led El Salvador through its war's middle years. Kidnapping of officers was a standing weapon of that conflict.

Inside, the president's official statement on the colonel's case is preserved. A communique lets a government speak once, formally, and stop. It gives nothing away beyond the words it chooses to print. Families and fellow officers had to read those words for any hint of hope. The file holds that formal voice from 1986, in a war where the fate of one captured officer could stir the whole country's politics.
cia-0000045250:
El Salvador's archbishop traveled to Panama for talks on the kidnapping, in a CIA record dated September 1, 1985. Shuttle trips by churchmen were the crisis's quiet diplomacy. Panama served again as the neutral ground for hard conversations.

Inside, the journey itself is the record's news, not its outcome. A traveling archbishop signaled that the talks had real weight. Governments watched his movements the way markets watch ministers. A ticket to Panama, in that season, was a kind of public statement all by itself. The file preserves the trip as officials abroad noted it, one more sign that the church had become the channel through which the case would be settled.
cia-0000049050: A CIA item from 1983 files material on Ricardo Sol Meza, kept with the Truth Commission records. Sol Meza's name runs through this series as the businessman tied to a death squad's funding. A personal file like this one gathers what the system knew about a single figure in the war's machinery.
cia-0000099450: Preliminary report of aircraft accident involving a C-123K, tail number 57-6293, near Ban Hong Sa, is declassified CIA document 0000099450, dated January 5, 1972. The heading gives the aircraft type, the tail number, and the place in full. Readers find a short accident report record, marked preliminary in its own title, preserved with the site designation LS-62 noted in the catalog heading as well.
cia-0000102950:
Crime and Unishment in the USSR is the heading, with punishment misspelled, on declassified CIA document 0000102950, dated September 5, 1984. Its text sorts Soviet labor colonies by regime, from regular colonies to strict, very strict, and special regime colonies. Assignment turned on the crime and the sentence imposed by law.

Inside, the state could shape a term around its need for workers on building projects, a practice called Khimiya. Exile could add two to five years after a prison term ended. Minor crimes could bring conditional labor at home, with pay cut for up to a year. The detail shows punishment tied closely to labor needs.
cia-0000107450: Meetings Between Representatives of Arab Communist Parties is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000107450, dated October 2, 1948. The heading records meetings among representatives of more than one Arab communist party. No country or city is named in the title itself. The brief record is a party meetings item from the autumn of 1948 in the files.
cia-0000112350: Moravian Ufo Thought to Be Falling Satellite is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112350, dated January 4, 1991. The title gives a sighting and a plain explanation in one line: a falling satellite. Moravian places the sighting over Moravia, as the heading states it. The brief record is a sighting item with its answer built into the title.
cia-0000118650: Intelligence Memorandum is the whole heading on declassified CIA document 0000118650, dated February 3, 1968. The title gives a form and nothing else: no country, topic, or person is named. A memorandum is the agency's plain working form, as the heading states it. The brief record is a form-only item, its subject left to the pages inside the file.
cia-0000119750: With information as of 10 p.m. on November 5, 1956, this CIA report covers Hungary the day after Soviet forces stormed back into Budapest. The revolution was being crushed as analysts wrote, and the report records the endgame hour by hour. By that hour the second Soviet intervention was a day old, and reports had shifted from the fighting itself to arrests, fear, and flight.
cia-0000132650:
Castro ready for an early seizure of Western oil plants fills a CIA item dated May 1, 1960. Taking the plants meant taking charge of the island's fuel and power at a stroke. The move would strike at the largest foreign firms still working in Cuba.

The item reports the plans as analysts learned of them that spring. The seizures did follow within weeks, in June of that year. For readers, the entry catches the step just before it was taken. It shows a warning reaching the file while there was still time, on paper, for the firms to act on it.
cia-0000132750: A subject line reading only Cuban, deleted, heads a CIA paper dated January 3, 1961. The real subject was cut out before release, leaving just the one word behind. What was deleted may well matter more than what was left standing. The short paper keeps the file in its cut state. It stands as a plain sample of the censor's hand at work.
cia-0000134250: Cuba under the West heading, plus a late item on the Soviet Union and Cuba, fill a CIA item dated July 5, 1960. Late items were fresh news stapled onto the day's briefing after it was typed. The late addition shows the Cuba file moving faster than the printing schedule. The short item covers both parts as filed.
cia-0000136150: The cable dated 4 April 1954 in the CIA files, now open, deals with Rennell, a single name standing as the whole subject. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136350: Aircraft involved in PBSUCCESS are inventoried in this 30 June 1954 LINCOLN cable. Losses have been two F-47s, one in a crash landing at SOMERSET plus mishandling, the other a battle casualty; Cessna types are also listed, some purchased by SYNCARP. The station recommends that soonest after CALLIGERIS is installed, three F-47s be given to the new government. The dry list documents how small the rebel air force really was.
cia-0000139450: A remote viewer insists a hostage will be released, in this April 1988 Project Sun Streak report, the government's psychic spying program under its later name. Viewer 079 remains adamant that Marine Lieutenant Colonel Higgins will be released; projected dates ran about 8 April, 22 April, and prior to June 1988. The summary says Higgins is very much alive and being moved about in the northeast section of Beirut in a navy-blue automobile, near white wall units and pillars with religious writings. Handle via Skeet channels only, the report warns.
cia-03179250: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1960/05/20, a CIA publication. The May briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-03448350: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1955/08/17, a CIA publication. Another August briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. The historical record keeps it. The archive guards it with care.
cia-06848450: <SANITIZED> MANEUVERING TO INFLUENCE THE MILITARY'S ATTITUDE TOWARD THE, a CIA document. The redacted maneuvering. This file preserves that declassified paper. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-06877050: ASSESSMENT OF CANIDATES TO HEAD THE NEW PRESIDENTIAL ADMINISTRATION, a CIA document. The candidates review. This file preserves that declassified paper. Later readers can locate it. The historical record keeps it. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cooke-manuscript-c1450:
The Matthew Cooke Manuscript, written around 1450, is the second-oldest of the Masonic Old Charges. Named for the nineteenth-century editor who published it, the Gothic Constitutions text stands as a bridge. Behind it lies the Regius poem; ahead of it, the later speculative ritual tradition of the lodges.

The Cooke text tells the craft's legendary history in fifteenth-century prose. Biblical builders and ancient geometers carry Masonry from the Flood to England. Rules for the craft follow the history, as in the Regius. Its plainer prose shows the charges settling into standard form. Together, Regius and Cooke give the two oldest witnesses to how masons first wrote down who they believed they were.
dickens-david-copperfield-1850:
Charles Dickens published David Copperfield in 1850 and called it his favourite child. The novel is his most autobiographical, drawn from his own hard early years. David's life, from birth to fame as a writer, fills its long, rich course.

David loses his mother, works in a London warehouse, and flees to his aunt. School, law, and love follow, with Dora, Agnes, Steerforth, and Micawber around him. Uriah Heep's false humility hides schemes that David helps to expose in time. Grief and growth shape David into a man who can tell his own tale. Dickens fills the margins with some of his most loved comic figures.
dods-philosophy-electrical-psychology-18:
John Bovee Dods taught electrical psychology in twelve lectures, printed as a course in 1850. Mind acts on body, he argues, through an electrical medium in the nerves. That claim made his book the founding American statement of the doctrine. Dods lectured widely, and his system fed the United States mesmeric movement.

The lectures move from first principles to healing and mental influence. Later mental healing lines, including New Thought, drew from his seed ideas. Dods writes as a preacher of a new science of mind. His electricity is part physics, part faith in progress. The book captures American mesmerism turning toward mind cure. It is a pivotal text of that turn.
doe-osti-3018491-design-of-transportatio: Cavities got frame-designed, and this DOE text transports 650 MHz units. The pages detail the coupler findings. The accelerator folks get their data. The couplers were high power. The data were accelerator. The MHz was 650. The frames were transportation. The power was high.
dumas-black-tulip-1850:
Alexandre Dumas published The Black Tulip in 1850, a Dutch historical romance of tulip mania. The jewel-like miniature of his art pairs political intrigue with horticultural obsession in fine balance throughout. It is shorter and tighter than his vast musketeer and Monte Cristo sagas of France.

Cornelius van Baerle, a tulip fancier, is jailed in the Dutch troubles of 1672 there. His jailer's daughter Rosa guards his bulbs and his hope as the black tulip nears bloom. A rival grower, Boxtel, schemes to steal the flower and its hundred-thousand-florin prize in Haarlem. The lynching of the De Witt brothers opens the tale in scenes of mob horror. Love and a flower, not swords, carry this compact tale to its bright close.
echr-1950:
The Council of Europe adopted the European Convention on Human Rights at Rome in 1950. It was Western Europe's answer to the tyranny and mass murder that had just wrecked the continent. Unlike a mere statement of ideals, the convention was built to be enforced by real courts.

The text guards rights such as life, liberty, a fair trial, free speech, and freedom of religion. People who claim a member state has broken those rights can take their case to the European Court of Human Rights at Strasbourg. Governments must accept the court's rulings. The system has grown into the most effective human rights machinery in the world, and its case law shapes law far beyond Europe.
emerson-representative-men-1850:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Representative Men in 1850, his lectures on great figures of the past. The set covers Plato, Swedenborg, Montaigne, Shakespeare, Napoleon, and Goethe in six searching biographical lectures for audiences. It is the great nineteenth-century theory of genius and heroism in the American grain of thought.

Emerson treats each man as the lens of an age, great because he sees for all. Plato stands for philosophy, Shakespeare for poetry, and Napoleon for the power of common will in action. He praises Goethe as the writer whose eye takes in the whole of modern life. Faults are not spared, for the hero is a use, not an idol, to Emerson. The book shaped how America talked about greatness, influence, and the debt owed exemplars.
etherology-and-the-phreno-philosophy-of-: Etherology, and the Phreno-Philosophy of Mesmerism, 1850. The etherology. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
etteilla-grand-etteilla-1850:
Etteilla, born Jean-Baptiste Alliette, invented cartomancy as a system in Le Grand Etteilla, seen here in the 1850 French edition. He was the first professional card reader to publish a full method. Meanings for all seventy-eight cards, spreads for laying them out, and the art of telling fortunes fill his pages.

Etteilla tied the tarot pack to Egypt, astrology, and ancient wisdom, building the lore later readers inherited. His reversed meanings and careful spreads still echo in modern practice. The book remains the first great system of tarot divination, the work of the founder of fortune-telling by cards as a trade.
europmc-pmc10026850:
Loyal and a large team show that T cells trained by common cold coronaviruses can boost responses to SARS-CoV-2, in a 2021 study. Whether such pre-existing cross-reactive cells truly help had been hotly debated. The team focused on CD4 T cells, the helper cells that coordinate immune attacks.

They found cross-reactive helper cells in many people, including some never exposed to the new virus. After infection or vaccination, these cells joined the response and sped it up. The work helps explain why immune responses to COVID vary so much between people.
europmc-pmc10273250:
Cui and a large team review photothermal nanomaterials in a 2023 paper. These are tiny engineered materials that turn light into heat with high efficiency. Shining near-infrared light on them can cook targeted tissue, which makes them attractive for killing tumors with limited harm to surrounding areas.

The review explains the physics of light-to-heat conversion in plain terms. It sorts the main material families and their strengths. It then covers uses in cancer therapy, imaging, and beyond, and the safety work still needed. The paper is a full guide to a hot field.
europmc-pmc10320150:
Lu and colleagues released MicrobiomeAnalyst 2.0 in 2023, a free tool for studies of microbe groups. A microbiome is the full set of microbes that live in a place, such as the gut. Studies of these groups make large and complex data sets. The tool helps users test, chart, and read such data.

Three new parts headline the update from Lu. One part cleans raw gene data and names the microbes in it. A second part joins microbe data with data on small chemicals from the same samples. A third part merges results from many studies to find shared patterns. The team showed these tools on data from a type 1 diabetes study.
europmc-pmc10420750: A scientific account of the United States Exploring Expedition of 1838 to 1842. The great naval voyage of discovery. This paper preserves that expedition's findings. Future scholars will discover it. History keeps its place secure. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc10858950:
Mallick and co-authors describe a shared archive of ancient human genomes in this 2024 paper. Ancient DNA is genetic material read from the remains of people who died long ago. More than 200 papers have published genome-wide data from such remains. Raw data are mostly public, but formats differ from study to study, which makes joint work hard.

The Allen Ancient DNA Resource, kept since 2019, cleans and unifies those records. It holds data at over a million DNA spots for each person. By late 2022 it passed 10,000 ancient people, and it had seen six public releases. The note serves as a citable record of the archive. The authors aim to give the field one versioned source that all can download and trust.
europmc-pmc11515850:
Vollmer and a large team pose 20 critical questions for machine learning research aimed at patient benefit in this 2020 paper. Machine learning and AI open new ways to use growing health data. Yet the wider literature lacks openness, clear reporting for replication, attention to ethics, and clear proof of effectiveness. The authors trace part of the problem to missing best-practice guidance specific to these methods.

Their 20 questions form a framework called TREE, for transparency, reproducibility, ethics, and effectiveness. Research groups can use them to shape study design, conduct, and reporting. Editors and peer reviewers can use them to judge submissions. Funders and regulators are also addressed. The questions were built for interdisciplinary health projects. The authors offer the set as a preliminary solution and invite wider adoption.
europmc-pmc1241550:
Welshons and co-authors argued small hormone-like exposures can act strongly in 2003. Estrogen-like chemicals from the environment reach hormone receptors. Standard lab safety tests use very high doses. The authors say that habit badly understates real activity.

Hormone systems respond at tiny receptor occupancy levels. Responses also saturate, so straight-line forecasts from high doses fail. Some responses rise then fall as dose increases. That pattern breaks the more-dose-more-effect assumption entirely. Welshons lays out mechanism-based reasons to test low doses directly. Natural hormone levels in the body set the relevant range. It is part one of a two-part series.
europmc-pmc1310650:
Zhang and co-authors surveyed RNA viruses in healthy human feces in 2006. The gut hosts many viruses, but the healthy RNA community was undescribed. Samples came from three specimens of two healthy people. Viruses were concentrated and their RNA sequenced in bulk.

Of 36,769 viral sequences, most matched plant pathogenic viruses. Pepper mild mottle virus was the most abundant fecal virus. It reached up to a billion particles per gram of dry feces. It also appeared in 12 of 18 healthy people across two continents. Pepper-based foods tested positive as the likely source.
europmc-pmc1489950:
Chunks of foreign DNA, called genomic islands, let bacteria adapt fast. Waack and co-authors built a program in 2006 to spot them. Such islands arrive by horizontal transfer, the passing of genes between germs. They often carry several genes for harm or partnership.

The program, SIGI-HMM, reads each gene's codon usage, the dialect of its DNA code. Foreign genes speak a unlike dialect from their host. The tool flags alien genes, guesses their donor, and masks the host's own busy genes. Tests matched known findings. Waack offers the program free, taking standard genome files as input.
europmc-pmc1800850:
Hutchinson, Chess and co-authors screened in 2007 for large RNA molecules that stay in the cell nucleus and never become proteins. Such noncoding RNAs were suspected to help control genes, but the big ones had drawn less attention than tiny ones. The team used gene chips to find copied RNAs that are enriched in the nucleus.

The screen turned up only three transcripts. One was XIST, a known noncoding RNA. The other two, named NEAT1 and NEAT2, sit less than 70 thousand DNA letters apart on human chromosome 11. NEAT2 is conserved across mammals to a striking degree, even more than XIST, which hints at real function. Microscope tests tied both RNAs to SC35 speckles, nuclear spots involved in processing messenger RNA.
europmc-pmc1949050:
Comeau, Krisch and co-authors found in 2007 that low doses of some antibiotics make bacteria produce far more virus particles. Bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, shape the whole biosphere, yet environmental effects on their production were little studied. The effect appeared with virulent phages that kill their hosts.

A low dose of cefotaxime, a cephalosporin antibiotic, raised one E. coli strain's output of its phage more than sevenfold. The team named the effect Phage-Antibiotic Synergy, or PAS. It recurred across varied host and phage pairs, including T4-like phages, with beta-lactam and quinolone antibiotics and with mitomycin C. All these drugs halt cell division and stretch bacteria into filaments. The synergy proved independent of the SOS stress response and was mimicked by cells that filament on their own, pointing to cell shape as the driver.
europmc-pmc2008650:
Kerr, Wyllie and Currie named and described apoptosis in 1972, a controlled way for the body to delete cells. The process balances mitosis, the division that adds cells. Its features suggested an active, programmed event, not random damage. Both normal and harmful signals could start or stop it. The authors set out its two stages and wide roles in tissue change.

First the nucleus and cell body shrink and split into membrane-bound fragments. Those fragments, called apoptotic bodies, are shed or taken up by nearby cells. Inside those cells they are rapidly broken down by enzymes. Apoptosis removes cells during embryo development and normal tissue turnover. It also occurs in untreated tumours and in shrinking tissues.
europmc-pmc2072850:
Fei, McLaughlin, Tarone and Olsen examined fluorinated chemicals and fetal growth in Denmark in 2007. PFOS and PFOA are man-made pollutants that persist in the body for years. Animal work suggested they might slow growth before birth. The team randomly selected 1,400 mothers and infants from the Danish National Birth Cohort. Blood was drawn early in pregnancy, between weeks four and fourteen.

Average maternal levels were 35.3 nanograms per millilitre for PFOS and 5.6 for PFOA, and those measures frame the exposure range studied here in this cohort of healthy single births. Only PFOA showed a link, with higher levels tied to lower birth weight by about 10.63 grams per unit, and confidence limits just excluding zero. Neither chemical consistently linked to preterm birth, low birth weight or small size for pregnancy length.
europmc-pmc2118050: A medical paper on chronic pancreatitis and the islands of Langerhans. The pancreas, studied. This article preserves that pathology research. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2125050: A medical paper on the possible importance of colloidal protection in protein phases. The protected colloids. This article preserves that chemistry. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2125250: Grafts still meet the body's guards, and this paper showed how the blood's clump-factors swayed the graft's fate. The team tracked which grafts lived. The guarded grafts, studied. The article keeps that graft study.
europmc-pmc2125350: Feeding rabbits pure cholesterol gave them diseased arteries, as this paper showed. Atheroma and other lesions appeared in the animals' vessels. The fatty diet's damage, documented. The article preserves that early cardiovascular research. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2125450: A medical paper with experiments on malaria parasite development in three American mosquito species. The vectors. This article preserves that parasitology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2128250: A medical paper on experimental syphilis in the rabbit, local dissemination and recurrence. The spreading pox. This article preserves that venereology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2128550: A medical paper on flagellar agglutinins. The tail antibodies. This article preserves that immunology. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. The historical record keeps it. Kept for readers. The archive guards it with care for all readers.
europmc-pmc2131650: A medical paper with studies on immunological relationships among the pneumococci, active immunization. The germs' kinship again. This article preserves that immunology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2140650: A biology paper with a cell for the measurement of cataphoresis of ultramicroscopic particles. The tiny movers, measured. This article preserves that biophysics. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140850: A biology paper on molecular structure of plant fibers determined by X-rays. The fiber's structure. This article preserves that botany. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2395250:
Tomoyasu and co-authors surveyed the red flour beetle's gene-silencing machinery in 2008. The technique is RNA interference, where small RNA pieces switch off matching genes. In the beetle Tribolium, silencing spreads through the whole body, a property called systemic RNAi, which makes the insect a strong lab model.

They searched the beetle genome for every gene tied to the silencing machinery. The beetle clearly shows the same body-wide response as the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, the classic case. Yet the worm's key spreading genes were missing in the beetle, and its machinery differed in detail. The authors concluded that insects likely spread the silencing signal by a different mechanism than worms do. Their catalogue gives researchers the parts list for finding that mechanism.
europmc-pmc2410050:
Matsumura and colleagues ran the first human trial of a micelle-packed cancer drug in 2004. The drug was doxorubicin, a potent but harsh chemotherapy agent, loaded into NK911, a carrier made of polymer micelles. These tiny spheres slip out of leaky tumor blood vessels and linger in tumors, a quirk called the EPR effect.

Twenty-three patients with solid tumors got the drug by infusion every three weeks, with doses rising by a fast-escalation plan. The main harm was a drop in white blood cells, severe at the top doses. The maximum tolerated dose settled at 67 milligrams per square metre of body surface, and 50 was set for the next trial phase. Blood levels of the carrier rose in step with dose. One patient with metastatic pancreatic cancer had a partial tumor shrinkage.
europmc-pmc2429950:
Tjitra and colleagues tracked malaria cases at a hospital in Papua, Indonesia, from 2004 to 2007 in this 2008 study. The region's malaria parasites resist many drugs, including the vivax species long dismissed as mild. The team recorded every outpatient and inpatient malaria case at the area's only hospital.

Malaria made up 16% of outpatient visits and 32% of admissions, with 60,226 outpatient cases in all. Among admitted patients, 22% had severe disease. Severe illness was actually more common in vivax infections, at 23%, than in falciparum infections, at 20%, and worst in mixed infections at 31% in this data. Severe anaemia, dangerously low red cell levels, drove most vivax complications. In children under one year, vivax caused 47% of malaria admissions. Overall 2.0% of admitted malaria patients died.
europmc-pmc2483250:
Perrone and colleagues compared lung immune responses to deadly versus mild flu in mice in 2008. The 1918 pandemic virus and bird flu H5N1 both cause severe lung damage in people, with swelling and massive inflammation. The team infected mice with rebuilt versions of these viruses and with gentler flu strains.

Using a cell-sorting method called flow cytometry, they counted immune cells flooding the lungs. The deadly viruses drew in far more macrophages and neutrophils, the two front-line cell types, and drew them in fast. The 1918 virus and the H5N1 isolate behaved very similarly in cell numbers and timing. One difference stood out: H5N1 provoked clearly higher levels of inflammatory signalling molecules in mouse lungs and in human macrophages grown in dishes. The authors suggested the early, excessive cell flood helps drive the lung injury that makes these infections fatal.
europmc-pmc2631150:
Need and a large team of collaborators scanned the genomes of schizophrenia patients in 2009 for both common variants and copy number variants, stretches of DNA deleted or duplicated. They genotyped 871 patients and 863 controls, then followed the top signals in four more cohorts totalling 1,460 patients and 12,995 controls. Everyone was of European origin.

No common variant reached genome-wide significance, and previously reported candidates found no support. The copy number analysis told a different story: eight patients and zero controls carried deletions larger than 2 million DNA letters, including two newly reported regions. That imbalance suggests very large deletions in a patient carry a high chance of mattering. Smaller deletions near the genes NRXN1 and APBA2 gained further support. The authors conclude rare harmful variants likely matter more than common ones in schizophrenia.
europmc-pmc2696450:
Blom and colleagues built in 2009 EDGAR, a software framework that compares related bacterial genomes automatically. Sequencing had made such comparisons feasible for whole genera, but matching genes across genomes by hand does not scale. EDGAR's core task is sorting genes into shared families, private singletons, and the common core every strain carries.

The system scores gene matches by ratios that correct for genome size differences, then precomputes comparisons for hundreds of genomes at once. Its database at launch held 582 genomes grouped into 75 genera. As a demonstration, the team compared ten genomes of Xanthomonas, a plant pathogen group whose family tree had been tangled by rival naming systems. EDGAR's tree matched careful traditional studies and rooted each strain more precisely than before. Web tools, including Venn diagrams and alignment plots, make the results browsable without programming.
europmc-pmc2721850:
Chaudhuri and co-authors built a method in 2009 to find all genes that Staphylococcus aureus, a drug-resistant hospital pathogen, needs to survive and grow. Such essential genes are prime targets for new antibiotics. Their method, called TMDH, inserts jumping DNA pieces at random and flags genes where no insert can survive.

Screening a library of about a million mutants, then rechecking missing genes with a second test, yielded three hundred fifty-one essential genes. Comparing that list with a related bacterium, Bacillus subtilis, revealed differences in both whole pathways and single genes. The list gives drug hunters a starting map, and the method can be reused in other pathogens.
europmc-pmc2726950:
Le Martelot and co-authors showed in 2009 that REV-ERB alpha, a clock-controlled nuclear receptor, shapes the daily rhythm of SREBP signaling in the liver. SREBP is a factor that switches on genes for making cholesterol and bile acids. Both processes rise and fall with the body clock, which times body functions to the day-night cycle.

In mice, loss of REV-ERB alpha disturbed the daily activity profile of SREBP and its target genes. That shifted cholesterol and bile acid balance across the day. The work places REV-ERB alpha as a link between the core clock and liver lipid control, tying the timing system directly to how the liver handles fats and bile.
europmc-pmc2734850:
Lawrence, Mitrou, and Zubrick compared in 2009 smoking and mental illness in population surveys from Australia and the United States. People with mental illness die early from smoking-related diseases such as heart disease and cancer. Many people who meet criteria for a mental disorder never seek treatment, so clinic samples miss the full picture.

In both countries, adults with a mental disorder in the past year smoked at almost twice the rate of adults without one. About one third of adult smokers had a recent mental disorder, with higher shares in women and the young. Most smokers with mental illness were not in contact with mental health services. Smokers under high distress also smoked more cigarettes per day.
europmc-pmc2791750:
Hayes and co-authors tested how well DNA-based breeding values predict merit in dairy cattle when herds mix two breeds. Breeders use these genomic values to pick young bulls before any calves are milked. Predictions built in one breed often fail in another, which hurts smaller breeds with few reference animals.

The team predicted values for young Holstein and Jersey bulls using single-breed and mixed reference herds, with three math methods. Standard prediction matched its own accuracy estimates within single breeds but not across mixed herds. Two Bayesian methods, which estimate each marker's effect, gained up to thirteen percent in accuracy from the mixed herd for some traits.
europmc-pmc2808350:
Lamba, McUsic, Hirata, Wang, Russell, and Reh grew light-sensing eye cells in 2010 from human induced pluripotent stem cells, which are adult cells rewound to a stem-like state. Retinal diseases that kill these cells, called photoreceptors, rank among the main causes of blindness, and replacement cells could one day restore sight.

Starting from skin cells, the team steered the rewound cells toward a retinal fate using their earlier recipe for embryonic stem cells. A glowing tag lit up true photoreceptors, letting the team sort out a pure batch. Planted into a normal mouse retina, the sorted cells settled into the tissue and switched on photoreceptor proteins, a step toward patient-matched transplants.
europmc-pmc2811150:
Dellicour, Tatem, Guerra, Snow, and ter Kuile produced the first modern global count in 2010 of pregnancies exposed to malaria each year. Malaria in pregnancy can kill the mother and harm the unborn child, yet planners lacked solid numbers outside Africa. The team combined malaria risk maps with United Nations population data for 2007.

They counted about one hundred twenty-five million pregnancies in areas where malaria circulates. Roughly eighty-five million of them fell in zones with Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, and tens of millions more where the vivax parasite occurs. The tally gives health programs a firm base for sizing drug and net needs for pregnant women.
europmc-pmc2838750:
Innocenti and Morrow hunted in 2010 for sexually antagonistic genes in fruit flies, genes where the version that helps males hurts females, or the reverse. Males and females thrive on different trait settings, so evolution pulls the same genes in opposite directions. The team measured adult fitness for one hundred genome copies, each tested in male bodies and in female bodies.

Fitness measured in males traded off against fitness measured in females, confirming the tug-of-war at the whole-genome level. By tying those fitness scores to each gene's activity in the two sexes, the authors produced the first genome-wide estimate of how many antagonistic genes the fly carries. They also built a candidate list with the genes' locations and jobs.
europmc-pmc2848550:
Nica and colleagues proposed a statistical method in 2010 for deciding which genome-wide association hits truly act by changing gene activity. Association scans flag DNA variants near many genes, and expression studies flag variants that alter gene output. But the two flags often coincide by chance, because nearby variants travel together in the genome.

Their Regulatory Trait Concordance score weighs the full local pattern of both signals, accounting for that correlation, and beat simpler correlation measures in simulations with one or two causal variants. Applied to published association loci, it singled out plausible causal genes, with a strong tilt toward immune conditions matching the blood cells used. A genome-wide extension also traces downstream effects of a disease variant.
europmc-pmc2859250:
Otto and co-authors used a new deep sequencing method in 2010 to map gene activity in the malaria parasite while it grows inside red blood cells. The method, called RNA-Seq, reads millions of RNA copies to show which genes are on. They sampled the parasite, Plasmodium falciparum, at seven points across its two-day cycle in the blood.

About seven in ten reads matched known protein-coding genes, and the patterns agreed well with older chip-based tests on the same samples. The data forced changes to more than one in ten gene models in the genome. Otto also confirmed most predicted splice sites, found hundreds of new ones, and uncovered over one hundred brand-new transcripts plus activity from genes long thought silent.
europmc-pmc2876750:
Van Loo and colleagues documented in 2007 a drug-resistant staph germ moving from Dutch farm animals into people. MRSA, a staphylococcus that resists standard antibiotics, was long a hospital problem. Starting in 2003 the Netherlands saw cases of a type that standard fingerprinting could not classify, and many patients had contact with pig farms.

The untypable strain traced to one genetic family common on pig and cattle farms. By the study period it caused over a fifth of all human MRSA cases in the country. Its features differed from both hospital strains and the community strains then known, marking a genuinely new animal route into people. Farming families and their contacts formed the risk group, which changed how Dutch screening was targeted.
europmc-pmc2885750:
Barbe and colleagues resequenced in 2009 the genome of Bacillus subtilis, the model bacterium for a huge branch of bacteria, a decade after the first version. The original sequence came from over thirty laboratories with uneven early-era technique, so errors had accumulated. Modern fast sequencing let the team rebuild the reference from scratch.

The unified sequence corrected the scattered mistakes of the consortium version and was reannotated to match the leading protein database. The authors frame the genome as two layers. The paleome holds genes needed to sustain and perpetuate life itself. The cenome holds genes a cell needs to thrive in its chosen niche. A trustworthy reference matters because thousands of gene-function claims rest on comparisons against this one bacterium's map.
europmc-pmc2906150:
Powers, Duarte, Kavazis, and Talbert reviewed in 2010 how reactive oxygen species, the cell-damaging molecules once blamed purely for harm, actually signal skeletal muscle to adapt. Working muscle makes more of these species, and so, paradoxically, does muscle left idle for long periods. Both exercise training and disuse remodel muscle, and the review argues the same chemical signal helps drive both remodelings.

The species flip redox-sensitive switches, including signal enzymes and the inflammation-linked transcription factor NF-kappaB, which then set gene programs for building endurance proteins or shedding unused tissue. The authors map where in the fiber the species are produced and which switches answer. Unanswered questions close the piece, especially how one signal yields opposite adaptations for training versus wasting.
europmc-pmc2915950:
Schaar, Brenneman, and Savitz reviewed in 2010 the behavioral tests used to judge recovery in rodent stroke models, where a therapy's promise must be read from movement, sensation, and thinking. Human stroke leaves devastating mixed deficits, and candidate treatments are legion, so animal outcome tests carry the field's translational hopes. The review surveys the standard battery, from simple reflex and walking tasks to fine paw skills and maze learning.

Each test catches a different slice of impairment: some flag any deficit cheaply, others isolate one modality like touch or forelimb use. No single test is perfect, and insensitive choices can bury a real treatment effect or flatter a useless one. Matching test sensitivity and timing to the stroke model is the authors' central advice for labs designing studies.
europmc-pmc3024950:
Atwood and coauthors profiled in 2011 which signaling receptors four widely used lab cell lines already carry on their own. The receptors belong to the GPCR family, a huge group that senses hormones, light, and many drugs. Lines such as human kidney HEK293 cells are often treated as blank slates for testing one added receptor, yet they quietly express many of their own.

Using gene chip arrays, the team measured the messages for hundreds of these receptors and over a hundred related signaling proteins. They covered four lines used often in receptor research, including mouse and rat lines. The resulting profiles are offered as an easy reference. Choosing a line whose built in receptors will not clash with a planned test can save months of confused results.
europmc-pmc3037350:
Lamarque and colleagues showed in 2011 how malaria and related parasites force their way into host cells. These parasites, called apicomplexans, must live inside cells and enter through a tight grip point that anchors them as they push in. Two proteins meet at that grip point, one from the parasite surface and one planted into the host cell wall.

Working with both the malaria parasite and its relative Toxoplasma, the team mapped exactly which part of the planted protein grabs its partner. Blocking that grip with lab made protein pieces stopped both parasites from entering cells. The pairing is kept within each species even though the proteins differ between species. The result names a clear weak point that future drugs or vaccines could target.
europmc-pmc3063350:
Stagg, Bachtiar, and Johansen-Berg asked in 2011 why some healthy adults learn new movement skills faster than others, pointing to a brain calming chemical called GABA. Adjusting GABA levels is known to be part of how the motor cortex rewires during learning. The team measured how much each volunteer's GABA dropped after a gentle electrical stimulation known to lower it, then tested motor learning inside a scanner on another day.

People whose GABA fell the most also learned the finger sequence task the fastest. Their motor cortex activity changed the most during learning as well. The link held at the individual level, not just on average. The authors suggest that a flexible GABA system is part of what makes a brain ready to learn. That could matter for stroke rehabilitation, where relearning movement is the whole task.
europmc-pmc3121750:
Chuong Do and colleagues ran an online gene hunt for Parkinson disease, reported in PLoS Genetics in 2011. Rather than recruiting through clinics, they gathered thousands of patients through a web-based company and surveys, then compared their DNA with a far larger control group. The design tested whether internet recruitment could power serious gene studies.

Two new DNA regions linked to the disease turned up, near genes involved in fat handling and cell recycling, and both held up in a separate group. Twenty known links were confirmed as well. Shared DNA patterns suggested genes explain at least a fair share of risk, though most of the genetic story remains hidden. The study proves web recruitment works and adds fresh leads on causes.
europmc-pmc3141050:
Kim van Wijck and colleagues measured gut damage from hard exercise in healthy men in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. During exertion, blood is diverted from the gut to muscles, a pattern also seen in illness, but its effect on the healthy gut was untested. Men cycled for an hour at a strong pace while the team tracked gut blood flow and damage markers.

Gut blood flow fell fast, and the deeper the fall, the higher blood markers of small-intestine cell injury rose. Leakiness of the gut wall also increased after exercise, in step with the injury markers. Liver measures rose slightly, kidney measures did not. Even in fit volunteers, an hour of hard cycling measurably injures and loosens the gut barrier, a finding relevant to athletes and patients alike.
europmc-pmc3145650:
Etay Hay and colleagues built detailed computer models of a key cortical nerve cell in a 2011 paper in PLoS Computational Biology. The cell type sends branches through all layers of the cortex and anchors its columns. Yet existing models could not copy both its body firing and its branch spikes at once. The team gathered extensive recordings from rat cells, in body and branches alike.

An automatic search method tuned channel densities across the cell surface until the models matched real firing patterns, including their natural variation between cells. The model set reproduces the main spike types and predicts testable behaviours. Analysing the set also revealed which mechanisms set the cell's dynamics and which bend with cell shape. The framework can now be reused for other neuron types.
europmc-pmc3161750:
Jianshe Lang and colleagues showed how a milk protein blocks the SARS virus from entering cells in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. The protein, lactoferrin, was known to rally immune cells against the virus, but a direct blocking effect was untested. Using a harmless stand-in virus carrying the SARS entry spike, they dosed human cells fitted with the virus's receptor.

The protein stopped infection in proportion to dose, acting at the attachment step before entry. It did not disturb the spike's grip on its main receptor, though. Instead it coated sugary chains on the cell surface that the virus uses as first landing pads. Stripping those chains, or flooding them with a similar sugar, copied the effect. The findings name those chains as essential entry helpers and suggest the milk protein as a defence lead.
europmc-pmc3198950:
Noel O'Boyle and colleagues presented Open Babel in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Cheminformatics. Chemists store molecular structures in many incompatible file formats, and converting between them is a constant chore in computer modeling. Open Babel is a free, open-source toolbox built to translate between those formats, handling more than one hundred and ten of them in the version described.

Beyond conversion, the toolbox supplies algorithms chemists need daily, such as assigning partial charges, detecting aromatic rings, perceiving bond orders, and producing canonical forms of a structure. The paper details the design of the new release and shows uses from conformer searching and two-dimensional drawing to filtering, batch conversion, and similarity searching. Developers can also embed it as a library in their own software.
europmc-pmc3207950:
Paul Magwene, John Willis, and John Kelly built a statistical framework for bulk segregant analysis with modern sequencing in this 2011 paper in PLoS Computational Biology. The technique hunts for genes behind a trait by pooling offspring that show the trait and sequencing the pool, looking for regions where allele frequencies shift.

Their method smooths the standard test statistic and accounts for two sources of noise: sampling when the pools are formed, and sampling during sequencing itself. Simulations explored how pool size and sequencing depth affect the power to detect trait-linked regions. Surprisingly, larger pools worked best, even though they dilute the signal. The authors show the approach can find even weak-effect loci, and they demonstrate it on a yeast experiment.
europmc-pmc3291550:
Snelders and co-authors asked whether farm fungicides could train a mold to resist medical drugs, in a 2012 study. The mold Aspergillus fumigatus causes serious lung disease, and doctors treat it with a small set of triazole drugs. Resistant strains carrying a paired genetic change had begun appearing in patients, including some who never took the drugs.

The team compared dozens of farm chemicals approved in the Netherlands over past decades with the medical drugs. Five farm triazoles matched the medicines closely in shape and in how they dock onto the target protein, and they produced the strongest cross resistance. Those five entered use just before the first resistant patient strain appeared, and lab tests showed spray pressure alone could push the genetic change further.
europmc-pmc3314950:
Mischo and colleagues showed that a yeast protein guards the genome while genes are being read, in a 2011 study. The protein, named Sen1, was known for helping to end the copying of certain RNA messages. When a fresh RNA strand sticks back onto the DNA it came from, it forms a loop that leaves one DNA strand exposed and fragile.

Without working Sen1, these loops pile up in baker's yeast and trigger unwanted swapping between DNA regions during gene reading. The protein's unwinding action normally clears the loops away. Genes for DNA repair also interact with Sen1, suggesting repair crews finish the cleanup. The authors argue that loop formation happens often during normal gene activity, and that stopping it is a core part of Sen1's job.
europmc-pmc3324550:
Bhullar and co-authors found widespread antibiotic resistance in bacteria from a cave cut off from the surface for millions of years, reporting in 2012. The cave, Lechuguilla Cave in New Mexico, holds microbial communities isolated for over four million years, untouched by human medicine. If resistance were mainly a product of modern drug use, these bacteria should have shown little of it.

Instead, many cave strains resisted a wide range of modern antibiotics, and some shrugged off fourteen different drugs. Resistance even covered a last resort drug used against stubborn infections. The team uncovered enzyme based tricks the bacteria use to disable drugs, including one gene closely related to resistance genes now circulating in hospitals. The authors argue that resistance is ancient and natural, built into microbial life long before pharmacies existed.
europmc-pmc3334750:
Gonçalves-Pereira and Póvoa reviewed how the body handles a major class of antibiotics in intensive care patients, in a 2011 paper. Beta lactam antibiotics kill bacteria only while their level stays above a threshold, so dosing depends on predictable drug handling. Critically ill patients, the authors suspected, break the predictions borrowed from healthy volunteers.

Surveying fifty seven studies covering six widely used drugs, they found striking variation from patient to patient. The space the drug spreads into and the speed the body clears it each varied more than two fold, tied partly to kidney function. Half lives and time above the killing threshold were nearly impossible to predict, especially in patients whose kidneys looked normal. Slow, prolonged infusions usually gave better coverage, and drug entry into infected tissues faltered in septic shock. The authors urge dosing guided by drug level monitoring.
europmc-pmc3367650:
Dumler and co-authors reviewed human granulocytic anaplasmosis in 2005, a tick-borne illness first recognized in 1990. The sickness is caused by a bacterium that lives inside neutrophils, the white blood cells that normally fight infection. Cases had been climbing in the United States since the disease was first described.

The review traces how the germ was separated from a related ehrlichiosis and renamed Anaplasma phagocytophilum. It describes the usual picture of fever, headache, muscle pain, low white cell counts, and mild liver injury. Dumler also explains how the bacterium changes the cells it infects. That grounding helps doctors spot, treat, and prevent a severe illness that is easy to miss.
europmc-pmc3383750:
Stuckler, McKee, Ebrahim, and Basu examined in 2012 how global producers drive rising use of unhealthy goods in poorer countries. The goods include soft drinks, salty and fatty processed foods, alcohol, and tobacco. Consumption was climbing fastest in low- and middle-income countries, while rich countries had largely leveled off.

Growth in poorer countries, they report, is running even faster than it once did in rich ones. Multinational firms have penetrated middle-income food markets about as deeply as rich-country ones. Sales of unhealthy foods track closely with tobacco and alcohol sales, hinting at shared industry tactics. Rising income alone does not doom a country; trade and investment deals shape the outcome.
europmc-pmc3431850:
Singh and Li reviewed in 2012 how two plastic chemicals, bisphenol A and phthalates, rewrite the chemical tags that control genes. Such epigenetic marks, on DNA and its packaging proteins, can change gene activity for life after exposure in the womb. The review gathers evidence from cell and animal studies.

In yellow mice, bisphenol A stripped tags near a coat-color gene, and feeding mothers folate or a plant estrogen blocked the effect. The chemical also altered tags in human breast and placental cells and shifted tiny regulatory RNAs. A phthalate loosened tags on the estrogen receptor gene in breast cancer cells, while another raised tag-writing enzymes in mouse testis. Some effects in rats passed to later generations.

everard-divine-pymander-1650:

The dialogues claim an age older than Moses in their own telling. Everard, a clergyman with mystical leanings, gives them plain, strong English. Seekers of secret lore treasured the book for generations afterward here. It carried strange old wisdom into a land at war with itself, and its influence ran through English occult thought for centuries.

frus-1861-d150:
A letter of 5 September 1861 went from William H. Seward to William Dayton in Paris. The letter is document 150 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

September letters from Seward turn to trade, ships, and the fine print of neutrality. The grand pleas of spring gave way to detail. This note to Paris shows high policy becoming clerk's work, which is where it was won or lost. Detail, Seward knew, was where neutral pledges were kept or quietly broken. Neutral pledges live or die in details, and Seward never forgot that truth. Fine print was where pledges lived or died.
frus-1861-d250:
Writing on 4 September 1861, James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 250 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d50:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 June 1861. The dispatch is document 50 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams wrote in a spare, exact style that Seward learned to trust. His June reports cover talks, notes, and the mood of the British press. For readers, they are a model of how a skilled envoy turns daily talk into clear word for his chief. Seward read Adams's reports with close care and often shared them with the cabinet. Cabinet eyes on his pages made Adams the best read envoy of the war.
frus-1862-d150:
Circular No. 24, dated 25 September 1862, is Document 150 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. A circular was not a private letter but a single set of orders sent at the same time to many American envoys and consuls abroad. So that all of them spoke with one voice.

Seward used circulars when Washington needed the same line taken in every capital at once. This one went out three days after Lincoln announced his emancipation plan, in a week when foreign governments were reassessing the war. It shows the State Department managing its whole foreign service as one body, not post by post.
frus-1862-d250:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 21 January 1862 in a letter printed as Document 250 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward, though it stands in the file after a later Seward letter.

The printers grouped some papers out of date order, so this report follows the dispatch it may have crossed at sea. Dayton's mail gave Washington its best read on Napoleon III's court, where policy could shift with one man's mood. Reports from his hand shaped how the Union handled France all year. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d350:
Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 December 1861, in a letter printed as Document 350 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mercier wrote two days before Washington settled the Trent affair by freeing the seized envoys. French diplomacy had counseled calm in that crisis, which Washington noted with gratitude. His letter belongs to the closing days of the year's worst foreign scare, when the French channel proved one of the steadiest Seward had. The French legation's notes were written in French and printed here in the Department's English. Cases in this channel often mixed the war at home with French designs in Mexico.
frus-1862-d450:
John Lothrop Motley, the American minister in Vienna, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 January 1862. It is Document 450 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, opening the Austrian file.

Motley was already famous as the historian of the Dutch republic when Lincoln sent him to Austria. Vienna was a conservative court, cool toward republics, and its view of the American war was shaped by its fear of revolution at home. Seward's opening order for the year armed Motley with the Union's case. The dispatch begins a file written by one of the most literary men ever to hold an American post abroad.
frus-1862-d50:
Seward wrote again on 19 April 1862, this time to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 50 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d550:
A second note of 30 September 1862 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Roest van Limburg. It stands as Document 550 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, beside its same-day companion.

Paired notes on one day meant separate subjects, each answered in its own letter under the Department's standing practice. The Dutch file had run that way since June, and the habit gives the modern reader a clean record: no mixed paragraphs, no buried answers. Van Limburg's government got from Seward that day two distinct statements it could file and quote. The pair closes the September Dutch exchange, one of the most orderly in a volume full of harder and hotter correspondence.
frus-1862-d650:
Dated 17 May 1862, this dispatch from Robert H. Pruyn reached Secretary of State William H. Seward as part of the regular mail from Japan. Pruyn was the American minister there, in the first weeks of his time in the post. The letter is document 650 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Note the dates around it: Pruyn wrote again and again that May, a sign of how much a new envoy had to report. His letters told Washington about the legation's talks and troubles in a land the United States had known for less than a decade. Each one adds a page to that early record.
frus-1863p1-d150:
On 9 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 150 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, carrying a round number in the count.

The middle sheet of Adams's 9 April set holds its own head of the brief, as his sets always did. That spring the heads were ships and the law that might hold them. This letter is the second of the three. With its mates, it rounds out a day on which the London post worked the full width of the Union's case in Britain.
frus-1863p1-d250: Document 250 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume is an untitled paper dated 28 July 1863. It sits inside the long run of letters between Secretary of State William H. Seward and Charles Francis Adams in London, the channel that handled relations with Britain during the Civil War. The catalog gives it no title or author, so its place in that correspondence is what the record shows.
frus-1863p1-d350: On 3 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 350 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d450:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State took up his pen on 7 April 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d50: This untitled paper is dated 25 October 1862 and printed as document 50 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It sits inside the group of Confederate letters in that part, between papers of Mallory and Memminger. The evidence gives its date and place in the run, but no title, writer, or name addressed.
frus-1863p1-d550:
William H. Seward took up his pen on 5 June 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d650:
On 29 October 1863, the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d150: The Joint Chiefs of Staff wrote to Ambassador Harriman in Moscow on November 20, 1943, and the letter is Document 150 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A message from the chiefs as a body to an ambassador was a weighty channel, used when military and diplomatic lines had to meet. The record gives the senders, the receiver, and the date. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d250:
A dinner meeting at Cairo involving President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill is covered by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. The fact of the meeting and the names of those present come from the President's Log, and no record of what was discussed at the dinner has been found.

The editors add one careful pointer. Later documents in the volume show that Roosevelt raised the future status of Hong Kong with Churchill at Cairo. There is, however, no sign showing whether that subject came up at this particular dinner or at some other meeting between the two men during the conference.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d350:
Steve Early, the President's secretary, telegraphed Harry Hopkins from Washington on 2 December 1943 with the American reaction to the Cairo communiqué. Sent by military channels, the message mixes celebration at the statement's reception with anger at how its secrecy was broken.

The communiqué, Early reports, was received with enthusiasm across the country, with great praise and jubilation in all quarters. That came despite Reuters' Lisbon dispatch. The dispatch printed virtually the whole Cairo story almost twenty-four hours before the release. It cut the statement's force. It also let German and Japanese propagandists broadcast their versions in the gap. Early urges shorter intervals between distribution and publication for any future communiqués, and a strict ban on sending their contents abroad before the release date.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d450: Document 450 is a short piece of editorial writing, not a 1943 dispatch. Historians in the Office of the Historian prepared notes like it for the Cairo-Tehran volume. They use the notes to add context the wartime papers lack. Sometimes they point to documents printed elsewhere in the series. The conferences covered here shaped Allied plans for 1944 and beyond. A reader gets orientation before returning to the primary papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d50: Roosevelt answered Hull on October 21, 1943, the same day the secretary's letter in this series was written. The reply is Document 50 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. With his secretary of state in Moscow and the Tehran summit five weeks away, the president kept a close hand on the talks. The record gives the date and the two men. The exchange is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d550:
President Roosevelt wrote to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on January 24, 1944, answering the flow of department business with a presidential message of his own. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

The Roosevelt-Hull channel ran both ways all winter: reports and requests went up, decisions and instructions came down. January 1944 was a month of consolidation, when the Tehran and Cairo results were being turned into policy on Poland's future, Germany's treatment, and the coming invasion. For readers, this message shows the President working the machinery of his own government between summits, in writing.
frus-1944-quebec-d150:
Eisenhower sent the Combined Chiefs his recommendations on taking command of the Dragoon forces on September 9, 1944. The southern France armies were racing north, and by September 15 they would be strong around Dijon.
