At that point, he proposed, operational control should pass to him, with directives going directly to General Devers.

Air arrangements fill much of the message: the Ninth Air Force would take over the tactical air command supporting Seventh Army, while the Twelfth Air Force kept helping until relieved. Supply, though, should keep flowing from the Mediterranean while American stocks there exceeded local needs. Eisenhower asked that the end of that arrangement be settled by agreement between Wilson and Devers.
frus-1944-quebec-d250:
Stalin answered Roosevelt's message on the Dumbarton Oaks discussions on September 14, 1944, in a secret, personal letter printed here in translation. He hoped the talks on a world organization would end successfully. But he laid down the Soviet condition: the order of voting in the proposed Security Council would decide whether the organization could work at all.

The Council, Stalin argued, must proceed on coordination and unanimity of the four leading powers on all questions, including those directly relating to one of them. That principle, he said, underlay the agreement reached at Tehran for the future struggle against aggression. Without unanimity among the leading powers, the consequences would be grave. He also complained of absurd prejudices that hindered an objective attitude toward the Soviet Union.
frus-1944-quebec-d50:
On September 2, 1944, Churchill wrote again to Roosevelt. The Quebec Conference would open ten days later. The State Department placed the message in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Churchill crossed the Atlantic that week aboard the Queen Mary. He wrote ahead to the President as he traveled. His September letters fixed the British agenda. They covered finishing the war in Europe. They covered settling Germany's treatment after defeat. They also covered Britain's part in the Pacific war. American aid formed part of that case too. For readers, the message shows a case argued in advance. Churchill then argued it in person.
frus-1945-50-intel-d150:
On 9 May 1946, the President’s Chief of Staff (Leahy) sent a memorandum to President Truman. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 150 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d250:
A text titled "Memorandum of Discussion at the 2d Meeting of the National Security Council" bears the date 14 November 1947. It stands as document 250 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. By law the CIA now stood where the Central Intelligence Group had stood, and the National Security Council sat above it.

Where no stenographer sat in, a memcon is the meeting. It holds the talk in the words of the man who wrote it up. So the talk could guide later work, each point is set down while its weight is still clear. The Council was still new, and its early meetings worked out how the president's top advisers would handle defense and foreign policy together.
frus-1945-50-intel-d350:
A memorandum from Robert G. Barnes reached William J. McWilliams of the Executive Secretariat on 25 August 1948. The State Department prints it as document 350 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was a season of stock-taking: the CIA was a year old, and its friends and critics were both writing things down.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d50:
Minutes of the 170th meeting of the Secretary of State's Staff Committee are dated 27 November 1945. Two numbered meetings within a week point to a heavy agenda at the department. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The staff committee was Secretary Byrnes's inner council on department business. Its minutes for late November belong to the weeks when the intelligence plans of State, War. The Budget Bureau were being forced into one shape. Readers should note the pace: the 168th meeting on the 20th, the 170th on the 27th. Institutions meet this often when a decision is near and the details will not settle themselves.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d150:
A new Polish cabinet in London leads the items in this 1 December 1944 briefing for the President. Titled “Special Information for the President,” the memorandum from Secretary Stettinius collects the notable foreign developments of the past few days. The excerpts are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Schoenfeld reports from London that the new Polish government is generally seen as the anti-Russian wing of the exile Poles. Against that, the Lublin Committee's chairman, Osobka-Morawski, has told the Soviet press that his organization will cooperate with Mikolajczyk. But the offer holds only on the platform the Lublin Committee itself supports. Two rival Polish authorities were thus hardening, weeks before the Big Three met.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d250:
Detailed staff talks, not more general talk, are what the Far East now needs, Harriman warned on 10 October 1944. This excerpt from his report to the President, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, looks past Churchill's Moscow visit to the planning that must follow.

Stalin has given full agreement, Harriman writes, not only to join the Pacific war but to enter it with full effort. What remains unknown is what Russia can actually do in the East. The limiting factors are logistics, about which the allies know very little. Churchill's talks with Stalin should therefore stress the weight of the detailed discussions agreed between General Deane and the Red Army Staff. Harriman adds that he has General Ismay's agreement on this line.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d350:
Roosevelt and Churchill lunched together at Livadia Palace at 1 p.m. on February 6, 1945, away from the full table. The record preserved here gives the setting and the company. Harry Hopkins, James Byrnes, and Ambassador Harriman sat on the American side. Sir Alexander Cadogan, the Foreign Office chief, joined Churchill.

No topics are listed in the portion that survives, so the lunch must be read by its place in the week. It fell on the third day of plenary bargaining, between sessions on Germany and the world body. Private talks like this one let the two Western leaders align before facing Stalin again.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d450:
Ambassador Harriman's memorandum gathers his three conversations of February 10, 1945, into one record. At 2 p.m. he called on Molotov at Koreis, at Molotov's request. Molotov handed him, in English translation, the draft of Stalin's political conditions for Russia's entry into the war against Japan. The terms had been discussed with the President on February 8.

Harriman told Molotov there were three amendments he believed the President would wish to make before accepting. Two more conversations followed at Livadia Palace, the last at 4:30 p.m. with Stalin and the President present. The subject was the Far East, on its political side. The secret price of Soviet entry enters the record here.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d50: Churchill sent Roosevelt a further message on 10 January 1945, his third letter in three days. Filed as document 50 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta, it keeps the January sequence intact. The full text appears as the editors printed it, one link in the chain of cables that preceded the Malta meetings by three weeks.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d150:
President Truman set his staff a string of homework questions in a memorandum dated June 9, 1945. The memo to Acting Secretary Grew is document 150 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It responds to the British list of suggested subjects for the summit.

Truman asks for a brief, informal statement of the State Department's position on each British point, plus any subjects the Department thinks should be added. He also asks how the peace terms for Europe should be worked out. Should there be one conference like Dumbarton Oaks, with steady talks until proposals are agreed? Or should there be a series of meetings in different places? Last, he asks the Department's view of a 25-year treaty among the great powers to keep Germany disarmed, along lines Senator Vandenberg had proposed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d250:
Naval aide George Elsey traced the Korea trusteeship idea in an undated memorandum printed as document 250 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The note, prepared for the President's staff, pulls together what the Map Room files held on Korea before the conference.

The Cairo Declaration of 1943 had promised that Korea, enslaved by Japan, would in due course become free and independent. At Yalta, Roosevelt told Stalin he had in mind a trusteeship for Korea of Soviet, American, and Chinese representatives, lasting perhaps twenty to thirty years, with no foreign troops stationed there. Stalin said the shorter the better. By May 1945 Stalin had agreed to a four-power trusteeship adding Britain, and Truman so informed Chiang Kai-shek on June 15.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d350:
Willard Thorp answered MacLeish's draft on the aims of the German occupation in a note dated July 14, 1945. Thorp, deputy to the Assistant Secretary for Economic Affairs, wrote because he could not attend the Staff Committee meeting on Monday. He put his reactions on paper instead, and a copy went to Clayton at Babelsberg.

Present directives, Thorp argues, recognize no single basic objective. The government instead chases a series of aims, some immediate and some long-run, which can clash with each other. His list begins with the reform aim MacLeish stressed, then turns to the removal or destruction of much of Germany's war-making plant.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d450:
The British reply on Greek elections is relayed to Athens in Grew's urgent cable to MacVeagh of July 11, 1945. The Foreign Office telegram of July 9, Grew reports, answers the Department's aide-mémoire favorably. Britain accepts the proposal that invitations to supervise the Greek elections go to the Soviet and French governments from Washington and London, not from Athens.

That procedure departs from the strict letter of the Varkiza Agreement, both sides admit. Britain remains strongly opposed, though, to advising Athens to hold elections before the plebiscite, calling the order a matter of Greek internal politics. London deems it essential the invitations go out this week, so the matter can reach the Big Three talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d50:
Churchill laid out his fears about Soviet power in an extract from telegram number 72 to President Truman, sent June 4, 1945. It is document 50 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Much of the telegram is omitted in print, but the surviving passages show a Prime Minister deeply worried about the American army pulling back in Germany.

Churchill dreads the retreat of American troops to their agreed line, which would bring Soviet power into the heart of Western Europe behind what he calls an iron curtain. He still hopes the meeting date can be moved up, though he accepts July 15 if it cannot. He also says he must bring Labour leader Clement Attlee, so the other powers know they deal with the whole of Britain.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d550:
Britain's chiefs of staff set out a top secret memo at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945. It is document 550 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The paper asks what should happen to the Combined Chiefs of Staff system after Japan falls.

The British chiefs say the joint system has worked well since 1941. They warn that the world will stay troubled for years, and joint work will still be needed. Shared facts, common weapon design, and common training could all help both states. They ask both governments to keep the framework and the habit of consulting. They add that it need not clash with the new world security body's military staff.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d650:
London ambassador Winant reported British thinking on Palestine once more on July 14, 1945. His secret wire is document 650 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It gives the views of the Foreign Office's Eastern Department head, Charles Baxter.

Baxter named two outstanding points. First, it had always been understood that nothing definite would be done on Palestine until the war in Europe ended. That point was now reached, and the next step was being asked for. Second, the immigration quotas would run out by November. Before then, London must make what he called a very important decision. Trouble would almost surely follow either way, since Jews or Arabs would be roused. Baxter expected a short-term plan on immigration, with the big questions deferred to the post-election government.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1050:
Richard Miles, a secretary at the British Embassy in Washington, wrote to John deWilde on July 30, 1945. His short letter passes on an aide-mémoire about the draft directive on coal production in Germany. Miles presumes deWilde will hear from Potsdam about the talks held there.

The enclosure restates London's position. Britain has weighed the revised directive meant for the American commander in Europe. The Foreign Secretary has told Secretary Byrnes that Britain agrees with its terms. A directive in the same words will go to Field Marshal Montgomery as interim instructions for the British zone.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1150:
The Polish team at Potsdam spoke as a body in this memorandum of 28 July 1945. Earlier Polish papers had come from one man, Deputy Premier Mikolajczyk. A paper from the whole team carried a different weight: it was the joint stand of Warsaw's envoys at the summit.

By the last week, the choices on Poland were taking final shape. The team's paper made its shared case once more, on borders, on the vote, and on Poland's place in the new order. It is Warsaw's group effort in the home stretch of the talks. Read beside the solo papers, it shows the Poles closing ranks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1250:
The White House Map Room wrote to Ambassador Hurley in China on 25 July 1945. The Map Room was the president's own message center, the small staff that handled his secret traffic with posts and commanders around the world. Its cables spoke with his authority.

A Map Room message to an envoy carried the president's word without the forms of a department letter. Hurley in China received it as direct guidance from the top. This note shows that swift, private channel at work during the summit. It linked the president's traveling court to a distant post in a single step.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1350:
J. Rives Childs, the American representative in the talks about Tangier, reported to the acting secretary of state on 18 July 1945. Tangier, the port city at the mouth of the Mediterranean, had a special status shared by several powers. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Tangier was a small place with an outsized diplomatic file, since its rule had been shared before the war and seized by Spain during it. Childs took part in the talks meant to settle the city's future. His report shows a side negotiation running beside the Potsdam summit. Such quiet work filled most of the department's days, even in historic weeks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-150:
Formal State Department minutes record a meeting of July 31, 1945, the Potsdam Conference's last full day. The next day the leaders would adopt the final protocol. Minutes from this date sit near the summit of the second Potsdam volume's record. They state the business in the ordered form the Department favored.

End-of-conference minutes are thick with settled points. Readers watch topics close one by one. The plain record also shows what stayed open past the deadline. That mix of done and undone is honest history. The minutes give later disputes about Potsdam a firm text to argue from.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-50:
A rapporteur's report sums up the foreign ministers' meeting of July 21, 1945, at noon. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Three heads of business are reported in turn.

On the Council of Foreign Ministers, the ministers agreed it should be set up not later than September 1. Invitations to join its work would go to China and to France's provisional government before any public announcement. The drafting committee was asked to make a few minor changes to the proposal's text. German economic questions were put off until tomorrow, since the subcommittee's report had only just arrived. On Poland, the subcommittee chairman presented his report to the ministers. Its points of disagreement, the report signals, would have to go up to the heads of government.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d750:
The Soviet delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 26, 1945, as document 750. It came in the conference's second week, when the hardest trades were live. Soviet drafts tended to hold firm lines. This one joined the numbered record of the second Potsdam volume, beside rival American and British texts.

A late Soviet proposal shows Moscow's hand near the endgame. Readers can test what it asked against what the final protocol gave. The gaps and matches tell the story of the bargaining. The document keeps the volume's balance: the settlement was written by all three sides, each in its own words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d850:
Donald Heath, director of political affairs for the American group on the Control Council for Germany, wrote to Robert Murphy on July 17, 1945. Document 850 comes from the occupation machine in Germany itself. Murphy was the political adviser to the American command there. The letter joined the second Potsdam volume.

Letters from the Control Council staff show the settlement being run, not just debated. Heath's office handled Germany's daily political facts. Readers see the layer where summit lines met German streets. The document ties Potsdam to the occupation it governed. The men in Germany had to make the protocol work, and their mail shows them bracing for it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d950:
Marshal Zhukov, commander of Soviet occupation forces in Germany, reported to Stalin in this undated message, filed with the July 29, 1945 papers. He charges that American and British troops, while pulling back from land later assigned to the Soviet zone, took railway rolling stock without Soviet agreement.

His tables list 10,413 loaded goods cars, 2,139 empty cars, and 600 passenger cars removed. The Erfurt board alone lost 9,722 loaded cars to the Americans. Zhukov also counts 102 locomotives of all types. He asks Stalin to press the Allies for the stock's return. His zone, he says, faces an acute shortage of cars and engines.
frus-1950v01-d150: A third 1950 FRUS document from the national security volume. The administration's planners kept writing. This entry preserves that paper. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
frus-1955-57v16-d150: A 1955-1957 FRUS memorandum from the Suez Crisis volume. Nasser's nationalization shook the West. This document preserves that memo. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
gao-gaoreports-b-299150: ITT Electronic Systems quintupled its February 2007 protest — five case numbers, one radar fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles them all. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Five filings get one thorough answer. The radar fight got a full radar sweep.
gao-gaoreports-b-306050: Procurement provisions in spending bills got a legal review in this April 2006 GAO call, which examines the appropriations language. The decision reads the law. The ruling parses what the spending bills allowed. The law had the final word. The spending bills' words were parsed.
gao-gaoreports-b-308150: Housing in Cairo for Central Command drew GAO's fiscal eye in this March 2007 ruling, which tests the spending against the money law. The call reads the appropriations against the arrangement. The ruling decides whether the overseas housing deal was legally sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-250: SSA's totalization deals needed formality in 2005, and GAO's report says a more formal approach could improve the agreements. The review prescribes the paperwork. The cross-border workers deserved the clarity. The approach had to be formal. The cross-border workers deserved the clarity.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-650: Job training funds' outcomes were unknown nationally in 2005, and GAO's report says substantial money went to training, though results were unclear. The findings demand the proof. The report warns that the trainees deserved proven programs. The outcomes had to be known.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1050: The Interior Department's land appraisals needed fixing in 2006, and GAO's report says compliance with standards had to improve. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the public's land should not be sold on sloppy math. The appraisals had to be honest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-150: Chemical plant security needed more authority in 2006, and GAO's report says DHS was taking steps, though additional power was required. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the toxic tanks needed guarding. The authority had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-250: Federal IT investment data needed better accuracy in 2006, and GAO's report says agencies had to improve the reliability of the figures. The findings demand the truth. The report warns that the tech billions' numbers should be trusted. The information had to be accurate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-450: The 2004 election got a GAO post-mortem in 2006, and the report reflects on the nation's evolving election system. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the ballot box's machinery needed tending. The system had to evolve well. The ballot machinery needed tending.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-750: Medicare's communication networks needed locking in 2006, and GAO's report says the agency had to improve controls over key systems. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the health programs' wires carried secrets worth stealing. The controls had to be tightened.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-850: Human rights screening for security aid had lapses in 2006, and GAO's report says the North African gaps showed a need for more oversight. The findings target the holes. The report warns that the helping hand should not arm abusers. The screening had to be tight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-150: Public television's money maze got a GAO look in 2007, and the report examines the structure and funding of the system. The findings map the dollars. The report asks who should pay for the programming the market would not. The airwaves' orphan needed a patron.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-50: Customs' new bonding rules were working in 2007, and GAO's report says the revised policy cut the risk of uncollected duties, though uneven concerns remained. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the import bonds had to hold. The duties had to be collected.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-650: The weather service's new toy needed better plans in 2007 — GAO's report says the operations prototype wanted more rigorous groundwork first. The findings press for discipline before deployment. The report's moral: forecast the project with the same care you forecast the storms.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-750: Student-loan lenders were running wild in 2007 — GAO's report says the Education Department finally turned up the watch. The findings detail the tightened oversight of lender and school games in the federal loan program. The report captures the moment Washington noticed the student-loan gold rush.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-350: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on DOD Personnel Clearances: Improved Annual Reporting Would Enable More Informed Congressional Oversight. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-50: Congress's audit arm, GAO, wrote this 2007 report on the State Children's Health Insurance Program. It compares how states set up their plans, signed up kids, spent money, and ran ad drives — with a close look at states that covered grown-ups too. The findings show which state plans and sales pitches did the best job of reaching families who qualified.
gregory-great-morals-on-job-vol-3-part-1:
The first half of volume three of Gregory the Great's Morals on the Book of Job came out in 1850, in the Rev. James Bliss translation. The Moralia, written in the late 500s, is Gregory's verse-by-verse reading of Job and the largest work he ever produced. This part opens the final stretch of that reading.

Gregory is now deep into Job's long speeches and God's reply from the storm. His method stays the same: history first, then the teaching hidden in the words, then the moral for daily life. He lingers on pride, hidden sin, and the limits of human judgment. The volume carries the commentary toward its close in the following part.
gregory-great-morals-on-job-vol-3-part-2:
Volume three, part two of Gregory the Great's Morals on the Book of Job, published in 1850, closes the Rev. James Bliss English translation. It covers Books Thirty through Thirty-five of the Moralia, the commentary Gregory wrote in the late 500s, and it adds the indexes for the whole set.

In these last books Gregory works through the end of Job: the great speeches on God's power in nature, Job's humble reply, and his restoration. Leviathan and Behemoth become figures for evil and pride. Gregory sums up his lifelong theme, that suffering rightly borne purges the soul. The ending completes the most widely read Bible commentary of the early Middle Ages.
grimoire-pape-honorius-1850:
Spirits are summoned in the Grimoire of Pope Honorius, in this 1850 reprint of the 1760 Rome edition. Circles, prayers, seals, and commands promise power over demons. The classic French grimoire bears the name of a medieval pope, Honorius the Third, as its supposed and most unlikely author of all.

Priests were said to guard copies as tools of their office. Feared, banned, and endlessly reprinted, the book spread through rural France. Its rites mix church Latin with folk daring in equal parts. Few ritual magic books in French match its dark fame, and collectors of grimoires still rank it among the essential texts.
hawthorne-scarlet-letter-1850:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Scarlet Letter in 1850, his great novel of guilt and Puritan conscience. The book is the founding text of American psychological fiction in the judgment of many critics since. Hawthorne claimed to find the letter and tale in the Salem custom house attic papers there.

Hester Prynne stands on a Boston scaffold with her baby and a scarlet A for adultery. Her husband, presumed lost, returns as Chillingworth and vows to find and torment her secret lover. Dimmesdale, the young minister, hides his guilt while his health and mind waste in secret shame. Pearl, the wild child, links them all and demands the truth her elders will not speak. Hawthorne's symbols and gloom shaped how America writes about sin, shame, and hidden selves.
hermes-pymander-everard-1650:
John Everard put the Pymander of Hermes into English in 1650, the first English Hermetica. The text speaks as Hermes Trismegistus, the sage linked with Egypt and Greece. Its talks claim great age, and early readers prized them as ancient wisdom.

In these books, Mind speaks to Hermes and shows how the world was made. Soul, stars, fate, and man's fall and rise fill the talks. Good readers, the text says, can know God and be born anew. Everard's version fed English occult thought for two hundred years. The sample text shows spellings and speech of that age.
his-last-bow-pg2350: His Last Bow: Holmes comes out of retirement on the eve of war to catch a German spy. "There's an east wind coming." The great detective's farewell, patriotic and moving. The end of an era.
hohman-long-lost-friend-1850:
John George Hohman was a German settler in Pennsylvania who collected the charms and remedies printed as The Long-Lost Friend, in this 1850 edition. The book is a pow-wow manual: pow-wow here means German-American folk healing by prayer, charm, and rite. It became the foundational text of American folk magic.

Its short entries tell how to stop bleeding, cure burns, break fevers, protect cattle, and guard a house from fire and thieves. Most cures join a spoken charm in the name of the Trinity to a small rite or herb. Families kept the book in kitchens and barns for everyday emergencies.
holy-bible-wycliffe-forshall-madden-1850:
Long before print, John Wycliffe's followers put the whole Bible into English by hand, in the 1380s. The Wycliffe Translation presented here comes from the 1850 edition prepared by Forshall and Madden. It was the first complete English Bible, made a century and a half before Tyndale's famous version.

Owning or reading the translation could draw persecution, yet copies spread widely among ordinary believers. The language is the English of Chaucer's age, demanding but rewarding. Scholars use this edition to study how scripture first sounded in the mother tongue. The pioneer of all English Bibles deserves its place in any library of translations. Its survival through bans and burnings is a story in itself.
hottel-memo-1950:
An FBI field chief sent Washington a saucer tale in March 1950, and it became the bureau's most read file. Guy Hottel's memo of March 22 tells of three downed saucers and small dead crews, as told to an agent at third hand. The bureau never worked the claim and stands off from it now.

The tale came from a man in New Mexico by way of an Air Force contact, links too weak to hold weight. Hottel's crisp memo outlived its proof by far once the file came out. It is famed less for what it shows than for what it cannot. Students of Roswell lore meet it at every turn.
hutcheson-reflections-upon-laughter-1750:
Hutcheson's Reflections upon Laughter appeared first as essays in the 1720s and were reprinted in 1750 with remarks on the Fable of the Bees. The laughter essays take up a puzzle from Hobbes, who had called laughter a sudden glory at another's weakness. Hutcheson thought that account both false and unkind.

He shows that we laugh at incongruity, at odd pairings of dignity and meanness, often with no scorn at all. The remarks on Mandeville's Fable answer the cynical claim that private vice brings public benefit. Hutcheson defends a warmer view of human nature, the same benevolence his moral-sense theory requires. The piece is the lightest of his works, philosophy with a smile. It still reads as a model of how to correct a great thinker with good humor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenstein-bern:
Bernhard Löwenstein (1821–1889) was an Austrian rabbi born at Meseritz, in the province of Posen, and he is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch. Recommended by Ludwig Philippson, he was elected preacher at Szent Miklos in Hungary in 1845. There he became known as a pioneer of the modern synagogue service in Hungary.

In 1857 Löwenstein left Szent Miklos for the rabbinate of Butschowitz in Moravia, and soon afterward he was called as rabbi to Lemberg, where he died. The article describes him as an impressive preacher and a tireless communal worker who was twice decorated by the Emperor of Austria. It also notes his sermons and a volume of poems, “Jüdische Klänge,” published at Brünn in 1862, making the entry a useful short record of a reforming rabbi’s career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mandel-paul-103:
Paul Mandel, a Hungarian jurist and deputy, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Nyirbator on January 6, 1839, he studied law at Budapest and Vienna. In 1875 his native city elected him to the Hungarian Parliament. He was still holding that seat in 1904.

The article follows his work inside the legislature. He joined the law committee in 1881 and helped frame laws on guardianship and copyright. The office of royal notary public also bears his hand. His speeches won wide attention more than once. In 1878 he spoke against capital punishment. In 1884 he argued for religious freedom, and in 1885 against the anti-Semites. The short entry preserves a lawyer who used a long parliamentary career to defend civil and religious liberty in Hungary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marx-david-1045:
David Marx was chief rabbi of Bordeaux. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He was born at Landau, in Bavaria, in 1807. He trained at the rabbinical school at Metz and led a Jewish school at Nancy. Bordeaux chose him as chief rabbi in June 1837, ahead of the usual age for the office, and he died in February 1864.

The entry describes a reforming and much-loved rabbi. In 1841 he proposed bringing confirmation to Bordeaux, when the rite still looked like a dangerous novelty. He founded a nursery and an infirmary. He also stepped in for Jewish children kidnapped by Catholic proselytizers. Napoleon III gave him the Legion of Honor in 1852, and at his funeral the cardinal archbishop ordered every church bell in Bordeaux tolled.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-media-latin-med:
Media, the ancient land south and west of the Caspian Sea, is surveyed for its place in Jewish history in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Richard Gottheil and A. V. W. Jackson. Its territory matches roughly modern Azerbaijan and the Persian districts toward Kurdistan. Scripture names the Medes more than a dozen times: Madai son of Japheth stands as their ancestor, and Shalmaneser planted the exiles of Samaria in Median cities.

Other threads follow. The "laws of the Medes and Persians" became a byword for rules that cannot be changed. Isaiah foresaw Media helping to overthrow Babylon. At Ecbatana, Media's capital, the scroll of Cyrus's decree for rebuilding the Temple was found, and the Median city Rhages carries much of the story of Tobit. The article then turns to Greek accounts of Median antiquity, beginning with fragments of Berosus and Ctesias.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-megiddo-once-me:
Megiddo was the fortress town of the plain of Esdraelon. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn survey it in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. It was the capital of a Canaanite king beaten by Joshua and was assigned to Manasseh, though its people were taxed rather than expelled. Solomon restored its ancient fortifications, and one of his twelve provision officers drew supplies from it. Kings died there: Ahaziah died fleeing Jehu, though Chronicles tells the story differently, as the article notes.

The great day of the city was its worst. At Megiddo, Pharaoh Nechoh met King Josiah in battle, and Josiah was killed. The “mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon” in Zechariah is read as its echo. Herodotus records the same fight under a garbled name. The article closes by weighing the rival identifications of the site, Al-Lajjun among them, the choice of Robinson.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-zion-be:
Menahem Zion ben Solomon, generally called Menahem Ziyyon, was a Polish rabbi and preacher. He died at Altona in 1681. Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn give him a brief notice in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served first as rabbi of Vladislav. Vladislav lay in the government of Suwalki in Russian Poland. Afterward he served as dayyan, or judge, at Cracow.

His one book is the "Nehamot Ziyyon," Consolations of Zion. It is a collection of twenty-two sermons. It was printed at Frankfort-on-the-Main in 1677. That was four years before his death. The entry rests on Wolf's Bibliotheca Hebræa. It rests on Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue too. It records nothing else of him. There are two posts and one volume of preaching. There is a death far from both his congregations, in the community at Altona.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-arthur-10:
Arthur Meyer, born at Havre in 1846, became one of the most powerful French journalists of his generation, as a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman records. As a young man in Paris he bought and edited the Revue de Paris, though it soon folded. He then reported for nearly twenty years for Le Gaulois and the Paris Journal.

In 1868 Meyer became part owner of Le Gaulois and made it the voice of the Bonapartists. After 1879 he bought the Paris Journal, Le Gaulois, and the Clairon, merging all three under the Gaulois name as the chief organ of the Clerical-Monarchic party. The entry ends on a sharp note: Meyer was one of the most vehement opponents of Captain Dreyfus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mines-and-minin:
Mines and mining barely existed in ancient Israel, and a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack, published in 1906, starts by saying so. Deuteronomy's hills that yield iron and brass probably mean stones hard as iron, the writers argue. Only surface iron ore and old copper-works in the Lebanon offer real evidence nearby.

Real mining knowledge shows up instead in the book of Job, chapter twenty-eight, whose author knew shafts that twist after the vein and lamps worn on miners' foreheads. The article matches verse to verse against Diodorus's account of Egyptian mines, where fire-setting cracked the rock. Its picture is of Israelites who knew mining as neighbors practiced it, not as an industry of their own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monotheism-1095:
Monotheism, the belief in one God, gets a careful Jewish Encyclopedia article from Joseph Jacobs and David Philipson in 1906, beginning by refusing an easy compliment. Renan had called the monotheistic instinct a Semitic trait; later research, the writers say, will not bear it out. Robertson Smith traced Semitic religion's ethical turn instead to its alliance with monarchy.

The Hebrews alone among Semitic peoples reached pure monotheism, and they reached it slowly — through the prophets' teaching, over centuries, before every trace of idolatry disappeared even among them. Hebrew tradition roots the belief in Abraham's religious awakening, and the article follows the legends that grew around that beginning. A theological entry that insists on history rather than essence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-of-smolen:
Moses of Smolensk was a Russian engraver known from a single document of 1284. Herman Rosenthal and George D. Rosenthal wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. The document, published by Professor Kunik, records a court decision in a suit about a bell. Under the signature of Duke Feodor of Smolensk it adds: Moses, engraver of Feodor, made this seal.

The document never calls Moses a Jew, and the entry argues the point. The name Moses was not in use among Russian Christians of that time. The Russians of the day also knew nothing of engraving seals and coins. On those two grounds the scholars conclude that the duke's seal maker was a Jew, a lone craftsman at a Russian court.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-myers-walter-11:
Walter Myers was an English physician and toxicologist born at Birmingham in 1871. Joseph Jacobs wrote his short Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied at Cambridge and at St. Thomas' Hospital, taking his medical degree in 1897. He then worked under Ziegler at Freiburg, Koch at Berlin, and Ehrlich at Frankfort.

Myers translated Ehrlich's work on the blood and won a Cambridge scholarship for research in pathology. With the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine he sailed to Brazil to study the causes of yellow fever. There he caught the disease himself and died at Para in January 1901. The entry calls him a martyr to science.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-elias-sa:
Elias Salomon Nathan was a German doctor with a second life in letters. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Eutin about 1806. He took his medical degree at Kiel in 1830. After a Polish campaign, he settled in Hamburg as a doctor.

Nathan died at Hamburg on July 5, 1862. Beside medicine, he gave his time to Jewish learning. Under the pen name Essenna, he translated a French history. Salvador's book on Moses and the Hebrew people became three German volumes. G. Riesser wrote the introduction for that edition. Nathan also published thoughts from a Jew's diary in 1837.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-netherlands-114:
The Netherlands became a great refuge for persecuted Jews. Joseph Jacobs and E. Slijper wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews appear in its provinces well before Holland itself. Nimeguen, its oldest settlement, had Jews by 1404. A cemetery came in 1382, a synagogue by 1426.

Utrecht expelled its Jews in 1444 for good. Till 1789 no Jew might sleep a night there. Spain's rule brought edicts against Jews and lax Christians. Freedom came with independence from Spain in 1581. Maranos reached Amsterdam in 1593, turned away elsewhere. Their trade tied Holland to Morocco and Brazil. Six hundred Jews sailed for Brazil in 1642. Amsterdam's Jewish quarter grew, but it was no forced ghetto.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ocana-11650:
Ocaña was a town in Castile, in Spain. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish group lived there from an early date. At first its members held full rights in the town. In time the Christian folk began to curb those rights.

King Fernando the Fourth told the town board to stop. He said the Jews must keep the rights past kings gave them. A false charge of child murder was laid on them there. A Christian had killed a boy and hid the body. He put it in a Jewish house to cast blame. The plot failed, and the truth came out. In 1391 many Jews were killed at Ocaña. Others were forced to take baptism against their will.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oral-law-11750:
The Oral Law is the body of laws and teachings said to have been given to Moses by word of mouth, alongside the written Torah. Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands next to the written law of Moses. Rabbis teach that God gave both to Moses. The written part is the five books of Moses.

The oral part held laws, rules, and plain sense of texts. Moses was told not to write this part down. He was to pass it on by mouth to the folk. In a wide sense it holds much more than that. It holds all sense drawn from the written Torah by scribes. It holds the rules those scribes set in place too. So it takes in the Mishnah and the Tosefta. It takes in the law tracts of the Midrash as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paggi-angelo-11:
Angelo Paggi was an Italian scholar of the Hebrew tongue. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Sienna on May 4, 1789. He died at Florence on June 7, 1867. Leon Vita Monseles trained him in Hebrew in his youth.

Angelo read the books of Italy and of Rome as well. For a short time he worked in trade for his bread. He soon left trade to open a school of his own. In that school he brought in a clear, sound way to teach. From 1836 to 1846 he led the Jewish school at Florence. Ill health then forced him to give up that post. He still wrote and taught in private for years. He wrote grammars of Hebrew and of the Chaldee tongue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paul-de-burgos-:
Paul de Burgos was born Solomon ha-Levi, the leading Jew of Burgos. He was born about 1351 and died in 1435. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served as rabbi of Burgos before his baptism.

In 1390 he was baptized and took the name Paul de Santa Maria. His wife Joanna refused and stayed in her faith. Paul rose fast in the Church and the court. He became Bishop of Cartagena, then Archbishop of Burgos. He also turned hard against his former people. As chancellor he drafted an edict that cut Jewish rights.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pharisees-arama:
The Pharisees were the popular religious party of the Second Temple age. Kaufmann Kohler wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They stood against the priestly Sadducees. Their name means those who separate themselves for holiness. They spoke for the heart of the Jewish people.

Pharisees kept the Law as the scribes read it. Tradition, not the letter alone, guided their reading. They formed a brotherhood with strict entry pledges. Members swore purity, full tithes, and care for others' goods. The New Testament paints them with hostile strokes. Josephus, writing for Romans, softens them into philosophers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pillar-12150:
The English word pillar covers several Hebrew terms. The Executive Committee and J. F. McLaughlin wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One term means the door-posts of a gate. The chief term, mazebah, means a standing stone. Excavators found eight such stones in a row at Gezer.

Such stones marked graves, like Rachel's tomb stone. They witnessed treaties and marked the borders of land. Some served as rough altars for poured offerings. Moses set twelve pillars at Sinai for the tribes. Baal shrines and Tyre had pillars as well. Later law codes banned them as idolatry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pollak-ludwig-1:
Ludwig Pollak was an Austrian scholar of old art, born at Prague in 1868. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took his doctorate at Vienna in 1893. The Austrian state then sent him for a year to Italy and Greece. He settled in Rome and lived there from that time.

Pollak made a long study tour in 1900. It took him through Egypt, Syria, and Asia Minor. In 1898 he joined the German institutes for old art as a member. His book of 1900 treats two vases from one Greek workshop. His book of 1903 lists classical gold work owned by a Russian envoy. Both books came out at Leipsic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-press-moses-ale: Moses Alexandrovich Press was a Russian engineer born in 1861. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He trained at the Institute of Technology in St. Petersburg. He wrote for a journal on roads and travel there. He wrote for journals of the city's engineers as well. At his death in 1901 he was at work on a book. It treated the share of Jews in trades in western Russia. He died at Sankt Blasien that year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-purims-special-:
Special Purims are local feasts kept by single towns or families. Gotthard Deutsch, M. Franco, and Henry Malter wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Each marks a rescue from some past danger. The danger may have threatened a whole town. It may have threatened one family alone. The feast copies the great Purim in its form.

On the set day a scroll is read aloud. It tells the tale of the event in full. The reading takes place in the synagogue or at home. Set prayers are said for the day as well. Some of these days join fasting with feasting. The article lists known cases town by town and house by house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ramathaim-zophi:
Ramathaim-Zophim is named as Samuel's birthplace in First Samuel. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The article warns that the present text is corrupt. The usual reading breaks Hebrew usage, it argues.

The writers propose reading the verse in a different way. A man of Ramathaim was a Zophite of Mount Ephraim. Zuph was a district south of Ephraim, near Benjamin. No clear details fix the town's exact site. Still, Samuel's home city lay in that district. The short entry is a lesson in careful Bible reading. One small wording change shifts the whole sense.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rehumai-iii-126: Rehumai III was one of the early saboraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died in 505, in the month of Nisan. In Erubin 11a he appears with his peer R. Jose. Each man explains an earlier authority's words differently. Sherira, Halevy, and Grätz are the cited sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ries-elias-elka:
Elias Elkan Ries was an American electrical engineer born on January 16, 1862. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Randegg in Baden, Germany. His parents brought him to America at age three.

The article says he schooled in Baltimore and New York. He also attended lectures at Johns Hopkins University. In 1876 he became a telegraph operator. He worked for the Edison Company and other firms. Back in Baltimore he developed his own inventions. He founded the Ries Electric Specialty Company in 1891. Since 1896 he has lived in New York City. His patents number about one hundred fifty. They cover telephones, lamps, rail welding, and motor controllers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenfeld-morri:
Morris Rosenfeld was a Yiddish poet born at Boksha, in Russian Poland, on December 28, 1862. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He worked as a tailor in New York and London, and cut diamonds in Amsterdam.

Rosenfeld settled in New York in 1886 and joined the staffs of Jewish papers. He later edited the New Yorker Morgenblatt and spoke at the Fourth Zionist Congress. His first book, Die Glocke, held revolutionary poems he later tried to destroy. Das Lieder Buch, from 1897, made his name in many lands. Leo Wiener's English version, Songs from the Ghetto, appeared in Boston in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saadia-12950:
Saadia, without more, names a Bible commentator whose land and age stay uncertain. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Rapoport first showed he is not the famous Saadia Gaon.

The Daniel commentary long ascribed to the Gaon belongs to this Saadia instead. Matthews held that the Ezra and Nehemiah commentary is his as well. Saadia knew both Talmuds and the Targum in great depth. He quotes earlier interpreters under one general term, seldom by name. His readings often rest on swapping letters of like sound or class.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salvador-joseph:
Joseph Salvador, also Joseph Jeshurun Rodrigues, was an English philanthropist flourishing about 1753. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His family came from Holland with money invested in commerce.

Salvador ranked among the merchant princes of England's Jews in his day. His firm negotiated loans for the British government after Sampson Gideon's death. He was elected a director of the Dutch East India Company, a first for a Jew. He presided over London's Portuguese congregation and its deputies' committee. Lisbon earthquake losses and the company's failure ruined him late in life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schapiro-moses-:
Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Moses ben Phinehas Schapiro. He was a Russian rabbi and printer. Schapiro was born probably at Koretz, in Volhynia, about 1758. He died at Slavuta in 1838. His father was the Ḥasidic rabbi Phinehas of Koretz. Moses became rabbi of Slavuta in 1808.

That year Schapiro began a new edition of the Talmud. It far surpassed earlier editions and sold out fast. Rival printers at Kopys broke the rabbis' twenty-five-year ban to compete. Schapiro answered with a second edition from 1817 to 1822. A bitter feud with the Romm press of Wilna followed. His sons began a third edition at Slavuta. Then a bookbinder's suicide in their shop brought a murder charge. After a harsh trial the sons were flogged and sent to Siberia. The press was closed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scopus-13350:
Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Scopus. Scopus is a height seven stadia north of Jerusalem. Tradition says the high priest welcomed Alexander the Great there. Josephus gives its name as Saphein, rendered in Greek as Skopos. The Greek word means prospect. From that height one can see Jerusalem and the Temple.

The Talmud places the Alexander meeting at Antipatris instead. Grätz blamed a confusion between similar names. The article finds Josephus more plausible. Scopus later hosted Roman camps in the war on Rome. Cestius Gallus camped there first. Titus then leveled the ground from Scopus toward the city. In Jewish law Scopus counts as a boundary of Jerusalem. In 1889 diggers found a rock-cut canal at the hill's foot. It may be the Temple's water conduit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-set-off-sometim:
Set-off, sometimes called a counter-claim, lets a defendant answer a claim with one of his own. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Roman law called the idea compensatio. The goal is one judgment that settles both sides at once.

Talmudic law allows the idea, though it gives it no name. When two men beat each other, damages can cancel out. The court then awards only the difference. Beyond that case, the entry finds just hints in the Talmud. One passage in Bava Kamma is the main text later writers cite. Readers see a fair legal tool traced through sparse early sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shemaiah-13550:
Shemaiah was a prophet who served during the reign of King Rehoboam. Emil G. Hirsch and Isaac Broydé wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. God sent him to stop Rehoboam from making war. The northern tribes had just revolted and formed their own kingdom.

Shemaiah told the king that split was God's own will. Israel would stand as a separate state, he said. Later, Egypt's King Shishak invaded Judah and besieged Jerusalem. Shemaiah spoke again when the princes humbled themselves. God would not pour out wrath through Shishak, he promised. Twice this prophet's words spared Jerusalem, the entry shows. Once they stopped a civil war, and once they softened an invasion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-lady-rach:
Lady Rachel Simon was an English author born in London on August 1, 1823. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. She was the daughter of Simeon K Salaman and Alice Cowen. Her home drew many noted guests. In 1843 she married John Simon.

From age seventeen she kept a diary called Records and Reflections. In 1893 she published fifty years of it, from 1840 to 1890. She also wrote a work on the Psalms called Beside the Still Waters. The entry adds a note on her son Oswald John Simon. He was a communal worker and author in his own right.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-abr:
Solomon ben Abraham ben Jehiel was an Italian rabbi at Rome. Isidore Singer and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He flourished in the eleventh century there. He was nephew of Nathan ben Jehiel, author of the Aruk. A generation after Nathan's death he joined the rabbinate of Rome.

For a time Solomon presided over that rabbinate himself. He also headed the high school founded by Nathan. His authority shows in the questions put to him by others. He explained why the Eighteen Benedictions are not said on Sabbaths. He also answered questions from Menahem ben Solomon repeatedly. One responsum from Rome to Paris bears his signature first.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sperling-jacob-:
Jacob Hirsch Sperling was an Austrian teacher of religion at Lemberg. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Lemberg in 1837. He taught at the Jewish school and the German gymnasium there. He backed the Haskalah movement in Galicia with energy.

Sperling was also a gifted Neo-Hebrew poet of his time. He wrote for many Hebrew and German Jewish periodicals. He coedited the Jüdische Presse and the Neuzeit in Lemberg. He founded the societies Ahawah we-Haskalah and Shomer Yisrael there. His poems include a life of Rapoport in verse. He also wrote an epic poem in five cantos, Horodot.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stier-josef-140:
Josef Stier was a Hungarian rabbi born on April 12, 1844. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Neustadt-on-the-Waag in Hungary. He studied at Presburg, Vienna, and Breslau. He earned his doctorate in 1869 and ordination in 1872.

In 1872 Stier became chief rabbi at Stein-am-Anger in Hungary. He also taught Jewish religion at the local gymnasium. Later he moved to Berlin for a rabbinate. He has held that Berlin post since 1890. His books include a work on Ferenc Deák from 1875. Others treat priests and prophets, and honor in the Bible. One 1896 book weighs theism against natural science. The entry lists a rabbi active in print and pulpit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sword-hereb-bar:
The sword was the standard blade weapon of ancient Israel. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its Hebrew name is hereb, with barak as a poetic form. Men wore it at the hip on a belt. A sheath guarded the blade when at rest.

Some swords were double-edged for cutting and thrusting. Ehud's short dagger-like sword fills one famous story. He drove it, haft and all, into Eglon's belly. Blades were usually iron, rarely bronze, in Israel. Israelite swords likely matched Assyrian and Egyptian shapes. Some ran straight, others curved like daggers. The Bible gives no full descriptions of types. The entry rebuilds the weapon from scattered verses and phrases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tarnow-14250:
Tarnow is a town of Austrian Galicia with an old Jewish community. Isidore Singer and Ignaz Schipper wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. An organized community existed by the mid-1500s. The town belonged hereditarily to the lords of Tarnow. Jews lived under those lords' jurisdiction.

In 1637 a privilege placed Jews under castle protection. It let them trade on equal footing with citizens. Popular jealousy and magistrates killed that privilege in 1654. Plague, fires, and Swedish attacks then ruined the town. Its overlord restored the Jewish privilege in 1670. The town's survival required the Jews' return. A deal set Jews' share of town taxes at thirty percent. Later lords confirmed the privilege repeatedly. The entry shows rights traded against a town's needs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-texas-14350:
Jewish settlers in Texas, from republic days to statehood, fill this long article. Cyrus Adler and Henry Cohen wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Texas was an independent republic from 1836 to 1845. It joined the Union in 1845, left in 1861, and returned in 1870.

Samuel Isaacs arrived with Austin's first colonists in 1821. He earned 320 acres by serving the republic's army. Other pioneers traded, farmed, and held town office. Michael Seeligson became mayor of Galveston in 1853. Jewish soldiers fought at Goliad and the Alamo. One Jewish surgeon served in Sam Houston's army. The article names dozens of these early Texans.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-toronto-14450:
Toronto, capital of Ontario in Canada, had four organized Jewish congregations in 1905. Cyrus Adler and Clarence I. de Sola wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Holy Blossom was the oldest, begun in 1845. It organized formally in 1852 and dedicated a synagogue in 1857.

Goel Tsedek dated from 1880, and Shomerei Shabbas from 1891. Chevra Tillim followed in 1895. Smaller new congregations kept growing in importance. Aid work flourished alongside the synagogues. The city had benevolent societies, a burial society, and a Talmud Torah. Zionist groups numbered four, and a YMHA served the young. About 7,000 Jews lived among 207,971 residents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tushiyyah-lit-s:
Tushiyyah was a Warsaw publishing house founded in 1896 for Hebrew books. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its name means sound knowledge in Hebrew. Though a private business, it worked like a publication society. Its aim was to spread new Hebrew literature widely.

Ben-Avigdor founded the house and served as first editor. Its program promised good and useful Hebrew books. Youth would gain knowledge, morality, and civilization from them. Scientific books in all branches were also planned. Novels, biographies, poems, and histories all appeared. Its textbooks taught Hebrew by modern methods to children. Authors like Frischman, Brainin, and Berdyczewski published with it. The house much encouraged young Hebrew talent.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vatke-johann-ka:
Johann Karl Wilhelm Vatke was a Christian scholar of the Hebrew Bible. Crawford Howell Toy wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Vatke was born in Saxony on March 14, 1806. He died in Berlin on April 19, 1882. He taught at the University of Berlin from 1830 onward.

Vatke's key book appeared in Berlin in 1835. It dealt with the religion of the Old Testament. On the Pentateuch, he took the boldest view of his day. He denied that Moses wrote any of it. He also treated Deuteronomy as the earliest of its books. Critics attacked him, yet his teaching shaped later scholars. He is counted a forerunner of Graf, Kuenen, and Wellhausen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wahl-moritz-cal:
Moritz Callmann Wahl was a German writer on language. He was born on March 28, 1829, at Sondershausen. Isidore Singer and W. Salzberger wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died on October 15, 1887. He studied Oriental languages at Leipsic. His teachers were Julius Fürst and H. L. Fleischer.

Wahl taught in England, then worked in business at Lyons. He finally settled at Erfurt. There he founded a business academy. His research focused on proverbs across languages. He wrote on proverbs in Hebrew and Aramaic writing. He also studied English proverbs before Shakespeare. Proverbs in Shakespeare's own plays drew a book as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weiss-wilhelm-1:
Wilhelm Weiss was an Austrian mathematician. He was born at Ridka, Bohemia, on February 3, 1859. Isidore Singer and Alexander Kisch wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Prague on June 18, 1904. His father, a village teacher, taught him first. He studied at Prague, Leipsic, and Erlangen.

Weiss took his doctorate in 1887. He taught math at Prague's German technical school. He climbed its ranks year by year. In 1900 he became a full professor there. From 1901 to 1902 he served as dean of engineering. The brief entry marks a steady academic rise.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wisdom-hebr-gre:
Wisdom, in Hebrew hokmah, joins insight with skill. Kaufmann Kohler wrote this long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Wisdom means grasping the nature of things deeply. It also means performing hard tasks with craft. The word is both a human and divine trait. Scripture traces all wisdom back to God.

God's spirit made Joseph wise before Pharaoh. It filled Bezalel with skill for the Tabernacle. Solomon's wisdom came as God's direct gift. The wise formed a class beside priests and prophets. Kings sought their counsel on hard matters. Wisdom grows by watching nature and history. It also grows by study and wise company. The entry surveys wisdom across Bible and rabbinic thought.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zeror-raphael-j:
Raphael Jedidiah Solomon Zeror (1681-1737) was an Algerian rabbi of note. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Algiers, he died in that same port town. He came of a house of great Talmud men of old.

His grandsire was chief rabbi of Algiers in his day. With the rabbis of his town he signed a ban writ. That writ was the ban on Nehemiah Hayyun of ill fame. He read world books with care all his life long. Logic, the frame of things, and earth lore drew him most. He gave time to verse craft in those years as well. He won fame as a deft healer of the sick in town. He ran a wide trade by sea and by land at once. His pupil bound his replies and notes as one book.
keyhoe-flying-saucers-are-real-1950:
Donald Keyhoe, a retired Marine Corps major, published The Flying Saucers Are Real in 1950. The book grew out of his hit article in True magazine the year before. It was the first major book of civilian UFO research and launched a movement.

Keyhoe gathers pilot reports, radar cases, and his talks with Air Force men. He argues the saucers are craft from other worlds and that the Air Force hides what it knows. His charges set the tone for decades of UFO writing: keen sightings, official silence, public doubt. Later UFO books followed the path Keyhoe cut here.
king-richard-ii-pg2250:
William Shakespeare's history play King Richard II follows a king who loses his crown. Richard rules England with weak judgment and heavy taxes. His cousin Bolingbroke returns from exile, gathers support, and forces him to give up the throne.

Alone in prison, Richard looks back on his fall. He breaks a mirror and says he has no name and no title left. A quiet garden scene adds a moral lesson about careless rule. Readers value the play for its rich verse and its sad picture of power lost. The play asks what a king is once his crown is gone. Its speeches give that question a sad, musical force.
long-lost-friend-hohman-1850:
John George Hohman, a German immigrant healer in Pennsylvania, first published The Long-Lost Friend in 1820. This edition of 1850 carried his collection of charms and cures through German America. The book became the classic grimoire of Pennsylvania Dutch pow-wow, the folk healing tradition of that region.

Its pages give words to say over burns, bleeding, toothache, and sick cattle. Bible verses, short prayers, and folk recipes stand side by side. Pow-wow practitioners treated the book as a license and a toolbox in one. Families kept copies for daily use across generations. Everyday magic for farm and family is here in its most durable American form, still consulted today.
mellon-ms-12-a-collection-of-alchemical-:
Mellon MS 12 is a paper manuscript of about 1450, held at Yale. The Beinecke Library in New Haven keeps the book today. Its texts are alchemical works ascribed to Ramon Llull, with extra matter.

The works came into English from French and Catalan forms. A later hand added leaves on thin paper in the 1500s. Wheels, tables, a tree of the art, flasks, and a furnace are drawn inside. Denis Duveen held the book once, and the Mellons gave it to Yale in 1965. Headings in red and slight pen work mark the text breaks. Such books show how the art passed from hand to hand.
mellon-ms-2-alchemical-miscellany-1350:
Mellon MS 2 is a parchment manuscript of about 1350. Yale's Beinecke Library holds the book, with 88 leaves. The record calls it the first such practical book in the Mellon set.

Its texts came in part from Arabic sources, with European adds. Works by Geber, Avicenna, and Rasis stand in the contents list. Richard de Fournival's work on the art stands there too. Three scribes wrote the book in a clear gothic hand, in Latin. Leaves from a German song book serve as its pastedowns. That reuse shows how old parchment was prized and kept.
mellon-ms-33-alchemical-miscellany-1550:
Mellon MS 33 is an English paper manuscript of about 1550. Yale's Beinecke Library holds the book, with 128 leaves. Brown calf covers it, though the back strip is now lost.

Most texts inside are alchemy turned into English by Robert Freelove. Jean de Meung's book on the mineral stone is one such work. The Radix Mundi, turned in 1550, stands in the list too. Khalid ibn Yazid's secrets of the philosophers close the named set. At least three scribes shared the work of this copy. Their hands shift from neat script to rougher forms as it goes.
mellon-ms-36-alchemical-miscellany-1550:
Mellon MS 36 is a paper manuscript from Italy, dated about 1550. Its maker wrote Lapis Philosophalis, the philosopher's stone, on its back. The parchment cover is home made, from a used deed sheet.

One Johannes Baptista F. compiled the book of Latin alchemy texts. The record calls his copies corrupt, as was common for such sets. Practical steps and poems in the vernacular stand among the texts. Small ink drawings of flasks, furnaces, and a Bain-Marie fill the front leaves. The book is worn and wormed, and loose in its cover. Its gear drawings still show the tools of the old art.
notes-and-queries-number-11-january-12-1:
Number eleven, dated Saturday, January 12, 1850, returns to Sir E. Dering's household book. E. Rimbault handles that note this time. Bayswater and its origin, Eva daughter of MacMurrough, and Billingsgate follow. Plagiarisms, or parallel passages, get a note on borrowed lines. Fly leaves yield a fourth set of notes.

Opinions on English historians reach Lord Clarendon in a second part. Miscellanies treat books by the yard, the thistle of Scotland, and humble pie. By hook or by crook, the origin of grog, and Dr Faustus all appear. Queries ask about catacombs and bone houses, and contradictions in Don Quixote. Colonel Blood's house also draws a question.
notes-and-queries-number-12-january-19-1:
Hudibras leads number twelve, dated Saturday, January 19, 1850, with a passage explained by E. F. Rimbault. The Field of the Brothers' Footsteps and the receipts of the Beggar's Opera follow as notes. Bolton Corney continues on books and authors, and Rimbault adds more notes on Cunningham's London. Sewerage in Etruria sits oddly among them.

R. Monckton Milnes asks about St Thomas of Lancaster, and J. R. Planché about the Black Prince's shield. M. A. Lower asks for the origin of the name Shylock. Minor queries hunt the origin of snob, of cannibal, and of the word poghele. Pictures in churches and flaying for sacrilege draw graver questions.
notes-and-queries-number-13-january-26-1:
Domingo Lomelyn, jester to Henry the Eighth, opens the notes in number thirteen, for Saturday, January 26, 1850. Edward Rimbault writes that piece. Marlowe and the old Taming of a Shrew, beetle mythology, and old painted glass follow. Churchwardens' accounts for St Margaret's, Westminster, give local colour.

Lord Braybrooke asks after Catherine Pegge, and J. P. Collier after William Basse and his poems. Minor queries touch a Christmas hymn, the circulation of the blood, and Lord Bacon's psalms. Luther and Erasmus reappear as a query. Answers in the miscellanies settle the etymology of muffins and the seal of Killigrew. Defoe also gets a word.
notes-and-queries-number-14-february-2-1:
Reprints of old books, by J. P. Collier, lead number fourteen, dated Saturday, February 2, 1850. Catacombs and bone houses get a note in answer to an earlier query. Lines attributed to Hudibras and fly leaf notes, in their fifth part, follow. The Pursuits of Literature closes the notes.

The Reverend J. Jebb sends nine queries at once, and Barryana gets one more. Minor queries chase Norman pedigrees, Dr Johnson's library, and the derivation of calamity. Replies settle the Field of Forty Footsteps and the meaning of pokership. The etymology of Armagh and matters of the Revels also come in. Gray's Elegy and Shylock fill the miscellanies.
notes-and-queries-number-15-february-9-1:
Wages in the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries open number fifteen, for Saturday, February 9, 1850. The Reverend L. B. Larking compares those wages. Marlowe and the old Taming of a Shrew return, from S. Hickson. Shakespeare's use of monosyllables gets a note from C. Forbes. Fly leaf notes reach part six.

William J. Thoms asks for folk lore, in the form of metrical charms. Allusions in the Homilies draw a second query. Minor queries touch Pope's translations of Horace, Arabic numerals, and dog Latin. The cuckoo as Welsh ambassador charms the list. Replies settle Selago and Samolus, and portraits of Luther and Erasmus.
notes-and-queries-number-16-february-16-:
Daniel Defoe and his ghost stories lead the notes in number sixteen, dated Saturday, February 16, 1850. Pet names follow, from the Reverend B. H. Kennedy. Lacedæmonian black broth gets a note, plus a hint to intending editors. Folk lore notes cover Easter eggs, buns, and a Gloucestershire custom.

C. H. Cooper asks about the White Hart Inn at Scole, and others about passages in Pope. Belvoir Castle draws a query of its own. nsc-68-1950:
NSC-68 was a top-secret report delivered to President Truman in 1950 by the National Security Council. Paul Nitze led the team that drafted it, weeks before the Korean War began. The paper set out how the United States should face the Soviet Union across the whole world.

It warned that the Soviet bloc sought world domination and that time favored the side that built strength fast. The report called for a huge rise in military spending, a stronger alliance system, and readiness to fight limited wars. Truman held back at first, but Korea made the plan real. Declassified years later, NSC-68 reads as the blueprint that militarized the Cold War for four decades.
openalex-w1969321150:
Amy Vogler, Paul Keim, and co-authors studied plague in Madagascar. The hosted sample carries a fuller title than the catalog. It names Yersinia pestis, the plague bacterium, in Madagascar. Plague reached the island in 1898, they report. It remains a real human health problem there.

The disease persists mainly in the central highlands. In the 1990s it returned to an old port area. The team traced the bacterium's family history and spread. Genetic tools of molecular epidemiology guided the work. Partners worked in Arizona, Berlin, and Madagascar. Knowing plague's routes helps target control on the island. The catalog title names only the wider Yersinia genus.
openalex-w2037915750:
Raul Aguirre-Gamboa, Hugo Gomez-Rueda, Emmanuel Martinez-Ledesma and colleagues built an online tool for cancer gene research. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Gene signatures may predict cancer outcomes. Testing them across many datasets is slow work. Biologists and doctors needed an easier route.

Their tool, SurvExpress, needs only a list of genes. It holds data from over twenty thousand samples. The data cover more than twenty tissue types. Users can run survival analysis through a web page. The tool compares how well signatures predict outcomes. It also estimates patient risk groups. Fast checks help researchers discard weak signatures early.
openalex-w2047571950:
Santiago Signorelli, Pablo Dans, Laura Coitino and colleagues proposed a new chemical link between two plant stress molecules. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2015. Stressed plants build up proline, an amino acid. They also build up GABA, a protective compound. How the two connect was not fully clear.

The team used computer chemistry to model proline reactions. Harmful oxygen radicals surge during plant stress. Their model showed proline reacts readily with those radicals. That reaction can produce a step toward GABA. The route needs no enzyme to work. It offers a fresh way to explain GABA buildup. Proline may thus protect cells in more ways than thought.
openalex-w2079455750:
Jonathan Friedlaender, Francoise Friedlaender, Jason Hodgson and colleagues mapped mother-line DNA diversity in Melanesia. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2007. Melanesian peoples are well known for their diversity. The pattern behind that diversity was hard to grasp. Mother-line DNA traces family roots through women.

The team checked over a thousand DNA samples. Samples came from thirty-two groups across the region. Group differences were shaped by island and island size. Language ties also shaped the pattern. Remote inland groups differed most from the rest. Shore groups were less distinct from each other. Within-group diversity was lowest in remote groups. Marriage and migration patterns likely drive these contrasts.
openalex-w2110515650:
Bruno Fontanella, Janete Ricas and Egberto Ribeiro Turato examined saturation sampling in qualitative health research. Their paper appeared in Cadernos de Saude Publica in 2008. Clear reporting marks rigorous qualitative work. Saturation sampling is a common stopping rule. Researchers stop when new interviews add nothing new.

The authors analyse how the concept is defined. They discuss closing a sample by theoretical saturation. Intentional samples raise acceptance problems, they note. Judging sample size in advance is another difficulty. Valuing repeated themes against rare differences matters too. Misused terms for closure are also criticised. The paper offers cleaner guidance for health researchers.
openalex-w2116146250:
Santiago Madrinan, Andres Cortes and James Edward Richardson profiled the paramo, a high Andean grassland. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Genetics in 2013. Paramos sit above the treeline in the northern Andes. They are rich in species found nowhere else. Their youth makes them a model for fast evolution.

The authors compared diversification rates across biomes. Paramo lineages split into new species very quickly. Their rates topped other famous young hotspots. Cold, wet conditions define this high habitat. Islands of grassland may speed species formation. The paramo is Earth's fastest evolving hotspot, they argue. It is also its coolest one. Protecting it preserves evolution in action.
openalex-w2149507050:
S. Patiño, Jon Lloyd, R. Paiva, and colleagues published this study in Biogeosciences in 2009. They measured branch xylem density, a wood trait tied to how trees grow, survive, and reproduce, across the Amazon Basin. Wood density varies between trees, species, and places, and the team wanted to know what drives that spread.

They sampled over sixteen hundred trees from nearly six hundred species at eighty-seven sites. Values ranged widely, from very light to very dense wood. Species identity explained about a third of the total variation, and environment about a quarter more. Even wide-ranging species shifted their density predictably from place to place. The trait is thus part inherited and part shaped by local conditions.
openalex-w2167969650:
Nicolas Guillemot, Michel Kulbicki, Pascale Chabanet, and Laurent Vigliola published this study in PLoS ONE in 2011. They examined functional redundancy in the coral reef fishes of New Caledonia, among the richest fish communities on Earth. Redundancy means several species share the same ecological job, which should buffer an ecosystem against losses.

Divers counted fish along transects and sorted species by the jobs they perform. The link between species counts and job counts followed a rising power curve with no plateau. Species spread across jobs in a clearly non-random way at moderate richness. Some jobs gained backup species fast, others only at high richness. Habitat changed the pattern little. Low overall redundancy warns that losing a few key species could hurt.
