openalex-w2557804650: M. Aguilar heads the long author list on this 2016 Physical Review Letters paper. It reports a precision measurement of the boron to carbon flux ratio in cosmic rays. The data came from the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer aboard the International Space Station, across the wide energy range named in the title. The preserved sample holds only the title page and author affiliations, with no readable abstract or results. The measured ratio and its meaning therefore cannot be stated from the evidence kept here.
openalex-w2800497750:
Jayalaxshmi Mistry, Isabel Belloni Schmidt, and Ludivine Eloy, with Bibiana Bilbao, wrote on savanna fire management in Ambio, published online in 2018. Fire policy in South American savannas long meant fighting every blaze. Brazil and Venezuela have begun shifting toward managing fire with local communities instead. Both countries' experiences anchor this perspective.

New initiatives measure success by shrinking wildfire extent through planned early burning. They also opened real dialogue between government agencies and local communities about fire. The authors warn that participation still needs deepening. Institutions risk swallowing local knowledge systems instead of sharing power with them. Equitable, intercultural governance is their central demand. Fire, they argue, is a cultural practice as much as a hazard, and policy must treat it that way.
openalex-w2904710350:
Daniel Gaitán-Cremaschi, Laurens Klerkx, and Jessica Duncan lead this review on food system diversity, out online in 2018 in Agronomy for Sustainable Development. Dominant food systems follow a productivist model: vast amounts of cheap, standardized food. That model now looks unsustainable, socially and for nature. Transitions to alternatives need a clear picture of what food systems exist.

Research on sustainability transitions abounds, but a practical way to sort food systems was missing. The authors review how transitions might unfold and build a framework. It rests on the Multi-Level Perspective on socio-technical transitions, merging social and natural science concepts. The framework aims to classify existing systems and spot promising ones. Promising systems could seed the move toward sustainability. For policymakers, such mapping turns a vague call for change into a map of starting points.
openalex-w2909905050:
Scott D. Tiegs, David M. Costello, and Mark W. Isken lead a global river study in Science Advances in 2019. Rivers and their banks process organic carbon arriving from land. That carbon may become greenhouse gas, enter food webs, or wash into long-term storage. Processing speed decides which fate wins, yet global patterns were unmapped. Standardization problems had blocked worldwide comparison until now.

The team deployed a peer-sourced network of researchers across the planet. Everyone ran the same cotton-strip assay, measuring decomposition strength in fabric. Strips went into river channels and adjacent riparian zones simultaneously. Baselines like these let scientists quantify human impacts on ecosystem functioning globally. Climate and land-use drivers can then be tested against real rates. The study turns scattered local methods into one planetary instrument.
openalex-w2993330950:
Federico Coccolini, Ernest Moore, Yoram Kluger, and colleagues present these guidelines in the World Journal of Emergency Surgery in 2019. They come jointly from the World Society of Emergency Surgery and the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma. The subject is injury to the kidneys and urinary tract.

Such injuries occur in roughly ten to twenty percent of abdominal trauma cases, in adults and children alike. Good care weighs the exact injury, the patient's circulation, and any other injuries. For children, avoiding surgery is the preferred approach when safely possible. The guidelines stress team care, joining urologists, radiologists, trauma surgeons, and intensive care doctors around shared rules for treatment choices.
openalex-w3041632850:
Manfred Lenzen, Mengyu Li, Arunima Malik, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2020. It weighs the world's social and economic losses from the coronavirus pandemic against its environmental gains. Lockdowns cut production and consumption, and the effects cascaded through international supply chains.

Using a global multi-regional economic model and data available by May 2020, the team captured direct and spill-over effects. They estimate consumption losses in the trillions of dollars, with well over one hundred million full-time jobs and large income losses tied to them. At the same time, greenhouse gas and air pollutant emissions fell sharply. Asia, Europe, and the United States were hit most directly, above all in transport and tourism.
openalex-w4360620450:
Yogesh Dwivedi, Nir Kshetri, Laurie Hughes, and colleagues ask what changes when tools like ChatGPT write research text. Their opinion paper appeared in the International Journal of Information Management in 2023. Dozens of scholars from many fields contributed their views. Generative conversational AI can draft, summarise, and edit in seconds, which tempts busy researchers and raises hard questions about honesty and credit.

The paper gathers perspectives on the chances, challenges, and wider effects of such tools. It covers research itself, professional practice, and public policy. Benefits include speed and access for writers working in a second language. Risks include errors, bias, and blurred responsibility for published words. The authors aim to help journals and institutions set sensible rules early.
openalex-w7204238750:
Nayara Oliveira Rosa led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on lifestyle and polycystic ovary syndrome, one of the most common endocrine and metabolic problems in women of reproductive age. The syndrome connects to insulin resistance, obesity, abnormal blood lipids, high blood pressure, glucose intolerance, type 2 diabetes, and higher cardiometabolic risk. It also affects fertility, the menstrual cycle, excess androgen signs, mental health, and quality of life.

Recent studies, the review reports, show that lifestyle interventions can improve both metabolic and reproductive measures, lowering body mass index, waist size, blood sugar, and lipid values. The authors also note a May 2026 global consensus proposing to rename the condition polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, stressing that it is a multisystem disorder, not just an ovarian one.
openalex-w7204955450:
Girlaynne Michellyne Farias Santos and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva published a Portuguese-language review in Brazil in 2026 on the family-school relationship in the inclusion of children with autism spectrum disorder. Diagnoses have risen steadily, and the diagnosis itself is challenging for families, often bringing conflict born of not understanding the disorder. The review searched three sources for work on how the family-school relationship can help or hinder the autistic child's growth at school.

Family conflicts can cross the home's walls and strain the relationship with the school, the literature shows. Yet school is the most favorable environment for the child's growth in every aspect, where children with specificities share unique moments in society and are effectively inserted into wider environments. The relationship between the two institutions is decisive.
openalex-w7206176250:
Lucas Dias Mendes, Ary Canellas Machado Neto, and Mac Fatima Lucia Cartaxo Machado de Castro review delayed pressure urticaria and its effects on mental health. In the condition, painful red welts rise after lasting pressure on the skin, as from straps or tight clothing. Their 2026 narrative review searches studies from 2010 onward on quality of life, anxiety, depression, and how nerves and the immune system interact.

Chronic hives in general are already tied to anxiety and depression, and this form adds a heavy load because it lasts and often resists standard antihistamine treatment. The authors discuss how stress systems in the body may stir up skin cells and worsen flares. Advanced treatment with omalizumab looks promising, they conclude, but direct proof of mental health gains still needs forward-looking studies.
openalex-w7208737150:
Fabio Andrade de Moura leads a team mapping a decade of Brazilian research on digital technology in astronomy teaching. Their state-of-the-art review covers academic production from 2013 to 2023 on software, simulators, and other digital tools used to teach astronomy. The authors set out to map what exists, sort its themes, and see how the tools actually enter educational settings.

Beyond listing studies, the review looks for trends, repeated patterns, and gaps across ten years of work. Questions of this kind matter because astronomy is a subject where digital simulation can show what no classroom can hold: orbits, scales, and motions far beyond direct experience. By organizing the field's output, the authors give later researchers and teachers a chart of where Brazilian astronomy education has leaned on technology, and where it has not yet gone.
openalex-w7213639650:
Lucas Daniel Verbiski Kulik and Patrícia Fernanda Silvério sort out who should capture and rescue wild animals in Paraná. Their 2026 mixed-methods study reviews law and internal rules, plus response data from the state military police and fire service. Urban wildlife calls repeatedly draw several agencies at once.

Main responsibility falls on environmental bodies, the study concludes. Those include the state water and land institute and municipal environment offices. Military police and firefighters hold a subsidiary role, limited to set situations. Unclear competence creates duplicated effort when agencies are called without coordination. A standard operating proposal is offered so responses to wildlife incidents become clearer, faster, and less wasteful.
openalex-w7213971250:
Cristiane Fonsêca Ximenes De Castro and co-authors study mothers of children with neurodevelopmental disorders in Fortaleza, Ceará. Their 2026 exploratory research works through a primary care territory and a municipal public school. Ten mothers of children with autism or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder gave semi-structured interviews.

Heavy bodily and social overload marks the accounts. Institutional support networks are fragile, living conditions are precarious, and gender inequality deepens under socioeconomic vulnerability. The title quote, a mother saying she stopped being herself, captures that loss of self. Atypical motherhood is named a public health problem. Shared, collective duty for care is demanded, through policy across sectors.
openalex-w7214081850:
Larissa Nascimento Pinto and Rafael Coelho Rodrigues follow patients moved from a psychosocial care centre to a mental health outpatient clinic in Bahia. Their 2026 study analyses 127 records from 2022 to 2024 in a Recôncavo municipality. Transfer reasons, care offered, and clinical course after referral were investigated.

Most users received medication-centred care after transfer. A majority were seen only for in-person medication, some had home drug administration, and few also received psychotherapy. Non-adherence at the centre and travel difficulty justified many transfers, while many records gave no reason at all. Crises occurred in a significant share. Weak transfer flows, the authors conclude, risk turning advancement into abandonment.
openalex-w7214173650:
Aguinaldo Hygor Oliveira Matos and colleagues study street races run by the Military Police of Pará as community outreach. Their 2026 article joins literature on community policing and police legitimacy with institutional and press documents. Free or low-cost races are framed as a privileged meeting space between police and civil society.

Named events include a colonel's race held for over five decades, a Tiradentes race that drew fifteen hundred people in 2025, and a special operations sunset run with about five thousand entries. Measurable gains in police-community bonds, staff health, and institutional image are reported. No systematic impact evaluation exists, they caution. Stronger research on effects on safety perception and public trust is needed.
openalex-w7214190650:
Francilino Paulo de Sousa leads a large team on Brazil's new National Education Plan. Their 2026 library and documentary study draws on scholars of the state, public policy, educational planning, and democratic management, plus normative and institutional documents. A new plan opens a fresh cycle of debate on Brazilian schooling's direction.

The history of educational planning in Brazil is traced first. Limits in carrying out the previous plan are then identified. Federative coordination, financing, and cutting educational inequality stand among the central challenges discussed. Turning legal determinations into effective action inside teaching systems is the core difficulty, they argue. The plan's fate will be decided in budgets and federation politics, not in its text alone.
openalex-w7214923950:
João Henrique Rolde led a twelve-author 2026 literature review on rebuilding the alveolar ridge, the bone that holds teeth, using bone blocks from other species or made from synthetic materials. Losing ridge volume makes it hard to place dental implants well. The reference solution, the patient's own bone, costs a second surgical site, is limited in amount, and resorbs unpredictably, which motivates the search for substitutes.

Collagen-containing xenogeneic blocks performed comparably to the patient's own bone in the reviewed studies. They needed no donor site and had unlimited supply, though implant survival was slightly lower in some work and wound opening with graft exposure could occur. Synthetic materials conducted new bone growth adequately and suited small defects or combinations with other substitutes. Both options are viable, the authors conclude, with choice depending on defect shape, patient health, complication risk, and surgeon experience.
openalex-w7219772050:
Adriana Santos Merisio led a 2026 literature review on the dentist's role in detecting child abuse through oral examination. Abuse, whether physical, sexual, psychological, or by neglect, is a public health problem with high underreporting. The narrative review gathers clinical studies, World Health Organization guidance, forensic dentistry manuals, and Brazil's child and adolescent statute to describe warning signs and the professional's ethical and legal duties.

Many assaults leave marks on the head, neck, and mouth, the review shows. These include bruising around the face and mouth, tears of the lips and the small fold under the tongue, broken teeth, repeated marks, and injuries that do not match the caregivers' story. Sexual abuse can leave suction marks and palate bruising, while neglect shows as severe untreated decay, strong bad breath, ruined oral hygiene, and repeated missed treatment. Dentists sit in a privileged detection position, the authors argue.
phrenology-and-the-scriptures-by-john-pi:
John Pierpont's Phrenology and the Scriptures began as a lecture given by special invitation before the American Phrenological Society at Clinton Hall, New York. The preface, written by the publishers, Fowlers and Wells, urged him to print it. A quoted notice from the New York Evening Mirror calls it a remarkable lecture on the harmony of phrenology with the Christian scriptures.

Pierpont, a minister and poet, distinguished the animal mentality from the moral and spiritual powers in man. He applied phrenology to give a better exposition of those elements. The pamphlet, entered for copyright in 1850, is a clergyman's case that head-reading and the Bible can agree.
phrenology-explained-and-exemplified-185:
Eneas Mackenzie's Phrenology Explained and Exemplified, published by the author in London, begins by defining its word. Phrenology, from the Greek for mind and discourse, means that our intellectual faculties, moral virtues, base urges, and animal emotions may be known by bumps on the skull. These correspond to organs of the brain beneath, strong in proportion to their size.

Mackenzie credits Dr. Gall, a physician from Tiefenbrunn in Swabia, as the science's discoverer and champion. He adds the caution that exercise and education shape the faculties, so actions cannot be positively predicted. The little book is a mid-century primer of the system.
phrenology-proved-illustrated-and-applie: A hosted sample showing only the Google Books digital-copy notice pages that precede this scan, with no page of the work itself visible. The catalogue record names the book Phrenology Proved, Illustrated, and Applied, accompanied by a chart, and credits O. S. Fowler, dating this edition 1850. Its long title promises the location of the phrenological organs in the head and a view of the moral and intellectual powers.
plos-pbio-0020050:
Haoxing Xu, Jie Jin, Louis J. DeFelice, and their team reported a surprise about metal transport in PLOS Biology in 2004. A protein called DMT1 is the main route for iron to enter mammalian cells. A mutation that keeps turning up in the protein revealed something extra: a path for calcium entry.

Mutations that appear again and again often mark a spot a protein cannot do without. Here, studying that spot exposed a hidden side of DMT1's work. The finding widens the picture of how cells handle metals, where iron and calcium traffic may cross. It may also help explain odd symptoms in people and animals with faults in this transporter.
plos-pone-0000050:
Karla Eger, Mark Sundrud, Alison Motsinger, and co-authors showed in 2006 that one class of immune cells is far from uniform. Natural killer T cells patrol for abnormal cells and can release signals that steer the whole immune response. A key question was whether they can reprogram those effector functions, switching the kind of signal they send.

The team found human natural killer T cells are heterogeneous in that capacity: some can reprogram, others are more fixed. A mixed population changes how doctors should think about using these cells in therapy, since the helpful subset may need to be picked out. The study maps variety where earlier work had assumed sameness.
plos-pone-0000150:
Roman H. Khonsari and Vincent Calvez published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It addresses concentric demyelination, a striking pattern seen in some brain lesions where myelin, the insulation around nerve fibers, is lost in rings. The authors model how such rings could arise through self-organization in the human brain.

Ring-shaped damage is hard to explain by simple spreading. A self-organization model shows how local interactions can build the pattern without a ring-shaped cause. The work offers neurologists a new way to think about an unusual lesion pattern. It also shows how maths can suggest mechanisms for diseases that are hard to study directly.
plos-pone-0000250:
Sagi Levy, Jan Ihmels, Miri Carmi, and colleagues published this yeast genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Budding yeast is a single-celled fungus and a workhorse of genetics. The authors lay out the strategy of transcription regulation in this yeast. It is the overall logic by which the yeast decides which genes to switch on and when.

A strategy-level view shows design principles: how one regulator can serve many conditions, and how the system stays flexible. The authors draw that logic from genome-wide data. Understanding yeast regulation guides work in more complex cells, where the same principles apply with more parts.
plos-pone-0000350:
Gianfranco Diretto, Salim Al-Babili, Raffaela Tavazza, and colleagues published this plant engineering paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Carotenoids are the pigments that make carrots orange and supply vitamin A. The authors use metabolic engineering to raise potato carotenoid content, switching on a bacterial mini-pathway only in the tuber, the part people eat.

Potatoes are a staple for millions, so enriching them could fight vitamin A deficiency at scale. A tuber-specific pathway avoids burdening the rest of the plant. The paper reports the engineered potatoes' carotenoid gains, a step in the biofortification program for staple crops.
plos-pone-0000450:
Hu-Hui Lee and Richard R. Behringer switched a developmental gene on during cartilage formation and watched the result, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The gene is Wnt4, a signal that guides building in the embryo. Using conditional expression, a method that turns the gene on only in chosen tissue and time, they activated it during chondrogenesis in mice.

The outcome was dwarfism: the mice grew up short-limbed. Cartilage is the template that bone later replaces, so a signal that disturbs cartilage growth reshapes the whole skeleton. The experiment shows Wnt4's dose and timing must be tightly controlled for normal bone length, a lesson relevant to human skeletal disorders.
plos-pone-0000550:
A. D. McNaghten and colleagues argued for a fairer way to watch the HIV epidemic in the United States, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Existing behavioral and clinical surveillance drew on convenience samples that may not represent all persons with HIV. The authors set out the rationale for developing a population-based approach to improve representativeness.

If surveillance misses whole groups, programs aim at the wrong targets and disparities stay hidden. A population-based design samples so that every group counts in proportion. Methods papers like this one do quiet but durable work: they change the data every later decision depends on.
plos-pone-0000650:
Mike M. Moradian, Denis Beglaryan, Jill M. Skozylas and colleagues sequenced the full mitochondrial genomes of three Tetrahymena species for PLOS ONE in 2007. Tetrahymena is a single-celled ciliate used widely as a model organism. Its mitochondrial genome is divergent and unusual. Half of its 44 genes still lacked a definite function.

Those genes fall into known protein-coding genes and a group called Ymf genes. The title reports mutation hot spots and faster nonsynonymous change in the Ymf group. Nonsynonymous changes alter the protein a gene encodes, so their speed says something about evolutionary pressure. Comparative sequences like these help untangle how this odd genome evolved.
plos-pone-0000750:
Delphine Hu, Stefano M. Bertozzi, Emmanuela Gakidou and colleagues weighed what it costs to keep mothers alive in Mexico. Writing in PLOS ONE in 2007, they give Mexico's lifetime risk of dying from maternal causes as 1 in 370. The United States figure was 1 in 2,500. National efforts had improved maternal services over the prior decade, but progress toward Millennium Development Goal 5 was unclear.

The team assessed costs, benefits, and cost-effectiveness of interventions against maternal illness and death. Money spent on the wrong mix of services saves fewer mothers. Their accounting gives policymakers a ranked case for where the next peso does the most good.
plos-pone-0000850:
Allan Saul and Michael P. Fay analyzed how human immunity should shape vaccines that bundle several components against one target. Including multiple immunogens against one organism is a strategy pursued for many trial vaccines. It helps most where one immunogen alone cannot raise a strongly protective response. Many existing human vaccines already contain multiple components.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE question is design logic: given how human immunity actually responds, when do extra components help, and when do they compete? Immune responses can focus on a few dominant targets, wasting the rest. Sound design rules save vaccine developers from bloated formulas, and they matter most for hard targets like malaria and HIV.
plos-pone-0000950:
Marco Salemi, Brant Burkhardt, Rebecca Gray and colleagues traced how HIV changes inside different tissues, in PLOS ONE in 2007. As HIV infection advances, the virus often switches which cell door it uses, from CCR5 to CXCR4. The CXCR4 forms are especially deadly to young thymus cells.

Almost no work had checked which virus forms live inside the thymus itself. The team compare viral populations in lymphoid and other tissues. Their analysis gives the thymus a central role in the emergence of the CXCR4 forms. That finding ties a turning point in disease to one small organ where T cells mature.
plos-pone-0001050:
Yulei Wang, Catalin Barbacioru, Dov Shiffman and colleagues found a blood gene signature for a hidden artery swelling, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Thoracic aortic aneurysm is a bulge in the main artery near the heart. It usually gives no symptoms, yet it kills at high rates when it bursts. Surgery can prevent that, but finding who is at risk is hard.

The team hypothesized that gene expression patterns in peripheral blood could betray the aneurysm. A blood test for a silent, deadly swelling would change screening entirely. Their signature work is a first step: show the signal exists in an easy sample before building a clinic ready test.
plos-pone-0001150:
When a broken bone heals, the body rebuilds it using two routes: one that first lays down cartilage, and one that forms bone directly. Danielle Behonick and colleagues examined an enzyme's part in both routes, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The enzyme is matrix metalloproteinase 13, also called collagenase-3, which cuts collagen.

The enzyme was already known to matter in long bone development. The authors found it is expressed during adult skeletal repair and tested its role in regeneration after injury. Their work links the reshaping of the matrix around cells to successful bone healing in adults.
plos-pone-0001250:
The brain rewires itself as it adapts, but how its own activity changes the strength of its connections is largely unknown. Masako Tsukamoto-Yasui and colleagues report observations from the hippocampus, a region central to memory, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They describe active hippocampal networks undergoing spontaneous synaptic modification.

In their experiments, synapses changed strength without an external lesson driving them, following the network's own activity. The brain, in their phrase, is self-writable. Findings like these bear on how memories form and how networks stay stable while remaining flexible.
plos-pone-0001350:
Thousands of systematic reviews summarize health care evidence. Such reviews sit near the top of the evidence ladder in medicine. But their quality varies, and it should routinely be appraised. Beverley Shea and colleagues externally validated AMSTAR, a measurement tool for assessing systematic reviews, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They used the tool to appraise 42 reviews.

External validation asks whether a tool works in hands other than its makers'. AMSTAR has since become a standard checklist for review quality. The paper helped establish whether its scores are reliable and meaningful for judging the reviews on which clinical guidelines rest.
plos-pone-0001450:
Zhuofei Xu and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study that reads the full genome of a pig germ. The germ causes a lung ill in pigs that costs farms a great deal world wide. The strain they read is a type common in China. Its full gene code gives a base for all later work on this germ.

The full code lets labs compare this strain with kin strains from other lands, gene by gene. That base lets them spot vaccine and drug targets with far more care than before. It also lets vets track how strains spread and change. That is key for a disease that moves with the pig trade.
plos-pone-0001550:
Joseph Lemire, Ryan Mailloux, and Vasu Appanna wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on lactate use in human brain tumor cells. Lactate was long seen as a waste end of energy work without air. Its fate in brain chemistry was not pinned down. The team tested a human astrocytoma cell line, a model of a common brain tumor cell.

They show, for the first time in this line, that the cells can take in and burn lactate for energy. An enzyme inside the cell power units drives that use. The result recasts lactate as a fuel, not just waste. It may shape how brain tumors are fed and fought.
plos-pone-0001650:
Mikhail M. Pooggin, Johannes Fütterer, and Thomas Hohn compared a protein-making trick used by two plant viruses in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Cauliflower mosaic virus infects broad-leaf plants, while rice tungro bacilliform virus infects rice. Both are pararetroviruses, and both pack several genes onto one RNA strand. To read the later genes, ribosomes shunt: they start, then jump past a section to the next start point.

The authors asked whether the shunt parts from one virus work in the other, across the wide gap between the plant groups they infect. The full text gives the swap tests and how much protein each version made. Shared function across such different viruses hints that this jump mechanism is old and sturdy. It also gives plant science a tested tool for making several proteins from one gene strand.
plos-pone-0001750:
Henry Haeberle, Leigh A. Bryan, Tegy J. Vadakkan, and their co-authors studied touch sensor cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Merkel cell-neurite complexes are among the most sensitive touch receptors in skin, pairing epidermal Merkel cells with sensory nerve endings. Merkel cells are proposed to be the sensing cells that signal nerves chemically, but functional proof was thin.

The team reports that swelling-activated calcium channels trigger calcium signals in Merkel cells. Calcium signals are how such cells would pass the touch message onward. The full text gives the cell recordings and channel tests. Pinning a channel to the first step of touch helps explain fine fingertip sensitivity and may guide work on touch loss.
plos-pone-0001850:
Anandharaman Veerapathran, Rajnish Joshi, Kalyan Goswami, and their co-authors set cut-off values for tuberculosis blood tests in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Blood tests called IGRAs are a promising alternative to the tuberculin skin test. Reading repeated tests is hampered by lack of evidence on the best cut-offs for flips. A flip is the point where a result counts as newly positive or back to negative.

Using repeat testing data, the team derived cut-offs from how much one person's T-cell assay results vary. The full text gives the spread of results and the proposed thresholds. Health workers screened again and again, such as hospital staff, need such thresholds to avoid chasing noise as if it were new infection.
plos-pone-0001950:
Caroline Charlier and co-authors matched brain scans to illness severity in a fungal brain infection, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The infection, cryptococcal meningoencephalitis, strikes people with HIV and kills about one in five despite antifungal drugs. Doctors lacked a sharp way to grade how bad a case is.

The team studied brain images from sixty-two HIV-positive patients treated in the era of strong HIV therapy. They report that the brain lesions seen on scans correlate with how severe the illness is. If scan patterns grade a case well, doctors could sort who needs the most urgent and intense care.
plos-pone-0002050:
Toru Nakamura and co-authors compared the pattern of behavior in mice and men, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Mental functions, and how psychiatric illness warps them, are hard to reach with molecular tools, since objective measures of behavior in animals were lacking. The team instead studied laws of behavioral organization, the math shape of how acts are timed.

As the title states, they report a universality in that organization across mice and humans, and its breakdown in illness. If the timing laws match, a mouse's act stream can stand in for aspects of human mental state that genes alone cannot show.
plos-pone-0002150:
Tal Arnon, Gal Markel, Ahuva Bar-Ilan, and co-authors explored a new way to aim the immune system at cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Natural killer cells are immune cells that can kill tumor cells and infected cells. On their surface sit natural cytotoxicity receptors, including NKp46, NKp44, and NKp30, which help them pick out targets.

These receptors also exist in a loose, soluble form that floats free of the cell. The team worked on using those free forms to build new cancer immune therapies. If a receptor can be turned into a drug-like molecule, the killer cell's own targeting skill might be borrowed for treatment.
plos-pone-0002250:
Evelyne Derelle and co-authors described the life cycle and genome of a virus that infects a marine alga, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Large DNA viruses infect hosts from algae to humans and descend from an ancient common ancestor. In the oceans, algal viruses shape plankton blooms and steer the evolution of the tiny plants at the food web's base.

Their subject, OtV5, infects Ostreococcus tauri, a unicellular green alga of the open sea. The team charted how the virus grows and read its genome. Each such genome sharpens the picture of how giant viruses evolved and rule marine microbes.
plos-pone-0002350:
Ma-Li Wong, Chuanhui Dong, Karin Esposito, and co-authors analyzed blood thickening in depression and its response to treatment, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Major depressive disorder raises the risk of cardiovascular disease on its own, and depressed patients who suffer a heart attack face more cardiac complications afterward. One suspect link is stress-hemoconcentration, where stress squeezes fluid from the blood, leaving it thicker.

Using data from a randomized, double-blind trial, the team found stress-hemoconcentration was elevated in major depression and normalized with antidepressant treatment. A measurable blood change that tracks with mood treatment gives the depression-heart link a concrete, testable form.
plos-pone-0002450:
Work from Guerreiro and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Rita J. Guerreiro, Jennifer C. Schymick, Cynthia Crews, and others. Its subject is tDP-43 Is Not a Common Cause of Sporadic Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis. TAR DNA binding protein, encoded by TARDBP, was shown to be a central component of ubiquitin-positive.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002550:
In 2008, Park and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Sungsu Park, Hyejin Hwang, Seong-Won Nam, and others. Its subject is enhanced Caenorhabditis elegans Locomotion in a Structured Microfluidic Environment. Behavioral studies of Caenorhabditis elegans traditionally are done on the smooth surface of agar plates, but the natural habitat of C.

elegans and other nematodes is the soil, a complex and structured environment. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002650:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Stefan Koelsch and colleagues addresses cognitive components of regularity processing in the auditory domain. The catalog record names Stefan Koelsch first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Music-syntactic irregularities often co-occur with the processing of physical irregularities. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002750:
Bronwen Martin led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was iTRAQ analysis of complex proteome alterations in 3xTgAD alzheimer's mice: understanding the interface between physiology and disease. Authorship is credited in the record to Bronwen Martin and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by progressive cognitive impairment associated with accumulation of amyloid β-peptide. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002850:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Lihui Liu and colleagues addresses K-ras/PI3K-Akt signaling is essential for zebrafish hematopoiesis and angiogenesis. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Lihui Liu, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The RAS small GTPases orchestrate multiple cellular processes. The summary also notes a further point. Studies on knock-out mice showed the essential and sufficient role of K-RAS, but not N-RAS and H-RAS in embryonic development. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002950:
Huaiqing Chen, Yueyun Ma, Jun Yang and co-authors hunted genes needed for pneumococcal ear infection in 2008. Ear infection, or otitis media, causes most bacterial respiratory infections in children worldwide. Streptococcus pneumoniae is one of its three major causes, alongside two other bacteria named in the paper.

Little was known about which pneumococcal genes the infection itself requires. The PLOS ONE study screens for that genetic requirement, separating genes the germ needs in the ear from those it can lose. Such a list can guide vaccine and drug work aimed at a very common childhood disease.
plos-pone-0003050:
Pamella Wang, Gabriela Campanholle, Marcos Cenedeze and co-authors tested blocking the bradykinin B1 receptor in kidney injury in 2008. The team had earlier shown mice lacking that receptor were protected against renal ischemia-reperfusion injury, damage when blood returns after a cutoff. A drug blocker could offer the same gain without gene deletion.

Here they analyze the effect of B1 antagonism on that injury and whether blocking or deleting the receptor shifts the response. The title states antagonism is beneficial. Published in PLOS ONE, the work supports a drug route to protect kidneys after transplant or shock.
plos-pone-0003150:
David Pickar, Jessie Vinik and John J. Bartko survey drug treatment for schizophrenia in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Patients are often prescribed combinations from several drug classes, even though single antipsychotic use matches official labelling and the science behind combinations varies widely. The authors set out to gain current data on real drug treatment practice.

The title reports their main finding: off-label drug use was preponderant among schizophrenic patients in the data studied. Readers get a snapshot of how far practice can drift from labelled use. That gap matters for safety checks, cost, and for judging whether combined prescribing helps or harms.
plos-pone-0003250: Patrick S. Sullivan and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 comparing HIV care in two kinds of clinics. The title states the comparison: care quality in sites backed by the Ryan White Program versus sites not backed by it. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so this record does not state which group gave better care.
plos-pone-0003350:
Julien Sérandour, Stéphane Reynaud, John Willison and colleagues study insect attraction to aquatic plants in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Plants produce semiochemicals that sway insect attraction and repulsion. Generally, this attraction is closely associated with herbivory and has been studied mainly in air. The link between aquatic plants and insects was less explored.

The title reports ubiquitous water-soluble molecules in aquatic plant exudates determine specific insect attraction. Readers see chemical cues working through water rather than air. Those cues may guide insects to host plants for egg laying, with effects on aquatic food webs.
plos-pone-0003450:
Sergio Lizano and co-authors studied swapped genes in a strep germ for this 2008 paper. Streptococcus pyogenes causes strep throat and worse diseases. Its history suggests some genes came from another species wholesale. The swapped gene replaced the germ's own matching copy.

One such swap involved genes for pili, hair-like strands on the cell surface. The team tested how the foreign copy changed pilus gene control. Imported DNA had rewired the circuitry that turns those genes on. The study shows gene theft can reprogram a pathogen's surface. Pili help the germ grip host cells, so their control matters for infection.
plos-pone-0003550:
Jason G. Bragg and Sallie W. Chisholm modeled a stolen gene's payoff in this 2008 paper. Viruses of sea bacteria often carry a gene called psbA. That gene encodes D1, a core protein of photosynthesis. The host's own D1 decays during infection in the light.

A virus-carried copy may keep photosynthesis running while the virus replicates. Their model weighs the fitness gain of carrying that gene. Keeping the host's energy plant alive could yield more virus offspring. The math explains a strange case of genetic piracy in the ocean. Sea microbes drive much of Earth's oxygen output, so their viruses matter globally.
plos-pone-0003650:
Francesca Martinato, Matteo Cesaroni, Bruno Amati, and colleagues published this gene study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Myc is a protein that switches genes on and drives cell growth. It binds a large share of gene promoters across the genome. The team asked what it does to chromatin there.

They measured the chemical marks on histones, the spool proteins DNA wraps around, at Myc's target sites. The pattern of marks changed where Myc landed on the DNA. Those changes help explain how one growth switch can reset the activity of many genes at once, a process that goes wrong in cancer.
plos-pone-0003750:
Amets Sáenz, Margarita Azpitarte, Rubén Armañanzas, and colleagues published this muscle disease study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2A is an inherited disorder caused by faults in the calpain 3 gene. What calpain 3 does inside muscle cells was still little known.

The team profiled gene expression in tissue from patients with the disease. The portrait shows which genes change their activity when calpain 3 fails. That map gives researchers leads on the protein's real jobs in muscle and on how its loss leads to wasting.
plos-pone-0003850:
M. Mar González-Barroso, Irina Giurgea, Fredéric Bouillaud, and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Congenital hyperinsulinism makes newborns release too much insulin, driving blood sugar dangerously low. Faults in the pancreas's potassium channel explain many cases, but more than half had no known cause.

Mice lacking the protein UCP2 also mishandle insulin secretion. The team therefore searched patients for mutations in UCP2 and found them. The finding reveals a role for UCP2 in regulating insulin release and adds a fresh genetic cause to this infant condition.
plos-pone-0003950:
Nicolas Bréchot, Elisa Gomez, Marine Bignon, and co-authors studied limb blood loss in mice lacking a protein in 2008. Critical limb ischemia starves leg tissue of blood and can end in amputation. Macrophages, immune cells that guide healing, flood such tissue. Yet inflammation markers track with worse disease in patients.

Their PLOS ONE article used mice without thrombospondin-1 to test macrophage tuning. Shifting macrophage activation state protected tissue from necrosis in those mice. The result suggests calming one immune mode can save ischemic limbs. It points to immune tuning as a treatment angle for patients.
plos-pone-0004050:
Bernard A. Okech, Isaac K. Mwobobia, Anthony Kamau, and co-authors documented falling malaria in Kenya in 2008. Their team was surveying insects ahead of planned malaria control in Mwea. Meanwhile, cases at Kimbimbi sub-district hospital kept declining steadily. Why cases fell before interventions began was unknown.

Their PLOS ONE article credits integrated malaria management for the reduction. Integrated programs combine several control tools at once. Identifying what drove the decline mattered before adding new measures. The lesson helps other districts copy what already works. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004150:
Ricardo Palacios and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most genes exist in two copies, one from each parent, and the two copies are not always used equally. This uneven use, called allele-specific gene expression, may shape many human traits and diseases.

To map how common the pattern is, the team combined genotyping with gene activity measures across the human genome. They report that allele-specific expression is widespread, touching many genes and many biological processes. The result means that which copy of a gene came from which parent can matter far more often than once thought.
plos-pone-0004250:
Brian Fink and colleagues published this cell energy study in PLOS ONE in 2009. MitoQ is a version of the antioxidant coenzyme Q engineered to enter mitochondria, the cell's power plants. The team had earlier found that, surprisingly, it increased superoxide production in cow artery endothelial cell mitochondria fed certain fuels but not others.

Here they dig into that puzzle: how a mitochondria-targeted antioxidant, plus the choice of fuel, changes superoxide output. Fuel selectivity, which food molecules the mitochondria burn, turns out to shape the result. The findings warn that antioxidant drugs can behave as pro-oxidants depending on the cell's diet.
plos-pone-0004350:
Danuta Martuszewska and colleagues published this kidney cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tensin family of proteins is thought to link the extracellular matrix to the cytoskeleton, mediating signals for cell shape and motility. Dysregulation of tensin expression had previously been implicated in cancer.

The team report that tensin3 is a negative regulator of cell migration, a brake on cell movement. They also found all four tensin family members downregulated in human kidney cancer. Losing brakes on movement fits a cancer that spreads, which is why the family matters. All four were turned down, not just one.
plos-pone-0004450:
A small enzyme called PRL-3 helps melanoma cells spread, show Ran Song, Feng Qian, Yu-Pei Li, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. PRL-3 belongs to a family of enzymes named for the regenerating liver, where they were first found. Many studies had hinted that it aids the spread of cancers, called metastasis, but the proof was thin.

The team worked with B16F1 melanoma cells, in dishes and in animals. They found PRL-3 sits at the cell membrane, and that the cells need it to spread. Removing its effect cut the cancer's ability to move and invade. Pinpointing a needed helper of metastasis gives drug hunters a concrete target, and gives doctors a possible marker of cancers most likely to spread.
plos-pone-0004550:
A red tide coated seabirds in a slimy film and killed them in large numbers in Monterey Bay, documented by David Jessup, Melissa Miller, John Ryan, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. In November and December 2007 a widespread seabird mortality event struck the bay in California. It coincided with a massive red tide of the dinoflagellate Akashiwo sanguinea, a single-celled alga.

Affected birds had a slimy yellow-green material on feathers that were saturated and lost their waterproofing. The team links the deaths to a surfactant, a soap-like substance, produced by the bloom. Surf-like foam can strip the oils that keep seabirds dry and warm. Naming this mechanism matters, because such blooms are not poisonous in the usual way, yet can still kill at scale.
plos-pone-0004650:
A bacterium best known for harming newborns is turning up in the lungs of cystic fibrosis patients, report Vera Eickel, Barbara Kahl, Beatrice Reinisch, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Streptococcus agalactiae is a well-known pathogen for neonates and for adults with weakened immunity. Beyond the newborn period, it is rarely found in the respiratory tract.

Between 2002 and 2008 the team noticed it in respiratory secretions of a notable share of their cystic fibrosis patients. They describe this emergence of respiratory isolates. Cystic fibrosis lungs are a special environment where unusual microbes can settle. A new regular in that environment changes what doctors should test for when a patient's condition worsens without explanation.
plos-pone-0004750:
Heather Baskind and colleagues showed that a mouse gene keeps the role of a fly gene that controls gene on off states. In PLOS ONE in 2009. Two protein groups set lasting marks that keep genes active or silent. Those marks pass from mother to daughter cells, so cell identity holds through division and growth.

The mouse gene Asxl2 matches a fly gene in that system. The team tested if it does the same job in mammals. Proof of a shared role links fly genetics to human health. Such genes matter in development and in some cancers. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0004850:
Christian Quaia and colleagues measured viscoelastic properties of passive eye muscle in primates, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Viscoelastic properties of passive eye muscles are prime determinants of deficits observed following eye muscle paralysis, the root cause of several types of strabismus. Limited knowledge hinders ability of eye plant models to assist in diagnosis and surgical planning for patients with misalignment disorders.

Static forces and step responses define stiffness and damping. Accurate parameters improve surgical simulations. Eye movement models become clinically useful. The work is part one of a series. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004950:
What a mother eats in pregnancy can shape her children's lives. Earlier work showed a striking pattern in mice. Mothers fed too little protein had small pups. The pups grew fast to catch up, then lived shorter lives. Jian-Hua Chen and colleagues followed up in PLOS ONE in 2009. They tracked key proteins tied to lifespan regulation.

The team measured those proteins after birth in the catch-up offspring. Maternal protein restriction changed their levels. The results connect a poor start in the womb with ageing machinery. They help explain how early nutrition echoes across a lifetime.
plos-pone-0005050:
Two gene switches can control each other. Umashankar Singh and colleagues studied such a pair in PLOS ONE in 2009. One switch is HSF1, tied to heat shock and cancer. The other is NFIX, implicated in a brain tumor driven by PDGFB. Their molecular interplay was unknown.

A DNA sequence directs mutual transcription regulation between them. Each factor can dial the other up or down. The loop involves novel heat-sensitive protein interactions. The finding maps a new regulatory knot in brain tumors. It connects a stress factor to a developmental one. Understanding such loops matters for cancer biology. They show how tumors can lock growth programs in place.
plos-pone-0005150:
TB bacteria hide inside macrophages, the cells meant to kill them. To persist, they must survive chemical attacks. Yanmin Hu and Anthony Coates studied one of their defenses in PLOS ONE in 2009. The defense is an antioxidant enzyme called TPX, a thiol peroxidase. Macrophages blast invaders with oxidative and nitrosative stress. TPX helps neutralize that blast.

Both acute and persistent infections depended on TPX. Without it, the germ cannot hold its niche. The enzyme is a linchpin of the antioxidant complex. That makes it a target for new TB drugs. Persistent TB is the hardest to cure. A drug against TPX could shorten treatment. The study identifies a genuine vulnerability in a stubborn pathogen.
plos-pone-0005250:
The endoplasmic reticulum is the cell's inner membrane web, usually seen as one continuous system. Proteins and ions were thought to move freely through it. Kucharz and colleagues watched that web in living neurons and reported a change in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Stimulating NMDA receptors, key switches in neuron signaling, made the reticulum split into pieces. The split then reversed, and the web joined back together. Reversible fission shows the reticulum is far more dynamic than the static picture in most textbooks suggests. A web that can break and heal in minutes gives the cell a fast way to sort what it makes and where it sends it.
plos-pone-0005350:
Genome-wide studies in cattle need chips that read many DNA variants at once. Human genetics had already shown the power of dense single-letter variant genotyping. Matukumalli and colleagues developed a high-density SNP genotyping assay for cattle, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team built the assay and characterized how well it performs. A reliable cattle chip lets breeders map genes for milk, meat, and disease resistance. It brings the genomics revolution to the farm, where each mapped trait has direct economic value. One chip for the whole genome lets a small herd gain as much from gene maps as a large one. That spreads the gain to farms that could not pay for older tests.
plos-pone-0005450:
Daniel Ballhorn and co-authors studied wild lima beans in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Plants face many enemies in nature and defend themselves in several ways. Lima beans are known for asking for help from other insects by releasing scents when chewed.

The team focused on a more direct defence: the beans make cyanide-based poison in their tissues. In field tests, that poison proved to be an effective guard against enemies that eat the plants. The study shows that a plant can rely on its own poison, not only on help from allies, to stay safe.
plos-pone-0005550:
Andrea Aliverti and co-authors described a pump effect in the belly in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A large pool of blood sits in the vessels of the gut and nearby organs. That blood can be shifted toward the arms and legs when the body needs it.

The team measured trunk and body volume in healthy people while their belly muscles contracted. The measures showed how much blood the belly squeezes out with each contraction, like a pump. This pump likely helps keep blood flowing during exercise and when standing up quickly.
plos-pone-0005650:
Cathy Cailotto and co-authors studied night light and clock genes in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The body's master clock sits in the brain and sets daily rhythms for the whole body. Light at the wrong time can shift the clock and disturb organs such as the liver.

The team tested how light at night changes clock gene activity in organs outside the brain. They traced a role for nerve signals reaching the liver. The work helps explain why shift work and night light are linked to metabolic problems. Liver rhythms govern sugar and fat handling, so a disturbed liver clock can ripple through the whole body.
plos-pone-0005750:
Larisa DeSantis, Robert Feranec, and Bruce MacFadden read fossil teeth in 2009 to see how ancient mammal communities weathered a warm spell. Today's warming is reshaping mammal ranges and raising extinction risk. The long-term effects are harder to see without a past example.

Chemical traces in tooth enamel record what fossil herbivores ate and where they lived. The team used those traces across a past warming event. Shifts in diet and habitat show how communities bent under heat. Such deep-time evidence helps judge which modern species are most at risk as the planet warms again.
plos-pone-0005850:
Marian Tsanov and Denise Manahan-Vaughan linked brain rhythms to lasting memory change in 2009. The hippocampus shows a theta rhythm during exploration, thought to help encode new spatial information. Synapses strengthen or weaken in cycles tied to that rhythm.

The team found long-term plasticity, the durable rewiring behind memory, in proportion to theta activity. More theta meant stronger lasting change. That proportionality is a neat rule connecting a brain wave to a cellular outcome. It may help explain why alert exploration forms strong memories, and why rhythm faults in disease impair learning.
plos-pone-0005950:
Two blood measures guide care for people living with HIV: the CD4 cell count and the amount of virus in the blood. Eline Korenromp, Brian Williams, George Schmid and colleagues reviewed in 2009 how well each one forecasts illness when no treatment is given. Their PLOS ONE paper gathers data across many studies for a single reckoning.

A fair test must weigh how much each measure swings within one person and between people. The review weighs that swing against the risk of getting sicker per step of change. The result helps clinics, above all where tests are scarce, judge when treatment need is near and which measure deserves the most trust.
plos-pone-0006050:
Mandrills in the wild carry a virus much like the human leukemia virus HTLV-1. Sandrine Souquière, Augustin Mouinga-Ondemé, Maria Makuwa and colleagues used those monkeys as a living model in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper tracks the amount of STLV-1 carried in mandrills over chronic infection, and watches the T cell response shift alongside it.

The team also watched what happened when the immune system was suppressed. Virus load and immune answer move together in a dynamic balance, the study shows. A natural infection in a close primate relative offers a rare view of how such retroviruses settle in for life, knowledge that bears on the human cousin virus.
plos-pone-0006150:
A male fruit fly courts with song and dance, and the genes behind the show change over his life. Elizabeth Ruedi and Kimberly Hughes asked in 2009 whether age or experience drives that change. Their PLOS ONE paper measures courtship gene expression in male Drosophila melanogaster, against a backdrop of mutation screens that found the developmental genes behind behavior.

Age, but not experience, affects the courtship genes, the title reports. The calendar thus writes on the genome in a way practice does not. That split matters for the growing question of how much of behavior's variation is developmental and how much is lived, a question this simple fly system can answer cleanly.
plos-pone-0006250:
In complex diseases, the faulty proteins often belong to the same working pathways. Regine Bergholdt and colleagues applied that idea to type 1 diabetes in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They combined genetic data with maps of protein interactions to profile the networks involved.

Expression profiling showed which parts of those networks change in the disease. A network view can reveal weak points that single-gene studies miss. It also explains why many different gene faults can end in the same illness. The approach serves other complex diseases where gene lists alone have stalled.
plos-pone-0006350:
Drug advertisements in medical journals are a main source of medicines information for doctors. Noordin Othman, Agnes Vitry, and Elizabeth Roughead systematically reviewed studies of those ads' quality in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Despite worldwide regulations on drug promotion, ad information has been criticised as poor in several studies.

The review gathers the evidence on how pharmaceutical advertisements perform against standards. Misleading claims can steer prescribing toward costlier or weaker choices. A systematic picture beats scattered complaints when regulators weigh reforms. Doctors also gain grounds for reading ads with sharper scepticism.
plos-pone-0006450:
Hamish Innes-Brown and David Crewther studied a trick of the senses in PLOS ONE in 2009. In the sound-induced flash illusion, one flash shown with two or more beeps looks like two or more flashes. Earlier work showed the illusion fades as the gap in time between sound and flash grows. The pair asked what happens when sound and flash come from different places.

They tested how spatial mismatch between beeps and flashes changes the illusion. Their work maps the limits of how the brain merges sight and sound. When senses disagree in place as well as time, the merge can fail. Such limits reveal the rules the brain uses to build one world from many senses.
plos-pone-0006550:
Ying-Yu Huang, Markus Tschopp, and Stephan Neuhauss studied false self-motion perception in zebrafish for PLOS ONE in 2009. The zebrafish mutant belladonna carries a mutation in the lhx2 gene. That gene encodes a transcription factor. The mutation causes a defect in retinotectal axon pathfinding, the wiring from eye to brain.

Those wiring errors produce illusionary self-motion perception: the fish responds as if moving when it is not. Such a mutant reveals how visual circuits compute motion. It also gives a model for studying miswired visual systems. Zebrafish are ideal here because their larvae are transparent and easy to observe.
plos-pone-0006650:
Margret Berg Miller and co-authors sequenced a rumen bacterium's draft genome in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ruminococcus flavefaciens is a predominant cellulolytic rumen bacterium. It forms a multi-enzyme cellulosome complex that could play an integral role in its ability to degrade plant cell walls. The team analyzed diversity and strain specificity of its plant cell wall degrading enzymes.

The draft genome reveals the enzyme toolkit this bacterium carries. Rumen microbes let cattle turn grass into food; their enzymes also interest biofuel makers. Strain differences show the toolkit is not uniform. That diversity affects both animal nutrition and industrial enzyme hunting.
plos-pone-0006750:
Andrew Skilton and colleagues studied a small protein tag in fission yeast in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tag is SUMO, a ubiquitin-like protein. Cells attach SUMO to lysine residues on target proteins. SUMO shares a folded shape with ubiquitin despite different sequences. It can also link into chains of several units.

The team worked in the yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe. They asked whether SUMO chains are needed when DNA copying stalls. Replication arrest is a stress that can damage the genome. Their results show chain formation is required for the response. The finding separates single SUMO tags from chains as distinct signals. It clarifies how yeast protects its genome during copying stress.
plos-pone-0006850:
Hui Wei, R. Holland Cheng, and John Berriman imaged the three-dimensional structure of a bacteria-infecting virus in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bacteriophage phi12 wraps its genome in a lipid envelope. It belongs to the cystoviruses, a unique enveloped group. Its host is a plant-pathogenic Pseudomonas bacterium. The genome arrives in three double-stranded RNA segments.

The structure revealed an unusual double arrangement of protein shells. An incomplete outer lattice sits over a complete inner shell. Such layered architecture is rare among viruses. Knowing the layout clarifies how the virus assembles and infects. It also informs the wider study of RNA virus structure.
plos-pone-0006950:
Gregers Gram, Ingrid Karlsson, Else Marie Agger, and colleagues tested a vaccine adjuvant in PLOS ONE in 2009. Strong killer T cell responses are a prized feature of viral vaccines. Adjuvants are the helper ingredients that can coax such responses out. The team studied a new liposome-based adjuvant called CAF01.

They paired CAF01 with very small HIV-1 peptide antigens. Tests ran in transgenic mice carrying a human immune gene, HLA-A*0201. The goal was to raise CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes against those peptides. A working adjuvant of this kind could strengthen future HIV vaccine designs that rely on killer T cells.
plos-pone-0007050:
Rocío Montes de Oca, Christopher Shoemaker, Marjan Gucek, and colleagues mapped partners of a nuclear protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The cell nucleus is braced by a network called the lamina. Defects in that network cause diseases named laminopathies and connect to aging. One lamina-linked protein is barrier-to-autointegration factor, or BAF.

The team catalogued the proteins BAF associates with. Many partners turned out to regulate chromatin, the packed form of DNA. That partner list places BAF at the heart of gene organization. It gives laminopathy research new molecular leads to follow.
plos-pone-0007150: Wendy Lea, Jin Xi, Ajit Jadhav, and colleagues described a high-throughput approach for finding new general anesthetics in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their method was built to screen many compounds in a fast, systematic way. A pipeline like this matters because new anesthetics are rare. Faster screening could widen the options for safer drugs that put patients to sleep and wake them cleanly.
plos-pone-0007250:
Dorothy D. Sears, Philip D. Miles, Justin Chapman, and colleagues studied an inflammation-linked enzyme in obesity in PLOS ONE in 2009. Insulin resistance is now understood as an inflammatory condition. That view drives searches for genes that regulate inflammation in tissues that respond to insulin, such as fat tissue.

The enzyme is 12/15-lipoxygenase, which controls production of inflammatory signals. The authors feed mice a high fat diet and track early fat tissue inflammation. They report that the enzyme is required for the early onset of that inflammation and insulin resistance. The finding names a target for diabetes prevention research.
plos-pone-0007350:
Ida Autiero, Susan Costantini, and Giovanni Colonna modeled a longevity-linked human protein in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Sirt-1 is a nuclear enzyme that removes chemical tags from other proteins. It participates in glucose metabolism, insulin secretion, and many other pathways, acting on numerous different substrates as a multifunctional protein.

Sirt-1 is partly unordered, meaning sections lack a fixed shape. That disorder complicates structural study. The authors present molecular modeling and structure-function relationships for human Sirt-1. Their model helps explain how a flexible protein can regulate so many metabolic processes.
plos-pone-0007450:
Katherine Schouest and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on cell death control in the roundworm C. elegans. Germinal center kinases form a large, conserved protein family involved in growth, movement, and stress responses. One member, GCK-1, works in the worm's germline, the tissue that makes eggs and sperm. The team examined what GCK-1 does there.

They found GCK-1 acts as a brake. It restrains MAP kinase signaling and holds back apoptosis, the orderly self-destruction of cells. Without that brake, germ cells would die too readily. The finding identifies a control knob in a simple animal that many organisms share. It helps explain how reproductive tissue decides which cells live and which are culled.
plos-pone-0007550:
Olivier Chenu and colleagues published a feasibility study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on preventing pressure sores in people who sit for long periods. Pressure sores are injuries to skin and tissue caused by unrelieved pressure. People with paraplegia are especially at risk, since they sit long and cannot feel their lower limbs. The team tested a wireless device that reports sitting pressure through the tongue.

The device senses overpressure under the seated body and signals via a small mouthpiece. The tongue is sensitive and usually spared in spinal injuries, making it a good alarm channel. A warning prompts the user to shift posture before damage forms. Early results show the approach can work in practice. It turns an intact sense into a guard for a body part that cannot feel danger.
plos-pone-0007650:
Lee Samuel and Branko Latinkić published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the first steps of heart development. Cardiac induction is when embryonic cells are first told to become heart. It is thought to start during gastrulation, prompted by nearby tissue. Several signaling pathways had been implicated, including FGF, Nodal, BMP, and Wnt. Which signals fire first, and whether they need each other, was unknown.

Early activation of the FGF and Nodal pathways proved to mediate cardiac specification. Strikingly, they did so independently of Wnt and beta-catenin signaling. That splits the heart's recipe: two pathways start the job without the expected third. Correcting the recipe matters for growing heart cells in the lab. Stem cell recipes copy embryo logic, step by step. The study clarifies the opening steps of that logic.
plos-pone-0007750:
Yun-Cheol Kim and Sherie Morrison published a methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. It describes a fast, cheap way to purify plasmid DNA at the lab bench. Labs judge such methods on purity, yield, speed and cost. Most kits and protocols do well on some of these, but not all four.

Their method uses glass syringe filters as the key tool. The setup is built in-house from simple parts. It aims to give clean DNA quickly without pricey kits. A cheaper routine method can help small labs run more experiments on tight budgets.
plos-pone-0007850:
Isabella Bray and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines tiny RNAs in neuroblastoma, a childhood cancer of the sympathetic nervous system. The cancer is often fatal and starts in precursor nerve cells. One driver is MYCN, a gene that can become amplified, present in many extra copies.

The authors show that MYCN amplification and chromosome imbalances disturb microRNAs widely. Those small RNAs normally tune gene expression after transcription. Certain microRNA patterns were associated with patient survival. The links could lead to markers that flag high-risk children sooner, and perhaps to new treatment targets.
plos-pone-0007950:
Melanie Norgate and colleagues read the DNA of an Australian butterfly in PLOS ONE in 2009. The butterfly, Heteronympha merope, is used to study how species cope as the world changes. The team used DNA from the cell's power plants, a part passed down through mothers.

The DNA pointed to a split between butterfly groups late in the last ice age era. Past shifts in range, forced by cold and warmth, left clear marks in their genes. Knowing that past helps scientists guess how the species may move or thin out as the climate warms again.
plos-pone-0008050:
Yanyan Hong and colleagues vetted an antibody meant to find estrogen-making tumors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some breast cancers feed on estrogen made inside the tumor by an enzyme called aromatase. Drugs that block the enzyme help only when it is truly there.

The team mapped the exact spot their antibody grips on the enzyme, proving its aim. A trusted stain for aromatase in tumor tissue can match patients to the blocking drugs with more care. The vetting step is dull but vital: a test is only as good as its aim.
plos-pone-0008150:
Melissa Edeling and colleagues mapped which parts of a membrane-bending protein a zebrafish embryo cannot do without in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein family, PACSIN or syndapin, curves cell membranes during intake of material. The embryo needs it while building the notochord, the rod that precedes the spine.

Disabling one part at a time showed which shapes and prongs the work truly needs. Some parts proved vital; others could be spared. The map connects a protein's shape to a whole organ's making, a link that helps read human faults in kindred genes.
plos-pone-0008250:
Qingzhong Liu and colleagues tackled cancer data analysis in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Microarray data measure thousands of genes at once. Yet data sets usually contain only a small number of samples. That mismatch makes analysis both interesting and challenging. Choosing the right features is key when predicting disease from gene activity.

The team applied feature selection and classification to MAQC-II data. The data covered breast cancer and multiple myeloma samples. Picking fewer, stronger gene features can make predictions more reliable. Their work tests methods on a shared benchmark set. That helps other researchers compare tools fairly.
plos-pone-0008350:
Anwar M. Hashem and colleagues tested a compound against influenza in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Influenza viruses cause serious infections worldwide each year. Vaccines prevent many cases but have real limitations. Strains resistant to current anti-influenza drugs are increasing. New antivirals are therefore needed.

The compound, aurintricarboxylic acid, proved a potent inhibitor of influenza neuraminidases. Neuraminidase is an enzyme the virus uses to spread between cells. Blocking it is the strategy behind existing flu drugs. A fresh inhibitor could help when viruses resist the old ones in clinics.
plos-pone-0008450:
Lise Aksglaede and co-authors link puberty age and obesity in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Recent studies show puberty now starts at younger ages than in the past. Some think the rise in childhood obesity drives that trend. Fat tissue can affect hormones that set the timing of puberty. The team test that link with data on body mass before puberty.

They analyze how body mass relates to age at puberty. They check the pattern in their study group. The results help judge how much of the trend weight can explain. The paper gives facts for a debate that affects child health policy.
plos-pone-0008550:
Corinne Beurrier and co-authors test a protective factor for brain cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The factor is called CNTF. It can protect nerve cells in animal tests of damage from glutamate. Glutamate is a brain signal that harms cells when levels stay too high. How CNTF protects was still poorly known. The team test if it helps support cells clear glutamate faster. Those support cells, called glia, mop up glutamate near synapses.

They find CNTF protects striatal nerve cells by boosting that cleanup. Faster cleanup leaves less glutamate to overdrive the cells. The striatum is a deep brain area harmed in Huntington disease. Boosting cleanup gives a clear route to protect such cells.
plos-pone-0008650:
Per Sjödin, Thomas Bataillon, and Mikkel H. Schierup published a genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. They dealt with indels, short stretches of DNA that get added or lost. Such changes make up a large share of the differences between genomes. Yet they drew far less study than single-letter changes, partly because they are hard to type reliably.

The authors counted and compared indel events across recent human history. From those patterns they worked out how this kind of mutation tends to arise and spread. Their account gives these overlooked edits a firmer place in human evolution. It also warns that any reading of genome history ignoring indels will miss part of the story.
plos-pone-0008750:
Charles Baer and Dee Denver tested how random mutations affect the steadiness of gene activity. Their worm study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Traits are called canalized when they resist small environmental jolts. Logic says some hidden layer must absorb the jolts. The tiny worm Caenorhabditis elegans offered a controlled test. Lines carrying fresh spontaneous mutations were compared with steady lines.

Mutant worms showed gene activity that was less sensitive to random surroundings. In other words, new mutations buffered the readout rather than scrambling it. That surprise result challenges simple views of mutation as pure noise in evolution.
plos-pone-0008850:
F. Curtis Hewitt and R. Jude Samulski engineered a brand-new start site for DNA copying. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. DNA copying begins at spots called origins of replication. There, proteins grip DNA with exact specificity. In most higher animals and many viruses, those grips remain unknown. Model viruses offered a simpler place to learn the rules.

By reshaping the DNA-protein interface, they created a working novel origin. The build shows specificity can be designed, not just found. Engineered origins could stabilize gene therapy vectors. They also test theories of how natural origins evolved.
plos-pone-0008950:
Betiana Garavaglia and co-authors studied a stolen gene that helps a citrus pest survive, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bacterium Xanthomonas citri causes citrus canker, a damaging tree disease. Oddly, it carries a gene much like one plants use for their own signalling. No other known bacterium has this plant-like gene.

The gene makes a protein resembling plant natriuretic peptides, signals that keep leaves working. Plants normally shut down photosynthesis when attacked, starving the invader. The bacterium's copy of the signal counters that shutdown, keeping its food supply alive. Borrowing the host's own gene lets the germ live longer on the tree.
plos-pone-0009050:
Keiko Fujikawa and co-authors nominated two genes behind a spontaneous form of glaucoma, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glaucoma is a leading cause of blindness around the world. Pressure and optic nerve damage feature in it, but the molecular roots are murky. Few genetic animal models of the disease exist to study.

Mice lacking both VAV2 and VAV3 developed glaucoma on their own. VAV proteins relay signals inside cells, including in the eye's drainage tissue. The mouse model gives researchers a living system for the disease. The same genes now stand as candidates in human glaucoma too.
plos-pone-0009150:
John Arne Dahl and co-authors found a chemical tag split unevenly at the embryo's first fork, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A mouse embryo's first decision makes two lineages. The inner cell mass becomes the body; the trophectoderm becomes support tissues. Histone marks help lock in those early choices.

The team mapped methylation on histone H3 at lysine 27. On development genes, the mark sat asymmetrically between the lineages. One side carried the silencing tag while the other did not. That uneven start helps explain how identical cells first diverge. The split appears before the lineages fully separate.
plos-pone-0009250:
Emilio Herrera and co-authors published this rat study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glucocorticoid drugs given to premature babies reduce chronic lung disease. The trade-off is a higher risk of high blood pressure in adulthood. Excess glucocorticoids also drive free radical production and damage blood vessel linings.

The team tested whether antioxidant treatment could undo that vessel damage. They gave rats glucocorticoids after birth, then treated them with antioxidants. The treatment changed the peripheral vascular dysfunction the steroids had caused. That result supports the free radical explanation, and hints that the long-term harm of a useful newborn therapy might be softened.
plos-pone-0009350:
Bernhard Haubner and co-authors published this heart study in PLOS ONE in 2010. PI3K gamma is an enzyme with jobs in both immunity and the heart. In immune cells it promotes inflammation. In heart muscle it restrains contraction yet helps cells survive stress. That double life made its role in heart attacks unclear.

The team studied mice through heart ischemia and the rush of blood that follows. PI3K gamma protected the heart from that combined injury. Surprisingly, the protection came through a pathway that does not need its enzyme activity. A protein can thus guard the heart by its presence and partners, not only by its chemistry.
plos-pone-0009450:
Radina Soebiyanto, Farida Adimi, and Richard Kiang modeled flu spread in warm lands in PLOS ONE in 2010. Flu is often tied to cold, dry winter air. In the tropics and nearby warm zones, its timing is less clear. The team built a model that uses weather data, such as heat and damp air, to track transmission.
