The model aims to predict when flu will rise in places where seasons are weak. Tests against past data show how well weather alone can flag a surge. Health teams in warm regions could use such forecasts to time vaccines and staff. That would put help in place before cases climb.
plos-pone-0009550:
Kareem Carr and colleagues proposed a fast way to compare proteins in PLOS ONE in 2010. Classic methods align sequences letter by letter, which is slow on huge data sets. Their approach turns each sequence into a feature vector, a list of numbers. The numbers capture the counts and positions of building blocks in the sequence. Related proteins should then give close vectors.

Comparing vectors is far faster than aligning full sequences. The method loses some detail but gains a lot of speed. For very large collections, that trade can be worth it. It gives researchers a quick first pass to sort proteins before deeper study.
plos-pone-0009650:
Michelle Heupel, Colin Simpfendorfer, and Richard Fitzpatrick tracked grey reef sharks in PLOS ONE in 2010. These sharks range across the tropical Indo Pacific. Wide ranging animals might roam far, or each might stay near one reef. The team tagged sharks and followed their movements over large areas. They measured both long trips and fidelity to home reefs.

The tracking showed how far individuals travel and how faithfully they return. Such habits decide how well marine reserves can protect the species. A shark that stays home gains full shelter from a local reserve. A roamer needs protection across a wider map, and this study supplies that map.
plos-pone-0009750:
Irina V. Balyasnikova and co-authors published a brain tumor study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study uses human stem cells from marrow, fitted with a small antibody that locks onto a tumor-only marker called EGFRvIII. The aim was a better therapy for glioblastoma, the most lethal brain tumor.

Fitted stem cells slowed tumor growth in dishes and clung to tumors in mice far more than plain stem cells. Flank tumors grew 50 percent less with the fitted cells. Mice with brain tumors lived longer when given the cells, and longer still with a second dose two weeks later.
plos-pone-0009850:
Rod-shaped bacteria must divide in the middle, not near their ends. Suey van Baarle and Marc Bramkamp studied the system that enforces that rule in Bacillus subtilis. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bacillus subtilis is a model bacterium for cell biology.

Dividing off-center can create minicells, tiny cells with no DNA that cannot grow. The MinCDJ system prevents that error in this soil bacterium. It works by promoting divisome disassembly, taking apart the division machine at wrong sites. The result keeps each new cell complete and viable.
plos-pone-0009950:
Tropical sponges of one family hide more diversity than their shapes suggest. Judith Pöppe and colleagues used gene barcodes to reveal that hidden variety across the Indo-Pacific. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sponges are simple animals with no true tissues.

The barcode gene is COI, a standard marker for animal identification. It revealed new clades, branches of the family tree, within the family Irciniidae. Radiation patterns showed how lineages spread and split across the region. The family belongs to the sponge order Dictyoceratida. The sponges live across warm Pacific waters.
plos-pone-0010050:
The authors were Dayanidhi Raman, Jiqing Sai, Nicole Neel, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study covered a receptor called CXCR2 and cell movement. CXCR2 helps white blood cells and vessel cells move where they are needed. It shapes new blood vessel growth, wound healing, and sudden inflammation, plus long-term inflammatory disease.

The team studied a protein shortened to LASP-1 and its effect on CXCR2-driven migration. How cells move matters in both healing and in cancer spread. Pinning down a control protein adds one more possible point for future drugs to act on.
plos-pone-0010150:
The authors were Sueli Nakatani, Carlos Santos, Irina Riediger, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper built a test for hepatitis C virus types. Knowing a patient's virus genotype is the strongest predictor of response to antiviral therapy. Different genotypes respond differently, so typing guides drug choice and treatment length in the clinic.

The new method uses real-time PCR, a fast DNA copying and reading technique. It reads the NS5B region of the virus to assign the genotype. The authors designed two reaction sets and evaluated how well the test performed.
plos-pone-0010250:
The authors were Nicole Dietrich, Stefan Lienenklaus, Siegfried Weiss, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used mice to locate an immune sensor's signal source. Toll-like receptors are first-line sentinels that detect germs and trigger defense. The TLR2 family pairs up in varied combinations, letting it recognize parts from many different microbes with one flexible system.

The team found that activating mouse TLR2 induces type I interferon responses. Those antiviral signals came from endolysosomal compartments, recycling stations deep inside the cell. Placing the signal there refines models of how surface sensors produce antiviral messages.
plos-pone-0010350:
Venkata Dasari and colleagues tested stem cells against glioma, a deadly brain tumor, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A gene called PTEN normally brakes a key growth pathway in cells. Most gliomas keep that pathway, known as PI3K/Akt, switched on too strongly. The brake is weak or missing, so tumor cells move and grow freely. The team used stem cells from cord blood to restore the brake.

When those stem cells met glioma cells, PTEN levels rose in the tumor cells. The overactive pathway then quieted down. As a result, the glioma cells migrated less, a step toward spreading. Stem cells here act as a delivery and repair tool, not just spare parts. The work points to a treatment idea worth testing further.
plos-pone-0010450:
Mina Fadaee-Shohada and colleagues watched a food-poisoning bacterium meet rat brain-lining cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Listeria can cross into the brain and cause meningitis. The brain's ventricles are lined by ciliated cells that sweep fluid along. Those cells stand between infected fluid and brain tissue. The team grew rat lining cells with the bacteria and observed both sides.

Certain bacterial strains slowed the beating of the cells' tiny hairs. The cells themselves also changed behavior during the encounter. A weakened sweeping system might help bacteria settle and invade. Studying this border clarifies one route into the brain. It may also suggest ways to protect the lining during infection.
plos-pone-0010550:
David Sebinger and co-workers presented a low-volume method for growing embryonic kidneys in the lab in PLOS ONE in 2010. Growing whole organs in dishes lets scientists watch development step by step. Kidney culture is a classic version of that technique. It repeats many features of early kidney growth faithfully. The catch was that older methods blurred the organ's internal layout. Their new method used much less fluid and preserved anatomy better.

Kidneys grown this way formed the proper outer and inner zones. A faithful layout lets researchers trust the developmental signals they see. Low volume also saves costly growth factors. Better organ culture serves both basic science and future regenerative work. This methods paper upgrades a standard tool.
plos-pone-0010650:
Chris Crowder and colleagues surveyed Lyme disease bacteria inside ticks, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Several Borrelia species and strains cause Lyme disease. They are carried by Ixodes ticks across North America and Europe, and the mix differs by region.

The team typed bacteria collected from ticks on both continents. Ticks often carried more than one strain at once, and strain sets differed between sites. The strain a tick carries affects how illness may unfold in a bitten person. A clear map of that variety supports better tests and smarter local prevention advice.
plos-pone-0010750:
You-Hai Xu and colleagues compared two enzyme drugs for Gaucher disease in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gaucher disease type 1 stems from a faulty lysosomal enzyme that should break down a fatty substance. Without it, the substance builds up in liver, spleen, blood, and bone. Regular infusions of a working enzyme are the standard care.

Two products, velaglucerase alfa and imiglucerase, were tested head to head. In dishes and in mice with the disease, they performed very much alike. Comparable results give doctors and patients a real choice of supplier, which matters when a lifelong drug faces shortages.
plos-pone-0010850:
Wenjie Xie, Yafang Huang, Wenling Xie and co-authors published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chronic bacterial infection is known to raise cancer risk, usually blamed on long-term inflammation. The authors asked a more direct question: can material from bacteria act on cancer cells themselves and make them more aggressive?

They worked with a highly mobile breast cancer cell line that carries large amounts of TLR2, a sensor on the cell surface. A piece of bacterial wall from Staphylococcus aureus switched that sensor on, and the cancer cells became stickier and better at invading. Blocking the sensor erased those effects, and key growth pathways inside the cell switched on in step. Xie and colleagues show a germ's debris can directly push cancer spread, not just inflame nearby tissue.
plos-pone-0010950:
Katie Barott, Jennifer Caselle, Elizabeth Dinsdale and co-authors published this reef survey in PLOS ONE in 2010. Millennium Atoll, a remote coral island in Kiribati's Southern Line chain, is among the least disturbed reef systems left on Earth. During a 2009 expedition the team charted its lagoon, one of the most enclosed of any atoll, as a reference for what a healthy reef looks like.

They mapped physical conditions and life throughout the lagoon, from the rim reefs to the palm-like patch reefs webbing its center. Depths averaged around ten meters in most pools, and the deepest areas held broad platforms of one coral that formed a base for the branching corals dominating above. Barott and colleagues document a near-pristine ecosystem in detail, a baseline against which damaged reefs, and any future decline here, can be judged.
plos-pone-0011050:
Yosuke Kita, Atsuko Gunji, Kotoe Sakihara and co-authors published this face perception study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Recognizing a face depends both on where the eyes travel and on how the brain processes what they land on, yet those two halves are rarely measured together. The authors combined eye tracking with near-infrared spectroscopy, which reads blood oxygen changes in the frontal lobe.

Healthy adults watched morphing movies in which one face gradually became another, sometimes their own face turning into a familiar one, while the team recorded fixations and brain responses during identification. Kita and colleagues test whether different scanning strategies actually change how the brain identifies a face. Their conclusion, flagged in the title, is that looking patterns do not drive the identification process, a result that reframes how face training therapies might work.
plos-pone-0011150:
Gainotti, Fusari Imperatori, Spila-Alegiani and colleagues reviewed Italian law in PLOS ONE in 2010. People with dementia may join research even when they cannot consent for themselves. The authors asked how the law protects such participants and who may act on their behalf.

The study examined legal agency rules that let a representative decide for a patient. It weighed safeguards meant to balance science with personal dignity and safety. Clear rules matter as dementia research grows with aging populations. The review shows where Italian law gives protection and where gaps leave participants less covered.
plos-pone-0011250:
Bahlai, Xue, McCreary and colleagues compared soybean pesticides in PLOS ONE in 2010. Farmers often assume organic sprays are safer for the environment than synthetic ones. The team measured environmental risk from both kinds of products as actually used on soybeans.

Choosing organic products did not reliably lower environmental risk in their analysis. Some natural products harmed helpful organisms as much as man made ones. The lesson is to judge each spray by measured data, not by its label. Farm policy built on evidence can protect water, pollinators and soil life more honestly.
plos-pone-0011350:
Marjolaine Maher-Laporte and co-authors catalogued in 2010 the cargo packets that young rat brain cells use to move messages. Nerve cells ship RNA along their long branches inside parcels made of RNA plus proteins. Those parcels decide which proteins get built far from the cell body, at the branch tips where connections form. The exact mix inside each parcel type defines what it can do.

The team isolated parcels built around a protein called Staufen2 and listed the other proteins and RNAs traveling with it in embryonic rat brain. That inventory shows which partners work together to carry and control the messages. A parts list like this helps neuroscientists trace how growing brains wire themselves. It also gives later studies firm targets when they ask how faulty shipping may contribute to brain disorders.
plos-pone-0011450:
Douglas Plager and co-authors read gene activity in 2010 in tissue from patients with chronic sinus inflammation and nasal polyps. The condition often travels with asthma and makes breathing and smell miserable for years. Because its molecular roots are murky, the team compared its gene profile with that of atopic dermatitis, an allergic skin disease, to sort shared signals from unique ones.

The comparison separated allergy wiring common to both diseases from changes specific to the sinus tissue. That split matters for treatment: shared pathways might answer to existing allergy drugs, while sinus-specific signals need new ones. The paper gives drug researchers a cleaner target list. It also shows the value of comparing related diseases directly, instead of studying each in isolation and rediscovering the shared half every time.
plos-pone-0011550:
Maria Cristina De Rosa and co-authors built a three-dimensional model in 2010 of the molecular grip behind rheumatoid arthritis. In the disease, T cells mistake joint collagen for an enemy when it is displayed by a molecule called HLA-DR4, which many patients carry. The team modeled the full three-part complex: the T-cell receptor, the collagen piece, and the HLA display molecule.

A working model of the mistaken grip shows exactly which contacts hold it together, and therefore which contacts a drug would need to break. Blocking one defined complex is a far more selective aim than suppressing the whole immune system, as current treatments do. The model also helps explain why only certain collagen pieces and certain HLA forms combine into disease. Computational models earn their keep when they turn an autoimmune mystery into a shape a chemist can work on.
plos-pone-0011650:
Lina Thoren and co-authors studied a quality-control system for RNA in the liver, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells destroy faulty RNA messages that contain early stop signals, a clean-up process called nonsense-mediated decay. The protein UPF2 is a core part of that system, but its role in whole organs was still emerging.

Working in mice, the team showed UPF2 is critical for liver development, daily function and regrowth after damage. Losing it disrupts all three. The result reveals how much the liver depends on RNA surveillance, and it offers a new lens on liver failure and regeneration research.
plos-pone-0011750:
Patrik Sahlin and Henrik Jönsson modelled how cell division shapes growing sheets of tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In cell layers such as skin, dividing cells change both the shape and the neighbour pattern of the sheet. The rules that govern division are thus key to grasping how tissues grow in an even, orderly way.

Their model followed sheets that grow at the same rate in all directions. The runs show how division choices shape the traits of the sheet at large scale. That view of orderly growth helps explain how tissues stay smooth and whole while their cells keep splitting.
plos-pone-0011850:
Frank Boellmann and Russell Thomas used large screening methods in 2010 to find what controls the heat shock response in mammal cells. When cells are stressed by heat or damage, they quickly make protective proteins that help other proteins keep their shape. The response also stands in for the cell's wider quality control system, which weakens with age and in folding diseases.

Their screens singled out protein kinase C iota, an enzyme not previously placed in charge here, as a regulator of that response. Adding a new controller changes the map of how cells react to stress. It also gives researchers a fresh handle for studying why protein cleanup fails in aging and disease.
plos-pone-0011950:
Alan Yu reported in 2010 a link between how listeners handle sloppy speech sounds and their autistic traits. Speech varies constantly with context, and listeners normally compensate, hearing the intended sound rather than the shifted one. When compensation fails, odd hearings can seed lasting changes in how a language sounds.

Yu found that the degree of perceptual compensation tracks a listener's own autistic traits. That connection ties a core speech skill to the broader autism spectrum in the general population. It also gives models of sound change a human variable to include: languages evolve through listeners, and listeners differ in systematic ways.
plos-pone-0012050:
Anna Murzyn and co-workers showed in 2010 that a good yeast wages war on a bad one with a fatty acid it gives off. The good yeast, sold as a probiotic, is used to calm gut ills. Its foe, Candida albicans, causes thrush and worse ills of the gut, the skin, and the body's inner linings, and it is growing harder to kill with drugs.

The acid, called capric acid, stopped the foe yeast from growing its long threads, from clinging to walls, and from building the slimy films that shield it from drugs. Those three traits are just what make Candida so hard to clear from a sick body. A named weapon in the good yeast's kit could be copied by drug makers who need new ways to fight fungal ills.
plos-pone-0012150:
Jacob Udell, Julie Wang, David Gladstone, and co-authors weighed blood-thinning treatment after a major heart attack, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Survivors of a heart attack in the front wall of the heart often form a clot inside the heart, which can travel to the brain and cause a stroke. Many patients already leave hospital on two anti-clotting drugs, and adding a stronger blood thinner raises bleeding risk.

The study weighed that trade-off: fewer strokes against more bleeds, in an era when blocked arteries are reopened quickly. Clear numbers on both sides help doctors choose for each patient instead of following habit. It is the kind of evidence that quietly shapes discharge prescriptions for thousands of heart patients.
plos-pone-0012250:
Isabelle Schepens, Fabienne Jaunin, Nadja Begre, and co-authors identified the target of autoantibodies in a rare blistering disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Paraneoplastic pemphigus strikes people who also have tumors, destroying skin, mouth lining, and sometimes internal organs. Patients' immune systems attack a set of structural proteins, and one target, known only by its size and called p170, had never been identified.

The team showed p170 is a large protease inhibitor that guards tissues against enzyme damage. Naming the target completes the known set of this disease's immune targets and sharpens its blood test. For a disease this devastating, a complete target list is the ground every diagnosis and treatment study stands on.
plos-pone-0012350:
Biborka Bereczky-Veress, Nada Abdelmagid, Fredrik Piehl and fellow scientists traced how herpes simplex virus type 1 reaches the brain in rats, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Herpes brain infection is rare but often deadly, and survivors can face lasting harm. Earlier work showed that some rat strains fall very ill while others resist, so genes and entry routes both matter.

The team looked at the sheath cells that wrap nerves and at two sensors, TLR2 and TLR9, that spot invading germs. Their tests show how these cells and sensors shape the virus's path into the central nervous system. Knowing the entry route may help doctors find ways to block the infection before it reaches the brain.
plos-pone-0012450:
Juliane Bremer, Tracy O'Connor, Cinzia Tiberi and colleagues removed the enzyme Dicer from mouse Schwann cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Schwann cells wrap peripheral nerves in myelin, the insulation that lets signals travel fast. Dicer builds the tiny microRNAs that fine-tune gene activity, so deleting it tests how much myelination depends on that tuning.

Without Dicer, the cells multiplied more but failed to myelinate nerves. Growth and insulation, it turns out, are balanced by microRNA control. The result explains features of nerve diseases where myelination stalls and gives researchers a clean model for studying how insulation is switched on.
plos-pone-0012550:
Masahiro Azuma, Ryoko Sawahata, Yuusuke Akao and colleagues tested how fat-peptide molecules switch on killer immune cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Natural killer cells attack infected and cancerous cells, and dendritic cells can wake them using signals that engage the TLR2 sensor. The team used diacyl lipopeptides, small fat-tailed peptides, as the wake-up signal.

The exact peptide sequence decided how strongly dendritic cells activated the killers through TLR2. Sequence, not just presence, sets the immune volume. That rule helps vaccine designers build adjuvants — immune boosters — with predictable strength, rather than screening blind mixtures and hoping.
plos-pone-0012650:
Sysoeva, Tonevitsky and Wackermann asked why people judge the length of time so differently. Their 2010 study recruited forty-four healthy young men and tested how each one sensed time passing. They also read each man's variants in genes tied to serotonin, a brain chemical linked to mood.

Matching time scores to gene variants linked part of the difference to the serotonin system. Time sense feels basic, yet it shifts in many mental illnesses, so its biology matters. Small gene studies like this one are early steps toward explaining that variation.
plos-pone-0331050:
Abdulrahman Alshammari and co-authors introduce in 2026 a flexible family of statistical curves for how risk of an event changes over time. Many real risks first fall then rise, or peak once, and simple curves cannot bend that way. Their two measure family builds on any starting curve, and they study one version in depth with full maths for fitting and uncertainty.

Computer simulations checked bias and accuracy, and a test on COVID death records from Mexico compared the new curve with well known rivals. The new version fit best across several standard scores. The authors offer it as an easy tool for health and reliability work where risk is not steady.
plos-pone-0335050:
Phones and sensors that talk directly to each other, skipping the tower, can speed local wireless traffic. Abdullah Hadi Al-Quhali and colleagues simulated such device-to-device links inside a single 5G cell, testing ways to share the airwaves, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

One plan split the cell into inner and outer rings, each with its own share of spectrum. Another let nearby pairs reuse channels when other users were far enough away. Changing user density and placement showed how each plan affects dropped connections. The authors aim to cut outages in crowded city areas where direct links could relieve busy towers.
plos-pone-0338350:
Heng Liu and co-authors examined elite women's golf at the Paris Olympics in 2026 work published that year. They took the leading players from the 2024 Games and linked each single round score to thirteen measures of play, such as putting and reaching greens in few strokes.

Scores were lower when players reached greens on time and putted well, and higher when they needed many putts. A careful model kept seven measures as steady predictors and explained most of the gap between good and bad rounds. Because the sample was small, the authors checked the model hard for overfitting, and coaches can use its short list to focus practice.
plos-pone-0340550:
Emily Kiernan and Jakina Debnam Guzman report this 2026 PLOS One study of paying in public. It asks how paying where others can see changes what people will spend. More than two hundred sixty American undergraduates made a real purchase. They paid by debit card, credit card, or the app Venmo. Venmo was set to private, public, or friends-only visibility. Each person then stated what they would pay for ten household items.

The usual digital payment premium held for private and fully public payments. People paid more than with cash-like methods. But when purchases showed only to friends, willingness to pay dropped sharply. The authors link this to image management among frugal peers. Viewing others' transactions strengthened the effect. Stated preferences, though, did not move at all. The lesson: who sees a payment shapes spending, not just how the payment works.
plos-pone-0341850:
Khudhayr Abdullah Rashedi and Tahir Mehmood led a team that used just twenty-one compounds to probe a weak point in data science. Their 2026 study is not about predicting yields. It asks how trusty two popular math tools stay when samples are tiny but measures are many. The compounds are Schiff bases, a well-known group in chemistry. Each one came with a full infrared scan and a known yield.

The team ran both tools and checked each result by leaving one compound out in turn. Both tools proved shaky. Their answers swung a lot from run to run. The authors warn labs not to trust such models on tiny sets. They also urge full, open reporting when data are this thin.
plos-pone-0343050: Megyesiova and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on poverty across European Union countries. They used methods that weigh many factors at once to track poverty and social exclusion together. The frame was the first UN Sustainable Development Goal, which aims to end poverty. Comparing countries on many measures at once can show which policies travel well and which gaps persist.
plos-pone-0345550:
Chavez-Ecos and colleagues, in a 2026 review, weigh two genetic tests for confirming Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy, diseases that waste muscle in boys and men. A first test, called MLPA, hunts large missing or duplicated chunks of the gene. A second, newer sequencing test reads the gene in fine detail. The team pooled studies of patients already suspected of the disease.

The first test was good but imperfect, catching about four in five cases with high accuracy when positive. Sequencing alone found a similar share. The striking result came from using them in sequence: when the first test was negative and sequencing followed, detection rose to nearly every case. Bias checks looked clean, but the certainty of the estimates was rated very low. The authors still back the stepwise plan for patients whose suspicion stays strong after a negative first test.
plos-pone-0345850:
Artificial intelligence burns large amounts of power, so Amirreza Ahmadnejad, Mohammad Mehrdad Asadi, and Somayyeh Koohi designed a tiny light-based part that does one key neural network step. Their 2026 PLOS One paper presents a cavity, about ten micrometers wide, that bends light signals the way common activation rules do.

The part works at two linked light frequencies and uses only femtojoules of energy per step, in a space one hundred times smaller than earlier designs. Computer simulations checked the physics, and test networks using the optical step scored within half a percent of normal electronic versions. Small changes in the light input also mimic other activation rules.
plos-pone-0345950:
Tie Xu and colleagues proposed a collision avoidance system for groups of ships in 2026. Busy waters demand split second choices that follow sea rules, respect each captain's appetite for risk, and handle many vessels at once.

Their design first learns from past ship tracking data to predict moves and guess each vessel's risk attitude. Then a game based learning method plans avoidance, with the international collision rules built into the allowed actions. Tests on historical tracks and simulations showed advantages over older methods. Embedding the rule book directly is the key idea for safe automation at sea.
plos-pone-0346350:
Nura Alkali and co-authors survey in 2026 abnormal blood fat levels among people with diabetes in northern Nigeria. Patients at several centres gave data on heart risks, medicines, body size, blood pressure, sugar control, and kidney health. Abnormal fats raise heart danger, yet how often they are treated locally was poorly known.

About three in five patients had abnormal fats, linked more often to women and to protein in urine. Only about half of those affected took fat lowering treatment, almost all one drug class, and very few reached the target level. The authors call for wider access to other drug types and closer following of guidelines.
plos-pone-0347150:
Victoria DeRooy and Amanda Hansen pieced together the hidden highway that moves live baitfish across the United States. Anglers' minnows are farmed in a few states and trucked nationwide, and each shipment can secretly carry invasive species and fish diseases. Because no central registry exists, the authors filed public records requests with state governments and stitched the returns into one national picture for twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-four.

The records captured nearly forty million individual baitfish crossing state lines, plus hundreds of shipments with no count recorded. Arkansas, South Dakota, and Minnesota stood out as source states, and record-keeping quality varied sharply between states, leaving blind spots. The authors deliver regulators the first solid map of this trade, naming the busy routes where inspection would do the most good.
plos-pone-0347650:
Brett R. Moyer, a citizen scientist, reports five years of photographing leg bands on Black Skimmers along Florida's coast. Modern bands can be read from a distance, letting the public supply real research data. In this 2026 study, one observer logged more than a thousand band sightings covering three hundred forty-seven individual skimmers and traced where each bird was raised.

Northeast Florida drew big numbers of skimmers from Atlantic coast states, some from very far north. Birds from the nearer Gulf coast barely appeared, despite shorter distances. One young bird set a record dispersal linking the two populations. The project shows how one patient watcher with a camera can redraw a species' travel map.
plos-pone-0347750:
Justin Hardick and co-workers compare two ways of hunting respiratory viruses in nose swabs: broad genetic sequencing that reads everything present, and targeted panel tests that look only for known germs. Their 2026 study runs sequencing on one hundred swabs from two groups of sick patients who had already been panel tested.

The broad method agreed with the panel on only about a third of positive samples. It found no viruses in panel-negative swabs either. It did surface stray microbes, including an amoeba, in a fifth of one group's samples. Targeted panels proved more sensitive here for routine diagnosis. The result tempers enthusiasm for catch-all sequencing as a front-line test, at least with this approach.
plos-pone-0347850:
Desu Beriso Dama, Seltene Abadi Tesfamariam, and Abdi Mohammed Hassen measured thirty-six peanut varieties grown under irrigation at Dire Dawa in eastern Ethiopia, hunting for genetic diversity breeders can exploit. Peanuts supply food and oil and enrich soil, but Ethiopian yields suffer from a narrow genetic base. The 2023 trial recorded yield, plant traits, and oil measures, then mapped variation statistically.

Six trait clusters captured three-quarters of all variation, and the varieties fell into six family groups. Some pairs of varieties sat very far apart genetically, exactly the contrast breeders want for crosses. The authors name the most divergent pairs as parents for developing improved groundnut varieties suited to Ethiopian conditions.
plos-pone-0348150:
Sunny L Jardine and co-authors tested simple rules for choosing which river barriers to fix for migrating fish in western Washington in 2026. Agencies often rank dams and culverts by the habitat upstream, and the team asked how much that shortcut loses against full optimisation.

Judged against the best possible picks, ranking by total upstream habitat captured most of the gain when habitat amount was the only goal. But adding popular quality scores, such as natural land cover, cut success nearly in half. The lesson is sharp: a well meant quality bonus can mislead, unless it targets the habitat fish truly gain.
plos-pone-0348350:
Wang Yizhang and colleagues used a statistical optimisation method to green the making of cefotaxime sodium, a widely used antibiotic. Three knobs, reaction temperature, the amount of wash liquid, and the ratio of the salt-forming ingredient, were tuned together against yield, purity, and an environmental score. Single-factor trials had mapped the sensible ranges first.

The winning recipe ran cool, at a moderate wash volume and an even salt ratio. It delivered a stable, high yield with low impurities. Its crystals were clean and regular, confirmed by X-ray and microscope checks. Its green chemistry score came out excellent. The authors argue that designing for yield, crystal quality, and environmental performance in one experiment, rather than trading them off later, is how antibiotic manufacture should be modernised at factory scale.
plos-pone-0348450:
Quang Minh Ho and colleagues reviewed a decade of swine flu pneumonia at a leading Vietnamese infectious disease hospital, following 729 adults with confirmed H1N1 infection between 2009 and 2019. Their 2026 cohort study asked how often the infection turned to pneumonia, who ended up in intensive care, and which patients died despite modern treatment.

About one patient in five developed pneumonia. Of those, nearly half needed intensive care, over a third progressed to serious lung failure, and roughly one in twelve died. Age over sixty and existing illness multiplied intensive care risk enormously, and abnormal kidney, liver, and inflammation tests added warning. Intensified antiviral dosing showed no survival benefit. The authors urge close early monitoring of older, sicker patients.
plos-pone-0349350:
Hyunmin Koo and Casey Morrow searched the blood cells of twelve patients with long COVID for switched-on human endogenous retroviruses, ancient viral fossils in our DNA that can wake up. Their earlier work found a shared pattern of these loci active in one immune cell type. Extending the scan to all major blood cell types, they asked where the activity truly sits.

No consistent pattern appeared in B cells, T cells, natural killer cells, or dendritic cells. The signal concentrated in one monocyte class, where four retroviral loci were active and mostly absent elsewhere, and one locus also showed up in lung wash cells from COVID patients. A cell type carrying a distinctive viral-fossil signature could become a marker, or even a target, for understanding long COVID.
plos-pone-0349450:
Zhang Dongjiao, Zhang Yunlong, and Jiang Xu asked what makes people accept art and goods for museums made with smart software help. Museum shops now sell gifts whose designs come partly from generative tools. Their survey covered three hundred and twenty three users with direct experience, modelled across tech feel, cultural worth, inner value, and willingness to accept.

Good tech feel lifted both acceptance and sense of cultural worth. Cultural worth then raised the inner reward users felt, and that reward fed acceptance too. In short, a tool must work smoothly, honour the culture it borrows, and leave users feeling enriched. Shops that miss any leg of that chain risk cool public response.
plos-pone-0349750:
Md Mashiar Rahman and colleagues tested extracts from water hyacinth, a fast growing water plant, against a drug resistant staph germ. Tribal communities in the hills of Bangladesh eat the plant and use it for gut and liver complaints. The team made leaf and flower extracts with three solvents and profiled their chemicals in the lab.

Lab tests measured how well each extract slowed or killed the germ. Computer work on hundreds of plant compounds then searched for ones that could hit several germ targets at once. Two compounds stood out for strong binding in the models. Much more testing would be needed before any treatment claim, but a common weed now looks like a useful place to search.
plos-pone-0349850:
Supanida Mayurasakorn and two colleagues examine two candidate predictors of how well a first radioactive iodine treatment works in thyroid cancer, in this 2026 study from Thailand. After surgery, many patients with differentiated thyroid cancer receive radioactive iodine, and a tumor marker called thyroglobulin helps judge the likely result, though its level shifts with another hormone. The team tested a marker ratio designed to cancel that influence, plus the presence of cancer in a particular neck lymph node group.

Reviewing just over two hundred twenty patients treated over four years, they found neither the ratio nor the lymph node feature independently predicted a less-than-excellent response. Male sex, higher recurrence risk, more advanced stage, and a higher raw marker level did. The ratio performed about as well as the raw marker at separating outcomes, and the authors note possible statistical overlap and sample size as limits on their null findings.
plos-pone-0349950:
Miguel Fernando Molano and co-authors charted the shape and breakup of dimercaprol in 2026, a long used antidote for heavy metal poisoning whose basic chemistry was still incompletely mapped. Knowing its stable forms and fragments helps labs identify it and its remains.

Quantum calculations found five low energy shapes, with one consistently the most stable, held by internal hydrogen bonds. Mass spectrometry under hard ionisation broke the molecule in patterns the team explained through losses of water, sulphur compounds, and radicals, backed by calculated energies. The paired approach gives analysts reference behaviour for a drug older than most of its users.
plos-pone-0350150:
Mohammed Nashawi and co-authors described how non-infectious eye inflammation affects children in Saudi Arabia, where regional data were scarce. The condition, pediatric uveitis, can quietly damage sight if treatment lags. Their 2026 review gathered records for thirty-six children treated at two major centers between 2017 and 2023, tracking their care and vision over two years.

Joint disease of childhood caused just over half the cases, and most children had inflammation at the front of the eye, often in both eyes. Steroid drops and methotrexate were the main treatments at diagnosis. More than eight in ten children reached remission within two years, though some developed complications such as cataracts or scar tissue. The authors credit early diagnosis and newer biologic drugs, and they urge better screening and follow-up support.
plos-pone-0350250:
Yewulsew Godie Gela and Birtukan Gizachew Ayal tested short stories as a tool for English reading in northwest Ethiopian secondary schools in 2026. English is the language of instruction, yet many pupils struggle to understand what they read in it.

Two ninth grade classes of sixty pupils each were split into story taught and standard groups, with tests before and after plus interviews. Groups started level. Afterwards the story group scored far higher on reading tests, and pupils spoke warmly of the approach. A cheap, enjoyable text type delivering a gain that large deserves wider trials in similar classrooms.
plos-pone-0350550:
Yaping Sun and colleagues present a tuning method for car following models when roads turn snowy. Drivers space out differently on slick, low visibility roads, and standard models miss that shift. Five classic following models were tuned with road grip and visibility counted in. A time series encoder extracts snow scene features, while a physics guided network adjusts model settings on the fly.

Checked against a national driving data set and real snow driving tests, tuning accuracy beat a standard genetic search by about thirteen percent in snow. Gains held across all five model types. Better snow tuned models can sharpen traffic simulations, driver aids, and safety tests for winter roads.
plos-pone-0350650:
Samantha Fabian and colleagues unraveled how certain Aspergillus molds make lysergic acid amides, the ergot compounds behind both medicines and poisonings, with one enzyme doing a job that takes two elsewhere. In ergot fungi proper, two partner enzymes build the key precursor. Aspergillus species lack both, yet make the same products, and their gene clusters carry a single two-part gene instead. The team moved that gene into a test fungus to see what it could do.

The experiment was designed to prove the single gene's product can stand in for the pair, covering both assembly steps on the road to ergonovine and its sister compound. Confirming that swap rewrites a chapter of ergot biochemistry and hands synthetic biologists a compact part: one gene instead of two when engineering microbes to brew these valuable, dangerous molecules.
plos-pone-0350750:
Andrée-Ann Bolduc and co-authors exposed human natural killer cells to an extract of a smoked cannabis joint in the lab, asking what the smoke does to these front-line immune cells. Killer cells destroy infected and cancerous cells, and cannabis use is rising in Canada. Blood immune cells were treated with rising doses, and stress, damage, and killing power were measured.

The extract harmed the killer cells in step with dose, mostly by driving them into programmed death. At a mid dose, cell stress gases rose, self-eating markers climbed, DNA damage appeared, and the cells' power plants lost charge. Treated cells also killed target cancer cells less well, though they could still move and stick normally. The authors link the harm to runaway self-eating and failing mitochondria, a caution for heavy use.
plos-pone-0351150:
Rayyan Garba and seven colleagues map a diphtheria outbreak street by street in Kano State, Nigeria. Their 2026 study uses national surveillance data from April 2022 to December 2023. Nigeria's nationwide outbreak concentrated brutally in Kano, which reported about three-quarters of confirmed cases. Over ten thousand confirmed cases in the state were geolocated. Mapping software searched for clusters, and the cluster map was compared with where health facilities themselves cluster.

Cases bunched in the eight metropolitan districts. Facilities bunched there too, which can flatter detection. One district broke the pattern worryingly. Ungogo had the heaviest clustering of cases but the thinnest spread of facilities. Such mismatches are where outbreaks outrun response. Vaccination teams and treatment centres can now be aimed at true hotspots rather than spread evenly. For a disease that returned after decades of control, spatial intelligence is preparedness in its most usable form.
plos-pone-0351550:
Xue Yang, Xin Wang, and Miguel Ribeiro Ramos followed just over one thousand first year high school students in central China for a year. Surveys at both points measured how much good and harm students felt internet gaming brought, in the short and long run, plus signs of gaming disorder. About fifteen percent met disorder marks at the first survey and about fourteen percent a year later.

Heavier disorder at the start predicted feeling more costs from gaming a year later, both near and distant. Feeling costs or benefits at the start did not predict later disorder. Lived harm, not prior belief, seems to teach gamers the price. Programmes may work better by making real costs vivid than by lecturing on risks.
plos-pone-0351650:
Razia Sultana and colleagues fielded a friendly bacterium against rice blast, the fungal disease that can cut a rice crop at any growth stage. The bacterium, Pseudomonas mosselii strain PR5, lives inside plants and was applied as seed priming, seedling priming, and leaf sprays of its culture liquid, alone and combined, across three blast-prone rice varieties. A chemical fungicide and untreated, infected plants anchored the comparison.

Both the bacterium and the fungicide cut disease sharply against the infected control. Seed priming plus spray gave the lowest disease progress in two varieties, while the fungicide won the third. Treated plants also grew and yielded better. A seed treatment that lets farmers spray less chemistry is worth having in blast country, and this trial maps which delivery pairing works on which variety.
plos-pone-0351750:
Architecture students in China need strong English for their field. General English courses miss the special vocabulary of buildings and design. Rui Sun and Zhihao Chen designed a course to close that gap. They call it Architectural Art English. Their paper appeared in PLOS One in 2026. It explains how the syllabus was built.

The team surveyed about six hundred fifty students and teachers. Learners dreamed of study abroad and international teamwork. Yet their listening skills and field vocabulary lagged far behind. The new syllabus answers with seven real text types from architecture. Lessons mix language with subject content. Tasks mirror the work architects actually do.
plos-pone-0351850:
Sajidur Akash and seven colleagues investigate a mustard seed compound as a possible cancer fighter in this 2026 study. Cervical cancer kills many women in poorer countries where treatment access is thin. Black mustard seeds contain a plant sterol called gamma-sitosterol. Chemical profiling confirmed the compound in seed extracts. The team then tested the extract on cervical cancer cells in dishes, alongside safety and clot-related assays.

The extract killed cancer cells in a dose-dependent way. Computer modelling explored how the sterol might act inside the body. It docked favourably with cancer-related proteins, including neuropilins. Long simulations suggested those bindings stay stable. Drug-likeness checks looked acceptable as well. None of this makes a medicine yet. It does build a layered case, from chemistry to cells to simulation, that this seed sterol deserves proper preclinical development.
plos-pone-0351950:
Gitika Bhasin and seven colleagues compare twenty-five shortcuts for detecting insulin resistance. Their 2026 study recruited one hundred adults aged twenty-five to fifty-five. Half had prediabetes, half had normal blood sugar. Insulin resistance is the silent fault that precedes type 2 diabetes. Measuring it directly is clumsy, so doctors lean on indices. Some need blood tests, some combine lipids with body measures, and some use body measurements alone.

The prediabetes group carried more body fat and worse metabolic readings, as expected. Seventeen of the twenty-five indices correlated significantly with the standard laboratory measure. Among blood-based options, the triglyceride-glucose index discriminated well between the groups. So did the standard homeostatic model itself. The practical aim is triage. A cheap, validated index lets busy clinics flag insulin-resistant patients early, when diet and activity changes can still prevent diabetes from taking hold.
plos-pone-0352150:
Gaffney and colleagues, in a 2026 study of Medicare data, ask whether regions with more heart catheter specialists do more of the heart procedures that help least. Stent procedures can save lives in heart attacks, but for stable chest disease their value is doubtful. Earlier work hints that when specialists are plentiful, use rises. The team linked claims for all older Americans treated from 2019 to 2021.

Across about sixteen hundred hospitals, the share of stent procedures done for stable disease averaged much higher in regions richest in specialists than in the poorest. After adjusting for hospital and population differences, the gap stayed large and clear. The pattern fits a supply story: more operators, more marginal procedures. The authors stop short of blaming individual doctors, but they argue payment and oversight should reckon with how strongly local supply shapes the care patients receive.
plos-pone-0352250:
Lin and colleagues built a computer method to predict which drugs will bind which body proteins in a 2026 study. Lab testing of every drug and protein pair is slow and costly, so good predictions narrow the search. Their method reads drug shapes with a graph network that weighs the most telling parts, and reads proteins with a pre-trained language-style model.

Tests on three standard data sets beat older prediction methods, the authors report. Fuller reading of both drug structure and protein sequence drove the gain. Better shortlists mean chemists spend lab time on pairs most likely to work. The approach adds a fresh route for early drug discovery work.
plos-pone-0352350:
Zhengxiu Sun and five colleagues examine this 2026 PLOS One study of how being schedulable at any hour through apps like WeChat relates to job satisfaction in China. Using a nationally representative 2021 social survey, they asked whether workers whose shifts and tasks can be arranged anytime through messaging tools feel worse about their jobs, and why.

Always-on scheduling was indeed tied to lower satisfaction, and the link ran largely through two channels: more conflict between work and family life, and a stronger sense of pressure at work. The negative pattern concentrated among highly educated workers and professionals. The authors argue the findings show how communication tools quietly stretch the working day, with costs that fall unevenly across the workforce.
plos-pone-0352450:
Ruining Jin and co-authors examined how gender links to physical bullying among teenagers in India, and whether that link shifts with age. Bullying research leans heavily on Western samples, so they reanalyzed open survey data from a hundred sixty-nine school students. Students were grouped into early, middle, and late adolescence for the comparison.

Boys reported both more bullying of others and more being bullied themselves than girls did. The gap in doing the bullying grew wider in the later teen years. Because the pattern changes across adolescence, the authors argue that prevention work should not treat all teens alike: what fits a twelve-year-old may miss the point for a seventeen-year-old. The sample was small, so the findings are a starting point rather than a final word.
plos-pone-0353350:
Wen and colleagues, in a 2026 study, compare the chemistry inside the pulp of three citrus varieties grown in China. Flavor and nutrition live in that chemistry, yet varieties had rarely been dissected side by side. Using a scanning method that catches hundreds of compounds at once, the team profiled a mandarin type, a sour orange hybrid, and a yuzu relative.

The three pulps formed clearly separate chemical clusters. More than three hundred compounds differed between them, from the flavonoids tied to health claims to acids, aromatics, and bitter limonoids. The mandarin leaned into flavonoid pathways. The yuzu relative piled up organic and amino acids. The hybrid showed its own blend, rich in fatty acid and purine activity. Networks of linked compounds confirmed whole pathways shift together. The authors offer the maps to breeders chasing better flavor and to makers of citrus health products.
plos-pone-0353550:
Ahmad and colleagues, in a 2026 study, fine-tune a fast vision model to find defects in fabric as it is made. Flawed cloth is wasted money, and human inspection is slow and tiring. Mills also make plain and printed textiles side by side, so one detector must handle both. The team trained on cloth from a Pakistani mill and checked the model on three public data sets.

Their customized model, built on the twelfth version of the YOLO detector family, learned features aimed at varied defect shapes and used adaptive tricks to enrich training images. On the home mill's cloth it scored well across seven defect types, balancing catches and false alarms. On the public sets it again beat comparison methods, staying light enough for cheap computing. The authors present it as a universal inspector for mixed textile lines, ready for the factory floor rather than only the lab.
plos-pone-0353750:
Vinicius Oliveira and co-authors compare in 2026 how older adults in Brazil and Europe manage daily life, using a World Health Organization framework for care in ageing. Large ageing surveys from both places supplied measures of basic and tool based daily tasks, plus five areas of built in ability such as movement, memory, and senses.

Risk patterns differed by place: grip strength protected more in Europe, while walking speed mattered only in Brazil for basic tasks. Depression carried more risk in Europe, and hearing loss more in Brazil. Overall, decline began about ten years earlier in Brazil, which the authors tie to social and economic gaps.
plos-pone-0353850:
Tomioka and colleagues, in a 2026 study, link social life to oral frailty in older Japanese adults. Oral frailty means weakening of chewing, swallowing, and the mouth's overall function, and it predicts wider decline. Japan has universal dental care, yet gaps by income persist. The team asked whether social capital, meaning trust, reciprocity, and taking part in community life, protects the mouth.

Data came from a large national aging study, with more than thirty thousand people followed from 2019 to 2022. About one in five developed oral frailty risk over three years, more among poorer participants. People with richer social ties and stronger trust in neighbors had lower odds of oral frailty, at every income level. Joining in community activities also protected, and it helped poorer participants most. The authors suggest that building social connection is a health policy in itself, one that can narrow oral health gaps.
plos-pone-0354150:
Zhanyan Li and colleagues study in 2026 how people in China reacted online just after the first imported mpox case reached the mainland. They gathered comments under popular posts on a major social platform during the first two days. Language tools scored feeling in each comment and grouped the main topics of concern.

Comment volume peaked within two hours and faded fast after four. Most comments carried negative feeling, and concern centred on how the illness spreads and on attitudes toward it. High activity posts also drew stronger feeling. The authors argue that fast, place aware official messaging matters most in those early hours.
plos-pone-0354350:
Freihat and colleagues, in a 2026 global study, chart the burden of lung cancer from 2010 to 2050. Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer, yet counts of cases and deaths alone do not say how hard the disease hits each patient. The team combined three global data sources covering nearly two hundred countries, and added two severity measures.

In 2022 the world saw roughly two and a half million new cases and close to two million deaths, with tens of millions of healthy years lost. Men and richer regions bore more, by their measures. Two forward views were built: one holding 2022 rates fixed so only population change acts, and one extending each country's recent trend. Their severity frame pairs the share who die with healthy years lost per case, a fairer way to compare countries.
plos-pone-0354450:
Shanshan Hu, Chaxiang Li, and Wei Zhang explore in 2026 how older adults living with type two diabetes experience being cut off from others. Fourteen patients from a hospital clinic in Yichang, China, took part in face to face interviews. The team sorted what they heard into patterns at personal, family, and wider levels.

Many described pulling back after losses linked to illness and fear of decline. Others felt held back by overprotective families, shrinking friend circles, and brief talks with doctors. Poorly matched local services, hard to reach public spaces, and stigma added to the problem. The authors call for stronger family and local support.
plos-pone-0354750:
Kyuhyung Choi and co-authors published this 2026 study of immune activity inside the human dorsal root ganglion, the cluster of sensory nerve cells targeted by many pain treatments. Using public single-nucleus gene data, they asked whether immune activity there follows one pattern or several distinct ones.

Choi's group sorted a curated set of immune nuclei into seven recurring gene programs. Some programs clustered in particular spots instead of spreading evenly through the tissue. That patchy layout points to small immune niches rather than uniform swelling. Knowing where these programs sit could help doctors aim local pain treatments at the exact tissue zones involved.
plos-pone-0355550:
Kady D Waggle and colleagues describe how a hospital system runs routine genome sequencing of germs to catch outbreaks early and cheaply. Standard infection control often misses silent spread between patients. Their program sequences samples from high-risk germs every week, compares genomes to spot hidden clusters, and reports back to infection teams. The paper lays out staffing, workflow, and costs across two phases over three years.

In a typical week the team sequenced dozens of samples, with per-sample cost falling below a round threshold in the later phase once staff pay and supplies were counted. Results reached infection teams in a little over a week on average. Waggle and colleagues argue the routine is feasible for other hospitals and can pay for itself by stopping outbreaks sooner.
plos-pone-0355650:
Judith Legrand and fellow doctors test whether texture patterns on chest CT scans can tell whether chest lymph nodes in lung cancer patients truly hold cancer. Node status decides treatment, and scans alone often mislead. The study looked back at about one hundred ten surgical patients whose nodes looked suspect. Up to three nodes per patient were outlined in three dimensions. Texture features were extracted. Two machine learning models were trained across many repeated splits.

The stronger model sorted malignant from harmless nodes modestly well, far from perfect but better than chance. Three texture features recurred in the winning signatures, all capturing how uneven the node tissue looks. Legrand and colleagues present scan texture as a supporting signal for staging, not a replacement for tissue proof.
plos-pone-0355850:
Nicholas Dietrich and David McShannon test a popular fix for scarce medical images in this 2026 study: making synthetic training data. Their task was classifying emphysema subtypes in lung CT scans, where only a small set of real image patches was available. They compared three modern generative models, which learn to invent new scans, against simple geometric tricks like rotating and flipping real images.

None of the methods, alone or combined, improved the classifier's accuracy in a statistically reliable way over training on real images only. The best single result came from one generative model at an equal mix of real and synthetic data, but the gain was not significant. How realistic the fake images looked did not predict how much they helped. The authors say generative augmentation in tiny, texture-driven datasets needs better methods before it can be trusted.
plos-pone-0355950:
Chuanyin Liu and seven colleagues trace how microbes in shrimp pond mud break down a cyanobacterial toxin without oxygen, in this 2026 study. The toxin, microcystin-RR, threatens aquaculture and water safety, and knowing its fate in oxygen-free sediment matters for pond management. The team enriched a microbial community from pond sediment, fed it toxin labeled with heavy nitrogen, and tracked the chemistry and gene activity as degradation proceeded.

Three breakdown products were identified, pointing to a path that opens the toxin's ring, then strips pieces away step by step into short fragments and amino acids. One bacterium dominated the community, while a scarcer genus stayed unusually active. The enzymes doing the cutting appear to be an unconventional set, not the classic microcystin pathway, and nitrogen-cycling genes switched on alongside. The authors offer the map as a basis for building toxin-eating communities.
plos-pone-0356250:
Juan Ge and three colleagues study the link between sleep quality and type 2 diabetes in Chinese community patients who already live with chronic disease, reporting in 2026. More than nine hundred patients answered questionnaires, and the team scored their sleep with a standard index where higher scores mean worse sleep. Nearly two thirds of the group had diabetes.

Worse sleep went together with a higher share of diabetes, but the relationship was not a straight line. Once sleep scores passed a certain point, the odds of diabetes climbed steeply, then leveled off at still worse scores. The authors suggest that community health workers treat sleep checks as a useful extra tool. Helping the worst sleepers in this high-risk group, they add, could be a practical way to fight diabetes.
plos-pone-0356550:
Berna Dizer and three colleagues survey nurses about wounds caused by the medical devices attached to their patients, in this 2026 study from a Turkish state hospital. Tubes, masks, and monitors can press into skin and cause injuries that lengthen stays and raise costs. One hundred fifty nurses in intensive care and surgical units completed a questionnaire on their knowledge of, and attitudes toward, preventing such injuries.

Average scores suggested moderate knowledge and generally positive attitudes, yet only about a third of nurses reached the study's threshold for adequate knowledge paired with positive attitudes. Item-by-item results exposed stubborn misconceptions about prevention and healing, and knowledge did not line up neatly with attitudes. Because the study covered a single hospital, the authors are cautious, but they argue for structured, device-injury-focused training in nursing education and hospital programs.
plos-pone-0356650:
June Labbancz and three colleagues issued this correction in 2026 to their study of tomato plants under aphid attack. The original paper compared tomatoes grown with conventional and organic fertilizer and found that fruit quality held up under an uncontrolled infestation by green peach aphids. Meanwhile gene activity in the plants shifted toward breaking down stored resources. In the published version, the captions were correct but the eleven figures appeared in the wrong order.

The notice republishes the figures in their proper sequence. They cover gene co-expression networks in leaves and fruit, and links between gene modules and aphid presence or fertilizer type. They also cover enrichment analyses of the biological processes involved. Readers using the study's transcriptomic results should match each analysis to the corrected figure rather than relying on the original layout.
plos-pone-0357050:
Signe Nilssen Stafne and coauthors published a 2026 cohort study in PLOS ONE on physical activity in Norwegian women. Their pregnancies were complicated by gestational diabetes, blood pressure disorders, early birth, or a small baby. Such histories raise later heart disease and diabetes risk, making activity especially valuable, yet nobody knew if these women move less. Drawing on the large HUNT study linked to the birth registry, the team measured activity with accelerometers worn for several days.

About a quarter of the nearly four thousand women had adverse pregnancy histories, and they were less active than the others on total and vigorous activity. However, the gap largely faded once postpartum health and lifestyle factors were taken into account. This is hopeful, they say: lower activity is not fixed by pregnancy history itself but travels with health and habits support programs can target. Pregnancy complications should trigger activity support, not resignation.
plos-pone-0357450:
Azar Taheri Tayebi and colleagues compared in 2026 three ways to predict angler pressure: how many people will fish a lake or river, and where. Managers need such forecasts to guard fish stocks and to plan docks, parking, and wardens. The team tested three routes side by side.

One model was guided by what past studies in the field advise. A second was built with the help of a large language model. A third was purely data driven, fitted to records of past fishing. The head to head test shows what each route gains and what it misses. Agencies far beyond this study face the same forecast problem with thin data, and now have better grounds for picking a tool.
plos-pone-0357950:
Richard W. Nauman and colleagues published a 2026 immunology study in PLOS ONE comparing two strains of BCG, the vaccine bacteria also used as a bladder cancer treatment. North American treatment has relied on one strain, but supply problems have pushed interest in an alternative strain produced in Russia. Because much of BCG's benefit is thought to come from trained immunity, a lasting priming of the innate immune system. The team gave mice one dose of each strain and examined bone marrow weeks later.

Both strains expanded the blood-forming stem cells that seed immune responses. The long-used strain, however, produced stronger trained immunity, with immune cells releasing more inflammatory signals when challenged again, and it switched on more inflammation-related genes. The Russian strain primed the system more weakly. Such strain differences, the authors say, could matter for how well bladder cancer immunotherapy works if supplies force a switch.
plos-pone-0358250:
Raffa Mubeen led a team of six authors building a questionnaire on swallowing problems for nurses, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Dysphagia, trouble swallowing, puts patients at risk of choking and lung infection. Nurses are the front line for spotting it, but their knowledge varies. The team developed and validated a tool that measures both knowledge and self-rated competence.

Mubeen's questionnaire reveals training gaps clearly, before patients pay the price for them. Hospitals can aim teaching at the exact weak points instead of generic refreshers. Validating the tool matters: a questionnaire that does not measure truly is worse than none. With sound measurement, nurse training on swallowing safety can improve where it counts, at the bedside.
plos-pone-0358550:
Kristina Fuentes led a team of eight authors setting out a photovoice protocol centered on caregivers, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Caregivers know the flaws of health systems firsthand, yet they are rarely given a real voice in fixing them. Photovoice hands participants cameras, so their own photographs become the evidence.

Fuentes's protocol aims to strengthen health systems by working alongside caregivers, treating them as co-researchers rather than subjects. Photos can show barriers that surveys miss, from confusing signage to exhausting routines. Health leaders presented with images from daily caregiving find them hard to wave away. The protocol's care in design should make its later findings hard to ignore as well.
plos-pone-0358750:
Karin Johnson leads a team of seven studying how birth teams actually involve women in decisions during labor, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their setting is the Swedish rollout of TeamBirth, a care process built around team huddles meant to share decisions with the woman and her partner. The researchers observed twenty-three births, covering seventy-nine huddles, and interviewed sixty-five care providers across two labor wards during 2022 and 2023.

They found four rungs of engagement. At the bottom, staff simply instructed without explaining. Higher up came brief information, then genuine involvement in discussion, the most common pattern, though staff still decided. True partnership, with joint decisions, appeared least often. Limited Swedish skills, heavy workload, and emergencies pushed engagement down. The study shows a well designed process still bends under ward pressure, and names where support should aim.
plos-pone-0358950:
Mario Tudela-Petit and three colleagues test game design in gym class in PLOS ONE in 2026, comparing points and prizes against story and choice. Two hundred nine Spanish secondary students spent eight physical education sessions in one of three setups. One group got ordinary teaching. One got gamification built on outer rewards. The last got gamification built on inner drivers such as narrative and autonomy. Questionnaires before and after measured motivation, competence, and plans to be active later.

Both gamified groups trended toward feeling more capable, and that interaction with time was statistically real. Intention to stay active in the future rose only in the inner driven group. Other motivation measures stayed flat everywhere, and head to head comparisons between groups fell short of firm significance. The authors read the pattern as a nudge: playful design helps modestly, and meaning based elements may outlast rewards for keeping teenagers moving.
plos-pone-0359550: Drost and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study that asks a direct question about athletes and identity. When injury or illness leaves athletes unable to compete, does that loss track with how strongly they see themselves as athletes? A strong athletic identity can aid drive, yet it may deepen distress when sport stops. The study speaks to coaches and counselors who support sidelined players.
plos-pone-0359650:
Saba Karimi and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on diet and health. It assesses how much red meat adults with high blood pressure eat in excess, and then decomposes that excess, breaking it down into the parts explained by different factors. The method is a Wagstaff decomposition analysis.

Decomposition shows whether high meat intake in this group tracks income, education, place, or other influences, and by how much. Hypertension advice almost always includes eating less red meat, so knowing who over-consumes and why sharpens that advice. Nutrition policy researchers are the audience for this anatomy of a dietary pattern.
pmc-13198050:
Steven Dodd and colleagues evaluated a public involvement network for health research in a 2026 study. Public involvement means patients and community members help shape research, not just take part in it. Many such efforts fade fast and grant little real say, so the team studied a long-running network in northwest England.

The network, called CoREN, has linked researchers and community groups since 2019. Interviews and group talks showed it brokers ties, lifts community voices, and builds research skills in local groups. Power gaps between researchers and residents narrowed. Hurdles included a fuzzy role, slow bureaucracy, and thin reach into poorer and more diverse areas. Lasting funding is the key lesson.
pmc-13198450:
Costanza Spadini and colleagues tested a cobra-derived peptide against dog ear germs in a 2026 lab study. Canine ear infection is common and often involves drug-resistant bacteria and yeast. The peptide, called NCP-3, comes from Chinese cobra venom protein and kills germs with low cell harm in past work.

The team tested it on reference strains and field strains from dogs with ear disease. It killed all reference strains but one. Against a key staph germ, including resistant forms, it acted fast and at low doses, wiping out growth within five minutes. Higher doses were needed for other germ groups. It failed to reach kill levels for gut-type germs and the ear yeast. Gram-positive germs remain the best target.
pmc-13198550:
Safinaz M Elhadad and colleagues tested houseplants as indoor air filters in a 2026 study. Labs that handle chemicals can hold harmful vapors in their air. The team placed four ornamental species in a real drug-lab setting, as pots and as a green wall, and tracked vapor levels plus plant health.

One species, Cordyline fruticosa, cleared the most vapors, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide. It also scored highest on a pollution tolerance index and leaf traits. A second species cleared all fine dust particles in tests and cut gases well. Plants with tougher leaves and more complex surfaces cleaned best, per math models. Plant filters look like a cheap, green aid for indoor air.
pmc-13199650:
Tapas Paul and Sua Myong present a 2026 protocol for viewing single protein clusters. Biomolecular condensates are droplet-like protein clumps that organize cell work. Their earliest tiny forms are hard to catch with bulk tests, so the protocol pins single clusters down for close imaging.

Steps cover preparing a coated surface, forming clusters in a flow chamber, and catching them with antibodies for fluorescence imaging. The method tracks how fast clusters form, their relative size, and how molecules swap in and out. A worked example uses FUS, a protein tied to nerve disease. As a protocol, it reports no new findings; its value is a recipe other labs can repeat. Details point to a prior paper for full use.
pmc-13200350: Jingyi Zhao and colleagues are authors of a trial corrected in a 2026 note in the Journal of NeuroEngineering and Rehabilitation. The trial tested whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, magnetic pulses through the scalp, improves combined thinking-and-moving task performance in children with cerebral palsy. The note fixes a methods sentence about randomization and stimulation timing. It also corrects a results sentence, giving day-by-day test values that show group differences on days two and three but not day one. The original article has been corrected.
pmc-13200850:
João Pedro de Melo and colleagues synthesize evidence on kneecap lower-pole fractures in adults in a 2026 review. The patella is the kneecap, and its lower pole anchors the tendon that straightens the knee. Breaks there strain the whole straightening system and stir debate on best repair, so the team reviewed recent literature.

Their search of one database over five years found twenty-two studies, of which sixteen entered the review. Stable fixation methods favored bone healing and early return to movement. No single method won outright: choice still hinges on fracture pattern, surgeon experience, and cutting complications such as repeat surgery. The evidence base is case series, the weakest tier, so firm guidance awaits stronger trials.
pmc-13202650:
A calcareous tubeworm from the Sea of Japan gets its first complete mitochondrial genome in a 2026 study headed by Qinghua Bao. The research article sequences Serpula uschakovi, filling a gap for the genus Serpula, whose family is known for scrambled mitochondrial gene orders.

The circular genome runs just over twenty thousand bases and holds the standard thirteen protein-coding genes, two ribosomal RNA genes, and twenty-two transfer RNA genes. Its gene arrangement is heavily rearranged compared with the presumed ancestral pattern, yet it keeps a conserved block shared with the genus Hydroides. Family tree analysis placed the species as sister to Hydroides, informing tubeworm evolution studies.
pmc-13210750:
Plastic antibodies molded around a protein can fish it from mixtures, and a 2026 study headed by Nan Zhang improves the molding with multiple anchors. The research article imprints cytochrome C onto dendritic mesoporous silica nanospheres using a custom poly(ionic liquid) macromonomer that grips the protein at several points at once.

The support particles averaged about eighty nanometers with channels that let proteins move freely in and out. A thin imprinted skin formed on their surface, keeping the target's shape stable during capture according to simulations and spectroscopy. The material bound large amounts of cytochrome C selectively, kept most of its capacity after repeated reuse, and modeled well on standard adsorption equations.
pmc-13238250:
Peampring and Kiratiwudh test a simpler way to set up digital models of the upper jaw for artificial teeth. Making a well-fitting prosthesis on a virtual articulator, a digital jaw simulator, needs the jaw's plane and hinge axis placed exactly. Facebow instruments do this by hand, but the transfer is fiddly and error-prone.

Their custom transfer tool aims to carry the same measurements into the virtual setup more simply. The study measures both trueness, closeness to the real position, and precision, repeatability across tries, against a standard facebow. A simpler tool that matches the old one's accuracy would speed digital dentistry and cut remakes for patients.
pmc-13238750:
Wang and colleagues profile the immune life of enlarged adenoids in children, cell by cell. Adenoids that swell too much can block airways and disturb sleep, a condition tied to obstructive sleep apnoea in children. The team sequenced single cells from adenoid tissue of affected children and controls, capturing more than seventy thousand cells in all.

Paired with the gene readouts came each cell's antibody and T-cell receptor codes, showing which immune clones were present. The combined map reveals how the tissue's immune mix is remodelled in disease. Such maps can point to which cells drive the swelling, and whether drugs could calm it short of surgery.
pmc-13241450:
Olouladé and colleagues at Aarhus fused two neural network families to name heathland plants from the air. Standard image networks see pixels on grids, missing how plant parts relate spatially. Their PlantGraphNet turns image keypoints into graphs of connected plant regions. A convolutional backbone supplies appearance traits alongside.

On Danish aerial heathland data the hybrid reached near ninety-nine percent precision. That clearly beat image-only baselines on fine-grained species calls. Distributed training scaled almost linearly across rigs. Because decisions trace back to plant parts, the authors stress the system's interpretability for monitoring.
pmc-13241550:
Rosenberg and co-authors at the University of Michigan review how knee osteochondritis dissecans is managed in children and adolescents. In this condition, a patch of bone and cartilage inside the knee loosens or detaches. Treatment hinges on lesion size, stability, and whether the fragment can be saved. Imaging and arthroscopy guide the choice.

Stable lesions, especially in growing patients, get three to six months of rest-based care first. Drilling follows when rest fails to heal the lesion. Unstable but salvageable fragments can be fixed with screws, absorbable implants, or grafts. Lost fragments call for cartilage restoration procedures such as graft transfer or implanted chondrocytes, matched to lesion size.
pmc-13242350:
Sandra's team at Manipal review plant fibers that feed good gut germs, from inulin to FOS and GOS. These fibers feed Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, two helpful gut germs. Their fermentation yields short-chain fatty acids that nourish the gut lining. Makers now build them with enzymes, germ cultures, and controlled plant-fiber breakdown.
