Benefits found across studies cover barrier strength, calmer inflammation, and metabolic balance. Chain length and linkage type decide which gut microbes respond. Capsules and synbiotic pairings promise protected, colon-targeted release. Too-high doses, each person's own microbiome, rules, and plant costs still block wider use in care.
pmc-13242950:
Yuki Kurokawa and colleagues report a breast cancer case where surgery followed drug control of a lone liver metastasis. Their case report appeared in Surgical Case Reports in 2026. The patient, a forty-five-year-old woman, had hormone-sensitive, HER2-negative cancer treated five years earlier with breast surgery and follow-up therapy. When a single liver spot appeared as the only recurrence, she received hormone therapy plus abemaciclib, a CDK4/6 blocker.

The drug combination held the disease in check for a long stretch. Rather than continue indefinitely, with its costs to quality of life and finances, the team removed the liver lesion surgically. She has since remained free of recurrence over long-term follow-up. The authors note this is a rare report of resection after this drug class. They suggest carefully picked patients with controlled, solitary disease may gain from local treatment, even when hormone resistance is suspected.
pmc-13244250:
Abdallah Aldwekat and co-authors mapped the burden of Q fever's cause, Coxiella burnetii, across the Arabian Peninsula through a One Health lens. Their systematic review appeared in Transboundary and Emerging Diseases in 2026. The bacterium spreads from livestock to people and thrives where humans, animals, and environment mix. Searching six databases, the team gathered 320 papers and kept sixty-four that measured the germ in people, animals, or surroundings.

About one in five people tested carried antibodies, with most exposure traced to ruminants. Among farm ruminants roughly two in five were positive, peaking in Saudi Arabia at nearly three-quarters of animals. Tick-infested large animals were far more likely to be positive than tick-free herds. Birth products carried the highest detection rates of all sample types. The authors argue control must be joined-up across farms, clinics, and the environment, since the germ respects none of those borders.
pmc-13244350:
Erika Iacona and colleagues tested whether a structured outcome scale can surface what hospice patients need, person by person. Their mixed-method study appeared in Palliative and Supportive Care in 2026. Thirty-eight terminally ill patients at a northern Italian hospice completed the Integrated Palliative Outcome Scale, rating physical, emotional, relational, spiritual, and practical concerns. Interviews alongside explored what being at peace with oneself means to the dying.

Constipation, mouth discomfort, weakness, and drowsiness topped the physical list, with anxiety and worry for family close behind. Patients who understood their prognosis better tended to know their diagnosis better too, and both kinds of awareness came with less anxiety and more peace. Across repeat ratings most symptoms held steady while anxiety and low mood crept up. Interviews showed peace is built from relationships, faith, and unfinished business, not symptom counts. The authors back the scale as a planning tool for care.
pmc-13247550:
Yang and co-authors built a single-cell atlas of twitchy pediatric airways in this 2026 International Journal of Genomics study. Airway hyperresponsiveness, airways that overreact to triggers, underlies much childhood asthma-like disease, but averaging gene activity across whole tissue hides rare cell types. The team reanalyzed public single-cell sequencing data from bronchial brushings of affected children, clustering cells and tracing their developmental paths.

The atlas resolved the mix of epithelial and immune cells, including varied macrophage states, and highlighted variable genes tied to tissue remodeling. A network-pharmacology layer even mapped targets of a traditional herbal formula onto the cell data. The authors stress the work is hypothesis-generating computation: it needs healthy comparison tissue, fresh cohorts, and laboratory validation before guiding treatment.
pmc-13249750:
Orlob and colleagues introduce Vitabel, free software for making sense of intensive care data streams, in a 2026 Journal of Medical Systems paper. Monitors record heart and breathing signals thousands of times per second, and artificial intelligence needs such data cleaned and labeled before it can learn. Existing tools rarely handle the volume or the mess, so the team built a Python framework around interactive notebooks.

Vitabel loads, aligns, displays, and annotates medical time series with sensible defaults that users can extend. Three worked examples show it in action, and browser demos let readers try it without installing anything. Released under the MIT license, it aims to standardize the unglamorous labeling work that critical care AI depends on.
pmc-13250150:
Sheta and colleagues build a gel form of a possible sunscreen ingredient called dibenzalacetone. Their 2026 Scientific Reports paper tackles the ingredient's main flaw: it blocks both UVA and UVB light well but barely dissolves in water. The team loaded it into oleogels, oil-based gels stiffened with silica powder, using argan or jojoba oil.

Using a factorial design, the researchers varied the recipe and measured spread, stability, and sun protection. Argan oil gels scored highest, and one formula with the most silica and active ingredient gave the best protection factor. The gels stayed stable in light, let little ingredient pass through skin samples, and did not harm human skin cells in tests. The authors present them as promising bases for future sunscreens.
pmc-13250250:
Sulaiman reports a salvage success after a patient delayed the recommended second operation for a broken shinbone. The 2026 Case Reports in Orthopedics paper follows a forty-year-old man hurt in a road crash. His open tibial shaft fracture, with a broken fibula beside it, was first washed out, closed, and held with an external frame.

Doctors advised early conversion to a nail inside the bone, but the man declined for personal and financial reasons. X-rays showed alignment held while healing stalled for months afterward. In February 2025 the frame came off, a locking nail went in, and his own bone graft was added. Later films showed solid union with no deep infection, though the author warns that delay should never become routine.
pmc-13252750:
A journal notice from 2026 corrects the statement about data access in an earlier interview study. That study looked at family support after a family member's suicide. The first statement about the study's data was wrong, and this notice gives the right terms instead.

The new statement says the interview data are not public. This protects the privacy of those who took part, under an ethics approval from Ulm University. Those who took part agreed to study of disguised transcripts. They also agreed to a few quotes in print with names removed, but not to full release. A small set of extra quotes sits in a supporting table. Trained researchers may ask for the full disguised transcripts, subject to review. The publisher apologises for the errors.
pmc-13254750:
Martin Mossige and co-authors check how well surgeons in Norway report a grave problem after knee replacement surgery in a 2026 study. The problem is deep infection around the new joint, which can cost the patient function and health. The team read full case files for 423 repeat operations in Western Norway from 2010 to 2023 and judged each case by one shared rule set.

Of 170 repeat operations reported as infection, 94 percent were confirmed as true infections. Of the rest, 5 percent proved to be infections after all. Reporting was right in 94 percent of cases overall. The authors say the registry data can be trusted for quality work and for research on this problem.
pmc-13255650:
Jenny Castillo Cato and Kayleigh-Ann Clegg trace the rise of FemTech in a 2026 perspectives article. Women are half the world's population yet remain underrepresented in health research and funding. The article notes that only about six percent of private health investment goes to women's health, and that women's symptoms are often dismissed or misread as emotional.

FemTech, a term coined in 2016, covers technology built for women's health, from cycle tracking to pregnancy care and telemedicine. The authors argue the sector can widen access, push research forward, and chip away at deep gender gaps, though funding and bias remain steep barriers.
pmc-13256550:
Glicerina and colleagues replaced all the sucrose in whole-wheat biscuits with alternative sweeteners and measured what changed. Five polyols, trehalose, and fructose were each baked into biscuits, then assessed for structure, texture, and sensory appeal. Sugar shapes spread, crispness, and flavor, so full replacement is a stiff test.

Isomalt, maltitol, and trehalose preserved or improved the biscuits' structure, giving good dough spread and desirable crispness. Isomalt and trehalose biscuits also won the highest sensory scores, which the authors link to roasted and buttery aroma compounds detected in them. The study shows reduced-calorie whole-wheat biscuits can stay acceptable to consumers without any sucrose.
pmc-13257450:
Sirichan Larpnarongchai and colleagues in Thailand studied newborns with persistent pulmonary hypertension, a failure of blood flow to adjust after birth. Their 2026 paper is a retrospective cohort study covering a decade of cases. It asks which clinical factors track with days alive and free of a ventilator.

Among one hundred seventy-five babies, the middle value was twenty ventilator-free days in the first month. Very poor oxygen levels, several heart-support drugs, kidney injury, and ventilator-linked pneumonia each meant fewer such days. Babies whose illness followed respiratory distress syndrome fared worst. The authors caution that one hospital's records can only suggest patterns, not prove causes.
pmc-13258150:
Natalia Quirk and colleagues study how tuberculosis bacteria juggle two stresses at once: nitric oxide attack and scarce iron. Inside a host, Mycobacterium tuberculosis must answer both, and the gene sets involved overlap heavily. Their 2026 paper homes in on a two-gene unit called rv3839-rv3840.

Both stresses switched the gene pair on strongly. Deleting it changed the bacterium's behavior, letting cells grow more under long iron shortage and leave a protective growth pause early. Mutant cells also grew elongated and let a heme-making precursor pile up. The pair normally reins in heme production when iron and calm are in short supply.
pmc-13260150:
Eugenia Vercelli and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of how imaging data are reported in studies of kidney and urinary stone surgery. The team searched two databases for treatment outcome studies in adults published in 2020 and 2021 by selected journals. They recorded imaging type and timing, how stone burden was measured, and how stone-free status and treatment success were defined. From the gaps found, they built a seven-point checklist called iSTAR.

Of 122 studies included, 13.9 percent did not report preoperative imaging type and 5.7 percent omitted postoperative imaging type. Forty-three percent gave no definition of stone burden measurement, and eighteen percent gave none for treatment success. Success definitions ranged from zero millimetres of remaining stone to allowing four millimetres. Only 10.7 percent of studies scored a perfect seven on iSTAR.
pmc-13261750:
Rui Zhang and Sheng Lu write a 2026 letter on nail protrusion after elastic stable intramedullary nailing, a flexible-nail fixation for children's forearm fractures. The letter comments on a study by Brattgjerd and colleagues about keeping the implants in place instead of routine removal. The question is how far a nail may stick out before it irritates tissue.

The original data showed that when protrusion was under 3.3 mm, no implant was removed for irritation, a negative predictive value of 100%. A calculation put the upper 95% confidence limit for such removals at about 2.3%. Above the threshold, the positive predictive value was only 16%, so most protruding nails could still be retained. The letter warns against turning 3 mm into a rigid surgical target, since deeply seated nails are harder to remove later. It frames the threshold as a safety margin for ruling out risk, not a decision rule.
pmc-13262650:
Budi Haryanto and colleagues link peat fire smoke to sick children in Palembang, Indonesia. Seasonal haze from forest and peat fires blankets the city almost yearly. Their 2026 ecological study aligns a decade of air readings with over three hundred sixty thousand childhood respiratory infections.

Fine particles showed the strongest and steadiest relationships with illness. Rises in the finest fraction predicted more pneumonia cases the following month, matching how deeply such particles penetrate young lungs. Coarser particles tracked general respiratory infections more consistently. Sulfur dioxide's role wavered, though it may worsen particle effects. Child-focused air quality planning is their urgent recommendation.
pmc-13263250:
Xuejing Liu and co-authors test removing a gene-silencing protein from blood vessel cells in mouse breast cancer in a 2026 journal article. The protein, AGO1, helps switch genes off, but its role in tumor vessel cells was undefined. Mice lacking AGO1 only in those cells received implanted breast cancer cells, and tumors were compared with normal littermates.

Tumors in the modified mice were much smaller, and about half were undetectable by day 21. Their tumors had fewer blood vessels and more killer T cells and macrophages, immune cells that attack tumors. In dish tests, vessel cells without AGO1 made more of two signals that recruit immune cells. The authors propose vessel AGO1 as a treatment target.
pmc-13263350:
Elena Hofmann and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on precision treatment for ameloblastoma, a rare but locally aggressive jaw tumor. Standard care is major surgery that often harms appearance and function. The team profiled the tumors of 14 patients in detail, searching for gene changes that drugs could target.

Every tumor carried a harmful mutation, in genes including BRAF, SMO, HRAS, FGFR2, and PIK3CA. Thirteen patients received personalized drug advice, and eleven took matched therapies. Ten of those eleven saw their tumors shrink on scans. Four later had surgery with smaller removals than usual, and their tissue showed partial or complete response. The authors argue targeted drugs can ease the surgical burden.
pmc-13263750:
Oleksii Borikov and colleagues automate the fiddly measurement of red blood cell surface charge. That charge, the zeta potential, governs how cells clump and squeeze through tiny vessels. Their 2026 method films cells drifting in an electric field and lets software track every trajectory.

Healthy donors gave reproducible charge distributions, with a distinct minority of cells carrying far less charge. Flipping the field's direction changed readings, exposing a relaxation effect their protocol corrects by measuring both ways. Enzymes and a peptide that strip membrane components cut the charge sharply, proving sensitivity. Single-cell resolution replaces the guesswork of manual microelectrophoresis.
pmc-13263950:
Baiyu Wang led a 2026 study of fowl adenovirus type 4, a virus that harms chickens and costs farms a great deal. The team asked how the virus uses mitophagy, the cell process that clears worn-out mitochondria, the parts that make energy. They focused on one spot, residue 188, in the viral hexon protein.

In cells and in live birds, infection harmed mitochondria and switched on this clearing process, which helped the virus copy itself. Blocking the process cut virus growth about tenfold. Swapping residue 188 changed the effect: one change weakened it, and the reverse change strengthened it. The authors name that residue and pathway as targets for new drugs.
pmc-13264550:
H Joswig and colleagues published a 2026 study on whether trainee doctors can safely do guided brain biopsies, where a thin tool takes a tiny brain sample. Trainees need early practice, yet safety must not drop. The team compared cases done by supervised trainees with those done by senior surgeons at two centers.

In 217 biopsies, trainees did 60 cases and seniors 157. Complication rates were nearly the same, at 1.7 percent for trainees and 1.9 percent for seniors, all silent bleeds. Trainees were faster with frameless guidance, while seniors were faster with a head frame. Hospital stays were shorter in trainee cases. Trainee year did not predict results. The authors back supervised early training for this procedure.
pmc-13264650:
Andrew Nalley and colleagues present a 2026 review of scan findings in the jaw joint after radiation therapy for head and neck cancer. Radiation can stiffen the jaw, a problem called trismus, yet the joint changes behind it were scattered across small studies. The team gathered every study that imaged the joint after treatment.

They found 11 studies with 282 patients, using MRI, CT, ultrasound, and plain dental images. Chewing muscles most often showed signal changes, shrinkage, or swelling. The joint knob showed erosion, rough surfaces, or hardening in a smaller set of patients. Nearly half the patients, 44.7 percent, had trismus. No study reported changes to the socket or direct bone death in the joint. All studies carried moderate to serious bias risk, so the authors call for planned, standard studies.
pmc-13267750:
Alexis Ferrasse and colleagues present a 2026 study of a storage method that keeps DNA whole without freezers. Long-read DNA sequencing reads genetic variants and chemical marks from single long molecules. Today that requires deep freezing, which shuts out places without cold storage. Ensilication instead seals DNA inside silica, a glass-like mineral.

DNA kept this way at room temperature for 30 days sequenced as well as frozen samples. Across three standard reference genomes, read length, variant accuracy, and methylation patterns matched. The sealed DNA also survived repeated handling and harsh aging tests better than frozen DNA. In samples from two patients with rare disorders, it revealed a new variant and a disease-linked methylation pattern. The authors offer it for wider access to testing.
pmc-13269050:
Sarah Lukacs and co-authors published a review and combined analysis in 2026 on a fast microscope method for skin cancer. The method scans removed tissue with a laser and makes images at once, without slow lab steps. They tested how well it finds basal cell carcinoma, the most common skin cancer.

Sixteen studies with 1,387 tissue samples were pooled, using standard lab checks as the reference. Scanning took 7.0 minutes on average. For diagnosis, the method found 91.4 percent of cancers and cleared 91.1 percent of non-cancer samples. For checking surgery edges, it found 79.5 percent of leftover cancer. The authors say standard lab checks should still follow final surgery steps.
pmc-13269150:
Jana Mayer and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 comparing two ways to treat hip socket breaks in older patients. Some patients had small screws placed through tiny cuts, while others rested and let the bone heal. All breaks had moved little or not at all.

The study covered 151 patients treated from 2015 to 2023, with 92 in the screw group and 59 in the rest group. At first look, the screw group lost less movement during the hospital stay. After the team adjusted for starting movement and other health factors, that edge vanished. One-year death rates also lost their gap after adjustment. The authors draw no claim that surgery is better.
pmc-13269550:
S Bader and co-authors published an animal study in 2026 on brain cell stress during severe blood loss, treated with a balloon that blocks the aorta to hold blood pressure. Pigs were studied with either normal or raised pressure inside the skull. A brain chemical called glycerol, a sign of cell membrane stress, was tracked throughout.

Eighteen pigs underwent controlled blood loss and 90 minutes of full balloon blockage, nine in each pressure group. The balloon restored artery pressure and brain supply pressure in both groups. Glycerol stayed stable during blood loss, then rose steadily during the long blockage. Raised skull pressure did not worsen the response. The authors read the rise as membrane strain rather than permanent nerve damage.
pmc-13269650:
Habtamu Mesele Gebray, Gebre Hailu Dejen, and Kindsew Abi Menge published a case report in 2026 from Ethiopia about a 52-year-old man with asthma and two months of growing back pain. For about 15 years he had self-treated with steroid injections and tablets bought without prescription. His exam showed classic signs of steroid excess.

Doctors found a puffy face, a fat pad on his upper back, and a waist of 120 centimeters. Tests showed high white cell counts, poor blood sugar control, and low vitamin D. Scans revealed lung thickening, weak bones, many rib and spine fractures, and widespread fat overgrowth around his lungs and heart. The authors urge close supervision of long-term steroid use.
pmc-13271050:
Ying Li is lead author of a 2026 retrospective study, one looking back over five years, on Providencia rettgeri, a bacterium that causes hospital-linked infections and is gaining drug resistance. The work covers clinical features, resistance patterns, and resistance genes at a teaching hospital in northern China from 2021 to 2025.

The team collected 25 distinct isolates, most often from urine. A high 88.0 percent were multidrug resistant, and 52.0 percent resisted carbapenems, a last-line drug group. Gene tests found the same resistance gene, blaNDM-1, in all carbapenem-resistant isolates. One newer drug combination showed no activity against those strains, while another worked against 61.5 percent of them.
pmc-13271150:
Jure Demšar is lead author of a 2026 journal article introducing QuNex recipes, a way to write brain imaging workflows so they can be run, read, and repeated exactly. Preparing and analysing brain scans usually needs many software tools and fine settings, which makes full documentation for other teams hard.

Recipes live inside QuNex, an open-source, container-based platform for end-to-end imaging work across species and scan types. A recipe records every step and setting, mixing built-in commands with custom scripts and outside tools. Sharing just the software version, the recipe file, and the data should let others replicate a study with one command, the authors say.
pmc-13272250:
A. J. van Wesemael is lead author of a 2026 journal article on stool amino acid profiles in extremely preterm infants. Those are babies born before 28 weeks. The article covers their link to late-onset sepsis. That is a serious infection arising after the first days of life. Gut microbe and chemistry changes precede this infection, but what shapes stool amino acids was poorly known.

The study used matched groups: twelve infection cases and twelve controls in a discovery set, and eight plus eight in a validation set. Age after birth, full milk feeding, probiotics, and delivery mode all shaped stool amino acids. Before infection onset, two amino acids, threonine and glutamine, were lower in discovery cases; only threonine's dip repeated, weakly, in validation. Combined, threonine predicted infection only modestly.
pmc-13273150:
Godwin Pius Ohemu leads a 2026 multinational survey of perceived gaps in tackling antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to drugs. Stakeholders from 33 countries on five continents named the three areas they felt got too little attention. The team used theme analysis and an impact-effort matrix to rank priorities for One Health action.

Among 103 respondents from nine sectors, antimicrobial stewardship, meaning careful drug use, was the top gap at 18.8 percent, followed by environmental resistance and waste at 16.5 percent. Stewardship, infection control, surveillance, and animal health were classed as quick wins. No clear links appeared between gaps named and a respondent's sector or career stage.
pmc-13273950:
Yan Yuan and a large team report a 2026 journal article on a targeted drug for a rare brain lymphoma. The cancer, primary central nervous system large B-cell lymphoma, has the worst outlook of its lymphoma group. Many tumors carry a change in the MyD88 gene that helps cancer cells survive.

The team showed that this gene change raises levels of a protein called BTK, which in turn protects another cancer protein, PIM1. In mouse models, the drug orelabrutinib crossed into the brain, blocked BTK, and helped break down PIM1. Patients given orelabrutinib with methotrexate responded better and lived longer than a comparison group. Tumor DNA in spinal fluid matched tumor tissue better than DNA in blood.
pmc-13274150:
Jordan Stanford and colleagues present a 2026 journal article from a feeding trial comparing two whole diets in Australian adults. Diet shapes gut microbes, but how full eating patterns change microbial work was unclear. Thirty-four adults ate a healthy guideline-based diet and a typical Australian diet for two weeks each, in random order.

The healthy diet lowered the variety of gut microbes compared with the start, while the typical diet changed little. Still, 105 microbial pathways differed between diets, and ninety-nine rose on the healthy diet, mostly for building amino acids and vitamins. Combined microbe and blood-chemistry profiles separated the two diets with about ninety-two percent accuracy in held-out tests.
pmc-13274850:
Hiroyuki Tomari and a large team report a 2026 journal article on fever-causing contamination in disposable labware used for fertility treatment. Bacterial endotoxins can harm sperm and embryos, yet ordinary culture dishes and catheters are not guaranteed clean enough for IVF use. The team tested twenty products with a human cell-based pyrogen test, which detects fever triggers broadly.

Seven of the twenty products carried significant pyrogen, at levels the authors say could exceed reported safe limits in real IVF use. A low-temperature ozone and hydrogen peroxide gas treatment drove contamination below detection. Leftover peroxide on one dish type was baked off by a day of drying at eighty degrees, after which sperm survival and embryo development were unaffected.
pmc-13275750:
Maddalena Bolognesi and co-authors describe a 2026 observational study on tracking healthy aging through skin. The study used hyperspectral imaging, a camera method that records many narrow bands of light reflected from a surface. Hand skin is easy to reach and may show age-related change across the body.

The team collected just over one hundred hand images from healthy volunteers over forty years old. From each image they pulled more than two hundred light and texture measures. Fifteen of those measures best tracked aging, so the team used them to build reference curves for healthy skin. Volunteers also answered questions about lifestyle and how they felt about their health. The authors say this painless scan could become a simple tool for watching how people age.
pmc-13276350:
Qingfei Hu and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how a burrowing rodent of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau handles cold, thin air. Plateau zokors live underground, where burrows grow colder and lower in oxygen with altitude. Making cholesterol costs much oxygen, so low oxygen should suppress it, yet the team found the opposite.

With altitude, liver switches for cholesterol production turned up, not down. One key enzyme appeared in two cut-down forms whose balance flipped between low and high altitude. Blood cholesterol and oxygen use both rose significantly higher up. Body size also grew with altitude, following a classic rule linking size to cold climates. The authors conclude that cold, not low oxygen, drives the cholesterol rise, an adaptation to the chilly, damp burrow life.
pmc-13276450:
Jan Sodoge and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on mapping groundwater conflicts in Germany from news reports. Fights over groundwater are rising worldwide during droughts, but emerging hotspots in wetter Europe are understudied. News coverage can reveal where tensions flare and why.

The team mined more than twelve thousand news articles from 2000 to 2022. They scored each reported conflict by how often and how prominently it appeared. Conflicts proved widespread, with old hotspots recurring and new areas surfacing during the long 2018 to 2022 drought. Pollution and nature protection faded as stated drivers, while scarcity, farming, and drought itself gained. Reported conflicts matched measured water use and recharge only moderately. The authors caution that media habits and social context shape which disputes become visible.
pmc-13276950:
Virginia Simon leads a 2026 study of how depressed mothers read and respond to their babies through body movement. Postpartum depression is low mood after birth, and the study used a coding system that scores movement patterns in play. Mothers with and without depression were filmed playing freely with infants aged three to ten months.

The study included 68 mothers with depression and 61 without it. Depressed mothers showed more risk patterns and fewer protective ones, such as steady presence with the baby. Parenting stress tied to the child predicted several of those patterns, as did trouble managing emotions. Background factors also mattered, so the authors warn against blaming depression alone for the gaps.
pmc-13277150:
Yusuke Onoda and Ami Ogawa present a 2026 study of how seat cushions affect the effort of standing up from a chair. Sit-to-stand movement loads the hip and knee joints, which matters for people with weak legs. Fifteen healthy young adults stood up from five foam cushions that varied in springiness and hardness.

Springier cushions delayed the moment of leaving the seat and kept supporting the body longer, which lowered peak hip and knee effort. Softer cushions led people to swing the upper body forward more, raising hip effort to slow that motion. The authors give ranges for both traits that cut leg joint load, as a guide for chair design in care settings.
pmc-13277350:
Raquel Rodrigues da Costa Brilhante leads a 2026 scoping review of self-care for people with type 1 diabetes who use an insulin pump. Type 1 diabetes leaves the body unable to make insulin, so a pump delivers it steadily. The review mapped published evidence from ten databases plus gray literature, following standard mapping guidance.

Eighteen articles were kept. Three self-care behaviors stood out: managing blood sugar, giving meal-time insulin doses, and counting carbohydrates. Knowledge, freedom, sensor use, daily context, and responsibility shaped those behaviors. Deeper knowledge helped both patients and clinicians make better daily choices, the authors say. They call for studies that test ways to strengthen self-care in pump users.
pmc-13278050: Sarah Lafferty and Rebecca Lafferty are named on a 2026 installment of Curiositas, a quiz column titled Medicine in the Kitchen. The hosted text is a set of questions with licensed photos, and it gives no answers. Questions ask where Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, which honey is used medically and what germ-fighting traits it has, which enzyme grapefruit blocks, and which messenger chemical caffeine blocks to raise alertness.
pmc-13278250:
Chunrong Huang leads a 2026 content analysis of short videos about adenoid hypertrophy, enlarged tissue at the back of the nose in children, on three Chinese platforms. Parents increasingly meet this topic on Bilibili, TikTok, and Xiaohongshu, but quality is unclear. The team collected 220 videos with fresh accounts and had two reviewers score completeness, clarity, usefulness, and reliability.

Bilibili videos ran longer and scored higher on completeness than those on the other platforms. Differences in clarity and reliability between platforms did not survive strict statistical correction. Xiaohongshu videos were more actionable than TikTok's. Reviewer agreement was high. The results show uneven parent-facing information, with platform and uploader traits shaping quality.
pmc-13279150:
Maxwell Rowley and Dharshana Krishnaprasadh present a 2026 case of scalp sores in a newborn boy. The baby was two days old when he came to the emergency department. Staff saw grouped blisters with crusts on the left back scalp. A scalp sensor had sat at that spot during birth.

Tests showed herpes simplex virus type two, a germ that can cause grave harm in newborns. The illness class is skin eye mouth disease, where sores stay on skin and mouth surfaces. Cultures also grew a strep germ from the sores. Care teams gave strong germ drugs through a vein and did a full sepsis work up, meaning broad tests for spread. Early spot checks in pregnancy can lower such risk.
pmc-13279550:
Shan Xu and colleagues present a 2026 case study of a man past one hundred years old after COVID-19. For seventeen years he held a fragile balance despite severe frailty and stage three kidney disease. The team track thirty five months after infection and name the pattern a health collapse spiral. In their words, stress steps drove a one way, multi system slide.

Kidney function fell by more than sixty percent from its pre illness level. Albumin, a blood protein tied to nutrition, dropped as well. A swelling marker surged more than three hundred sixty fold at its peak. His daily self care score fell from eighty to zero. Hard to treat Pseudomonas lung and urine infections kept coming back. Care turned to comfort, and he died. Kidney, protein and swelling marks served as clear reserve gauges.
pmc-13279950: A. G. Manente and colleagues are the subject of a 2026 expression of concern for their 2013 study in Oncogenesis on estrogen receptor beta and mesothelioma cell growth. The editor alerts readers that splicing may sit between lanes two and three of a figure panel on the receptor, and between lanes three and four of a panel. The raw data are no longer on hand due to the study age. Readers are urged to read those data with caution. Four authors agree with the notice, and six did not reply to mail.
pmc-13280350:
Evangelia Florou and colleagues report a 2026 case of vanishing liver metastases in pancreatic cancer. Metastatic pancreatic cancer has a poor outlook, and shrinkage to surgery ready state is rare. Their patient was a sixty year old woman with pancreatic adenocarcinoma and extensive liver spread. Palliative chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX, a four drug mix, was her care path. Liver disease faded in full on scans, a complete radiological disappearance.

The primary tumour stayed controlled through the course. After a treatment pause, local progression led to a restart of chemotherapy, and the liver stayed clear. At thirty two months from diagnosis, she had pancreatic resection with clean margins. She stays alive and free of liver return at eighty four months from diagnosis. Select patients can gain long survival from tailored, multimodal care.
pmc-13280650:
Murat Büyüksefil and colleagues surveyed child dentists across Turkey for a 2026 study on how well they talk with young patients. Good talk can lower fear, raise trust, and make care go more smoothly. The team sent an online survey to dentists who treat only children. Three hundred thirty-one dentists took part and rated their own skills.

Most dentists rated their talking skills as strong. Teachers and dentists in private practice scored higher than those still in training posts. More years of work went with stronger scores. Younger dentists scored lower on some skills, such as speaking in the first person and guiding children fairly. The authors call for more hands-on talk training in dental school and beyond.
pmc-13281250:
Omar Alhumaidan and colleagues built a math model of what adults in Saudi Arabia eat in a 2026 study. Long-term diseases such as diabetes are common in the country. Good diet policy needs sound numbers on intake, yet direct surveys are rare. The team built a model from national data stretching back to 2010. The model treats each input as a range, not a set value, to honor doubt. It ran thousands of trials to judge whether diets meet body needs.

Grains topped the intake list, ahead of protein foods like meat and eggs. Daily energy intake was close in men and women. Checks against national spending data backed the model's soundness. Some groups fell short on key vitamins, with gaps the authors size up. They say the model gives policy makers a firmer base for food and health plans.
pmc-13281950:
Xinyang Jin and colleagues modeled dosing of a last-resort antibiotic in very ill patients in a 2026 study. The drug, colistin sulfate, fights germs that shrug off most other drugs. Getting its dose right is tricky, since kidneys clear it at varied rates. Ten intensive care patients with pneumonia took part. All had it by vein for three days or more. Blood was sampled after the fifth dose, giving one hundred thirty readings.

A two-room model of the body fit the drug's path best. Kidney strength proved the key dial for how fast the drug cleared. Played-out doses showed exposure plunging as kidney strength rose. A larger first dose lifted early levels and hit targets sooner. Eight in ten patients beat their infection in care, and seven in ten cleared the germ. No kidney harm was seen. The authors call the work a first sketch needing bigger studies.
pmc-13282250:
James C Marcus and co-authors present a 2026 evaluation of a daily diary that tracks symptom severity in a rare immune disorder. The disorder, systemic mastocytosis, involves excess mast cells, which can trigger flushing, itching, gut pain, and severe allergic reactions. The diary was tested in adults with the non-advanced form, using blinded data from two hundred thirty trial participants.

The diary's eleven items grouped cleanly into four symptom domains, forming a total score. Scores were steady over short gaps, agreed within themselves, and matched other symptom and quality-of-life measures well. They also separated patients by severity and moved when patients' status changed. The team estimated what score change counts as meaningful for a patient, at roughly a thirty to forty percent drop. They conclude the diary is reliable and fit for use in treatment trials.
pmc-13282350:
Guillaume David and co-authors present a 2026 study testing whether CT scan planning wrongly rules out a pelvic screw operation. Surgeons fix the front pelvic ring by passing screws through a bone corridor in the pubic ramus. Standard planning models that corridor as a straight cylinder based on the screw's outer thread width. The team reviewed thirty-three patients who had forty-two screws placed under live X-ray guidance at a trauma centre.

Standard planning called fifteen screws infeasible, over a third of the total. Yet after surgery, scans showed every screw sat accurately, with no breach of bone, joint entry, nerve or vessel injury, or redo surgery. Planning based on the screw's narrower core reclassified fourteen of those fifteen as feasible. One screw followed a curved path no straight model could capture. The authors say straight-line planning underestimates what skilled fluoroscopy, live X-ray guidance, can achieve.
pmc-13282550:
Md Ruhul Amin and co-authors present a 2026 study on the combined harm of microplastics and mercury to Nile tilapia, a widely farmed fish. Each pollutant alone is known to hurt aquatic life, but real waters carry mixtures. Two hundred forty young fish were kept for forty-two days in four groups: clean water, plastic only, mercury only, or both together. The plastic was a polyamide type used in textiles and nets.

Fish exposed to both pollutants accumulated more plastic, died more, and grew less than the other groups. Their blood shifted, with higher sugar and lower haemoglobin, the oxygen carrier, plus more cell and nucleus defects. Gills, gut, liver, and kidney showed severe structural damage. Growth hormone pathway genes were turned down in brain and liver. Liver antioxidant defences faltered while inflammation signals rose in a mixed pattern. The authors conclude the mixture aggravates harm beyond either pollutant alone.
pmc-13283150:
Wild boar parasites shift between alpine and Mediterranean Italy, a contrast Camilla Sangiovanni's field team tracked through 2026. One site is an alpine valley in Gran Paradiso National Park. The other is a low coastal park in Maremma with a warmer climate.

Seasonal dung samples were gathered from November 2023 to July 2025 along set routes. Lab counts measured eggs and cysts for each parasite type found. Three groups ruled the samples: Eimeria, gut strongyles, and lungworms of the Metastrongylus group. Burden levels differed between the two areas for main types. Lungworm counts fell as height rose, which may reflect host limits for its life cycle.
pmc-13283750:
Emergency appendix surgery six days after targeted radiation therapy is the unusual scene in a 2026 case from Kei Nakagawa and colleagues. The patient had a pancreas tumor treated with a radioactive drug that seeks tumor receptors. Staff worried about radiation exposure for the surgical team.

The 75-year-old man arrived with acute appendicitis and clear inflammation on lab tests. Keyhole surgery removed the appendix while meters tracked dose rates around him. Readings near the field stayed within accepted safety limits for staff. Urine readings were also low, and recovery was smooth with discharge on day four. Planned safety steps made urgent surgery workable.
pmc-13284750:
Eric Juriatti and co-authors report a 2026 surface study on tuning defect-rich molybdenum disulfide, a layered semiconductor. Defects strongly shape how such materials carry charge, yet their effects need careful measurement. The team used synchrotron light tools to probe bulk crystals after gentle argon and neon sputtering, then after adding a fluorinated cobalt compound layer.

Band patterns stayed visible after sputtering, but top-layer probes showed clear structural and electronic upset in the treated crystals. Adding the organic layer shifted the Fermi level for the neon-treated surface, with charge moving toward the cobalt atom. The work shows how surface defects plus molecular layers can tune energy levels in future devices.
pmc-13287250:
Jennifer Karas Montez and colleagues tracked survey data in 2026 from 1993 to 2019 to ask why schooling predicts self-rated health more strongly over time in the United States. They estimated the link separately for each state among adults aged 30 to 64, then tested personal and state-level explanations.

The schooling gap widened in 49 of 50 states, though by very different amounts. Household income was the single biggest contributor in most states, with jobs and obesity also playing roles. Smoking changes actually held the gap back in many states. Broad state conditions explained little. The authors argue that state-level study can guide efforts to narrow health gaps.
pmc-13287750:
Zafer Kurt tested in 2026 whether heated mud powder from Rize province in Türkiye can replace part of the cement in mortar, cutting the carbon cost of a basic building material. Mud was dried, ground, and fired at three temperatures, then swapped into mortar at shares up to forty percent by weight.

Strength tests at twenty-eight days peaked with a ten percent swap, reaching a value the author reports as 46.65 megapascals. Crystal, microscope, and light-based checks explained the inner structure behind the strength. Heavier swaps helped less. Kurt presents the fired local mud as a greener partial binder for construction, with the best firing temperature chosen from the trials.
pmc-13288950:
Luigi Russo and colleagues ask if gene risk scores change health habits. Their 2026 review pools all fair trials on the topic. Such scores sum many small gene effects. Telling people their score may spur change. Or it may do little at all.

The search found 27 trials in all. Most scores dealt with cancer or heart disease. Some dealt with diabetes risk. Pooling showed no clear gain on 22 outcomes. Diet, drinking, and exercise barely moved. Clinic visits and drug use barely moved. Mood scores barely moved. Many trial reports claimed more than their data showed.
pmc-13289050:
Michael R Kahn and colleagues probe daily rhythms in shock care in 2026. Their study uses a large Boston ICU dataset. Shock means blood flow fails the body. Drugs that raise blood pressure treat it. Dose needs may swing with time of day.

The dataset held 46,520 ICU stays in all. Stays ran from 2001 to 2012. The team kept awake adults on drug drips. All had drips for more than 24 hours. The final group held 468 patients. Doses were split by day and night hours. Whether dose needs truly swing with the time of day is the question the analysis sets out to answer.
pmc-13289250:
Barbara H Bardenheier and colleagues published a 2026 national survey study on depression, anxiety, and health care use in United States adults by diabetes status. Data came from the National Health Interview Survey for 2021 to 2023. The sample held 86 404 adults aged 18 or older who reported diabetes, pre-diabetes, or neither condition.

About 25.6 percent of adults with diabetes and 24.6 percent with pre-diabetes reported depression, versus 16.6 percent with neither condition in the survey. Anxiety showed a similar pattern. Rates ran higher among non-Hispanic white adults than in other racial and ethnic groups. Skipping medicine because of cost linked strongly to both mood conditions. The authors warn that mood care and diabetes prevention need to move together.
pmc-13289650:
Michael E Thase led a 2026 post hoc analysis of a phase 3 trial on lumateperone added to antidepressants for major depression. Loss of pleasure, called anhedonia, is a core and stubborn symptom. The trial enrolled adults whose current episode had failed one or two antidepressants, with high symptom scores at entry, and randomized them to drug or placebo for six weeks.

The added drug dose was 42 mg daily alongside standard antidepressant care in the trial. Anhedonia scores improved more with the drug than with placebo at every visit checked, with the largest gap at day 43 as reported. Gains held in those with high starting anhedonia and spread across single symptom items too. Broader relief beyond mood alone matters for daily function.
pmc-13289750:
Saki Hasegawa-Tamba and colleagues present a 2026 autopsy case of pulmonary veno-occlusive disease after cancer immune therapy. That rare condition blocks small lung veins and raises lung pressure. An 80-year-old man with lung disease, high blood pressure, and heavy smoking history had lung cancer surgery first, with no sign of the vein disease in tissue at that time.

After cancer returned, he got nivolumab plus ipilimumab, developed breathing and kidney immune problems, then improved on steroids. Ipilimumab stopped, and nivolumab alone ran for 22 months until worsening breathlessness and severe low oxygen appeared. Heart tests confirmed lung hypertension, but breathing failed fast and he died on hospital day 53 overall. Autopsy showed vein wall thickening.
pmc-13289850:
Nazila Dalir, Glenn S Parker, Rachel Amanda Masia, and Patricia Torres share a 2026 case series on two fiercely aggressive signet ring cell cancers of the colon. This rare subtype makes up under one percent of colon cancers and often spreads before discovery. Both patients arrived with blocking tumors needing major surgery, illustrating how fast and wide the disease can move.

One case was a 58-year-old woman with a rectal tumor invading the pelvis and spreading to nearby reproductive organs. The other was a 45-year-old man with a tumor at the splenic bend, spread across the belly lining, unstable microsatellites, and several cancer gene changes. Tailored, multi-pronged care is urged for such cases.
pmc-13290450:
Chronic pelvic pain in men leaves marks on the brain's wiring, Huipeng Ren and colleagues report in 2026. They studied men with chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome, comparing their cortical structure with healthy volunteers.

Thirty-one patients and 28 controls underwent high-resolution MRI, and cortical thickness was mapped across the Destrieux atlas. Patients showed thinning in several temporal, frontal, and occipital areas and thickening in a few others, and two regional measures tracked symptom and quality-of-life scores. Network analysis told a matching story: patients' structural covariance networks were more clustered and less globally efficient, suggesting more segregation and weaker integration. Ren and colleagues read the pattern as multi-level brain change accompanying a pain condition long treated as purely local.
pmc-13290650:
Old livestock pens keep feeding the savanna long after herders move on, Dennis Kipng'etich and colleagues show in a field study from 2026 in Kenya's Maasai Mara. In the Olare Motorogi Conservancy, they compared grass near corrals abandoned five years earlier with grass farther away.

Plots 5 to 55 meters from a corral held more standing grass biomass than plots 150 to 200 meters out, in both wet and dry seasons, with nutrient-loving decreaser grasses thriving closest. Diversity ran the other way: far plots held 18 species against 14 near plots, since a few strong competitors dominate the rich soil. Wildlife dung, a sign of use, piled up near corrals, especially in the dry season. The authors cast abandoned corrals as nutrient hotspots that managers can work with.
pmc-13290850:
Two of three women get too cold during keyhole gynecology surgery, Yingbo Ren and colleagues find in a prediction study from 2026. Cooling during surgery worsens outcomes, yet risk tools for this surgery type have been scarce, so the team built a simple scoring chart from routine data.

The study covered 424 patients at one center, operated on between January 2019 and February 2024, of whom 65.8% dropped below 36 degrees. Split-sample modeling kept just three risk factors: age, body mass index, and how long surgery lasted. The chart sorted high-risk from low-risk patients well in training, with an AUC of 0.788, and checks of accuracy and clinical value backed its use. Ren and colleagues propose flagging high-risk patients early so warming can start before body temperature falls.
pmc-13292450:
David O Ehizibolo and a large team investigate a 2026 blind spot in Nigerian foot-and-mouth disease control: the part sheep and goats play. Cattle usually serve as the indicator species, leaving small ruminants understudied. On Plateau State farms where the animals mix, the team sampled 138 sheep and 39 goats across nine local government areas, taking blood, oral swabs, and tissue from suspected cases.

Most animals, 71.2 percent of those tested, had antibodies showing past exposure, with sheep at 77.5 percent and goats at 48.7 percent in the results. Viral RNA appeared in 36.6 percent of oral swabs, and serotypes O and A were identified. Gene trees tied the sheep and goat viruses closely to cattle viruses on the same farms. The authors urge planners to count small ruminants in surveillance.
pmc-13292550:
Haymanti Bhanot compiles a 2026 question-and-answer installment in the STAR Protocols series, this time on organoids. These lab-grown tissue models mimic their organs of origin and open questions animal models cannot reach. Reproducibility, though, plagues the field, with results swinging between organoids and between batches.

Protocol authors and advisory board members answer practical questions from the bench. On batch variation, contributors blame timing, handling, and lot-to-lot differences in matrix gels and growth proteins, advising fixed passaging rhythms, gentle and consistent dissociation, and checking certificates of analysis when lots change. Another answer tackles uneven seeding: because organoids sink, tubes should be inverted gently so suspensions spread evenly across wells. The piece collects craft knowledge aimed at steadier, more comparable organoid experiments.
pmc-13292650:
Joyce R Mbwana and a large team trace a 2026 drug-resistance thread through children and chickens in Tanzania's rural Korogwe District. They collected Klebsiella pneumoniae complex isolates from children with and without diarrhea and from commercial and smallholder chicken farms, then sequenced the extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producers among them. The question was how closely the human and poultry germs relate.

Resistant isolates appeared in 14 percent of children with diarrhea and 7 percent without, and on 10 percent of commercial and 5 percent of smallholder farm samples in the survey. Sequencing found mostly true K. pneumoniae plus two sister species, spread across many sequence and capsule types. Fifteen clonal clusters turned up, chiefly among chickens on one farm. The gene blaCTX-M-15 dominated. The authors warn of possible cross-species spread and urge One Health action.
pmc-13292850:
Ibrahim Untan and Volkan Sabur ask, in a 2026 study, whether a simple blood ratio can flag severe illness in emergency patients with flank pain. The ratio compares albumin to globulin and reflects both nutrition and body-wide inflammation.

Charts covered 291 adults who had an ultrasound scan between August 2022 and May 2023, and 59 met the study mark for a severe visit. That mark needed at least two of four signs, such as kidney swelling or high inflammation. Patients in the severe group had lower ratio values on average. The ratio predicted severity on its own, yet added nothing beyond standard CRP and creatinine tests.
pmc-13293450:
Sian Calvert and co-authors set out, in a 2026 protocol, an updated review of ways to help adults use hearing aids more steadily. Hearing aids improve talk and quality of life, yet many owners wear them rarely or not at all.

The planned review will gather trials of support programs for adults fitted with at least one aid and pool results where fitting. A behavior framework sorting capability, opportunity, and motivation will guide how each program is classed. Knowing which strategies work, and which behavior levers they pull, should steer future research and clinic practice. No results are reported yet in this protocol.
pmc-13293650:
Rebecca K Simmons and co-authors warn, in a 2026 article, that gene-based low-oxygen scores are often misread in brain tumor research. Computer tools tag gene patterns as hypoxia signals, yet brain tissue normally lives at far lower oxygen than lab air.

Adult brain oxygen sits in the range of 1 to 7 percent, values the authors give, which should count as normal for brain, not oxygen-starved. No single gene pattern marks low oxygen in all cell types, so scores built in one cell may mislead in another. Careful experiments in each cell type are needed before such scores guide claims.
pmc-13293750:
Sudip Kunwar and co-authors join, in a 2026 study, drone-based light scans with gene mapping to find wheat genes behind yield traits. Gene hunts are limited by slow, low-volume trait measures, and light signatures may offer a fast stand-in for yield.

The team grew 341 diverse soft wheat lines over three years, with 273 light bands recorded by a drone sensor. Bands tied most to grain yield, grain weight, and grain count were folded into one score per trait. Gene mapping found 31 linked markers across both hand and light measures. One marker on chromosome 1A sat in a photosynthesis gene and linked to all three light scores.
pmc-13294050:
Liyan Zhang and coauthors build a 2026 prediction model for whether an ovarian-adnexal mass is cancerous, using clinic details plus ultrasound features. Records covered 930 patients with 1,380 masses confirmed by pathology between January 2020 and December 2025. Two senior sonographers, blinded to pathology, re-read every scan and settled disagreements by discussion.

Masses split into a training set of 966 and a validation set of 414. Screening, multivariable models, and Lasso selection fed a nomogram, while four machine learning methods gave comparison classifiers. A simple chart that flags risk before surgery could help triage referrals and spare benign cases from major operations.
pmc-13294150:
Shun Muroga and coauthors fuse many measurement types with machine learning in a 2026 study of carbon nanotube films. Film behavior swings with tiny structural shifts, and no single test captures the whole picture. Shape measures from electron microscope images, covering curl, alignment, junctions, and voids, were merged with Raman crystal signals, surface area, and electrical resistance.

Visual maps grouped films cleanly by crystallinity and tangling. Nonlinear models, led by XGBoost, predicted properties best under leave-one-out checks. Resistance hinged on junction spacing, crystal quality, and network links, while surface area hinged on junction density and void size. The interpretable setup offers a template for other complex materials.
pmc-13294850:
Sara Zekri, Esperanza Navarro-Pardo, and Francisco Alcantud-Marín review links between autism, gender identity, and gender dysphoria in a 2026 article. Some earlier work hints that autistic adults show gender diversity more often than the general population. The review limits itself to adults without cognitive impairment.

Searches of five major databases for work since 2013 yielded only 12 suitable articles, mostly small studies from Western countries. Findings point to a real connection between autism and varied gender identity, with some positive link to dysphoria as well. The authors urge larger, more balanced samples and better recognition of gender diversity when supporting autistic adults.
pmc-13295250:
Shengjie Wang and colleagues study tiny drifting animals in two nearshore systems of China's Beibu Gulf in a 2026 article. Zooplankton pass energy up food chains to young fish, yet nutrient pollution reshapes their communities. Surveys in Qinzhou Bay and the Beilun River mouth traced water quality gradients from inner to outer waters.

Salinity rose seaward while nutrients and pollution fell along the same line. Small copepods dominated, led by one species whose grip had tightened compared with older records. Modelling split pollution harm into direct effects, poorer food quality, and community narrowing, which together dragged total plankton biomass downward in enriched waters.
pmc-13295450:
Victória Ribeiro Silvestre and colleagues survey public views on antimicrobial resistance in Brazil in a 2026 study. Resistance threatens health, farming, and the environment together, yet public understanding in Brazil was poorly measured. An online questionnaire shared through social media between April and August 2025 fed the work.

After cleaning, 945 valid answers remained for analysis. Schooling level predicted knowledge and attitude scores most strongly, while age and gender effects wavered. Fewer than half correctly spotted antibiotics among common medicines, and only about a quarter disposed of packaging properly. Health worry drove interest in antibiotic-free goods, guiding calls for sharper public teaching.
pmc-13295650:
Sandro La Vignera and Rosita A Condorelli review falling sperm counts and testosterone in a 2026 article. Male reproductive measures have dropped markedly over five decades in many countries. The review gathers trend data, body mechanisms, and environmental drivers behind the slide.

Sperm concentration fell by roughly half worldwide between 1973 and 2018, with the pace quickening after 2000. Testosterone slipped steadily with age held aside, by about one to two percent yearly in several groups. Hormone-disrupting chemicals, weight gain, sitting habits, smoking, and heat all share blame. The authors favour combined care plus prevention through cleaner environments as the strongest long-term answer.
pmc-13295850:
Mohamed Abdeldayem and colleagues report a 2026 prospective study of dental implant repair after injury-related jaw bone loss. Twenty adults had defects rebuilt with bone taken from the hip crest, then received implants six months later once the graft had settled.

Thirty implants were placed and all but one survived, while graft width and height both grew markedly over six months. Implant firmness rose, bone loss at the edges stayed modest, and most patients said they were satisfied. One person had a hip wound that opened. The authors see hip bone grafting as a promising route to delayed implant repair.
pmc-13298550:
Women whose clotting disease also hurt their pregnancies show a more fired-up immune profile, Paula David and a large team report in 2026. From 663 people with steadfast antiphospholipid marks and proven clots, they picked 295 women with the clot form of the disease and a past pregnancy.

Of those, 115 women, or 39.0%, also met the pregnancy form's rules. That group showed more ANA marks, more triple-mark blood tests, and more low platelet counts. With other traits weighed, ANA stayed tied to the group, at an odds ratio of 1.94. Clot type and new clots, though, matched the rest. High blood pressure, not pregnancy past, flagged artery clots. The team say immune traits may help sort risk.
pmc-13300150:
Fat makes up about half the dry weight of the brain, and Wei Shao and five colleagues argue in a 2026 review that drifting lipid balance helps drive age-related brain disease. The authors place glial cells at the center of the story, with neurons as partners rather than sole actors.

They trace APOE-linked faults in cholesterol transport, lipid droplets that strain microglia, and ceramide paths that push neurons toward death. The same networks are then mapped onto Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and demyelinating disorders. Closing sections weigh food-based steps, LXR and RXR agonist drugs, nanoparticle delivery past the blood–brain barrier, and lipid profiling as an early warning tool.
pmc-13303150:
Most patients on nintedanib for progressive lung scarring held their ground for a year, Vanesa Vicens-Zygmunt and colleagues report in a 2026 real-world cohort from a single center. Fifty-five people with non-IPF fibrotic lung disease who started the drug as their fibrosis advanced had lung function compared against their own pre-treatment year. Breathlessness, side effects, and survival were tracked alongside.

After twelve months, 63.4 percent had stable or improved breathing capacity and 82.5 percent on the gas-transfer measure. Decline slopes flattened compared with the prior year, though not significantly. Three quarters reported side effects, diarrhea leading, and fifteen paused or stopped treatment. The authors read everyday practice as broadly matching trial expectations.
pmc-13303350:
Skin's hidden weave, not just its fibers, explains its springy stretch curve, Jia Li and colleagues show in a 2026 computer study. Block-face electron microscopy mapped collagen layout in fresh human skin, and a tensor method read fiber direction voxel by voxel. Those maps fed tissue models, set against versions that assume one even fiber layout throughout.

At the same stretch, the true-to-life model bore about four times the stress of the even-layout versions. It also gained its steep late stiffening from structure alone, with no need for nonlinear fibers. The method, the authors note, transfers to cornea, cartilage, arteries, and lungs.
pmc-13304650:
Ruoxuan Huang and co-authors profile the tissue under two mouth lining types in a 2026 study of what makes gums tough and cheek lining soft. The deep connective layer likely sets each surface's character and healing strength.

Human gum and loose cheek lining samples underwent gene sequencing plus protein and staining checks. Gum tissue carried more collagen-building gene activity and fewer attack-ready immune cells, with quieter defense cascades. Its inner chemistry also showed drained levels of a vitamin A product that guides surface growth. Such maps may steer graft design for lasting gum repairs.
pmc-13305250:
Keliang Zheng and colleagues use gene-based analysis to hunt changeable causes of tinnitus, the perception of ringing without outside sound, in a 2026 study. Aging, noise, smoking, and hearing loss are linked, but firm causal factors stay murky.

Thirteen lifestyle factors were tested with Mendelian randomization in a British biobank, then checked in a Finnish biobank. Belly size measures and blood sugar markers tied to tinnitus in the first group, and smoking tied in the second. When both groups pooled, only waist size kept a clear link. Trimming waistlines may be one lever worth testing in clinics.
pmc-13306050:
Xiaojun Zhang made a yellow pigment that also kills bacteria under light in a 2026 study using one-step combustion. Carbon was added to bismuth vanadate with citric acid serving as both fuel and carbon source.

At a citric acid ratio of 1.2, colour strength peaked with a reported b* value of 79.71 in the authors' measures. Light tests cleared 96.63% of a test dye and inactivated 99.99% of E. coli bacteria, far above the plain pigment. The powder also mixed well into plastic and glass, stayed stable with heat, and passed skin safety checks.
pmc-13306450:
Yugui Liu built a heat-reversible network inside recycled PET plastic in a 2026 materials study. Furan groups were grafted onto recycled chains, then linked with a partner compound through Diels–Alder bonds that break and reform with heat.

Higher linker shares raised gel content and crosslink density while swelling fell, with one mix showing the strongest network in reported checks. Heating traces showed bond opening near 143 °C and reforming near 124 °C in the given figures. The best mix kept strength after three re-pressing cycles and could heal damage, lifting recycled plastic performance.
pmc-13306650:
Syeda Sitara Waseem fused sound and video checks to catch deepfakes on small edge devices in a 2026 study. Single-mode detectors fail when an attack targets only one channel, so the design weighs each stream by quality in real time.

Benchmarks held 5472 audio and 1842 video samples, where fusion reached 96.7% accuracy and a 0.988 area score in reported results. Attack tests kept accuracy at 92.3% under a standard gradient method in the given figures. The model fits in 30.3 MB and runs at 20 frames per second on edge hardware. Such checks may help shield phones and ID tools from fake face and voice tricks.
pmc-13306850:
Martín Carballo-Pacheco optimised a plastic moulded to catch the antibacterial triclosan in a 2026 design study. Three recipe factors, two building acids and solvent share, were varied through a Box–Behnken plan to tune recognition strength.

The best mix gave a strong imprinting factor showing efficient target recognition in reported checks. Infrared scans confirmed the expected bond types, and microscopy showed a porous, clumped texture that opens moulded cavities to the target. Release ran in two phases over 48 hours, fitting a diffusion model with a score of 0.9754 in the given figures.
pmc-13307050:
Bo Wang tested how a clonal bamboo shares resources across uneven phosphorus patches in a 2026 pot study. Fragments joined a mother shoot, rhizome and daughter shoot, with phosphorus given evenly or placed at one end, and rhizomes left linked or cut.

Placed phosphorus raised growth of shoots sitting in rich patches and lifted total system mass over even feeding in reported results. Linked rhizomes boosted daughter mass and phosphorus stores against cut controls under every feeding pattern. Root shape shifts and sugar allocation patterns completed the picture of sharing at work.
pmc-13307650:
Miao An and co-authors mine in 2026 published herbal prescriptions for bovine viral diarrhea, a cattle disease with gut, lung, and breeding harms. They gathered 391 records from 2004 to 2024, covering 189 herbs used 2031 times in total across those records.

Data tools sorted herb traits, tastes, and pairings that showed up often, while network methods linked herb compounds to body targets and pathways. Docking runs added early guesses about how those links might work in the body. The map gives a tidy base for lab tests, yet the authors stress that real proof of benefit in cattle still lies ahead of any farm use.
pmc-13308550:
Belinda Cochrane and co-authors assess in 2026 a home based, team run service for lasting breathlessness in Australians with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The Macarthur clinic enrolled 89 patients with at least fairly severe lung block, gave each a nine week tailored plan, and scored breath, mind, and life quality over a year.

Mastery scores on a chest questionnaire rose by 0.5 points at nine weeks and by 0.8 points at 52 weeks in the cohort. Confidence, symptom load, and breath burden also held their gains at the late check in this study. Gains looked more like stronger coping and trust than like weaker breathlessness itself, which still marks real value.
pmc-13308750:
Jiaying Li and co-authors survey in 2026 how adults in China view immersive extended reality for health care, a field with scant public side data until now. Their poll ran from June to September 2024 and drew 35,861 adults across 33 top level regions and 800 towns with staged sampling.

Mean acceptance scored 63.11 on a 100 point scale, with wide swings by province and a fall with rising age. Richer social standing, past digital health use, and strong web health skill all tracked with warmer views of the tech. Past abuse, many siblings, and some health states tracked the other way. A short tree model spotted likely refusers far better than likely fans.
pmc-13310650:
Anna Piscone and co-authors study what happens when a DNA repair scaffold protein goes missing in breast cells in a 2026 article. Oxygen-driven DNA damage constantly threatens the genome, and the base excision repair path fixes the most common lesions. Two of its factors, APE1 and XRCC1, also steady the copying machinery.

Matched breast cell models lacking each factor were compared at rest and under oxidative stress. XRCC1 loss, more than APE1 loss, raised damage signaling and pushed chromatin fragments, rich in telomere DNA, into the cell body. Those cells also switched on an internal alarm path, inflammatory signaling, and aging traits. The authors name XRCC1 a key guard against stray DNA and float it as a treatment lever.
pmc-13310750:
Adriana Krenz and colleagues compare B cell clearing drugs for multiple sclerosis in a 2026 blood study. Drugs that remove B cells help many patients, and they can be given by vein drip or by skin injection. Whether the route changes the immune effect was unclear, so the team profiled blood cells in detail.

Groups held 25 patients on each of three drug plans, plus 20 healthy controls. All drugs cut B cells sharply. Patients on skin injections kept a higher share of memory B cells than those on vein drip. People who switched routes also gained memory share over eight weeks. Route may shape long term immune balance.
pmc-13310950: A short 2026 correction notice fixes swapped author names on a case report about complete androgen insensitivity syndrome. First and last names had been reversed for all authors of the genetic study. The correct lead name is Maria Francesca Astorino, followed by nine co-authors in full. The online version has been updated to match. The notice itself adds no new clinical data, results, or conclusions beyond the corrected byline.
pmc-13311450:
Hyun Bin Kim and co-authors detail a 2026 field test of a records-based tool that flags patients likely to carry drug-resistant gut bacteria on hospital entry. The bacteria, called CRE, resist carbapenem antibiotics.

The tool scored every admission at two Atlanta hospitals from June 2024 to March 2025 using current and past stay data. Of 853 patients approached, 342 agreed to stool or swab testing, and 11 carried CRE. Carriers had higher median risk scores than non-carriers, and the model's accuracy was modest. The team priced a screening program at the best cutoff to inform hospital policy.
pmc-13311750:
Meilan Chen and co-authors give their 2026 trial protocol on when to give dexmedetomidine to cut delirium after surgery in older patients with leg fractures. The drug may protect the brain, but the best timing is unknown.

Patients aged 65 and over having fracture surgery under spinal anesthesia will be split into three groups. One gets the drug before the spinal, one during surgery, and one gets salt water both times, using a double-dummy design. The main outcome is delirium in the first three days after surgery. Thinking scores, sleep quality, and pain are also tracked for later care guidance.
pmc-13311950:
Nicole Zhang writes a 2025 commentary on a qualitative study of pelvic floor problems among women living with multiple sclerosis. The discussed study found the problem common, distressing, and largely unmet by services.

Within ten years of diagnosis, most women with the disease face some pelvic floor trouble, on the cited evidence. The study's title quotes a clinician dismissing a patient with weight advice, capturing how concerns get silenced. Zhang argues nurses need knowledge of how these symptoms shake identity, autonomy, and control. She urges care shaped with patients, reaching beyond mobility to continence and sexuality.
pmc-13312050:
Wen Yu and colleagues report a 2026 randomized, double-blind trial of a long-acting local anesthetic for pain control after open heart surgery through the breastbone. They tested whether liposomal bupivacaine, placed in a superficial parasternal block, could beat the standard drug ropivacaine on pain and stress after surgery.

Forty-four patients having elective surgery with a heart-lung machine were assigned to one of the two drugs. The liposomal bupivacaine group reported lower pain scores from 18 to 72 hours after surgery, had lower levels of the stress markers angiotensin II and interleukin-6, and needed fewer extra pain doses. They also left intensive care sooner and recovered better, with no block-related complications in either group.
pmc-13312450:
Vinita Lal and colleagues report a 2026 surface science study of methanol oxidation on copper and on a copper surface dotted with single platinum atoms. Turning methanol selectively into formaldehyde on copper is an important industrial reaction. How product choice shifts with the amount of oxygen pre-loaded on the surface had never been mapped systematically on these single-atom alloys.

Using deuterated methanol with desorption and photoelectron measurements, the team found the lone platinum atoms slow the surface's own initial oxidation at low oxygen doses. Product choice, though, barely moved: formaldehyde stayed the main product on both surfaces across a wide oxygen range, peaking near a third of a monolayer. The platinum atoms did open a small oxygen-free route by splitting the molecule's O-H bond at very low temperature. Calculations agreed, showing platinum raises the barrier to oxygen splitting.
pmc-13313250:
Ying Wang and a large team report a 2026 antibody study aimed at Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a germ that more and more often shrugs off antibiotics. They sought a treatment that works no matter the drug resistance, by aiming at flagellin, the protein of the tail the germ swims with.

From a panel of 20 antibodies against flagellin FliC, they picked 16G10 as the lead for its strong binding. Mapping showed it grips a short stretch in the D1 domain, from Gly71 to Ile88, a site kept across types and key to building the tail. In lab tests the antibody clumped the germs, slowed swimming, cut entry into lung cells, and shrank biofilms. In mouse lung infection, even against a drug-proof strain, it raised survival, lowered germ counts, and calmed inflammation.
pmc-13314450:
Yehui Han and colleagues show how maize roots call in helpful microbes to beat salty, alkaline soil in a 2026 study. Carbonate-type salt-alkali stress cuts maize yields badly on the Songnen Plain of northeast China, and the joint answer of roots and microbes was not clear.

Field tests paired soil chemistry with microbe sequencing and broad chemical mapping of the root zone. Stress raised soil pH and salt readings and lowered organic matter and key nutrients, yet the thin soil layer around roots buffered the blow and kept a high capacity to hold nutrients. Microbe variety near roots even rose under stress, per the report. Root chemicals acted as signals that drew in helpful microbes and built a working web. The finds may guide ways to farm harsh soils.
pmc-13315450:
Gerda Deveikienė and colleagues report a rare case in 2026 of granulomatosis with polyangiitis starting during pregnancy. A 26-year-old first-time mother in her second trimester had worsening nose and sinus disease treated as severe bacterial infection, with repeated antibiotics and ear, nose, and throat procedures.

Her state worsened with coughing of blood and hollow lung lesions. Tissue tests showed dead, inflamed tissue with granulomas, and blood tests found anti-PR3 antibodies, confirming the disease near 22 weeks. Care was hard due to fast multi-organ spread, possible kidney harm, a fungal lung infection, and few pregnancy-safe drugs. Steroids, immunoglobulin, and azathioprine brought control.
pmc-13315750:
Adel Mahmoud Negm and co-authors mapped an oil reservoir in 2026 in the I and R fields of Libya's Murzuq Basin. The Upper Ordovician Mamuniyat Formation is the main reservoir there, shaped by glacial deposits and complex structure, so the team combined well data, seismic imaging, and 3D modeling.

Eleven wells showed quartz-rich sandstones with shale under 25 percent, effective pore space near 12 to 15 percent, and water share from about 20 to 55 percent. Seismic traits revealed a northwest to southeast fault system splitting the reservoir, and amplitude patterns marked sand-rich fairways with better quality rock.
pmc-13316650:
Daniel Marcano Zamora and a global team report a 2026 demonstration study that extends the World Health Organization GLASS surveillance system to Candida yeasts in the bloodstream. Drug resistance in these fungi is a rising threat, yet tracking had no shared global method.

Twenty-four laboratories were invited to collect cases under one protocol with shared software, covering infections confirmed between January 2017 and July 2021. Fourteen labs in 13 countries sent data, building a set of 3,447 cases for shared counting of species and drug resistance patterns. Sites also fed back on the tools through forms and meetings. The pilot shows standardized fungal tracking can work across very different health systems.
pmc-13316950:
Khaoula M'Rabt and colleagues present a 2026 case report on two sisters, aged 12.5 and 8 years, seen at a dental center in Rabat with pycnodysostosis, a rare inherited bone disorder also called Toulouse-Lautrec syndrome. Their parents are related by blood, matching the disorder's recessive pattern.

Both girls showed the classic signs: short stature, a beaked nose, short fingers, a wide jaw angle, and dissolving fingertip bones. The report lingers on face and tooth features, since dentists may be the first to spot the pattern and steer families toward diagnosis. Bone hardening from faulty bone-eating cells drives the syndrome, which affects roughly one to two people per million worldwide.
pmc-13318650:
