Raphael Groß and colleagues compare, in a 2026 retrospective study, two operations for sinus venosus atrial septal defects, a heart hole near the sinus node, looking mainly at rhythm problems afterwards. Records covered 110 adults and children treated in northern Bavaria between 2000 and 2025.

Seventy patients had the standard patch repair and forty the newer rotational Z-flap. Operations ran shorter with the flap, yet rhythm trouble appeared in 54.5 percent of all patients afterwards, and one pattern, sinoatrial block with junctional rhythm, was clearly commoner after the flap at 17.5 percent against 4.3 percent in the comparison. No one needed a permanent pacemaker, and leftover shunts or vein narrowing did not differ between the techniques.
pmc-13318750:
Giorgia Coratti leads a large consortium reporting, in 2026, on updating disease registries for spinal muscular atrophy. New disease-modifying treatments and newborn screening have reshaped the illness. Old centre spreadsheets and mismatched databases cannot track these changes. Registries must measure treated and untreated patients comparably over time.

Their group helped build the international ISMAR registry across the United States, United Kingdom, and Italy. It uses shared definitions, standard scoring, and trained examiners. Over seven years it has gathered natural history and real-world treatment data. The account describes why the registry scope is now being redefined again. Highly specialised centres led the first phase. Wider, harmonised monitoring is the next challenge for this fast-changing field.
pmc-13319050:
Ping Li and colleagues present a 2026 field experiment on cutting chemical fertiliser use for lettuce. Four treatments kept total nutrients equal. They ranged from chemical fertiliser alone to half replaced by organic manure, with biochar added in two arms. Yield, soil properties, and leaf chemistry were compared.

All three other mixes improved soil organic matter, pH, and available nutrients over chemical fertiliser alone. Lettuce yield and nutrient uptake also rose. The full mix of manure swap plus biochar did best overall. Leaf analysis showed richer phenolic acids and flavonoids under the new mixes. Manure mainly shifted tyrosine pathways, while biochar shifted nitrogen pathways. Leaf chemistry tracked soil organic matter, pH, and potassium most closely when links were checked.
pmc-13319650:
Sena Kaşıkçı and Ebru Şirinoğlu test ways to clear drug paste from young teeth with open tips in a 2026 lab study. Pastes placed inside a tooth to calm infection must come out cleanly before the final fill, and any paste pushed past the tip can cause harm. Sound based rinsing at two pulse types was put to the test.

Thirty two pulled lower canine teeth were shaped to mimic open tips and filled with one of two pastes. Fast pulse rinsing left far less paste behind than slow sonic rinsing for both pastes. Amounts pushed past the tip were alike across all groups. The newer paste cleared at least as well as the standard one, which supports it as a sound choice.
pmc-13319950:
Menglan Zhai and co-authors compare longer use of electric field therapy for a fast brain tumor in a 2026 study across many centers. The wearable therapy uses mild electric fields to jam tumor cell splitting and is given with drug and beam care at first. Whether keeping it on into the later drug phase adds gain was unclear, so records for two paths were set side by side.

One group of 68 people kept the fields into the later phase, while 32 stopped after beam care. Time without tumor growth was alike in both groups, near a year in each. Length of life ran longer in the kept on group by a few months on median counts, but the gap could reflect chance in this non random split. Scalp harm did not rise with longer use.
pmc-13320250:
Jennifer Hutchings and co-authors check whether a full body radiation shield slows heart attack care in a 2026 records study. Fast opening of a blocked heart artery is a core quality mark in heart attack care, with a goal of ninety minutes or less from door to balloon. A new shield system guards staff far better than aprons, but any setup delay would be a real cost.

Records for 133 straight heart attack cases at one center split 71 shield room cases from 62 standard room cases across a year and a half span. Door to balloon times ran close in both rooms, near fifty minutes in each, with no clear gap in any time slice. Better staff safety came with no loss of speed for patients.
pmc-13320550:
B Kaiser and colleagues release a 2026 data set on shock waves driven by high explosives through layered materials. Fast computer models that stand in for full physics runs need good training data, and no public set existed for this problem. The set, called HEAT, was built with a multi-material shock code from Los Alamos National Laboratory.

Two families of two-dimensional runs are included, one with an expanding shock cylinder and one with a rippled layered boundary. Each run tracks how shocks move through several materials at once, a task that needs rules for pressure, bending, phase change, and damage. The release lets machine learning teams train, test, and check fast surrogate models openly.
pmc-13322150:
Joyce O'Shaughnessy and co-authors test whether a 70 gene signature predicts who gains from stronger chemotherapy in a 2026 breast cancer analysis. Anthracycline drugs have shown no clear average benefit in hormone sensitive, HER2-negative early breast cancer. Data came from the FLEX study of high risk tumours classed by the MammaPrint signature.

Among 1106 patients in the lower high risk group, three year disease free survival matched between drug regimens, both at 95.9 percent in the study. In the highest risk group of 153 patients, the anthracycline regimen reached 100 percent against 94.8 percent without it, a 5.2 point gain. Benefit grew with genomic risk.
pmc-13322950:
Jing Ning and co-authors pool trial evidence on deep brain stimulation and thinking in Parkinson's disease, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. They searched four databases for randomised trials that set stimulation against best medical treatment, judging bias with a standard Cochrane tool.

Ten trials with 1,274 patients qualified. Stimulation groups fell more on verbal fluency and on a Stroop colour-word task than medical groups in the pooled results. Overall cognition, mental flexibility, depression and anxiety measures showed no clear difference between groups. The authors frame stimulation as a strong motor therapy with a narrow cost to word-finding speed, and they call for longer and more uniform mental testing in future trials.
pmc-13323250:
Alex Gittelman proposes a unified framework for rhythm coordination across brain, body and social life, in a 2026 theory article. Brains coordinate behaviour from milliseconds to days through cross-frequency coupling, where slow waves shape the timing and strength of faster ones.

The framework, called Temporal-Oscillatory Entrainment, sorts nine frequency bands into neural, biological and social groups. Hearing and movement form a privileged path, since coupling appears in the auditory brainstem near a natural rhythm band. Music training, breathing rhythms and social rhythm therapy give supporting cases across scales. The author argues that one nesting principle links neural timing with daily routines and group coordination.
pmc-13323950:
Kah and co-authors review immune based treatments for hepatocellular carcinoma in this 2026 article. This is the most common form of liver cancer, and it kills many patients worldwide. Drugs that release the brakes on the immune system have widened the options for advanced disease. Yet only a minority of patients gain lasting benefit from them.

The review blames the liver tumour environment, which is shaped by chronic viral hepatitis and fatty liver disease. Suppressor cells, exhausted T cells and natural killer cells, and blocking signals such as HLA G all help tumours escape. Kah surveys newer targets such as TIGIT and Tim 3, cell therapies aimed at glypican 3, natural killer cell treatments, and blood tests that track response. The authors argue that matching patients to treatments through biomarkers is the way to lift response rates.
pmc-13325150:
Bahriyenur Arabacı, Aslı Yüksel, and Canan Varlıklı turn sugar beet pulp into a light-driven catalyst for cleaning sugar factory wastewater in a 2026 study. The loop is neat: solid waste from the industry treats its own liquid waste.

Hydrothermal cooking made hydrochar from the pulp, which then supported graphitic carbon nitride. Best char yield, 36.74 percent, came at 200 °C for 60 minutes with 20 g of biomass. Under tuned conditions the pair removed 14.02 percent of total organic carbon from real effluent. That share looks low until the starting load, above 7000 mg per liter, is weighed. The char also made the catalyst sturdier for reuse.
pmc-13326350:
Yichao Liu and co-authors compare five drying routes for the medicinal herb Atractylodes chinensis in a 2026 study. Drying shapes both the active compounds and the prized aroma of the roots.

Sun, shade, hot air, microwave, and freeze drying were tested with an electronic nose and GC-MS. Freeze-dried and shade-dried batches kept the most functional compounds and the strongest odor response. Hot air drying lost the most on both counts. Volatile profiles centered on terpenoids, esters, phenols, and ketones. The freeze-dried batch stood out for atractylodin, atractylone, and bornyl acetate, which carry woody and camphor notes. Terpenoid building pathways dominated the chemistry shifts.
pmc-13326950:
Sameer Dal and a large team profile epileptic spasms that begin after infancy in a 2026 cohort study. Late-onset spasms are often missed, and older series left most causes unknown.

Records held 62 children seen from 2011 to 2021 with video-confirmed spasms and no hypsarrhythmia pattern. Median onset was 23 months, and diagnosis lagged by a median of 8 months. Only 24 percent were named correctly at first visit. Modern scans and gene tests found a cause in 95 percent of cases, led by structural brain malformations at 63 percent of the cohort. Steroid treatment stopped spasms in 29 percent, and vigabatrin in 35 percent, each favoring different cause groups.
pmc-13327950:
YuQi Ren and co-authors run a pilot causal study of an added drainage cut in glaucoma surgery in a 2026 article. Chronic angle-closure glaucoma is treated with lens removal plus freeing of stuck drainage tissue, and some surgeons also open the drainage meshwork from inside. Records covered 102 eyes, 54 with the standard operation and 48 with the added cut.

Weighted methods that balance group differences favored the added cut, with two-year freedom from failure at 0.682 against 0.425 and a weighted hazard ratio of 0.475 in the adjusted comparison. Scan-informed models also tried to forecast which eyes gain most. As a proof-of-concept pilot, the work supports a fuller trial rather than settling the question.
pmc-13328250:
Rulan Shangguan, Jiajing Xie, and Xiaofen Hamilton develop a scale for physical activity awareness in college students in a 2026 study. Young adults move too little, and how they perceive their own activity and surroundings may matter as much as fitness itself. Focus groups first mapped what awareness means to students.

Four parts emerged: personal awareness, social support awareness, environmental awareness, and awareness of activity recommendations. pmc-13329750:

pmc-13330550:

pmc-13331050:
Yanni Zhang and colleagues map world clinical trials of cytokine-induced killer cell therapy in a 2026 analysis. pmc-13333350:
Monica Pomaville and Jessica B Foster argue in a 2026 commentary that making CAR T cells from short-lived mRNA, rather than a lasting virus, could make brain tumor therapy safer for children. pmc-13333450:
Xiaogang Jin and colleagues compare students in China and Kazakhstan in a 2026 cross-cultural survey. pmc-13333750:
In New Hampshire and Vermont, César Alas-Pineda and co-authors surveyed cancer survivors about alcohol use in a 2026 study. The study measured drinking patterns, awareness that alcohol raises cancer risk, and survivors' wishes and obstacles around cutting down.

The cross-sectional survey drew 471 survivors aged 21 and older from two statewide online panels, and about a third had an alcohol-related cancer. Two-thirds currently drank alcohol, yet only about half knew alcohol increases cancer risk. Among current drinkers, 26.5 percent wanted to cut down within six months, and many in that group drank around seven drinks a week. pmc-13336350:
Zhigang Chen and Xing Li wrote a 2026 commentary on research linking gum disease to anxiety through a signaling pathway running from the mouth to the hippocampus. pmc-13336450: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws the Advanced Science article by J. Lin and co-authors on an injectable hydrogel meant to promote tolerance of transplanted kidneys. pmc-13336750:
Noortje Maria Petronella Overwater and co-authors review protein feeding in critical care in a 2026 article spanning the ICU stay and recovery after it. Muscle melts away fast in severe illness, yet many patients still miss protein targets. Big studies of high protein intake disagree, with some showing no gain or even harm in certain groups.

The authors argue for doses matched to each patient, guided by body type grouping and deeper biological typing. They discuss the hard problem of measuring body makeup, shown through a case study, and whether blood markers can guide dosing. Barriers that keep patients underfed also get attention. Better tailoring could protect strength and life quality for survivors.
pmc-13336950:
Igor D. Luzhansky leads a 2026 team that watches single nerve fibers heal inside living mice. Peripheral nerves sit deep in soft tissue, so tracking injury and regrowth over time at fine detail has been hard. Their implant places a flexible, clear silicone window in the skin over the mouse sciatic nerve.

The window gave steady optical access for over one month without harming nerve function in the reported use. Three microscope modes imaged labeled axons and Schwann cells, natural collagen, and blood vessels together. The team followed fiber breakdown and regrowth, support cell moves, and matrix-guided pathfinding across injury models, including gap repair. pmc-13337650:
Xiao-Tao Wang and co-authors offer a 2026 review on how exercise helps the adult hippocampus make new neurons. The hippocampus supports learning and memory, and new neuron growth there is tied to flexible connections between brain cells. Weak growth has been linked to Alzheimer's disease, epilepsy, and brain injury.

By pulling together what is known about cycle control in the dentate gyrus, the review points to exercise as a practical way to support brain health.
pmc-13339650:
Yuto Iwasaki, Akinori Sato, and Tomoyuki Miyao build fast machine learning predictors of molecular reactivity in a 2026 study. Methyl cation and anion affinities gauge how sites attract or donate charge, but quantum calculation is slow. Their surrogate models use a pretrained molecular encoder.

pmc-13339750:
Jinyoung Oh and a large team study how peptoid chains fold in a non-water solvent in a 2026 study. Peptoids mimic peptides but attach side chains to nitrogen, blocking normal folding bonds. Their shapes in chloroform, a stand-in for membrane interiors, were unknown.

pmc-13343250:
Jikun Wang, Yihan Wang, and Xiwu Zhang review plant polysaccharides against cancer in 2026. Chemotherapy's heavy toxicity and weak targeting push interest in gentler options, and these natural plant sugars stand out for hitting many targets at once with low toxicity and good body tolerance.

pmc-13343350: Jianjun Nie and co-authors issued a brief 2026 correction notice for their study of photodynamic therapy paired with a recombinant mussel mucin dressing for skin darkening after inflammation. The notice adds missing chemical name labels to Figures 7, 8, and 9, which show mucin production steps, antioxidant scavenging assays, and membrane testing. The figures and the study's results and conclusions stand unchanged.
pmc-13343950:
Shaowen White and co-authors solve a sixty-year puzzle about Epstein-Barr virus and the amino acid arginine in 2026. Starving infected cells of arginine was long known to wake the virus from latency. Why stayed unknown. The team screened amino acid cuts in Burkitt lymphoma and stomach cancer cell models.

pmc-13344850:
Cristina Conte and co-authors report a 2026 case of an unexpected chest mass that traced back to a patient's surgical past. pmc-13346050:
Qingfeng He and co-authors show that waist size catches fatty liver risk that body mass index misses in a 2026 health-check study. pmc-13346850:
Dong Zhou and co-authors load full-arch zirconia prostheses to failure in a lab study published in 2026, comparing support by four implants against support by six. pmc-13347650:
Jiaqi Liu examines fluorine-free fire foams held up by silica particles and a mixed surfactant pair, in a single-author study from 2026. pmc-13347950:

pmc-13348150:

pmc-13349750:

pmc-13349950:

pmc-13350050:

pmc-13350250:

pmc-13351150:

pmc-13351650:

pmc-13351950:

pmc-13353350:

pmc-13354950:
Albandari Alharbi and co-authors surveyed 531 adults in the United Kingdom in 2026 about continuous glucose monitors for type 2 diabetes. pmc-13355250:

pmc-13358850:

pmc-13359150:

pmc-13360050:

pmc-13361250:

pmc-13361650:

pmc-13363250:

pmc-13367150:

pmc-13367550:

pmc-13369950:

pmc-13371750:

pmc-13372250:

pmc-13373850:

pmc-13374650:

pmc-13375550:

pmc-13379450:

pmc-13380050:

Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis arise from changes in intestinal microbes together with the immune system. Their analysis compares gut communities and their chemical activity in patients and controls. Naming which microbial jobs are lost or overdone suggests new treatment angles, from diet to live microbe therapies. The work shaped how bowel disease is viewed as a system disorder.
pmc-3810850:
Zhang, Kapli, Pavlidis, and co-authors present a general method for delimiting species from sequence data, with applications to placing species on family trees. Sequence-based delimitation is central to DNA-based taxonomy, to surveys of microbial communities, and to metabarcoding studies. Existing approaches rely either on simple similarity thresholds or on complex, compute-heavy evolutionary models.

Their method seeks a middle path that is both principled and practical. Deciding where one species ends and another begins affects conservation lists, ecological counts, and identification of specimens from environmental DNA.  DNA barcoding of insects and fungi drove much of the demand behind it.
pmc-4287950:
Anders, Pyl, and Huber presented HTSeq in 2014, a Python framework for high-throughput sequencing data. Many tools exist for standard steps in this kind of analysis. Once a project departs from standard workflows, though, researchers must write custom scripts of their own.

HTSeq makes that custom work faster and safer. It provides building blocks for reading, counting, and sorting sequencing data in Python. A common task is counting how many reads fall on each gene. With a solid library for the basics, labs can focus their code on the new question they are asking instead of file handling.
pmc-4687950:
Whiting, Savović, Higgins, and their colleagues developed ROBIS, reported in 2016, to judge bias in systematic reviews. Many tools assessed bias in primary studies, but reviews themselves can also be biased. ROBIS was built to fill that gap for reviewers of reviews.

The team used a four-stage process: set the scope, review the evidence, meet in person, and refine the tool by piloting. ROBIS checks how a review searched, selected, and combined studies, and whether its conclusions follow. Umbrella reviews and guidelines rely on underlying reviews being sound. A tested tool for spotting weak reviews protects the decisions built on them.
pmc-5520850:
Yang, Fan, Mao, and their team found in 2017 that circular RNAs can be turned into proteins on a wide scale. Back-splicing of gene messages creates large numbers of circular RNAs in human cells. What most of these circles do in the cell was still largely unclear.

The team reports that a chemical mark on RNA, the most common such mark, drives the making of proteins from these circles. That was a surprise, since circles lack the start cap that straight messages use to begin protein making. Proteins from circles would add a hidden layer of gene products. The find widened the known roles of circular RNAs in the cell.
pmc-6146950:
James Dahlhamer, Jacqueline Lucas, Carla Zelaya, and colleagues reported United States pain figures for 2016 in this 2018 report. Chronic pain shapes work, mood, and health care use across the country. Knowing how common it is guides policy and funding.

Using a national health survey, the authors estimate that about one in five adults had chronic pain. A smaller share had high-impact pain that often limits life or work. Rates were higher in women, older adults, and rural areas. These baseline numbers are still quoted when pain policy and opioid policy are debated.
pmc-8431850:
David Stirling and co-authors described CellProfiler 4 in 2021, the newest version of a free program that measures features in microscope images. Images hold far more information than the eye can tally, and modern microscopy produces datasets far too large for manual scoring. Automated, objective measurement has become essential for image based biology.

The update focuses on speed, utility, and ease of use, letting researchers process big image sets faster and with less friction. The authors explain what changed under the hood and in the interface. CellProfiler is a workhorse in drug screening and cell biology, so improvements here quietly raise the throughput of many laboratories.
pmc-9438950:
Giulio Formenti and colleagues built Gfastats in 2022, a tool that sums up genome assemblies and helps researchers work with them. Labs now produce new reference genomes at great speed. Each one needs a clear report card: how long it is, how many pieces it comes in, and how far it can be trusted. New data types and new methods keep changing what that report card must show.

Gfastats builds its reports from assembly graphs, the maps that assembly software draws as it works. It can also convert files between formats and let users trim or join pieces of a genome build. Teams check these numbers at each step to judge when a genome is done, so a fast, sound tool sits inside many projects.
pmc-9825450:
Typhaine Paysan-Lafosse, Matty Blum, and co-authors reported in 2023 the recent developments in InterPro, a database that classifies proteins into families. InterPro also marks the domains and conserved sites that reveal what a protein does. This report covers version ninety of the resource and the services associated with it.

The authors describe new member databases and data added, improvements to the website, and growth in the classifications offered. InterPro merges many specialist collections into one search, so a single query checks a protein against all of them. Keeping such an integration current is constant work, and these periodic reports let users see what changed beneath a tool many treat as fixed.
reichenbach-researches-magnetism-1850:
Karl von Reichenbach announces a new force in his Physico-Physiological Researches, in William Gregory's 1850 English version. Sensitive persons, he reports, see flames and glows around magnets and crystals. He names the unseen energy the odic force and builds a vast system of trials to prove its presence in nature.

Earnest and elaborate, the work sought new forces with a chemist's care. Reichenbach had real fame as the finder of creosote and paraffin. Critics could not repeat his sensitives' visions under strict test conditions. The book remains the pivotal work of fringe science in its century, a serious mind's bold reach beyond the known map of nature.
sendivogius-new-light-of-alchymie-1650:
Michael Sendivogius was a Polish adept at the courts of emperors whose Novum Lumen Chymicum taught a generation of chymists. This 1650 English translation, A New Light of Alchymie, carried his treatise to Boyle and Newton. Both men studied Sendivogius with close attention.

He teaches that a hidden food of life, drawn from the air and the sun's rays, feeds metals growing in the earth. The philosophers' stone, in his account, concentrates that food until base metals ripen into gold. His clear, confident system made him the most readable of the great alchemical teachers. His name for that hidden food, the seed of nature, passed into wide use.
smith-dictionary-greek-roman-biography-m:
Volume Two of Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology appeared in 1850, continuing the alphabet of ancient lives. William Smith's team of scholars worked from the Greek and Latin authors directly. The aim was a complete record of the classical world in persons.

Each article weighs the ancient evidence, cites its sources, and untangles fact from myth. Long lives like those of the Caesars sit beside brief notices of minor poets and kings. The volume holds hundreds of engraved coins and portraits as well. Together with its mates, it formed the standard English guide to classical biography.
sydenham-works-vol2-1850:
Thomas Sydenham built his fame on careful notes taken at the sickbed in seventeenth-century London. R. G. Latham translated his Latin writings for the Sydenham Society. This second volume of the English Works followed the first in 1850 and completes the set.

Here Sydenham treats smallpox, gout, and several other common diseases of his day. He explains the cooling treatment he used for smallpox and describes his own painful attacks of gout. Throughout, he trusts what repeated observation shows over what old books claim. The volume rounds out the record of his clinical method, and it shows why later doctors admired his honest, practical style.
tennyson-in-memoriam-1850:
Alfred Tennyson's closest friend, Arthur Hallam, died suddenly at twenty-two in 1833. Tennyson grieved for seventeen years, writing short lyrics whenever sorrow or hope moved him. He published the gathered sequence, 131 lyrics with prologue and epilogue, as In Memoriam in 1850, without his name at first.

The poems swing between despair and a hard-won trust that love survives death. Tennyson wrestles with new geology and evolution, which seemed to make nature careless of human life. Ring out, wild bells and other sections became famous Victorian touchstones. Queen Victoria kept the book beside her Bible after her husband died. It remains the century's deepest meditation on faith and doubt.
the-divine-pymander-in-xvii-books-hermet: The Divine Pymander in XVII Books, 1650. The Hermetic classic. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
the-pacing-of-the-sentinel-or-the-soul-o: The Pacing of the Sentinel, 1850. The soul on duty. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
tob-0150:
Aleister Crowley summed up his system in Magick in Theory and Practice, the best-known manual of ceremonial magic of the twentieth century. His definition is famous: magick is the science and art of causing change to occur in conformity with will. The book lays out both his theory and his rites.

Yoga, ritual tools, invocations, and the holy books of Thelema all find their place in the scheme. Crowley writes as teacher, showman, and scold by turns. The work remains under copyright, and no public-domain text is distributed with this entry. Its record here marks the place the book holds in occult history.
tob-10450:
Jakob Boehme, a German shoemaker who became one of the most original religious thinkers of his century, staged Dialogues on the Supersensual Life as conversations between a master and a disciple. The subject is the life beyond the senses. Boehme wrote in dense, image-rich language drawn from craft, nature, and Scripture.

Master and disciple discuss how the soul falls, how it is reborn, and what heaven and hell truly are. Boehme treats both as states within the soul as much as places after death. Readers willing to move slowly get a strange, vivid system that influenced later German philosophy and Protestant mysticism alike.
tob-13150:
F. Max Muller, the German-born Oxford scholar who edited the Rig Veda, surveyed Hindu thought in Six Systems of Indian Philosophy. Muller did more than any other Victorian to bring Indian texts to English readers. The book gathers his long study into one course.

The six systems, or darshanas, are Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, and Vedanta. Muller explains each one's view of the soul, the world, and release, and shows how they argue with each other. His survey gave the English-speaking world its first ordered map of Indian philosophy and still serves as a clear, if dated, first guide.
tob-13450:
Swami Paramananda, an Indian teacher who carried Vedanta to America, translated the principal Upanishads into clear English. The Upanishads are dialogues and teachings from ancient India, placed at the end of the Vedas. Teachers and students sit in forests and ask what the Self truly is.

Their answer is bold: Brahman, the ground of all things, and Atman, the self within, are one. Famous lines like thou art that sum up the claim. The talks use stories, riddles, and bold images to lead hearers past fear and death. Paramananda's plain style keeps the focus on those central claims.
tob-4050:
Volume three of Wordsworth's Poetical Works collects poems of his middle years, including the lyric England knows best, I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud. The daffodils poem, composed after a walk with his sister Dorothy, turns a remembered field of flowers into a theory of memory itself: nature stored, then repaid with interest in solitude.

Sonnets, memorial verses, and meditations on time surround the famous lyric. The Lake District's poet is at his most musical here, chiming public sonnets about liberty with private recollection. For readers working through the eight volumes, the third shows Romanticism's everyday sublime at working strength, neither manifesto nor epic, but lived attention.
tob-4150:
Nicholson's Mathnawi continues in volume two, covering the middle books of Rumi's vast Persian poem. The reed flute's cry still frames the teaching: the soul, cut from its source, longs to return. Tale follows tale, of lovers parted and seekers tested, each glossed by Nicholson's commentary.

Fools, kings, saints, and talking animals all carry lessons about pride, love, and the polishing of the heart. Nicholson spent his later life on this translation, and its authority rests on that labor. Verified from the 1919 edition record, volume two deepens the poem's argument: behind every story stands the one Beloved.
tob-9350:
Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish thinker of the first century, expounded the commandments of Moses in On Special Laws. His project joins Athens to Jerusalem: the Torah's rules, read with Greek philosophy, yield lessons in virtue that any rational reader can honor. Allegory is his master key.

Festivals, sacrifices, and laws of purity become teachings about the soul's health and the city's order. Philo writes for Jews tempted by Greek thought and Greeks curious about Moses alike. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. His bridge between the two worlds carried traffic for a thousand years, into church and synagogue alike.
turgenev-diary-superfluous-man-garnett-1:
The Diary of a Superfluous Man, written by Ivan Turgenev in 1850, is Englished here in Constance Garnett's translation of 1899. A dying young landowner named Tchulkaturin keeps a journal in his last weeks. He looks back on a life in which he always arrived one step too late.

His one love was taken by a livelier rival, and even his duel ended in farce. Turgenev gave Russian writing a lasting type in this hero: clever, feeling, and unable to act. Other stories in the volume extend the study of missed chances. The superfluous man haunted Russian novels for the rest of the century. Garnett's version kept the tale in English classrooms for decades.
un-ga-res-a-69-50:
Glowing goods in the wrong hands are the fear behind Resolution A/69/50, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Radioactive goods serve health, farms, and power plants across the world. Yet the text voices deep worry at the risk that terror groups may gain, move, or use such goods in a device that spreads radiation and fear.

Stray and smuggled atomic goods, loose from all state checks, add to the threat. Such a device, if used, would harm health and foul the land. World pacts built to bar and crush that risk are recalled with weight. States are urged to keep radioactive stock under firm guard, in store and on the road.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly resolution 69/50 (2014) aims to keep radioactive sources out of terrorists' hands. The Assembly calls on member states to keep terrorists from getting or using radioactive materials. It calls on them to join the International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism. It calls on them to strengthen steps to track, secure, and guard radioactive sources. It backs the International Atomic Energy Agency's Code of Conduct on the Safety and Security of Radioactive Sources. It backs its Incident and Trafficking Database, and efforts to recover stray 'orphan' sources.
un-sc-res-1350: An official UN record text, Resolution 1350 is catalogued in this library with a 2001 date. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1450:
Kenya came under formal Council review in Resolution 1450, adopted on 13 December 2002 by fourteen votes to one. On 28 November a bomb had wrecked the Paradise Hotel at Kikambala near Mombasa. The same day, missiles had nearly hit an Israeli airliner leaving Mombasa. Al-Qaida claimed both attacks.

The Council condemns the hotel bombing and the missile attempt in the strongest terms. It sends deep sympathy to Kenya, to Israel, and to the victims' families. All states are urged to help find and bring to justice those who planned and paid for the attacks. The text restates the Council's resolve to fight every form of terror.
un-sc-res-1550:
Six more months for the Golan Heights observer force came in June 2004. The force, called UNDOF, watches the cease-fire line between Israel and Syria. A report from the Secretary-General on the force was before the Council that month. The file's header date sits a day before the report it cites, so the month is the safe dating. Resolution 1550 was adopted unanimously in June 2004.

The Council called on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. That text demanded a cease-fire and peace talks after the October war. UNDOF's mandate was renewed for six months, until 31 December 2004. At the end of that period, the Secretary-General had to report on developments. His report also had to cover the measures taken to put Resolution 338 into effect. The renewal followed the standard pattern for this long-running mission.
un-sc-res-1650: Adopted in 2006, Resolution 1650 is part of the Security Council's formal record, kept here through a Wikisource transcription. Every resolution is a small treaty among fifteen delegations about what the UN will say and do. This entry holds one such agreement entire, in the order and wording the members finally settled on.
un-sc-res-1750:
UNMIL was extended with a drawdown plan attached on 30 March 2007. The Secretary-General's report of 15 March lay before the Council. Liberia's government was improving governance, fighting corruption, and regaining control over the country's natural wealth. Fighters had largely been reintegrated, though jobs for them were scarce. UNMIL worked closely with the United Nations force in Côte d'Ivoire on border security.

The Council extended UNMIL's mandate until 30 September 2007. It restated its intention to let the Secretary-General shift troops between UNMIL and the Côte d'Ivoire mission as needed. He was asked to present a detailed drawdown plan for UNMIL, with benchmarks for handing security to Liberian hands. The government was called to press its reforms in close coordination with the mission. The Council noted the Special Court for Sierra Leone's aim to finish its work in good time.
un-sc-res-1850:
At the end of 2008, Resolution 1850 declared the Council's support for the Israeli-Palestinian peace talks restarted at Annapolis. It was a rare Middle East text that the United States helped draft and all members backed. The members called the negotiations irreversible.

Inside, the text backs the two-state goal, praises both sides' commitments, and urges donors to fund the Palestinian Authority. It also calls on regional states to support the process and cut ties with violence. Adopted days before the Gaza war began, it preserves the last shared statement of a peace effort about to collapse.
un-sc-res-1950:
Resolution 1950, adopted on 23 November 2010, took up Piracy off Somalia. Pirate attacks had spread deep into the western Indian Ocean. Ransom payments kept climbing, and captured suspects were often freed for lack of courts. Somalia's government had asked for the naval powers to be renewed.

The Council renews those powers for twelve more months. States working with Somalia's government may enter its waters and use all necessary means against pirates. Warships, aircraft, and seizures of pirate gear all stay allowed. Kenya and the Seychelles win praise for trying suspects in their courts. The text presses all states to make piracy a crime and to share proof for trials.
un-sc-res-250: Preserved as Resolution 250, this Security Council text carries a 1968 date in the catalog record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-350:
A new United Nations force for the Golan Heights was created by the Security Council on 31 May 1974. Israel and Syria had just signed an Agreement on Disengagement, worked out under resolution 338 (1973). The Secretary-General had reported on how a force should be set up, with annexes on its terms. The Council welcomed the disengagement agreement as a step in applying the 1973 cease-fire call.

The Council set up the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force at once, under its own authority. It asked the Secretary-General to take the needed steps in line with his report. The force was established for an initial six months, open to renewal by later resolution. The Secretary-General had to keep the Council fully informed of developments. The observer force took its place between the two armies on the Golan, where renewals every six months became a fixture of the region for decades.
un-sc-res-450: Security Council Resolution 450 survives in the official record, and the catalog dates it to 1979. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-50:
Fighting in Palestine after Israel's founding brought a truce call in May 1948. On 29 May 1948 the Security Council ordered a halt to all armed force for four weeks. The call went to every government and authority involved. It was made without judging the rival claims of Arabs and Jews. The aim was simply to stop the shooting.

During the truce, no side could bring fighting men into the region. The ban covered Palestine and seven nearby states, from Egypt to Yemen. Men of military age who did arrive could not be trained or mobilized. Arms imports and exports were also frozen. United Nations mediators used the pause to press for a settlement.
un-sc-res-650:
Nicaragua's contra fighters were set to lay down their arms in 1990. The Central America observer group needed a bigger mandate to help. On 27 March 1990 the Security Council approved the Secretary-General's report on the region. It authorized, on a standby basis, an enlarged role for ONUCA. Armed personnel would be added to its strength. The group could then take part in the voluntary demobilization of the resistance.

The Secretary-General had to keep the Council fully informed. The Central American presidents' own peace agreements drove the process. The Council praised their efforts and urged all parties to honor their pledges. The step turned a small observer team into an armed demobilization mission.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Short-term judges for the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal are the business of this text, passed on 27 April 2001. These posts, called ad litem judges, let the tribunal run more trials at once without adding permanent seats. The Council had created the system the year before, as the tribunal's workload kept growing.

The text forwards to the General Assembly the nominations the Secretary-General had received, as the tribunal's Statute requires. The list runs to dozens of lawyers and judges named by countries on every continent. From it, the Assembly would elect a pool of ad litem judges, and tribunal panels could then draw on that pool case by case.

A suicide bomber struck a beach hotel near Mombasa, Kenya, on 28 November 2002. The Paradise Hotel was popular with Israeli tourists. The same day, attackers fired missiles at an Israeli airliner leaving Mombasa. They missed. Al-Qaida claimed both attacks in December. Resolution 1450 followed on 13 December 2002, with only Syria voting no.

The Council condemned the bombing in the strongest terms. It offered sympathy to Kenya, Israel, and the victims' families. All states were urged to hunt down those who planned and funded the attacks. That duty flowed from Resolution 1373, the post-September 11 counterterrorism law. Members pledged stronger resolve against terrorism everywhere.

Côte d'Ivoire's path to a UN seat ran through this line of 1960. On 23 August, the Council adopted Resolution 150 without dissent. The Republic of Ivory Coast had claimed freedom from France weeks before, on 7 August. It was one voice in the great chorus of the Year of Africa.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Ivory Coast. The Assembly acted the next month. Seventeen African states joined the UN in 1960 alone. Ivory Coast stood in that cohort. Their arrival changed the world body's balance for good. A new bloc of votes now shaped its debates.

The Golan Heights watch gained six more months in the summer of 2004. On 20 June, the Council adopted Resolution 1550 without dissent. It had read the Secretary-General's fresh report on the observer force. That force, UNDOF, guards the truce line between Israel and Syria. The line dates from the end of the 1973 war.

The text calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 at once. That 1973 order links a ceasefire to peace talks. The mandate then runs to 31 December 2004. A closing report from the Secretary-General is due at the end. This text is one link in an unbroken chain of renewals.

Burundi's transition had just ended in success when its United Nations operation, ONUB, was extended on 21 December 2005, until 1 July 2006. Authority had passed peacefully to an elected government and institutions. Burundians are congratulated on that outcome, and the regional initiative, the African Union, and ONUB are thanked for their parts in it.

The mission stays in place to support the new authorities while many challenges remain. Temporary redeployments between ONUB and the Congo mission are authorized, under set conditions, so the two operations can back each other up. The government is urged to complete its disarmament and security reform programme, and donors are called on to keep funding Burundi's development and recovery.

Resolution 1750, passed on 30 March 2007, keeps the UN force in Liberia for six more months. A UN report that March won warm words, as did Liberia's strides at home. The state had curbed graft and won back grip on its mines and woods. Donors, West African states, and the African bloc won thanks for their aid. The force, UNMIL, drew praise too. It worked hand in hand with the UN team in the next-door state on border safety.

The new term ran to September 2007. Sound gains in bringing ex-fighters back to civil life were noted. Yet their fate in the end hung on real jobs in shops, farms, and trades. The growth of the police and the new army also drew the Council's eye.

Support is declared on 16 December 2008 for the Israeli-Palestinian negotiations launched at Annapolis. The November 2007 Annapolis Conference had restarted talks aimed at a two-state settlement under the Road Map. The Quartet's November 2008 statement backed the process, and the Council now added its own weight.

The Annapolis negotiations are declared irreversible, and both parties are called on to meet their Road Map duties, including freezing settlement activity and fighting terrorism. All states and world bodies are called on to support the talks and the Palestinian Authority's institution building. Stronger diplomacy toward a comprehensive Middle East peace is urged, including on the Syrian and Lebanese tracks, and a possible meeting in Moscow in 2009 is welcomed.

Somali piracy authorizations are renewed for another year in Resolution 1950, adopted on 23 November 2010. Pirate range and capacity were growing into the western Indian Ocean. Ransoms and weak embargo enforcement were fuelling the trade. Captured pirates were often released for lack of courts able to prosecute them. The Transitional Federal Government consented and asked for renewal.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews for twelve months the authorizations in Resolutions 1846 (2008) and 1851 (2008). They let states and organizations cooperating with the Transitional Federal Government enter Somali waters, seize pirate boats, and fight piracy and armed robbery at sea. It commends the EU's Operation Atalanta, NATO operations, and Combined Task Force 151. It praises Kenya and Seychelles for prosecuting suspects and stresses the authorizations apply only to Somalia and create no customary international law. Member states are called on to criminalize piracy and cooperate on prosecution.

North Korea's weapons programs stand behind Resolution 2050, adopted on 12 June 2012. Earlier resolutions had punished the country for nuclear and missile work and had created a Panel of Experts to watch over the sanctions. The panel's interim and final reports were now before the Council. Members again called the spread of nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons a threat to peace.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the panel's mandate until 12 July 2013. It sets deadlines for a midterm report and a final report with findings and advice, and asks for a work plan within thirty days of the panel's new appointment. The panel serves the sanctions committee, which is urged to discuss the panel's work with it on a regular basis.

Israel planned to hold a military parade in Jerusalem on 2 May 1968, and the Council moved to stop it. Resolution 250 was adopted unanimously on 27 April 1968, after the Council heard statements from Jordan and Israel. The Council judged that the parade would raise tensions in the area. It would also harm the chances of a peaceful settlement. The short text calls on Israel to refrain from holding the parade. The Secretary-General was asked to report on how the resolution was carried out.

Resolution 350, adopted on 31 May 1974 by thirteen votes to none, creates the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force. Israel and Syria had just signed an agreement pulling their forces apart on the Golan Heights, following up the ceasefire that ended the October 1973 war. The Secretary-General's report, with annexes setting out the force's design, reached the Council the same week.

The Council welcomed the disengagement agreement and set up the observer force under its own authority at once. The Secretary-General was told to take the necessary steps, following his report. The force was created for an initial six months, renewable by later resolutions. Nearly five decades of renewals followed, making this founding text unusually consequential for its length.

Southern Lebanon stayed violent in 1979, and the United Nations force there could not deploy in full. Obstacles blocked UNIFIL's work in the south. Violence against Lebanon had displaced civilians, including Palestinians. Resolution 450, adopted on 24 June 1979, renews the force.

The Council strongly deplored the violence and the loss of innocent life. Israel was called on to stop its acts against Lebanon's unity and territory at once. Its incursions were named, and so was its support for armed groups inside Lebanon. UNIFIL's work was praised, and the force's goals were restated. Its mandate was renewed for six months, until 19 December 1979. The old armistice machinery between Israel and Lebanon was to be revived as well.

The first truce order for Palestine came two weeks into the first Arab-Israeli war. On 29 May 1948, the Council adopted Resolution 50. Israel had declared itself a state days before. Neighboring Arab states had invaded at once. The Council said it sought a halt to the fighting. Neither side's rights, claims, or stance would be judged by the pause.

All governments must order a stop to armed acts for four weeks. No fighting men may enter the region in that span. War goods may not flow in or out either. Jerusalem's Holy Places must be kept safe, with access for worship kept open. The UN Mediator and the Truce Commission will watch the truce. Army observers will back them, and weekly reports are due.

Nicaragua's Contra war was dying in the spring of 1990. A new elected leader was set to take power. The Contra camps had to empty by pact. Resolution 650 passed with no dissent on 27 March 1990. It backed the chief's report of 15 March. The UN team in the area was small and bare of arms.

That changed, on one condition. The team could grow and take on armed staff. Its new job was to help Contra men lay down their guns by free choice. This was a first for UN peace work in the region. Demobilization by consent, not force, was the theme. The chief had to keep the Council fully briefed. Within weeks, the Contras stood down, and the team watched it happen.
van-helmont-ternary-of-paradoxes-1650:
Jan Baptista van Helmont argued three strange claims in A Ternary of Paradoxes, Englished by Walter Charleton in 1650. The Flemish doctor and chemist challenged the medicine of his day on wound cures, on wine, and on man's likeness to God. Charleton's version became the key English text of Helmont's new way of healing by chemistry.

The magnetic cure of wounds claims that sympathy can heal at a distance, without touch. The piece on tartar explains the stony crust in wine casks and, by likeness, the stones that form in the body. Readers of the age found here a bold new medical scheme, strange and fertile, that helped turn medicine toward tests and trials.
wordsworth-prelude-1850:
William Wordsworth worked on The Prelude for fifty years and never published it himself. He called it the poem on the growth of his own mind and read it aloud to Coleridge. After his death in 1850, his family published it in fourteen books, and it proved to be his life work.

The poem follows Wordsworth from childhood in the Lake District through Cambridge, London, and revolutionary France. He recalls stolen boats, skating at dusk, and the terror and joy nature taught him. Disillusion with the French Revolution forces him to rebuild his faith in the mind itself. The Prelude is the great autobiographical poem in English, and Romanticism's central document.
zoist-vol-08-1850:
Volume eight of The Zoist covers March 1850 to January 1851. Eight years in, Elliotson's journal remains mesmerism's English headquarters in print. Cases of trance, with and without surgery, lead the contents. Cerebral physiology, the study of brain and mind together, keeps its column.

Somnambulist reports grow stranger as spiritualism dawns next door in America. The journal watches the new rappings with a mesmerist's claim to the ground. Its thirteen volumes, ending in 1856, hold the movement's full primary record. Volume eight marks the run's later middle. The fight with the medical press cools into habit. The archive's weight keeps growing.
